By the spirit of the Ottawa Ankle Rules, nothing here mandates an X-ray right now. Practical plan below.

Rest of Sunday

  Walking out: take it easy, shorter steps, turn on the uninjured foot. If someone can grab you a ride home, accept it — less swelling than limping the subway.
  Ice: 15-20 min on with a thin cloth barrier, 40+ min off. Repeat 3-4 cycles through the afternoon/evening. Skip direct ice on skin.
  Compression: snug elastic wrap or sleeve, figure-8 around the heel/ankle. Tight enough to support, not enough to cause numbness or color change in the toes.
  Elevation: above heart level for the first 48h whenever you're sitting or lying down. Two pillows under the calf works; foot flat on the couch does not.
  Pain/swelling meds: ibuprofen 400-600 mg with food is fine short-term (a few days) for swelling + pain. If your stomach is sensitive or you'd rather not, acetaminophen per label works for pain but won't touch the swelling much.
  Avoid today: running, cutting, jumping, hot baths/heat, alcohol (worsens swelling), and massage directly over the swollen area.

Gentle movement progression

  Day 0 (today, after the first evening): pain-free ankle alphabet. Trace A-Z in the air with your big toe, slow, both directions. No pushing into pain.
  Day 1-2: ankle pumps (full flex, full point), seated heel raises. Walk normally inside the apartment as comfort allows.
  Day 3-5: resistance band 4-way — dorsiflexion/plantarflexion, then inversion/eversion at light tension. 2-3 sets of 12-15 each direction. If band work feels fine, switch ice → 10 min moist heat before the session.
  Day 5-7: standing calf raises (two legs → single leg), weight shifts side-to-side and forward/back.
  Week 2: balance progression — single-leg stand 30s eyes open → 30s eyes closed → on a folded towel or pillow. Add light hopping only when single-leg stance is steady and pain-free.
  Return-to-run checklist: full pain-free ROM, single-leg calf raise x15, single-leg hop x10 without pain. Usually cleared 10-14 days for a mild sprain.
  Soccer: linear running first (jogging → sprints), then cutting/pivoting last. Expect 3-4 weeks before full pickup games feel trustworthy. Given your left-calf history from last summer, also pay attention if the right calf starts complaining from favoring — that's a pattern to interrupt early.

Urgent evaluation — go to ER or urgent care now

  Cannot bear any weight at all, even after a few hours of rest
  Visible deformity, new bony prominence, or a "pop" with immediate large swelling
  Open wound over the joint (possible open fracture)
  Numbness, pins-and-needles, or toes turning white/blue/cold
  Severe pinpoint pain when you press the medial malleolus, lateral malleolus, base of the 5th metatarsal, or the navicular — those would meet criteria for an X-ray
  Calf becomes painful, swollen, warm, or tender to squeeze in the next 24-48h (DVT risk with reduced mobility — worth flagging given your calf history)

Routine evaluation — call PCP or sports med within a few days if

  Swelling hasn't started to improve by 72h
  Still limping noticeably past a week
  Recurrent giving-way or a feeling the ankle is unreliable on uneven ground
  Pain persists over a bony point I listed above (image then, not emergently)
  Things worsen after initial improvement, or never feel fully back to normal in 2-3 weeks

If swelling stays mild, you regain comfortable walking in a couple of days, and the alphabet doesn't hurt, you're on the expected path. Recheck the signals above as your daily reference and you won't miss the warning signs.

Bottom line: no, they cannot count 18,800. Replaying the full 10,000-point batch almost certainly produced ~8,800 duplicates on top of the points already accepted in the first response.

What actually happened, in order:

1. Request 1 (10,000 points) reached the collector. The collector admitted 8,800 and dropped 1,200 due to per-key/per-tenant rate limiting. From the collector's point of view, the 8,800 are durable and already moving through the pipeline.

2. The response was HTTP 429 with Retry-After: 2 and a body containing partial_success with rejected_data_points: 1200. That body is not decorative — it is the collector telling you "I accepted this many, I rejected that many, here is why." HTTP status and Retry-After describe the throttling posture; the body describes what was actually accepted.

3. The client waited 2 seconds (correct honoring of Retry-After) and resent the same 10,000-point batch.

4. The collector had no record of having seen those 8,800 before, because OTLP/HTTP has no built-in idempotency token. It accepted all 10,000 again. Those 8,800 now exist twice downstream.

Why the duplication happens:

OTLP does not require exporters to attach per-point identifiers that a collector could use to dedup on resend. The protocol's partial-success body tells you how many points were rejected, not which ones. So a naive client that treats "429 + Retry-After honored + 200 on retry" as success has no way to avoid resending the already-accepted subset. The server side cannot save you either — it has no standard hook for "I have seen this exact point before."

This is a load-bearing distinction in OTLP: HTTP status alone never establishes whole-batch acceptance. A response body with partial_success applies to both 200-with-rejections and 4xx-with-partial-acceptance responses.

What the client should do instead:

The reliable patterns are:

a. Sub-batch until partial failures are tractable. If the OTLP export is broken into N small batches (say 100–500 points each), a partial-success body now tells you which sub-batches were fully accepted and which need retry. You only resend the sub-batches whose count of accepted + rejected does not add up to the sent total. This is the most common practical fix.

b. Track and replay only the rejected subset. If the exporter maintains its own sequence numbers, content hashes, or export ids per point, it can replay only the points that were rejected. This requires bookkeeping on the client side and is the only way to get exactly-once behavior with standard OTLP.

c. Idempotent data design. If each data point carries attributes or a name that uniquely identifies its semantic content (e.g., a cumulative counter keyed by resource + metric + timestamp + attributes), the collector or downstream can dedup. This is workload-specific and not something a generic exporter can do for you.

d. If retrying the full batch is unavoidable, switch from cumulative to delta temporality where possible, so a replayed point either updates a counter correctly or is a known-acceptable re-observation. This still costs you storage and processing on the server side; it just avoids inflating sums.

What the customer should hear, in one line:

"Honing Retry-After was the right thing to do for the 429, but the 429's body said only 1,200 of your 10,000 were rejected — the other 8,800 were already accepted. Resending the full batch replayed those 8,800, so the downstream sees roughly 18,800 events with 8,800 duplicates. Count delivered as 10,000 (the second response, after dedup) plus the 1,200 retried separately, not 18,800. The fix going in is to chunk exports small enough that partial_success lets you identify and retry only the rejected points."

One operational note for your side: if this customer pattern is recurring, it is worth checking whether ingest-edge / metrics-router is returning 429 with a partial-success body in a way the docs call out. The protocol-level gotcha is "429 with partial_success means partial acceptance," and most off-the-shelf OTLP exporters do not handle that combination — they treat 429 as a pure retry-the-batch signal, which is exactly what bit this customer.

SANITY CHECK — FAIL-CLOSED REDESIGN
North Pier token-workflow pilot, post 2024-04-23 failure-path exercise

THE BUG IN ONE LINE
Generation wrote into the live output dir before validation ran, so a failed validation leaves the workspace in a mixed old+new state that a later manual commit can capture.

FAIL-CLOSED REDESIGN (sketch)

  Phase A — build in scratch, never touch live output
    - Create <output>.scratch/<run-id>/ alongside the live dir
    - Write ALL artifacts (CSS + platform JSON + anything else) into scratch only
    - Live dir is read-only for the duration of the run (lockfile optional)

  Phase B — validate the complete set
    - Run schema/lint/semantic checks against the WHOLE scratch output
    - Coverage must include CSS, not just platform JSON — the current gap is what made the failure look silent on the artifact side
    - Pre-conditions up front: canonical package loadable, schema fetchable, registry reachable if publish is in-loop

  Phase C — decide
    - Any validation failure OR unexpected exception:
        discard scratch, leave live output byte-identical to start-of-run, emit "generation failed" with reason, exit non-zero
    - Full success:
        atomically swap scratch into live output, publish to registry, emit "generation complete" with run-id, exit zero

  The two invariants that make it fail-closed:
    (1) live output dir is only ever updated by an atomic swap from a fully-validated scratch
    (2) any non-success path is required to leave live output unchanged

DECISIONS WORTH FLAGGING FOR ANYA (these shape the redesign)

  1. Swap-then-publish vs publish-then-swap. Both are fail-closed on the filesystem, but they disagree about which side is canonical during the gap. Pick one and document the recovery story for the other side.

  2. Atomic swap mechanism. rename(2) on the same filesystem is atomic. Pattern: write <output>.new, fsync parent, rename <output>.new -> <output>. Alternative: versioned dirs + a "latest" symlink updated only on success — naturally crash-safe and pairs well with the drift detector.

  3. Crash recovery. A crash mid-run leaves scratch behind. On startup, sweep for orphaned <output>.scratch/ and discard. Optional pending-marker file written before Phase A starts, cleared on Phase C exit, makes the sweep unambiguous.

  4. Manual-commit defense (the specific risk you called out). Even with a perfect generator, a human `git add .` can capture partial output if the output dir is checked in. Three options, ordered by strength:
       a. .generation-status file in live output, set to "complete" only at end of Phase C success. Pre-commit hook rejects != "complete". Works if output dir is in git.
       b. Gitignore the generated output entirely; canonical package + registry are source of truth, output is derived on demand. Removes the manual-commit class of bug. Worth checking whether the current pilot shape can move here.
       c. Hash-pin each generated file to a registry version; pre-commit hook cross-checks. Strictest, most wiring.
     The right answer depends on whether the pilot currently commits generated output — that question is for Anya, not me.

RESIDUAL RISKS THE REDESIGN DOES NOT FULLY CLOSE

  - Concurrent runs racing on the same live dir. Lockfile in a stable location; second run waits or fails fast.
  - Filesystems without atomic rename (some NFS / network mounts). Detect at startup and refuse, or fall back to the versioned-dir + symlink pattern, which is closer to atomic even there.
  - Validation gaps. Fail-closed only closes checks you actually run. Anything outside the check set can still leak into scratch — but scratch is wiped on failure, so live output stays clean. Today's failure becomes tomorrow's check, not tomorrow's mixed-state bug.
  - Partial publish from the registry (some artifacts accepted, some not). Treat registry publish as an atomic batch or define explicit per-artifact failure semantics. Worth nailing down before the redesign lands.

WHAT I'M LEAVING WITH ANYA
  - The redesign shape above (scratch → validate → swap or discard)
  - The four decisions above, framed but not chosen
  - Pilot design choices, rollout sequencing, drift-detector updates, and the gitignore-vs-pre-commit-hook call

## Diagnosis

The histogram metric is `router_request_duration_seconds_bucket` — the unit suffix `_seconds` is authoritative. `histogram_quantile()` returns a value in the **same unit as the bucket labels**, so the LHS of the comparison is in seconds.

The threshold literal `300` is therefore compared as `300 seconds`, not `300 ms`. Staging confirms it exactly:
- Real p99: 470 ms = **0.470 s**
- Expression evaluates: `0.470 > 300` → `false` → alert stays green while the dashboard (which formats `_value * 1000`) reports 470 ms

So the bug is a unit mismatch in the threshold, not in the histogram or the dashboard.

## Corrected expression

Pick one of the two and remove the other from the codebase — having both forms in nearby alerts is how this regresses:

**A. Threshold in ms (recommended — keeps the human label and the literal aligned):**

```
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(router_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) * 1000 > 300
```

**B. Threshold in s (matches the metric unit):**

```
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(router_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) > 0.300
```

Annotation update (so the summary can't drift if someone later flips the expression):

```
summary: "metrics-router p99 exceeds {{ $value }}ms (threshold 300ms)"
expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(router_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) * 1000 > 300
```

- **Boundary correctness**: cases at 299 / 300 / 301 ms pin the comparison to a strict `>` at exactly 300 ms. No off-by-one in either direction.

ROOT CAUSE
A naive local timestamp is ambiguous during the NY fall DST fold: 01:00–01:59:59 occurs twice (once at UTC-04:00, once at UTC-05:00). A dedup/sort key on (account_id, event_time) collapses both instants into one bucket and silently discards a real event. The producer's "all values are NY local" claim does not resolve this — both occurrences are NY local. Local-time-as-unique is the bug.

MINIMUM SAFE SCHEMA (replaces the single event_time column)
- event_time_local : VARCHAR(32) — ISO-8601 wall time, no offset. Preserves producer's value verbatim. Required.
- event_time_offset : SMALLINT — signed minutes from UTC (-240 EDT, -300 EST). REQUIRED for any row whose local time falls in a DST fold window; strongly recommended for every row.
- event_time_utc : TIMESTAMP — canonical instant, indexed. Derived at ingest as event_time_local + event_time_offset, or via IANA America/New_York + a documented disambiguation rule when offset is absent.
- account_id : required, non-null (unchanged).
- schema_version : SMALLINT, default 2. Legacy v1 rows (naive only) tagged and routed separately.

Optional but cheap: event_time_tz VARCHAR(64) IANA name, default 'America/New_York'. Eliminates implicit-tz bugs if the producer ever changes zone.

VALIDATION (reject the row, never coerce)
- event_time_local must parse as ISO-8601 (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS[.fff]).
- If the local time falls in the NY fall-back fold (01:00–01:59:59 on the transition day) OR the spring-forward gap (02:00–02:59:59 on the spring day): event_time_offset is REQUIRED. Reject otherwise.
- For all other rows: event_time_offset is optional. If absent, derive from America/New_York + date. If producer supplied an offset, it must match the derived value; reject on mismatch.
- event_time_local + event_time_offset must round-trip to a single UTC instant. Reject if the local time does not exist in the named zone (catches spring-forward gaps).
- Sanity bounds on event_time_utc: reject if more than ~7 days future or before the room's retention start. N is a producer-SLA choice but should be small.
- Per-(account_id, local_date) event_seq, if the producer emits one, must be strictly increasing. Not required as a schema field; useful as a secondary integrity check.

BACKFILL
- Do not synthesize offsets for v1 (naive) rows inside the fold window. Picking one of the two instants silently corrupts the dataset. Quarantine these rows (separate table or is_ambiguous_v1=true flag) and exclude from dedup-collision logic until the producer re-emits with explicit offset.
- v1 rows outside the fold window: offset is derivable from America/New_York + date; safe and idempotent. Tag backfill_source='derived_offset_v1'.
- Backfill is a separate, versioned operation. Do not mutate v1 in place. Write v2 rows; downstream reads v2 only after cutover.
- Coordinate re-emission of fold-window v1 rows with the producer before v2 cutover, or accept a documented gap in coverage for those dates.

DOWNSTREAM DEDUPLICATION + SORT
- Replace key (account_id, event_time) with (account_id, event_time_utc). Same for sort — local-clock ordering is wrong across DST (an EST 00:30 sorts before an EDT 23:30 on the same local date, but in UTC they're an hour apart, not same-day).
- Coordinate the key change with the workflow owner before cutover. Until cutover, quarantine v2 rows so the old workflow does not double-count or mis-sort.
- During the transition window, do NOT mix v1 and v2 in the same dedup pass. A v2 row's UTC instant will not collide with a v1 row's naive value and you will double-count. Run v1 dedup on legacy storage; v2 dedup on the new path.

DST REPEATED-HOUR HANDLING (the specific failure)
- Treat the fold as a permanent schema requirement, not a transition-day exception. It occurs every year for any DST-observing zone.
- Minimum durable fix: offset (or UTC) on every row, not just fold-window rows. Per-row cost is trivial; optionality is what causes silent loss.
- If the producer cannot emit offset today, three safe paths exist; the unsafe path is "keep ingesting naive and hope": (a) reject the room until offset is added, (b) admit with a written exception that fold-window rows are quarantined and v2 cutover is on a dated plan, (c) admit with offset derived under a documented rule (e.g., pre-transition wins) — acceptable ONLY if the producer attests all fold-window events are pre-transition. Anything else re-creates the loss.

ADMISSION
That decision stays with Iris. The above is the floor the contract must meet; anything less re-creates the silent loss the workflow is exposed to today.

TOP LINE: do not merge as-is. The cache is unsafe in three obvious
ways with more underneath. Point Wes at the parser-cache pattern
(Nadia's 3/29 dual-key fix; the parser-canary gate required miss-rate
normalization on top of p99 baseline) as the in-repo prior art.

CORRECTNESS RISKS

1. Identity collision. Key is rule.Expr but the matcher captures
   gen.MissingLabelMode and gen.Normalizer. Two gens with identical
   expr text but different modes or normalizers collide; the first
   Store wins for the life of the cache and the other gen silently
   inherits wrong semantics.

2. Failed-reload or speculative-compile poisoning. If compileRule
   runs during reload validation or canary build before commit and
   the candidate gen is later discarded, the discarded gen's
   matcher is still in the process-global cache under rule.Expr.
   The active gen then loads the discarded gen's semantics.

3. Concurrent compile across two new gens. Canary-style reloads race
   on identical expr text. Both miss, both compile, both Store, last
   writer wins. The losing gen's callers get the wrong matcher.

4. In-flight swap drift. A request evaluating under gen A at swap
   time may load gen B's matcher on the same expr key. Routing
   flips mid-request.

5. Immutability hole. NewMatcher likely takes gen.Normalizer by
   reference. If the matcher captures that reference and the gen is
   mutated later (debug hook, a config path that bypasses reload),
   the cached matcher changes behavior under active callers.

6. Unbounded growth. Every unique rule.Expr ever seen is retained
   forever; no eviction on gen swap.

SAFE CACHE IDENTITY

Cache key must encode the full compile-time identity, not just expr:

    (generation_id, hash(expr || gen.MissingLabelMode || gen.Normalizer))

generation_id is a monotonic uint64 allocated at config parse, never
reused. Hash once per rule at compile, not on the hot path. Cleaner
equivalent: bake MissingLabelMode and Normalizer into the matcher at
compile, key on (generation_id, expr), and treat matchers as
immutable post-compile. Within a single gen, expr uniquely identifies
the matcher because the gen has fixed every other input.

GENERATION LIFETIME

Move the cache off process-global and onto the generation:

    matchers map[string]*Matcher  // owned by ConfigGeneration

Build during reload under a reload lock, then activate by atomic
pointer swap of the active-gen pointer. The old gen, including its
matchers, is unreferenced and GC'd. Memory bounds come from gen
turnover, not from cache eviction policy.

CONCURRENCY BEHAVIOR

Compile-at-reload is the default. Lookup after activation is a plain
map read on the gen object; no read lock needed if the gen is
immutable post-activation. If runtime compile is needed for hot-added
rules, use sync.Map keyed by (generation_id, expr) with LoadOrStore,
and copy or freeze every NewMatcher input at compile time so
post-compile mutation cannot leak through the cached matcher.

FAILED-RELOAD BEHAVIOR

Build matchers into the candidate gen's local map only; do not Store
to any shared cache. Activate (atomic pointer swap) only after the
candidate gen's full build succeeds. On failure or abort, drop the
candidate; its matchers go with it. The active gen's matcher set is
untouched, and no in-process shared cache holds a partial build.

FOCUSED TESTS (must pass before merge)

1. Identity (mode). Two gens, identical rule.Expr, different
   MissingLabelMode -> distinct matchers; the matcher returned for
   each gen reflects that gen's mode on a shared input.

2. Identity (normalizer). Same expr, different Normalizer (e.g.,
   lowercase vs preserve-case) -> distinct matchers, distinct
   routing decisions on labels with mixed case.

3. Reload with semantic change. gen A mode=drop, gen B same expr
   mode=allow. After swap, inputs that previously dropped now allow;
   old drop behavior is gone from the active cache.

4. Failed-reload isolation. Start compiling gen B with a new
   MissingLabelMode, abort before activation. Active gen A's routing
   on the shared expr is unchanged; no gen B matcher is reachable
   from any caller path.

5. Concurrent compile on a fresh gen. Two goroutines call compileRule
   with the same expr; exactly one NewMatcher runs; both callers get
   the same *Matcher pointer.

6. In-flight swap. A long-running evaluation that started under
   gen A finishes using gen A's matcher; activation that races the
   evaluation does not change the in-flight decision.

7. Immutability. Build a gen, cache its matchers, then mutate the
   gen's Normalizer via a test-only seam; cached matchers' behavior
   does not change.

8. Memory bound. 1000 gen swaps with disjoint rule sets; heap holds
   only the active gen's matchers plus the previous gen during the
   swap window. Verify with runtime.MemStats or a sentinel large
   object in the retired gen.

CANARY GATE

Same as the parser-canary: in addition to p99 returning to baseline,
matcher-cache miss rate must normalize post-swap. A sustained miss
spike after activation means the cache key or generation lifetime is
wrong, not the workload.

A 2/10 ache on a two-foot hop means the lateral ligaments are still irritable under plyometric load. Bouldering loads the same lateral ankle on every foot placement — edging, smearing, foot swaps, and especially any pressure that pushes the foot into inversion. Even an "easy" V0 with no drops, no dynos, and no high steps still puts shear through that exact spot, and a missed foot at low height is plenty to re-roll the ankle you just protected for four days. Holding off costs you a few sessions; re-rolling costs you another month. Skip bouldering this week.

Progression before bouldering or soccer. Each gate must be completely pain-free and matched to the other side before the next.

1. Strength
  - Keep doing the four-way band work (inversion, eversion, plantarflexion, dorsiflexion) at moderate tension
  - Standing bilateral calf raises → eccentric heel drops off a step → single-leg calf raises
  - Gate: 3 x 15 single-leg calf raises, both sides, zero pain

2. Balance
  - Single-leg stand, eyes open → eyes closed → on a foam pad → with reach perturbations
  - Gate: 30 seconds single-leg eyes closed, steady, no pain
  - Then: same on a pillow or BOSU with arms moving as if reaching for holds

3. Hopping
  - Re-test the two-foot forward hop daily; the 2/10 should drop to 0/10 within 2–3 days
  - Two-foot side-to-side, then forward-back
  - Single-leg forward hop → single-leg lateral hop → single-leg diagonal hop
  - Gate: 10 pain-free single-leg hops in each direction (this is the bar from your prior return-to-run checklist, and bouldering should clear the same bar)
  - Then: single-leg triple hop for distance with a clean stick landing

4. Sport-specific layering, only after the hop gate clears

  Bouldering re-entry, in this order:
  - Standing foot placements on the wall at body weight only — practice edging on a large hold at waist height, no climbing
  - Low traverse (V0–V1 moves), flat feet on big holds, downclimb every move, no commitment above a pad
  - One easy session with your stated restrictions still applied (no drops, no dynos, no high steps) — only if every move is fully pain-free
  - Final gate: one symptom-free session, then a quiet next morning, before you drop the restrictions

  Soccer re-entry, in this order:
  - Walk-jog intervals on flat ground → continuous easy jog → easy run
  - Linear sprints at 50 → 75 → 100%
  - Straight-line plant-and-cut at 90° → multi-directional cutting at low speed
  - Non-contact ball work (passing, trapping) → controlled dribbling → reactive play
  - Full session only after a non-contact practice is asymptomatic the next day

Three back-up cues to stop and reassess at any step, not just pain alone:
  - the 2/10 lateral ache coming back
  - any renewed swelling
  - a feeling of apprehension or "my ankle doesn't trust this" on a move you've done hundreds of times

Any of those means drop back two steps in the progression for a couple of days, not push through.

Safe semantic correction. The bug is that the shadow path uses the decoded label value as a cache identity, while the active path keys by the raw (pre-decode) label. Whenever a raw label contains `%2F`, the shadow retains a second entry for the decoded form, which is exactly the 84k → 1.9M / 1.4 GiB growth pattern you're seeing (and why heap moved while allocations didn't — pure retention, not allocation rate). The active path's raw-before-decode rule is correct and must be preserved; the shadow path's cache identity is the thing to fix.

Bounded cache identity:

- Key = the raw label bytes exactly as received on the wire (no normalization, no decoding).
- One slot per unique raw value. `route/foo%2Fbar` and any decoded view of it are the same slot.
- Decoding is a read-through transformation performed against the cached decision, never an axis that produces a new key.
- Bound: |keys| ≤ |unique raw labels observed on the active path|. For the current canary window that upper-bounds the shadow cache at the active-path key count, not at active-path key count + decoded variants.
- TTL/eviction identical between paths so the shadow cannot outlive the active decision it's mirroring.

Focused tests, in order, each gating the next:

1. Identity-bound test (the regression). Feed the active path's recorded raw label set for the 2024-04-24 canary window plus its `%2F`-bearing subset through both paths. Assert: shadow cache key cardinality equals active-path key cardinality (no double-counting on decode), and shadow heap stays within the active-path cache footprint plus a fixed per-entry overhead.
2. Raw-before-decode preserved. For every label `L` in the fixture, the active-path decision on raw `L` equals the active-path decision on decoded `L`. This is the rule the active path already satisfies — the test pins it so the shadow-side fix can't quietly regress it.
3. Divergence replay. Replay the 2024-04-24 label-value buffer through both paths in lockstep, assert zero divergence on the full decision (route, drop, series id), not just on encoded-slash labels. This is the durable regression fixture called for in the 2024-04-29 investigation.

Verdict: do both, with the priority on generator determinism and the semantic comparison as a guardrail layer — not as a replacement for the hash gate.

The reasoning. The drift check is doing exactly what it was designed to do: two runs produced different bytes, and it reported that as a fail. The bug is in the generator, not in the check. If you "fix" this only by adding semantic comparison in the drift check, you're papering over the nondeterminism. Now any two runs could produce different byte output and you have no way to know whether a given diff was "just" reordering or an actual semantic change — you've weakened the signal the check was supposed to give you. Conversely, if you "fix" this only by sorting keys in the generator, you've handled this case but the next time someone changes the serializer, or a new map type creeps in, or the Figma-side path changes order, the same class of bug returns. You want both: deterministic generation is the contract, semantic comparison is the diagnostic.

This is the same root-cause class as the metrics-router parser dual-key issue from 3/29 — Go map iteration order leaking into something that should be deterministic. The fix shape is identical: pick a canonical serialization order at the source, and don't rely on the downstream consumer to notice. Worth telling Anya that this isn't a one-off in the platform; it's a pattern.

Tests that distinguish meaningful drift from formatting churn without weakening publication safety.

  1. N-run determinism invariant. Run the generator ≥ 50 times from the same canonical package with no inputs changed. Assert byte-equal output across all runs (hash each artifact in the staging dir; require all hashes identical across the 50 runs). This is the primary regression test for this bug.

  2. Root-cause focused map test. Construct a canonical package whose offending structure is a map with at least ~32 keys where insertion order differs from sorted order. Generate twice; assert byte equality. This isolates the iteration-order regression from any other determinism drift.

  3. Semantic-normalization property test. Take a known-good generated Android JSON. Apply a fixed battery of formatting-only mutations (key reorder at every nesting level, whitespace/indent changes, insignificant trailing zeros, key quoting style). Parse each result to a canonical AST (recursive sort, normalized numbers) and assert deep equality against the baseline. This proves the semantic comparator correctly classifies these as non-drift.

  4. Mutation-classification property test. Property-based: take the baseline artifact, mutate it across a structured space of {semantic, non-semantic} edits — semantic edits change a value, rename a token, add/remove an entry; non-semantic edits reorder, reformat, change insignificant whitespace. Assert the drift check blocks publication on every semantic edit and either passes or explicitly labels every non-semantic edit as "formatting churn" in a diagnostic report. Pass/fail is the hard gate; labeling is the guardrail.

  5. Publication-gate isolation. The hash-based gate and the semantic comparator must be separate code paths. Write a test that disables or corrupts the semantic comparator and confirms the hash gate still blocks publication on any byte diff. This is the test that prevents a future "let's just compare semantically" change from silently weakening the publication safety property.

  6. Two-layer report structure. When the byte diff is non-empty but the semantic diff is empty, the drift report must read "formatting churn, not drift — publication blocked pending investigation" rather than "drift detected". Block publication, but give the operator a usable diagnostic. Test the report content, not just the exit code.

  7. End-to-end determinism + semantic guard. Integration test: generate the full package twice, hash all artifacts, then run the semantic comparator across both generations. Assert (a) all artifact hashes match across runs for the same canonical package, and (b) the semantic comparator returns "equivalent" on every artifact pair, including a deliberately introduced benign reordering, so you have evidence both layers do what they claim.

How this should land with Anya, given how she prefers her authorship handled: frame the assessment as the engineering call with the rationale, separate the observed problem (one map serialized in traversal order) from the pilot hypothesis (deterministic generation + semantic guardrail) from the safeguards still needed (the seven tests above, of which 1 and 2 are required before the next run and the rest can roll in over the next sprint). The drift check did its job; the staging fail-closed behavior held publication safety; what's needed now is to make the generator keep its determinism promise and add the semantic layer as a diagnostic, not as a softer gate.

Support note — customer-safe explanation for the 429 burst on 2024-05-02:

What we observed:

  - The 429 responses were concentrated in traffic from one customer account,
    not spread across our user base. Other accounts on the same fleet
    continued to be served at their normal baseline rate.
  - That account's requests were arriving in tightly synchronized bursts
    roughly every ten seconds, all targeting a single region.
  - The request bodies, after our servers decompressed them, were larger
    than typical for that endpoint.
  - Fleet health was normal during the window: CPU had headroom, memory
    was flat, the request queue stayed well within its usual band, and no
    other region saw elevated rejection rates.

What the 429s meant:

  - Every rejected response carried a short randomized delay in the
    one-to-three-second range telling the sender when to retry.
  - Requests that arrived inside the admission window were processed
    normally. Nothing that got through was dropped or damaged.
  - Nothing reported as rejected was accepted on a follow-up without the
    sender first waiting and retrying. The retry-after guidance is what
    the sender should actually use.

What we recommend the sender change:

  1. Add jitter to the retry timer. A fixed 1s, 2s, or 3s sleep after a 429
     will still produce synchronized waves once many workers pick the same
     value; a randomized delay within that 1-3s window spreads the load.
  2. Smooth the ten-second pulse. If the workload naturally lines up on a
     tick, distribute the work across the full ten seconds instead of
     firing it at the top of each tick. Per-request offsets on the order
     of tens to a few hundred milliseconds are usually enough.
  3. Reduce the post-decompression size where practical. We saw bodies
     that expanded substantially after decompression. Smaller compressed
     payloads, or chunking a large request into a few smaller ones sent
     over a longer window, avoids the per-request admission cost and
     also reduces the synchronized pulse.
  4. If single-region targeting isn't required, spreading a fraction of
     the load to a second region keeps any one region's admission budget
     from being the bottleneck.

What we are not changing on our side:

  - The fleet is healthy and no rollback or capacity change is planned.
  - The one-to-three-second retry window is the guidance the sender
    should follow. We are not asking for longer or shorter delays.

How the sender can validate the fix:

  - After smoothing the sender and adding retry jitter, their own
    rejection rate should fall back in line with the rest of the
    customer base within a few minutes.
  - A small residual rate after that is expected tail behavior, not a
    regression on our side.

Internal add-on (do not send to customer):

  - 82% concentration in one tenant, single-region, 10s pulse, large
    decompressed bodies, fleet CPU peak 61%, queue peak 24%, other
    tenants at baseline, randomized 1-3s Retry-After honored, no
    reported-as-rejected requests admitted. Evidence is sufficient to
    attribute to sender shape and to recommend sender-side smoothing.
  - No fleet action recommended; do not raise rate limits, do not touch
    the 1-3s floor, do not propose rollback.

Short answer up front: the negative value proves a counter reset, not data loss; manual offsets in the collector are unsafe because the exporter cannot know the server's last stored value and any offset hides or invents gaps; a reset-aware `increase()`/`rate()` treats the post-restart value as the contribution of the new series and recovers a sensible rate across the restart.

What the collector actually did
- Before restart, the last exported cumulative value was 18,442. The monotonic counter kept climbing; the last pre-restart sample you have on disk is, say, 18,500.
- On restart, the in-memory counter state is gone. The next export reads the underlying SDK counter from zero, exports 37 (requests received since the process came back up).
- Timestamped samples continue arriving and ingest-edge accepts them — that is consistent with the counter reset happening client-side, not at ingest.

Why the dashboard went negative
- A raw five-minute delta subtracts the previous cumulative from the current cumulative. Across the restart, that subtraction is 37 − 18,442 = −18,405. The negative number is the size of the gap between the server's view of "where the counter was" and the freshly-collected "where the counter is now." It is the *signature* of a reset, not evidence of dropped requests.
- Pre-restart samples keep arriving for a short window in your dashboard because OTel batches and your query window straddles the restart; that further confirms the discontinuity is exporter-side.

Why a manual offset in the collector is unsafe
- The collector has no authoritative knowledge of the last value the backend persisted. Whatever offset a human writes into the config (e.g. `+18,442`) is a guess about state the collector never saw.
- It hides real gaps. If the new process drops or fails to observe requests during its warm-up, or if the restart takes ten seconds, the offset will silently fill that hole and the counter will look continuous while a chunk of traffic is missing.
- It breaks on the next restart. The offset has to be re-derived each time, otherwise you either double-count (offset applied on top of an already-offset view) or you scramble the series. This makes restart behavior dependent on operator memory, not on the data.
- It violates the monotonicity guarantee that downstream systems rely on. A monotonic counter, by definition, never decreases; injecting an arbitrary additive discontinuity at process start turns the series into a non-monotonic one that looks like a counter, and reset-aware queries will still detect the discontinuity and correct for it — so the "fix" doesn't even work.
- The right place to interpret a reset is the query layer, where the full series is visible and resets can be detected from the actual samples.

How a Prometheus-style reset-aware query should behave
- `increase()` and `rate()` walk the samples in range and, for each step, check whether the next sample is lower than the current one. If it is, that is treated as a counter reset; the contribution of that step is the post-reset value, not the difference.
- Worked numbers for an 8-minute window that straddles the restart, with pre-restart final sample 18,500, post-restart samples 37 and 120:
  - Pre-restart contribution: 18,500 − 18,442 = 58
  - Reset step contribution (new value, not 37 − 18,500): 37
  - Post-restart contribution: 120 − 37 = 83
  - `increase()` over the 8-minute range: 58 + 37 + 83 = 178
  - `rate()` per second over 480 s: 178 / 480 ≈ 0.371 req/s, i.e. roughly 22 req/min — a sensible, smooth checkout rate that does not show a spike or a dip at the restart.
- For the dashboard to do this in practice, it needs to query through a backend that speaks PromQL/OTLP-with-reset-handling (Prometheus, Mimir, Cortex, the vendor's rate/increase functions) rather than emit a raw client-side cumulative delta. The counter series itself does not need to change; the query does.

Net for the customer: tell them the negative is a reset artifact, not lost requests, and that the fix is to switch the panel to a reset-aware rate or increase query (or to a backend that applies this logic), not to paper over the counter in their collector.

Forty minutes is plenty. Salt the pasta water heavily (it should taste like the sea) and get it on now.

Sequence:
1.  T-40  Large pot of water on high, lid on. Wide skillet out.
2.  T-35  Water boils: drop pasta, cook 1 minute less than the package time.
3.  T-32  While it cooks, drain the chickpeas, strip and tear the kale (stems out), thinly slice 3-4 garlic cloves, zest the lemon and set the zest aside, halve the lemon.
4.  T-25  In the skillet: ~3 tbsp olive oil, sliced garlic, a pinch of red-pepper flakes, medium-low. Gentle sizzle 2 min — pale gold, not brown.
5.  T-22  Add kale, a small splash of pasta water, a pinch of salt. Stir to wilt, 3-4 min.
6.  T-20  Add chickpeas, several grinds of black pepper. Warm through, 1-2 min.
7.  T-18  Pasta's at the 1-min-from-done mark: lift it into the skillet with tongs, carrying the starchy water with it. Splash more water if it looks tight. Toss hard over medium heat 1-2 min — you want a loose, glossy sauce clinging to the noodles, not a puddle. This emulsion step is what keeps it from going gluey.
8.  T-15  Off heat. Taste for salt. This is your base.

Serving and holding:

Plate Anya's portion now and finish her bowl at the table — lemon zest, a squeeze of lemon, a few passes of Parmesan. Tear bread alongside.

For Devika, hold the rest of the pan off heat entirely. Residual warmth keeps the noodles loose for 30-40 min without overcooking them; that matters more than keeping the burner on. When she's about 10 min out, put the skillet on low, splash in 2-3 tbsp water, and toss until it loosens and steams (~60 sec). Plate it, then do the same lemon + cheese finish.

If she's joining well after 45 min, portion her share into a bowl now with a drizzle of olive oil and a tbsp of water, cover with a plate, and leave it on the counter. Reheat the same way — low heat, splash of water, short toss — when she walks in.

Two notes:
- Acid and cheese go on at service, not in the pan. Lemon dulls and cheese tightens if it sits.
- The 1-min-underdone + finish-in-sauce step is the real anti-gum move. Starch, olive oil, and a hard toss make an emulsion; without that, the pasta clumps no matter how you hold it.

Short answer: yes — including generation in the key blocks cross-generation reuse (two semantically equivalent (expr, normalizer, defaults) tuples across gens A and B cache twice instead of once) while doing nothing to bound the package-level `compiled sync.Map`. Each gen that ever calls matcherFor leaves its entries behind for the process lifetime. That's the worst of both shapes: per-gen cache cost, no per-gen cleanup. The gen key does correctly fix the in-flight-under-A-loads-B hazard that motivated the revision, so the keying direction is right; the lifetime model is still wrong. Findings by axis, then the explicit requirements.

1. Cache identity
   - Key = (gen, expr). This is what stops a goroutine holding gen A's pointer from accidentally loading gen B's matcher after activate — same direction as Nadia's 2024-03-29 dual-key parser fix, applied one level up. Correct for that purpose.
   - Defaults are passed to Compile but not in the key. If defaults can vary per call site (per route, per tenant, per request), two callers with the same (gen, expr) but different defaults will both receive the matcher built by whichever caller populated the slot first. That's a silent semantic bug, not just a perf issue. Either bake defaults into Generation, or include a defaults identity in the key.
   - Compile failure path is undefined. matcherFor calls `Compile(expr, defaults)` returning *Matcher and then unconditionally `LoadOrStore(key, matcher)`. If Compile returns nil/zero on failure, the next `value.(*Matcher)` on that key panics, and the bad value lives in `compiled` forever. Compile must return (matcher, ok/err) and matcherFor must not cache failures.
   - Immutability of Generation is not enforced. Keying by gen does not save you if the matcher captured `gen.Normalizer` (or any other gen field) by reference and the struct is later mutated. Make Generation effectively immutable after publish, or snapshot the relevant fields before Compile.

2. Generation lifetime
   - There is no lifetime. Entries live until process exit.
   - activate only swaps the active pointer. It does not publish, prime, retire, or evict anything in `compiled`. There is no invariant linking "which matchers are reachable as authoritative" to "what is in the map."
   - In a router that survives hundreds of reloads, that's hundreds of generations' worth of compiled regexes/parsers, each with a Generation reference the rest of the system has moved past. The longer the process runs, the worse the leak, with no observable trigger.

3. Failed-reload behavior
   - matcherFor has no concept of "reload." It writes to `compiled` under whatever gen the caller hands it. A reload that fails mid-build has populated the global cache with whatever it managed to compile, keyed by the would-be gen's ID. That gen never activates, but its entries stay forever — and a later retry with the same gen ID will hit those stale, partially-built entries via Load instead of recompiling. So the cache can both leak memory and silently serve broken matchers from a failed attempt.
   - Required: failed reloads build into a gen-local map that is discarded on failure and never touches the shared table.

4. Concurrent readers
   - sync.Map + LoadOrStore is correct for the read/miss race on the same key. Many concurrent matcherFor(gen, expr) calls converge on one Compile and one entry. Fine.
   - In-flight correctness across a swap is now safe: a goroutine that captured gen A's pointer mid-evaluate looks up (A, expr), gets A's matcher, and is unaffected by activate(B).
   - Residual hazard: any caller that does `active.Load()` and then reads fields off the returned *Generation later is fine only if Generation is immutable post-publish. Make that a hard contract; do not rely on convention.

Explicit requirements for what's still missing

Generation lifetime
- A matcher's authoritative lifetime is exactly one activation window: from activate(next) until the next activate(next') that supersedes it. After that supersede, the previous generation's matchers are unreachable from the public lookup path.
- The active generation's matchers must be the only ones a reader can reach. No fallback to older gens, no opportunistic reuse.

Cleanup
- On activate(next), the previous generation's matchers must be released in the same critical section that publishes next's: the previous gen's local map is dropped, and any references in the shared table to that gen are cleared. No reliance on the GC to "eventually" reclaim.
- Bounded live set: at most two generations' worth of matchers live at any instant (previous + next during the swap), collapsing to one after.
- No process-global unbounded retention across reloads. `compiled` must not accumulate across generations.

Concurrency
- matcherFor is safe under concurrent invocation (sync.Map or RWMutex+map are both fine; LoadOrStore pattern is fine).
- The active-generation pointer is swapped atomically (atomic.Pointer[Generation]). A reader sees either fully-populated old gen or fully-populated new gen, never a half-built one.
- Generation is effectively immutable after publication. Per-reload state is built into a snapshot before activation.
- matcherFor takes (gen, expr) from the caller's pinned gen pointer, not from a re-read of the active pointer mid-evaluation.

Failed-reload behavior
- Reload builds matchers into a Generation-scoped local map. Never into the shared table.
- On any reload failure (Compile error, validation error, partial build): discard the local map entirely. Shared cache unchanged. Active generation unchanged. Nothing partial is published.
- On reload success: publish the new gen's local map into the shared table, then atomically swap the active pointer. A reader that observes the new active pointer observes the new map fully populated — no torn view.
- A retry of a previously-failed gen ID must not inherit stale entries from the prior attempt. Either gen IDs are monotonic-on-success-only (skip the failed ID, take the next), or every attempt rebuilds its local map from scratch and prior attempts never published.

Cache identity (precondition for the rest being meaningful)
- The key must include everything that affects matcher semantics: expression, the normalizer (or an immutable snapshot of it), and the defaults identity. If any of those vary between calls with the same key, the cache is unsafe.
- Compile failures (nil, err) are not stored in the cache.

Working from the three categories you closed with Iris (deploy movement, ownership, incident load) plus the cross-cutting fields in the contract doc (service_id, last_source_event_at) and the four-state null-replacement rule.

DEPLOY MOVEMENT
  version_from               ALLOW          customer-meaningful version; pass through
  version_to                 ALLOW          customer-meaningful version; pass through
  environment                TRANSFORM      restrict to environments the customer subscribes to; normalize labels (no internal codenames)
  state_transition           ALLOW          derived (started / completed / rolled_back); single canonical vocabulary
  deploy_id                  TRANSFORM      externalize to opaque, externally stable ID; no internal linkage, no raw job identifier
  completed_at               TRANSFORM      UTC, normalized; suppress sub-second precision unless required for ordering
  deployer                   EXCLUDE        replace at presentation with the service-facing support label (see ownership)
  rollback_of                ALLOW          surface only when policy permits (see Q5)
  chat_links / job_ids       EXCLUDE        internal context; provenance IDs and permission refs stay internal too

OWNERSHIP
  service-facing support label       ALLOW          on-call / escalation path string, stable per service
  current owner team (internal)      TRANSFORM      collapse to the support label at presentation; never expose the team name as a distinct field
  employee names                     EXCLUDE
  internal owner-map record          EXCLUDE

INCIDENT LOAD
  count_in_window            TRANSFORM      bounded window + k-anonymity floor (see Q1, Q2)
  rate_per_service           TRANSFORM      same floor
  raw incident records       EXCLUDE        individual events never exposed
  time_window                TRANSFORM      bounded rolling or fixed (policy: Q2)
  suppressed / stale / permission-denied cells  ENUMERATE  no nulls; explicit state with last-known-good or window-start fallback per (Q7)
  freshness indicator        POLICY (Q9)    expose to customers, or internal only

ENUMERATED NULL STATES (no field collapses to null)
  unknown                    value cannot be determined from source
  not_applicable             field does not apply to this record
  not_authorized             caller lacks permission for this field on this service
  temporarily_unavailable    source is degraded; will retry

CROSS-CUTTING
  service_id                 ALLOW          public service identifier
  last_source_event_at       ALLOW          timestamp of last successful upstream update; signals freshness
  provenance IDs             EXCLUDE        audit-trail identifiers stay internal
  permission refs            EXCLUDE        internal access context only

UNRESOLVED PRODUCT-POLICY QUESTIONS FOR THEO

 1. Aggregation floor. What is the minimum count (k) for an incident-load cell to be surfaced, and what state do sub-floor cells take — "insufficient data", or fully suppressed with no row at all?
 2. Time-window shape. Is the incident-load window a fixed rolling window (e.g., last 7d / 30d) or a fixed calendar window, and is the choice customer-configurable per service or global?
 3. deploy_id externalization. Is the external ID a freshly minted opaque value per deploy, or a stable transformation of an internal ID? Who owns the mapping table and its retention?
 4. Support-label semantics. Does "service-facing support label" mean the escalation path at the time of the event (time-varying) or the current label (snapshot)? This affects historical deploy movement.
 5. Rollback visibility. Are all rollback relationships surfaced, or only those the customer would otherwise care about (e.g., affecting their subscribed environments)? Are there rollback classes we always hide (e.g., infra-only)?
 6. Retention horizon. How long does the externally visible deploy-movement feed persist — last 90 days, last 12 months, or indefinite for the customer's services?
 7. Null-state customer surface. Of the four enumerated states, which are surfaced to customers and which are logged internally only? Customers likely do not need to see "not_authorized" as a distinct value if a confidentiality-preserving omission is acceptable (see Q12).
 8. Timestamp policy. UTC always, or region-local for the customer's region? Affects how completed_at and last_source_event_at are formatted.
 9. Freshness signal. Is last_source_event_at surfaced as a customer-visible freshness indicator, or is it internal-only telemetry? If surfaced, do we expose staleness thresholds?
10. Support-label consistency. Must the label match strings used in other customer touchpoints (status page, support tickets), or can Lantern carry its own label?
11. Environment labels. Are "dev / staging / prod" the customer-facing vocabulary, or do we expose only the subset the customer subscribes to and use a uniform label otherwise?
12. Permission asymmetry. When two customers have different permissions on the same service, does a permission-denied field surface as "not_authorized" to the caller who lacks it, or is the field simply omitted (confidentiality over transparency)?
13. Contract versioning. Does the external contract carry a version field visible to customers so they can detect contract changes, and is there a public changelog?

The "low hum that stops" during drain is the key signal: the pump is getting power but can't move water. Most often that's a clogged filter; less often it's a failed pump impeller. Here's a quiet sequence that stays inside your stated limits.

1. Kill the breaker first. No noise, mandatory. Standing water around the sump plus the motor you're about to look at — don't chance it, even though nothing has tripped yet.

2. Pull the lower rack and look at the sump floor. The filter is the round mesh cylinder (sometimes a flat disc) sitting under the lower spray arm. Note anything obvious — broken glass, bone, a small utensil, a pit, a paper label. Don't reach past the filter into the impeller area.

3. Bail the standing water. Cup or sponge into a bucket. Lowering the level reduces splash when you remove the filter and lets you see what you're doing.

4. Remove and clean the filter. Usually a quarter-turn counter-clockwise, then lift. Rinse under the kitchen tap with warm water and a soft brush. Don't "wash" it back in by running the machine — that can shove debris into the pump you decided not to open. Reseat firmly; a filter that isn't fully locked is a common reason a pump hums without pumping.

5. One quiet drain test — not a full cycle. Most dishwashers have a Cancel / drain-only mode (or Start, then immediately Cancel/Drain). It runs the pump for about 1–2 minutes. This is the one noise you should accept, because it gives a definitive answer:
   - Water level drops and the pump sounds normal → fixed, run a normal cycle later.
   - Same low hum, no water moving → stop here.

Stop and contact building maintenance if any of these are true:

- Filter was clean (or is now clean) but the drain test still hums without moving water. That points at the pump impeller or a blocked drain hose — past your "don't open the pump housing" line and into a maintenance / appliance-tech repair.
- You see water at electrical connections, smell anything off, or the breaker behavior changes.
- The filter won't come out, or you find something broken inside the sump.
- This is a building-supplied unit — for anything past filter cleaning, building maintenance is the right call regardless of your troubleshooting, since the repair is on their asset.

What to tell them, in one sentence: "Standing water after cycle, no leak, no trip. I cleaned the filter. Drain pump hums but doesn't move water." That puts them at the pump/hose diagnosis without you having to disassemble anything.

One extra, since it's quiet: if your sink has a small cylindrical chrome cap next to the faucet (an air gap), you can unscrew the cap and look for gunk under it — that's another drain-side blockage that mimics a pump failure, and checking it is silent.

  The real defect is "decode pool pinned for ~15 s with no on-call signal." Treat that as the follow-up, not the saturation itself. If a decode-worker-saturation alert does not exist, the absence is the finding.

Admission correction

  Wrap the gzip decoder in a small semaphore sized to (decode workers − 1) so health checks and one worker of headroom are always free. This is the lowest-risk concurrency change: it cannot reject traffic that would have been admitted, and it cannot lose points because the post-decompression body-limit check and the existing commit path are untouched.
  Account for the decompression cost in admission, not just bound it. Either reserve a decompress slot from the same semaphore that gates accepted work, or charge a decompress token against a token bucket sized to decode-worker capacity. Pick one. Doing both is over-correction and will fight itself. The goal is that the admission path now sees decompression as part of its work, not as invisible pre-work.

Concurrency correction

  Two tenants were enough to pin the pool. Add a per-tenant concurrent-decompression budget (roughly decode_workers / N, with N chosen so one tenant cannot monopolize). Isolated to the existing tenant-id path; no schema change, no impact on tenants that behave well.

Observability correction

  Decompression is pre-admission and the queue metric is post-admission. Do not pretend the queue metric measured this work — it did not, and renaming or retro-fitting it after the fact would corrupt historical comparisons. Add separate signals instead:
    decompress_wait_ms (histogram, per request) — the actual wait these 17 requests sat in.
    decompress_in_flight (gauge) — live concurrency.
    decode_worker_utilization (gauge, 10-s window) — saturation.
  Add a decode-pool-saturation alert at "utilization ≥ 100% for > N seconds." This alert, had it existed, would have fired within the first 3–4 seconds of this event.
  State the queue-metric caveat up front in the postmortem timeline, not buried. Anyone reading the postmortem needs to know that "queue wait" was green while this was happening, or the next on-call will read it wrong again.

Explicit non-recommendations

  No body-limit change — bodies were below it; it was never the constraint.
  No Retry-After change — see above.
  No retrofit of the queue metric — its semantics are valid; the fix is a new metric for the missing work, not redefining the old one.
  No per-request reject path for high compression ratio. Compression ratio is not a signal of malice here; these were legitimate bodies that simply cost more to decode. Rejecting them would be a correctness change dressed as a safety one.

Scope: governs the customer-facing incident-load summary endpoint exposed under the limited external preview. Enforced at the API/data layer, not at presentation.

1. SERVICE SCOPE
- Customer sees only services tied to their tenant subscription.
- Service identifiers returned are customer-facing names mapped from internal. Internal labels, internal owning-team identifiers, and routing labels are not returned.
- Eligibility is governed by the standard tenant-service mapping; preview enrollment does not extend service scope.

2. FIXED CUSTOMER-VISIBLE WINDOW
- Window options are a closed, contracted set (e.g., trailing 7d, trailing 30d, trailing 90d; calendar month; calendar quarter). The customer cannot specify custom ranges.
- Smallest bucket granularity is one calendar day. Smallest window is 7 days. Sub-day, per-shift, and per-on-call windows are not exposed.
- The closed set and the window definitions are versioned. Changes require contract notice.

3. AGGREGATION
- Per-service rollup only: one record per (customer-visible service, contracted window).
- Returned aggregates: incident count, MTTR, severity mix (proportions, not raw counts). All three are computed over the same window and follow the same suppression rule.
- No per-team, per-owner, per-individual, or per-incident field is returned.
- Cross-service comparative framing is not provided by the API. A customer may compare across their own subscribed services on a like-for-like basis only; the contract does not promise any ordering or ranking.

4. SUPPRESSION
- A suppression threshold N (proposed N=5) applies per (service, window) to incident count and to every derived aggregate — MTTR and severity mix included. Open decision owed to Theo at this meeting: confirm the threshold extends to MTTR and severity mix, not counts only.
- Below threshold, the field's value is replaced by a suppressed-state indicator (suppressed: true). The actual count is not returned, and the affected aggregate is not returned alongside it.
- Suppression applies regardless of customer subscription size, number of subscribed services, or volume of activity. The rule does not weaken as scope narrows.
- Suppression is enforced at the API contract layer, not in UI presentation.

5. ZERO VALUES
- 0 (zero) means: zero incidents were recorded for this service in this window. Zero is a real reading and is returned as such.
- suppressed: true is distinct from 0. It means: at least one incident was recorded, but the count (and its derived aggregates) falls below the suppression threshold.
- The two states are not collapsed. A customer reading 0 is reading "no activity," not "activity hidden." If the team later decides collapsing the two is preferable to remove residual inference, that is a contract change requiring notice.

6. PROHIBITION ON INDIVIDUAL ATTRIBUTION AND MANAGER-READINESS INTERPRETATION
- No individual attribution. The summary returns no person names, initials, on-call identifiers, responder IDs, team labels, or shift identifiers — directly or by join with another endpoint.
- No manager-readiness interpretation. The summary returns, and the API does not enable the customer to derive, any field whose natural use is to evaluate an internal team or individual for performance, promotion, staffing, or restructuring. This includes, but is not limited to: per-team counts, comparative team metrics, severity mix split by team, MTTR split by team, responder attribution, and any framing that positions one team as better, worse, faster, or more reliable than another.
- The prohibition holds regardless of how many internal teams operate a service. When only one team operates a service, no team-level field is exposed; the absence of a team field is not itself a signal.

7. PROVENANCE AND FAILURE SEMANTICS (per external-data contract)
- Every response carries a provenance stamp identifying the internal incident-definition version, the window-definition version, and the suppression threshold in effect at the time of the query. A response without the stamp is invalid.
- If the upstream count or aggregate is incomplete, delayed, or recomputed, the response returns an explicit data-state indicator (state: incomplete | recomputing | delayed) and does not silently substitute 0 or a stale value.
- Auth: every response is scoped to the caller's tenant. Cross-tenant queries are rejected at the API.

Decision: hard fail on the proposed label shape. Don't add `pod_uid` or `container_id` to `customer_request_errors_total` as written.

Why, roughly:

Cardinality. Existing series grow with (customer, service, region, status_class, route_group). With ~900 emitting services and 40-120 live instances per service, adding both identifiers multiplies the series count by 40-120x. If the existing label set already produces, say, 50 distinct combinations per service, you go from ~45k series to ~2-5M series. That's the full label budget of metrics-router and shard-keeper consumed by one metric family, before you account for cross-region replication and scrape buffering.

Churn. Both identifiers rotate on every redeploy. If a service redeploys at any routine cadence (rolling deploys, node drains, autoscaler events), you're invalidating a large fraction of those series every cycle. High-churn labels break `rate()` over restart windows, balloon the index, and push shard-keeper through continuous re-mapping. This is the same shape that made `error_detail` a hard-fail family.

Drill-down framing. "Which instance failed" is an operational question, not a customer-facing one. The customer-facing metric answers customer-impact questions (which service, region, route group is degraded for which customer). Forcing instance identity onto it pays the cardinality cost on every dashboard, alert, and SLO query, for a question that only a small minority of queries actually need.

Safer design that preserves drill-down:

1. Leave `customer_request_errors_total` as-is. Keep customer, service, region, status_class, route_group. That's the aggregate / dashboard / alert surface.

2. Emit a sibling metric at the same instrumentation site, e.g. `instance_request_errors_total` (or a narrower `pod_request_errors_total`), carrying `pod_uid` + `container_id` + the same `service`, `region`, `status_class`. Namespaced to the ops stream — different routing, shorter retention (24-72h), explicit owner. Cardinality and churn are contained to a metric that operators query, not one that every dashboard pulls.

3. Preserve drill-down via join, not via label. The operator workflow becomes: from the customer-facing aggregate, identify (service, region, time window) → query the sibling instance metric filtered by that window → identify the failing pod/container. The link key is `(service, region, status_class, time)` — bounded, stable. Drill-down is preserved without the cardinality hit on the broadly queried metric.

4. If a single metric is non-negotiable, the least-bad version is a bounded `instance_group` label (deployment name, replica set, instance class) on the customer metric, with true instance identity kept in logs/traces/exemplars. Bounded, low-churn, and still gives operators "which deployment is hot" without per-pod cardinality.

Preflight note: the sibling-metric path itself still needs a cardinality preflight — per-service instance caps, retention floor, and explicit owner of the new label budget. That's the same shape as the label-cardinality preflight open questions; this proposal is a good forcing function to close them before the sibling metric lands.

Short version for the proposal author: the dimension you want isn't wrong, it's just on the wrong metric. Move it next door, keep the customer-facing aggregate clean.

The accounting axis is the failure. Weighting the semaphore by compressed bytes decouples admission budget from the resource the cap is meant to protect: worker time and memory during expansion.

The 40-request run already proved this. Tiny compressed bodies held workers 9 to 13 s while ordinary admission stayed "responsive." That is not proof the design works; it is proof admission and decompression are out of sync. "Responsive admission" under compressed-byte weighting only means compressed bytes were not the bottleneck. The worker pool was, and nothing in the accounting noticed.

WHY COMPRESSED-BYTE WEIGHTING IS INSUFFICIENT

Compressed bytes measure wire and storage cost. Decompression cost is dominated by expanded bytes: CPU, allocation, worker hold time. The two correlate weakly. A 1 KB compressed body can expand to 1 MB or more (100:1 and beyond) on repetitive JSON, base64-wrapped blobs, or pre-encoded frames. Under compressed-byte weighting, a client can claim most of the admission budget with a few large compressed requests while tiny-but-high-ratio requests consume nearly zero budget and tie up workers for seconds. The semaphore therefore bounds neither decompressed bytes in flight nor worker hold time, which are the actual scarce resources. decode_wait_seconds reports the symptom (queueing) but does not control the cause, and the current test cannot distinguish "no one is waiting" from "no one can get admitted cheaply enough to wait."

REVISED BOUNDS (single mechanism, not two)

Keep the 4/pod and 2/tenant active-decode caps, but reweight the existing semaphore by decompressed-byte units rather than compressed bytes:

  - Estimate expanded size at admission from Content-Length (if advertised and trusted) plus a bounded peek pass. Reject with 429 before any worker is taken if the estimate exceeds a per-request hard cap (proposed: 8 to 16 MiB).
  - Charge the semaphore by estimated decompressed bytes. The 4/pod cap becomes "4 x per-worker decompressed budget" (e.g., 4 x 16 MiB = 64 MiB decompressed in flight).
  - Re-check expanded size after the first chunk; release permits back if actual expansion is smaller; cancel and 429 if larger than the cap.
  - Express the 2/tenant cap in the same decompressed units so a tenant cannot arbitrage compression ratio.
  - Bind each active decode to a wall-clock budget (proposed: 2 s soft / 5 s hard). Expiry cancels the decode, releases the permit, and returns 429 with the existing 1 to 3 s Retry-After distribution.
  - Add a decompress_in_flight gauge covering both concurrent decodes and decompressed bytes, so decode_wait_seconds and the gauge move together.

Do not layer a second token bucket on top of this. The two will fight.

LOAD-TEST ASSERTIONS BEFORE ACCEPTING THE RUN AS PROOF

The 40-request run is not sufficient. Required:

  1. High-ratio torture. 40 requests with compressed:decompressed ratio at or above 100:1. No single worker holds a decode more than 5 s. Peak decompressed bytes in flight stays under the configured pod cap. 429s carry Retry-After in the 1 to 3 s range.

  2. Mixed-ratio sweep. 40 requests with ratios spanning 1:1 to 1000:1. Admission latency and shed count track decompressed budget, not compressed budget. If they track compressed budget, the weighting is still wrong.

  3. Adversarial client. A single source sends deliberately tiny compressed, huge expanded payloads (compression-ratio DoS). Per-tenant cap of 2 holds; other tenants are not starved; per-request worker time stays bounded.

  4. Cancellation drill. Cancel mid-decode on a 1000:1 request. The permit is released and the worker is free within a bounded interval (sub-second). The gauge drops accordingly.

  5. No-regression. Repeat the original 40-request run with realistic ratios (10:1 or less). Ordinary admission queues stay responsive and the new caps do not reintroduce starvation.

  6. Pressure-signal correlation. Under sustained overload, decode_wait_seconds and decompress_in_flight rise and fall together within one scrape interval. If one moves without the other, the accounting is still misaligned.

Only when all six pass should the prototype be treated as proven.

You're right about the Acquire UAF, and there are two more races in the same family plus a cache-identity hazard. Reviewing against metrics-router's existing generation model, not assigning ownership of any of this to Wes.

The UAF you flagged

Thread A: g = active_generation.load()         # reads pointer to X
Thread B: Publish(Y) — exchanges active to Y, sets X.retired=true,
                          readers.load()==0 (A hasn't bumped yet), free(X)
Thread A: g.readers.fetch_add(1)               # write to freed X

The increment has to land on a generation object that is still live and still the active one. Splitting the load from the bump makes that unsound.

Related races in the same shape

  - Publish has the mirror TOCTOU: between `old.readers.load() == 0` and `free(old)`, an existing reader can Release, and the free races with any thread that has already loaded `old` but not yet bumped. In the current pseudocode, with no re-check, "loaded but not yet bumped" threads can be in that window indefinitely.
  - Release has the same TOCTOU: `fetch_sub` followed by a separate retire check can free under a thread that has re-acquired the same generation pointer (which the pointer-reuse problem below makes possible).
  - Pointer-as-cache-identity is unsafe. Once `free(X)` happens and a later generation is allocated at the same address, an entry keyed by `(X, expr)` collides with `(X', expr)` for a different generation. Cache identity has to be a monotonic `generation_id` assigned at construction, not the object pointer.

What needs to be true

  1. One atomic refcount per Generation. The "active pointer holds one ref" and "each reader holds one ref" are the same counter; whoever decrements to zero with retired==true frees.
  2. Acquire bumps before returning, with a re-check that the active pointer still equals the object we bumped. If it doesn't, undo the bump.
  3. Publish transfers exactly one ref (the one it pulled out of the atomic pointer) and decrements it after marking retired. No separate `readers.load()` check.
  4. Published Generation is effectively immutable — normalizer and any other compile-input fields snapshotted into the candidate before matchers are built, so post-activation cache reads need no read lock (matches the 5/6 immutability-test convention).
  5. Failed reload never touches shared state. Speculative or canary compilation has to stay in a generation-scoped local map; ReloadFailed only frees the candidate, and the candidate's matcher table is dropped with it.
  6. On retire, evict that generation_id's entries from the matcher cache so total cache size is bounded; generation_id keying alone doesn't bound it.

Recommended shape (drop-in for metrics-router's matcher-cache acquisition/retirement):

  Acquire():
    loop:
      g = active_generation.load(acquire)
      g.refcount.fetch_add(1, acq_rel)
      if active_generation.load(acquire) == g:
        return g
      if g.refcount.fetch_sub(1, acq_rel) == 1 and g.retired.load(acquire):
        free(g)
        # eviction of (g.generation_id, *) from matcher cache happens here

  Release(g):
    if g.refcount.fetch_sub(1, acq_rel) == 1 and g.retired.load(acquire):
      free(g)
      evict (g.generation_id, *) from matcher cache

  Publish(candidate):
    # candidate.generation_id is monotonic; matcher map already fully populated;
    # candidate is effectively immutable (normalizer snapshotted)
    old = active_generation.exchange(candidate, acq_rel)
    old.retired.store(true, release)
    # old carries one ref from the exchange; drop it
    if old.refcount.fetch_sub(1, acq_rel) == 1:
      free(old)
      evict (old.generation_id, *) from matcher cache

  ReloadFailed(candidate):
    # No Acquire can have pinned it (Publish never ran), so refcount is the
    # one held by the failed-reload path itself. Drop and free.
    if candidate.refcount.fetch_sub(1, acq_rel) == 1:
      free(candidate)
      evict (candidate.generation_id, *) from matcher cache
    # Precondition: candidate never wrote to the shared matcher table.

What this preserves

  - Generation isolation: a reader pinned before Publish keeps its ref and its `(generation_id, expression)` cache hits; no cross-generation reuse.
  - Failed-reload cleanup: candidate dies with its local matcher map; shared table untouched.
  - Bounded cache: eviction is tied to the same atomic-decrement-to-zero that frees the generation.
  - No ownership implication for Wes — this is the metrics-router matcher-cache contract; backup/oncall handoff is unchanged.

Suggested review-side checks before this lands

  - Immutability test (already on the list from 5/6): mutate the published generation's normalizer through the test seam, confirm cached matcher behavior is unchanged.
  - Stress test with Publish concurrent with N Acquire/Release pairs on a pinned reader; assert no UAF and no cache-key collision across generations.
  - Assert cache size returns to baseline after several reload-then-retire cycles (bounded-size check, not just correctness).
