FOAM ALONE: NOT ADEQUATE

Four reasons, in the order that matters for your setup:
1. Foam carries no load. The rigid side panels are what brace the case laterally so the unit's weight doesn't tip it forward off the bracket rails. Loose foam stuffed into a 1¼" gap is just a draft plug, not a structural member.
2. Kibo chew and ingestion risk. XPS, EPS, and open-cell foam all shred easily with a paw or a chew, and spray foam off-gases before it cures. A dog who can already reach the screen from the sill will reach foam in minutes.
3. Foam degrades on the outer face. UV plus summer heat makes it crumble within a few weeks; the seal fails and you end up with foam crumbs on the outer sill.
4. Foam isn't positively fastened. Even foil-faced foam tape just adheres to the accordion panel. A nudge or compressor vibration dislodges it. The rigid side panel must be mechanically secured, not glued or taped.

PET-SAFE TEMPORARY CONTAINMENT (until the rigid filler is in place)

Your instinct to close the bedroom door is the right call. Hold that line:
- Bedroom door closed, AC unplugged, both stay that way until the rigid panel is in and verified.
- If the bedroom door has to be open for any reason tonight, put a pressure-mounted pet gate across the doorway. 36 inches tall handles most mid-size dogs. Walk-through gates are fine.
- Pull furniture away from the sill so Kibo can't stage a jump to the screen from a chair or the bed. Right now the screen is the only thing between him and the outer sash edge, and the gap is right next to it.
- Do not run the AC with the gap open even with the door closed. The case wasn't designed to be supported on the bracket rails with one side panel missing; an unbalanced case is a forward-tilt risk.

RIGID FILLER PANEL: MATERIAL

- ½" or ¾" exterior-grade plywood, or ⅛" hardboard (Masonite), cut to the exact gap profile. Acrylic or lexan also works and adds chew resistance if you want a belt-and-suspenders option; both need pilot holes.
- Paint or seal all edges before installing. The outer face sees weather.

RIGID FILLER PANEL: SIZE AND FIT

- Measure the gap at top, middle, and bottom. Sash frames are rarely perfectly parallel, and that's likely why the factory accordion panel can't close it. Cut to the tightest dimension and shim where needed, not the loosest.
- The panel fills the space between the AC's INNER accordion panel and the outer window frame. It does not replace the accordion panel. The accordion panel must be extended and locked per the manual first; the rigid filler handles only what the accordion can't.
- Bottom edge rests on the window sill. Top edge tucks under the locked upper sash or the upper frame. The fit should be snug by friction before any fasteners go in.

RIGID FILLER PANEL: FASTENING (mechanical, not adhesive)

1. Extend and lock the AC's inner accordion panel per the manual. This is the load-bearing side.
2. Slide the rigid panel into the gap, sill to top.
3. Fasten the panel into the inner accordion panel's metal frame with two #8 or #10 sheet-metal screws (one near the top, one near the bottom), through pre-drilled pilot holes in the panel. The screws bite into the AC's own side flange, not the sash wood.
4. Optional: a small L-bracket at the bottom edge anchoring the panel to the sill keeps it from sliding out if the AC is ever removed for the season.
5. For a draft seal, run a thin strip of closed-cell weather-strip tape (about ½" wide) on the outer face where the panel meets the sash. This is cosmetic — the screws are what hold it. Construction adhesive or silicone is not acceptable as the primary fastener.

PRE-USE CHECKS — STRUCTURAL (do these first, before plugging in)

- Push firmly on the rigid panel from inside. No movement, no bowing, no daylight appearing around the edges.
- Pull outward on it from outside (have Devika do it while you watch inside). No movement.
- Tug the inner accordion panel. It should not compress, shift, or pop loose.
- Grasp the top corners of the AC case from inside and push down. No rocking on the bracket rails. The case should sit flat with a slight backward tilt (about ¼" to ½" rise at the front) so condensate drains to the rear and not into the room.
- Confirm the lower sash is locked and the upper sash is seated on top of the AC and locked. The sash lock is what prevents the unit from being tipped outward off the bracket.

PRE-USE CHECKS — ELECTRICAL

- Plug directly into the wall outlet. No extension cord, no power strip, no cube tap. Window AC units draw too much steady current for any of those, and a warm-room dog investigating a cord protector is a separate problem you don't want.
- Confirm the circuit isn't shared with another high-draw appliance (microwave, space heater, hair dryer on the same breaker). If it is, anything else on that circuit stays off while the AC runs.
- Run fan-only for 5 minutes before switching to cool. Listen for rattling — a vibrating panel means a screw is loose or a shim is missing.

PRE-USE CHECKS — PET-SPECIFIC (do these last, right before Kibo comes back in)

- Walk the sill and the floor under the AC. No foam scraps, no offcuts, no dropped screws. Anything chewable within reach will be found.
- Power cord routed behind furniture or through a rigid cord protector. No dangling loop he can grab.
- Pet gate goes back up at the bedroom door whenever the room is unoccupied, even with the rigid panel in place. The panel protects the window; the gate protects the door and the cord.
- First re-entry: watch him for 10 minutes. If he goes for the panel, the sill, or the screen, redirect and treat the gate as permanent for that room until you've watched him ignore it across a few hot days.

STOP AND CALL THE CONTRACTOR BACK IF

- The bracket rails show any movement when you push down on the AC. The bracket was just replaced and signed off, so this is the specific case where the user's standing rule about not treating vendor sign-off as proof of subsequent steps applies — verify independently.
- The rigid panel cannot be made to fit without daylight wider than about ¼" along any edge. That suggests the gap is outside the normal range of AC side-panel design and may be a sash-fit issue.
- The lower sash won't lock, or the gap is on the inner sash edge rather than the outer sash edge. Different problem, different fix — and the contractor who did the bracket should be the one to look at it.

ASSESSMENT
Likely a normal load response. Mild stiffness around 1/10 showing up roughly 2h after play, with gait and stairs preserved, no swelling, no focal tenderness, no instability, and no in-play pain fits a normal post-load tissue response in the lateral ankle complex after a graded return. It is not a red flag in isolation, but treat the next 24-48h as an observation window.

THIS EVENING
  - Ice 15-20 min on / 45 min off if it feels hot or tight (you have no swelling, so skip if it isn't bothering you)
  - Compression sleeve or light wrap if it eases the stiffness
  - Elevate while seated or on the couch
  - Gentle pain-free ankle ROM: alphabet (toes trace letters), calf stretch, eversion isometrics against a pillow - no end-range forcing
  - No additional load today: no extra walking-for-exercise, no running, no plyos
  - Sleep normally; if you wake with stiffness, repeat the ROM in the AM before judging the next session
  - OTC NSAIDs only if you want them for comfort - not required

NEXT-SESSION CRITERIA (all must hold before you play again)
  - AM stiffness 0/10, or only transient (resolves within 5-10 min of walking)
  - No overnight or morning swelling
  - No focal tenderness on ATFL or CFL palpation
  - Single-leg balance >=30 sec each side, no wobble on the right
  - Pain-free single-leg heel raises (>=20 reps, or matched to the left)
  - Pain-free single-leg hop in place, symmetric distance
  - No feeling of looseness or apprehension on the right
  - Warmup again: ~15 min, jogging -> dynamic mobility -> band work -> accelerations -> planned cuts at 70-80%
  - If everything clears, repeat 35 min easy; hold duration flat across two clean sessions, then add 5 min

STOP SOCCER AND SEEK EVALUATION IF ANY OF THESE APPEAR
  - Stiffness worsens, or pain rises above 1-2/10
  - New swelling, bruising, or warmth around the lateral malleolus
  - Pain on palpation of the ATFL, CFL, or anterior talofibular region
  - Giving way, looseness, or "trust" loss on the right ankle
  - Pain or apprehension with single-leg balance, hops, or cuts
  - Locking, catching, or sharp pain on any motion
  - Calf pain, swelling, or tenderness (DVT check - low risk, but not zero)
  - Numbness, tingling, or color change in the foot
  - Symptoms that don't fully resolve within 48-72h

General guidance only, not a clinician. If anything in the stop list shows up, see one.

Pre-operation inspection — bedroom window AC, in order. Do these before plugging the unit in. Anything outside the listed pass conditions is a stop.

1. Panel movement (interior side)
   - With the unit still unplugged, slowly slide each accordion panel outward as far as it will travel, then back, twice.
   - Pass: panels move smoothly, no contact with the plywood filler, no binding, no bowing in the filler.
   - Stop if: filler flexes when panels move, screw heads catch the sash channel, panels no longer reach their full travel, or you hear creaking at the bolt points.

2. Sharp edges and pet-accessible surfaces
   - Visually trace the filler perimeter at Kibo-nose height (roughly 6–30 in off the sill). Run a clean cotton sock or paper towel along every edge the dog could reach.
   - Pass: foam weather-strip covers every cut plywood edge, no splinters snag the sock, no exposed screw threads, no gap a tongue or paw could slip into between filler and frame.
   - Stop if: any plywood edge is reachable and uncovered, any screw tip protrudes, foam is torn/missing, or the filler can be wiggled by hand (means fasteners or friction fit are not actually doing their job).

3. Sash restraint
   - Upper sash is locked; verify the lock engages fully (not just visually — pull up on the sash with one hand, confirm zero lift).
   - Pull the sash down onto the filler at three points: left edge of filler, center, right edge. There should be no daylight change and no rocking.
   - Pass: lock fully engaged, filler does not shift under hand pressure, sash stop or weatherstripping still bears on the filler.
   - Stop if: sash lifts under hand pull, filler rocks, filler pops out of friction fit, or the sash lock only partially engages because the filler is shimming it open.

4. Cord clearance (line cord)
   - Trace the line cord from the unit to the outlet. It must not pass through the sash, over the filler, or under the locked sash meeting rail.
   - Pass: cord exits the room through a route that does not cross any moving sash part and is not pinched by the locked sash.
   - Stop if: cord is pinched anywhere, runs where opening the sash would cut it, or lies on a walking path Kibo can reach.

5. Exterior gap check
   - From outside (or by mirror/phone camera), look at the gap between the filler perimeter and the window frame along top, bottom, left, right.
   - Pass: daylight ≤ ~¼ in at every point, foam tape fills any smaller slivers, no light beam visible through a continuous opening.
   - Stop if: any continuous light gap > ~¼ in, foam tape is missing/gapped, or the filler does not sit flush against the frame at top or bottom.

6. Test loading — how hard to push without misloading the bracket
   - With two people, hands at the bottom corners of the chassis only. Push straight inward (toward the room) at increasing effort: 5 lb, 15 lb, 30 lb. Hold each for 5 seconds.
   - No rocking, no diagonal force, no push on the top of the cabinet, no push on the filler itself, no one-handed test.
   - Pass: unit does not shift on the bracket rails, no creak from bracket or sill, no gap opens at the filler.
   - Stop if: any rail-to-bracket movement, any sound from the sill/bracket, the unit tilts, the filler shifts, or the bracket deflects — that means a partial load path, not a confirmed mount.

Stop conditions (master list — any one halts operation)
- Filler moves, rocks, or separates under hand force.
- Any screw is loose, missing, or backed out; any pilot hole has stripped.
- Sash lifts, sash lock does not fully engage, or filler shims the lock open.
- Daylight > ~¼ in anywhere on the filler perimeter, or foam tape has a gap.
- Any plywood edge, screw tip, or bracket corner is reachable by Kibo without the foam seal covering it.
- Cord is pinched, routed across a sash line, or within reach of the dog.
- Bracket or sill produces sound or visible movement under the 30 lb push.
- Unit rocks front-to-back or side-to-side more than ~1/8 in when nudged at the top corners.

If everything passes, the unit can be plugged in and run on fan-only for 2–3 minutes before switching to cooling, with Kibo still out of the room and someone present. Re-inspect the filler and sash at 30 minutes of operation, then again at 2 hours — heat and vibration can settle a friction fit the static check missed.

Flushing order

1. Pull the aerators off the kitchen cold tap and bathroom cold tap first — sediment collects in the small mesh screens and will keep the stream looking dirty even after the lines are clear.
2. Run the kitchen cold tap on full cold. The initial sputtering + 2 minutes of cloudiness then clearing is a normal post-shutdown pattern; keep it running another 2–3 minutes past clear so any settled material in the branch line is pushed through.
3. Run the bathroom cold tap on full cold the same way.
4. Move to hot. The bathroom hot tap's faint yellow is almost certainly the water heater refilling and pushing sediment out of the tank — slower to clear because it has to flush through the heater. 5–10 minutes of running is normal. If it's still tinted after 10 minutes, that's reportable.
5. Kitchen hot last, same approach.

Opening two taps at once (e.g. kitchen cold + bathroom cold in parallel) increases flow and pushes air and sediment out faster.

Drinking water

- No boil-water notice from management + cold tap cleared = cold water is fine to drink now.
- Going forward, after any low-use period (overnight, returning from a trip, post-shutdown), let the cold tap run 30–60 seconds before filling a glass or kettle.
- Don't drink or cook with hot water straight from the tap — standard guidance, and extra relevant right after the heater refilled.
- If you want a buffer: fill a pitcher from the cold tap and refrigerate.

Appliances — only after every tap runs fully clear

Dishwasher: run an empty rinse/quick cycle, no detergent, no dishes. If it completes and the drum water at the end is clear, return to normal use.
Washing machine: run a rinse-and-spin cycle with no clothes to flush the supply hoses. Clear drum at the end = good to go.

If either cycle leaves cloudy or tinted water in the drum, don't run a load yet — flush longer at the taps and retry.

When to report to management

- Cold water stays cloudy or tinted for more than ~5 minutes of running (points to the building riser, not your apartment).
- Hot water stays yellow for more than 10 minutes of running.
- Visible particles from any tap.
- Any sewage odor.
- Pressure that stays low or sputtering that doesn't resolve.
- Yellow tint also appears in the cold water (rules out the heater and points building-side).

Coupling the schema bump with the generator bump is the right shape — the 2024-05-14 incident was specifically the un-coupled version (generator 0.9.0 against a schema-2 canonical, correctly rejected by the schema guard as workflow drift, not a broken generator). The remaining risks in Anya's sequence are around ordering, test scope, and the strength of the freeze.

Partial-publication risks (in priority order)

1. Schema-bump before generator-pin window (step 1 → step 2). Even on an isolated branch, the canonical package is the source of truth. If the workflow auto-publishes the canonical to a registry on schema change, step 1 alone ships schema-3 tokens into the registry while the manifest still says 0.8.x. Downstream consumers with `>=2` ranges silently pick it up. Need an explicit "canonical is not republished on this branch" mechanism, not just a branch-name guard.

2. Consumer-pin and shared-CI-pin are coupled by claim, not by mechanism (step 2). "Pin together at 0.9.0" is fine if both live in the same manifest entry that takes effect atomically. If the consumer pin is in `package.json` and the shared-CI pin is in a separate tools manifest applied by a different step, a partial-apply reproduces the prior failure mode in mirror image — generator alone or consumer alone bumped. This is exactly what the memory says shouldn't happen.

3. Step 7 freeze is enforced by assertion, not by artifact gating. "Keep 0.8.4 published until the matrix passes" needs a definition of what gates publication (CDN version pin, registry dist-tag, manifest version constraint in the consumer), and who/what enforces it. Otherwise a clean step 4 lets someone declare "matrix passed" and bump. The freeze has to be load-bearing in the publish path, not a policy statement.

4. Generated artifacts vs. canonical-publication ambiguity. Step 7 says "0.8.4 outputs published" — does that mean all four targets, or just the canonical? If the four generated targets are gated but the canonical package itself moves to schema 3 in the registry on step 1, consumers who pull canonical directly see the schema bump even with 0.8.4 artifacts frozen. Needs an explicit answer: the canonical package version stays at the schema-2 release until matrix pass.

5. Step 6's "zero publication" is checked at the generator boundary, not the registry. If the schema-validator fails before generation but the publish step is independent, "zero generated" doesn't mean "zero published." The test needs to verify registry/CDN state, not just CI logs.

Misleading-comparison risks

6. Semantic-fixture comparison across four targets is circular if all four fixtures came from the same 0.9.0 generator. A bug that emits the same wrong answer in CSS, iOS, Android, and docs (e.g., a unit-conversion or token-name collision) passes all four comparisons trivially. Fixtures need an independent authorship trail — not regenerated from the generator under test.

7. Step 5 only exercises the CSS drift detector. The matrix claims four targets but the negative test edits one CSS variable. iOS/Android/docs drift detectors may use different mechanisms (plist diff, content hash, generated-doc n-gram check). An edit-per-target is needed, or the test silently covers only one of four guards.

8. Step 4's 20-iteration byte stability catches within-target nondeterminism, not cross-run drift. If the schema bump takes effect on a downstream cache between runs 1 and 21, that's invisible to byte stability within one process. Also doesn't catch the case where the generator is byte-stable but the consumer's parser interprets the output differently between runs (e.g., a CSS variable ordering change that's semantically equivalent but breaks a regex downstream).

9. Step 5/6 run on the same workspace as step 4. A negative test on a contaminated environment can pass for the wrong reason — residual artifacts from the green path can mask a guard that would otherwise fail. The red-path tests should run on a fresh checkout, or at minimum with the green-path outputs cleared.

10. Step 1's schema-3 content is unspecified. If schema 3 was authored to match what 0.9.0 expects, the comparison is between two views of the same source. The pilot memory explicitly says schema 3 shouldn't be bumped merely to satisfy 0.9.0 — worth confirming with Anya whether 0.9.0 actually requires schema 3, or whether the bump is orthogonal and can be deferred.

Questions to put to Anya before the rerun

- Is schema 3 required for 0.9.0, or can 0.9.0 run against schema 2 with a feature flag? If orthogonal, decoupling the schema bump removes risks 1, 6, and 10 in one move.
- Where exactly do the consumer pin and the shared-CI manifest pin live, and is the apply atomic? (Risk 2.)
- What is the registry/CDN mechanism that enforces "0.8.4 stays published"? A version pin, a dist-tag, a manifest constraint? (Risk 3.)
- Does "0.8.4 outputs" mean all four targets including the canonical package, or only the generated artifacts? (Risk 4.)
- For step 6, is "zero publication" verified by reading registry/CDN state, or only by CI logs? (Risk 5.)
- Who authored the semantic fixtures, and is the authorship trail independent of the 0.9.0 generator? (Risk 6.)
- Does step 5 get a per-target edit, or just CSS? (Risk 7.)
- Do steps 5 and 6 run on a fresh checkout, or on the post-step-4 workspace? (Risk 9.)

If Anya can answer these and the freeze mechanism is wired into the publish path rather than asserted in prose, the sequence is sound. The structural shape is right; the holes are in the seams between steps and in what counts as "pass."

Plan: warm sweet potato + chickpea bowls over rice with tahini-yogurt sauce and a quick wilted kale.

The shape of the plan — most cooking done by 9:00, only the kale and a final warm-up of chickpeas done after Devika texts — is so that the kitchen is quiet when she walks in and the bowl still feels fresh.

What holds vs. what waits
- Holds well (do early): roasted sweet potatoes, rice, tahini-yogurt sauce.
- Goes sad if done early (wait for the text): kale (wilts dull, slumps), chickpeas (best fresh-warmed in a hot pan).

Timeline from 8:30

8:30 — Oven to 425°F. Cube both sweet potatoes about ½-inch. Toss with olive oil, a generous pinch of cumin, one minced garlic clove, salt. Spread on a sheet pan. Start the rice on the stove in your usual ratio.

8:35 — Sweet potatoes in. Make the sauce: a few heaping spoonfuls each of tahini and yogurt, a squeeze of the half-lemon, one grated garlic clove, salt, and a splash of water until it loosens to a drizzle. Cover, set on the counter. It will sit fine for an hour.

8:45 — Strip the kale off the stems, tear, wash and spin if needed. Leave it raw in a bowl with a towel over the top. Do not cook yet.

8:50 — Drain the chickpeas, pat dry with a towel, toss with a pinch of cumin, salt, and a thread of oil. Set in a bowl. Not cooking yet.

~9:00 — Sweet potatoes should pierce easily. Pull the pan, turn the oven off, leave the door cracked so they don't over-brown. Fluff the rice, drop a clean towel between pot and lid, leave on the off burner. Sauce and kale sit.

9:00 → wait for the text. Cooking is done.

After she texts she's leaving (you have ~15-20 min until she arrives)

1. Hot skillet, medium-high, thin layer of oil. Chickpeas in, leave them alone for 2 min, then stir. Another small pinch of cumin and the rest of the minced garlic. ~4-5 min total — warmed through, some color, doesn't need to be shatter-crisp.

2. Pull chickpeas into a bowl. Same pan, splash of oil, kale in with a pinch of salt. Toss 60-90 seconds — just wilted, still bright. Small squeeze of lemon.

3. Plate: rice, then sweet potatoes, then chickpeas, then kale on top. Drizzle tahini-yogurt sauce. Final squeeze of lemon across each bowl.

If she's later than expected
Rice and sweet potatoes genuinely hold 20-25 min off-heat. If it's longer, sheet pan back into a 325°F oven for 3-4 min. Sauce may tighten — stir in a teaspoon of warm water before drizzling.

If she's more tired than expected
The bowl travels. She can eat on the couch or in bed — no table required, no decisions to make.

The PR itself isn't fetchable from this app surface, so I'm grounding the review in the code block you pasted plus the runbook context (v2.19.4 randomized 1–3s Retry-After behavior, ingest-edge staging rollback-drill hygiene). Going through your four dimensions in order.

**Permit ordering and cleanup**

The order `global.acquire` → `tenant.acquire` → `defer tenant.release()` → `defer global.release()` is correct for LIFO: global is held longest, tenant is released first. Good. But the cleanup is incomplete for two paths:

1. The `tenant.acquire` failure path returns directly without releasing global. If `tenant.acquire` errors with anything other than `context.Canceled` (e.g. a timeout that is *not* a cancellation — different error type from the context package), the already-acquired global permit leaks until GC. This is the same shape as the cancellation bug you flagged, just on a non-cancel error path. Fix: release global before returning on any tenant-acquire error, or acquire tenant first then global and only release what was acquired.

2. The order of `defer`s means `tenant.release` runs before `global.release`. That's fine — but it means if `tenant.release` itself panics or blocks, global is never released. Not likely, but worth a `defer` ordering note in the PR description so reviewers don't re-litigate it.

The recommended rewrite, scoped to what you pasted:

```
global.acquire(ctx)
if err := tenant.acquire(ctx); err != nil {
    global.release()   // <-- missing today
    return canceled(err)
}
defer tenant.release()
defer global.release()
```

**Allocation-before-limit behavior**

The append loop checks `decompressed > bodyLimit` *after* the `output` buffer has already been grown by `len(chunk)`. With a single large chunk (e.g. a 14 MiB block from gzip with a low compression ratio on a 1.86 MiB wire payload — the 2024-03-22 shape), the buffer is extended past the limit before the check fires. Two issues:

- Memory exposure: `output` can transiently hold up to `bodyLimit + maxChunkSize` bytes. If `bodyLimit` is the existing 10 MiB envelope and `maxChunkSize` is the gzip decoder's buffer (commonly 32 KiB, but configurable up to ~1 MiB on some decoders), this is bounded but non-zero.
- The 2024-05-16 prototype was judged internally sound because it "aborts immediately when the limit is crossed" — that abort is correct, but it happens *after* the over-limit allocation, so the abort itself is real but the memory savings from it are not. If the intent of the prototype was to *cap* decoded memory at `bodyLimit`, the current PR doesn't deliver that.

The clean fix is a pre-check before append:

```
for chunk := range decoder {
    if decompressed + len(chunk) > bodyLimit {
        return bodyTooLarge()
    }
    output = append(output, chunk...)
    decompressed += len(chunk)
}
```

**Cancellation**

Two distinct cancellation surfaces, both real:

1. `tenant.acquire(ctx)` returns `context.Canceled` (or `DeadlineExceeded`) because the request was canceled while waiting for the tenant permit. The current code does `return canceled(err)` — but `tenant.release()` and `global.release()` are both deferred *after* the failed tenant acquire, so neither runs. Global leaks. This is the bug you explicitly flagged.

2. Cancellation during the decode loop itself. The current loop does not select on `ctx.Done()` between chunks, so a canceled request still gets processed up to the next chunk boundary and only then errors out. For gzip that's typically the next 32 KiB block — not catastrophic, but it means cancellation latency is bounded by chunk size, not by request cancellation. At 1–3s Retry-After cadence this is mostly cosmetic, but it's worth a sentence in the PR.

Fix for (1): acquire tenant first, then global — that way only one permit exists at a time on the failure path, and the deferred release for the one you have runs automatically:

```
if err := tenant.acquire(ctx); err != nil {
    return canceled(err)         // no permits held
}
if err := global.acquire(ctx); err != nil {
    tenant.release()
    return canceled(err)
}
defer tenant.release()
defer global.release()
```

This also fixes the non-cancel tenant-acquire error path noted above.

**Minimum regression tests**

Before acceptance, the PR needs tests that exercise each dimension independently, not just an end-to-end "happy path":

1. Permit ordering: a unit test where the global semaphore is mocked to count acquires and `tenant.acquire` returns a synthetic error. Assert `global.release` ran. Repeat with `tenant.acquire` returning `context.Canceled` — assert global released, tenant never released.
2. Allocation-before-limit: a test that streams a single chunk larger than `bodyLimit` (or a synthetic decoder that yields one big chunk). Assert (a) `bodyTooLarge()` returned, (b) `len(output) <= bodyLimit` (no over-limit allocation), (c) the rejection metric incremented, (d) Retry-After is in [1, 3]s.
3. Cancellation: cancel the context *during* `tenant.acquire` (e.g. cancel from a goroutine after a short delay). Assert both permits released and no leak counter incremented. Also: cancel mid-decode-loop and assert the request returns within one chunk interval, not after the full stream.
4. Retry-After preservation: the randomized 1–3s value must be unchanged from v2.19.4. The cleanest test is a statistical one — run the overflow path 1000 times and assert the Retry-After distribution lies in [1, 3] and is not collapsed to a single value (regression guard against the randomization being dropped).
5. (Not strictly regression, but worth adding.) The 2024-03-22 1.86 MiB / 14,889,779 byte gzip case as a recorded fixture — that exact input should now return 413 at the limit, not after.

**Summary for the PR thread**

Not accepting as-is. The cancellation/global-leak path and the allocation-before-limit ordering are blocking. Reordering to tenant-first then global fixes both with one change. The append check should move before `append`. Tests 1–4 above are the minimum; the 1.86/14.9 MiB fixture is strongly recommended. Retry-After randomization should be preserved explicitly with a statistical guard.

Review of Wes's 5/22 matcher-cache revision:

READER PATH — sound, under standard EBR assumptions.

The pin-before-load (epochs.Enter then active.Load) and swap-before-retire (active.Swap then epochs.Retire) order match the pattern needed to keep `gen` alive across `Match`. Combined with monotonic generation_id (no allocator-reuse collisions) and `gen.Lookup` scoped to the generation, the use-after-free and retire/publish TOCTOU patterns from the prior rejection are closed.

Two things the snippet does not show but the reviewer should confirm before merging:
  - epochs.Enter pins (reads epoch + bumps the pinned count) atomically, before the caller observes active.
  - epochs.Retire(old) blocks until all reader epochs pinned at or before the swap have drained.

If those hold, the reader is fine.

RELOAD PATH — still leaks failed candidates. This is the same defect the prior rejection flagged, in a slightly different shape.

The constructor publishes to the process-wide registry before validation, and the failure path does not retract:

  generationRegistry[candidate.ID] = candidate.Matchers   // pre-validation write
  if err := Validate(candidate); err != nil {
      candidate = nil                                     // local pointer dropped
      return err                                         // registry entry kept
  }

That directly contradicts the rule from the prior rejection: build only in a generation-scoped local matcher map, never write the shared matcher table, and free the candidate with its local map.

Consequences:
  - generationRegistry grows by one entry per failed reload, with no upper bound. Each entry pins the full compiled matcher set for the failed candidate.
  - Live traffic is unaffected — the reader path goes through active.Load, not the registry. But anything that reads the registry (diagnostics, admin tooling, an alternate lookup path) sees ghost generations forever.
  - During the validate window the unvalidated candidate is already visible in the registry to any concurrent registry reader. Not a UAF risk for live traffic, but a real visibility-leak window.
  - The inline comment ("The validation-failure path does not delete generationRegistry[candidate.ID]") makes clear this is intentional in the patch, not an oversight. That is the part to push back on — the prior rejection was on exactly this point.

Fix: validate against a local matcher map first; register in generationRegistry only after Validate returns nil. The failure path must either not register, or delete the entry on error.

A separate, smaller question the snippet leaves open: what is generationRegistry's intended lifecycle on the success path? If it is meant to hold "all generations ever published," there is no Retire-side cleanup shown. If it is meant to hold "currently live generations only," then successful generations leak on retire as well. Worth resolving before this lands — the patch is silent on it.

The candidate design is structurally sound: tenant_id at the front of the cache key makes cross-tenant collision impossible by construction; including denies in policy_generation invalidation prevents stale-deny persistence; a single 403/not_authorized envelope is the right shape — implementation must use byte-identical bodies for "exists-but-denied" and "does-not-exist" cases or existence leaks via response diffing.

1. Revocation invalidation mechanism: revocation must trigger either (a) a policy_generation bump for the affected tenant, or (b) an explicit purge of (T, S, *, *, g_current) entries on the revocation event. The design is silent. Pick one and instrument it. Tests 2.1–2.4 cannot pass without this.
2. policy_generation is per-tenant, not global. Confirm. Otherwise a single role edit forces a fleet-wide cache miss.
3. The "unknown" state for permitted-but-absent must be a typed discriminator in the wire schema — not null, not empty string, not an error string. It must round-trip and aggregate (5.2 depends on this).

RERUN MATRIX

1) Cross-tenant cache reuse
   Setup: tenant A, subject S_A, resource R, action allow, g1 — allow path warmed. Tenant B, subject S_B (identifier-string collision with S_A), resource R, g1 — no membership, decision will be deny.
   1.1 — Action: request (A, S_A, R, allow, g1). Expect: cache HIT, allow served. Verify: served-from-cache log.
   1.2 — Action: request (B, S_B, R, allow, g1). Expect: cache MISS against A-keyed entry; B-keyed entry served (deny). Body = 403/not_authorized. Verify: cache lookup log shows no A-entry hit; storage inspection shows two distinct entries keyed by tenant_id.
   1.3 — Negative control: an unrelated tenant C with no entry at g1 must MISS cleanly, never fall through to A or B.
   Pass: 1.1 hit, 1.2 miss-against-A + correct deny, 1.3 clean miss; storage shows tenant_id-scoped partition.

2) Membership revocation
   Setup: tenant T, subject S, role grants access to R at g1. Cache holds (T, S, R, allow, g1).
   2.1 — Action: revoke S's role (or remove S from T); wait for invalidation to land; request (T, S, R, allow, current_g). Expect: cache MISS at current generation; decision recomputed; result = 403/not_authorized. Verify: deny observed; cache lookup log shows no hit at current_g.
   2.2 — Storage inspection: no allow entry remains for (T, S, R, allow) at current generation. Verify: post-test scan.
   2.3 — Concurrent: revocation commits while a request for (T, S, R, allow) is in flight. Specify outcome — either "old decision served then revalidated at use" or "new deny at arrival"; never "allow served after revocation commit." Verify: replayed race test, assert against the specified outcome.
   2.4 — Partial revocation: S loses access to R but retains access to R2. After invalidation, (T, S, R, allow) is deny and (T, S, R2, allow) is allow. Verify: per-resource invalidation, not blanket purge of legitimate allows.

3) Policy-generation changes

Verdict: yes, the completion rule violated the stated lateness contract. The first completion fired at +31s, the configured allowance is 90s, and the 312 late records all arrived in [+31s, +78s] — inside allowance, excluded from the first result, present in the corrected result. The 0.8% delta (312 / 38,721) is exactly that exclusion. Upstream is clean (stable accepted-point count, normal commit latency, no delivery loss), so this is rollup-service-local completion timing, not a data-path issue.

Mechanism: the completion trigger fires on a signal that arrives before `window_end + lateness_allowance` — either an upstream watermark at +31s, or an idle / no-new-events rule that ignores the configured allowance.

Assertions that should gate a fix:

1. First compaction of window N is invariant under arrivals in `[window_end, window_end + lateness_allowance]`. Any record arriving in that interval with a timestamp in window N is included in window N's first published result.

2. Completion of window N cannot fire before `window_end + lateness_allowance` unless a named upstream signal (watermark, EOS marker, source-idle threshold above the allowance) certifies no unprocessed record with `ts ≤ window_end + lateness_allowance` remains. Time-based completion that ignores the allowance is non-conforming.

3. Records arriving in `[window_end, window_end + lateness_allowance]` roll up only in their original window — never in N+1 or later. The "next compaction pass" is the correction surface for in-allowance late records, not a re-rollup destination, and must not produce double counts.

4. Determinism: given the same input events and the same lateness setting, the first compaction result is byte-identical to the corrected result. Post-fix, 39,033 must equal the first-published count for 14:05–14:10.

5. Undercount bound: for any window, `|corrected − first| ≤ records whose arrival > window_end + lateness_allowance`. In this incident that bound is 0 (all 312 were in-allowance). A regression asserting exactly 0 here is appropriate; an aggregate SLO asserting bound ≤ out-of-allowance count across windows is appropriate long-term.

6. Completion-trigger source must be named and documented — idle timer, scheduled cadence, or upstream watermark — with a stated precedence when they conflict. The current ambiguity between +31s and +90s is itself part of the defect.

7. Regression test: inject records arriving at +0s, +30s, +60s, +89s post-window-end and assert all four appear in the first compaction of window N.

Out of scope for this review: the upstream data path (clean), the operational correction (data-platform's), and the next-pass reprocessing semantics beyond the no-double-count requirement above.

Soft tacos with a raw cabbage slaw on top. One pan, ~15 min active, well inside your 25, cabbage stays crunchy.

  Plan, in order:
    1.  Prep while the pan heats. Slice the cabbage as thin as you can (skip the core). Slice 2 scallions, keep the whites and greens separate. Halve and slice the avocado. Crumble or shred a small handful of cheddar (~1/2 cup).

    2.  Pan on medium. Drain the beans, add them with 3-4 big spoonfuls of salsa verde (about a third of what's left). Warm 3-4 min, mashing some beans so it goes saucy, not soupy. Salt to taste. Scrape into a bowl and cover.

    3.  Same pan, medium-high, small splash of oil. Fry 4 eggs (2 each) or scramble all 8 softly if you're hungry. Salt as they go.

    4.  While the eggs cook, slaw in a bowl: cabbage + scallion whites + 1 spoonful of salsa verde + pinch of salt. Toss, let it sit 2-3 min. The acid + salt just barely tenderizes the outer layers; the crunch stays.

    5.  Warm the tortillas last so they stay pliable — 20 sec per side in the empty pan, or stack and microwave 30 sec wrapped in a damp towel.

    6.  Build: tortilla, beans, egg, slaw, avocado, scallion greens, cheddar. The cheese softens from the egg. Drizzle extra salsa verde if you want it looser.

  Timing:
    0-5 min   prep + beans warming
    5-12 min  eggs + slaw assembled
    12-15 min tortillas + plating
    15-25 min slack, eat at your pace

  Why this keeps the cabbage crisp:
    It's dressed, not cooked. Salt pulls a little water out and salsa verde's acid softens just the surface; the ribs stay crunchy against the soft egg and warm beans. Dress it at the last minute if you want even more snap.

Safe immediate guidance
- Keep both appliances unplugged. Don't recreate the dual-load condition on that outlet.
- The GFCI resets and each appliance works alone on it — good sign, but don't push it.
- For now, run the kettle OR the toaster oven by itself. Avoid stacking other high-draw items (microwave, coffee maker, Instant Pot, toaster) on the same circuit at the same time.
- Kitchen counter receptacles are usually split across two circuits that alternate along the counter. If the kettle trips on one outlet, try the outlet on the other side of the sink (different circuit). Two high-wattage appliances on different circuits is fine.

Low-risk checks you can do yourself
- Look at the outlet face, the wall plate, and both plugs: any brown/yellow discoloration, melting, or scorch marks?
- With nothing plugged in, plug a small lamp into that GFCI. Press TEST — lamp should go off. Press RESET — it should come back. If TEST doesn't trip the GFCI, the device itself may be failing; stop using the outlet and call maintenance.
- Smell the outlet briefly (don't touch your nose to it). No odor is normal. Any plastic/ozone/burning smell = stop, leave the breaker off, call maintenance.
- Plug each appliance into that GFCI by itself and run it 1–2 minutes. If either trips the GFCI alone, that appliance has a fault — don't keep using it, and have both the appliance and the outlet inspected.
- At the breaker panel (door open, don't touch anything inside), glance at the breaker for that circuit: any scorch marks, or does it feel obviously warm? If yes, leave the breaker off and call maintenance.

What NOT to do
- Don't run the kettle and toaster oven together again "to test it" — that's the same overload you just saw.
- Don't keep pressing RESET after a trip without changing the conditions.
- No extension cords, power strips, or outlet splitters behind a kettle or toaster oven.
- No 3-to-2 prong cheater plug, no swapping in a regular (non-GFCI) outlet, no bypassing ground.
- Don't keep using the outlet if any of the warning signs below appear.

Clear signs to leave the circuit OFF and call building maintenance or a licensed electrician
- Burning, ozone, or "hot plastic" smell from the outlet, plug, or wall.
- Brown/yellow discoloration, melting, or scorch marks on the outlet, wall plate, or plug prongs.
- Buzzing, crackling, popping, or sizzling from the outlet.
- Outlet face feels warm or hot to the touch while in use (a barely-warm outlet under heavy load is one thing; a hot face is not).
- Outlet is loose — the plug wobbles or won't seat firmly.
- GFCI won't hold RESET, or trips immediately with nothing plugged in.
- Repeated trips with only one appliance running.
- Tingling or mild shock when touching an appliance, the plug, or the outlet.
- Visible sparks when plugging or unplugging.
- Tripping returns even after you stop stacking loads.

Is this consistent with an overload?
Yes, this is consistent with an overload. A kettle (~1,200–1,500 W) and a toaster oven (~1,200–1,800 W) together pull roughly 20–27 A on a circuit that's typically 15 A or 20 A. Running both off one receptacle is a textbook overload. Three things argue against a hard fault and support overload as the cause: (a) the circuit holds when each appliance runs alone, (b) no heat, smell, discoloration, buzzing, or visible damage, and (c) the trip happened only under combined load.

One nuance worth knowing: a GFCI receptacle trips on ground-fault current (an imbalance between hot and neutral, around 4–6 mA), not directly on overload — that's the breaker's job. So the trip you saw was most likely either (1) the breaker behind the GFCI tripping on overload, which cuts power to the whole GFCI, or (2) the two appliances together producing enough combined leakage current to cross the GFCI's threshold even though each was individually clean. Both are benign once you stop stacking loads. As long as the GFCI resets cleanly, holds with single appliances, and none of the warning signs appear, you can keep using it for one high-draw appliance at a time — and call maintenance if anything in the warning list above shows up.

Bottom line: most likely an overload, no immediate danger given what you've observed, but stop stacking loads on that outlet and watch for the warning signs.

Diagnosis: both, and the second one matters more than the first.

The extracted contents and modes match, so at the level of "did the generator produce the right files" there is no semantic drift — this part is harmless packaging metadata. But the raw archive hash is the contract under which schema-3 + generator 0.9.0 are pinned, and that contract is currently broken across OSes. So the block is correctly fail-closed on the wrong gate: it is rejecting on archive bytes when the real drift check should be on canonicalized content, and it should simultaneously be flagging the packaging pipeline as non-deterministic until the raw hashes agree too.

Root causes visible in the artifact comparison:

  Timestamps. Linux writer stamps every entry with a fixed UTC instant (13:52:00 UTC), so the Linux archive is internally consistent and timezone-clean. macOS stamps entries with file mtimes in local time spread across four seconds (09:51:58 to 09:52:02). Even after you correct to UTC, those four seconds still differ. So the two writers are not using the same epoch model: one is using a pinned build epoch, the other is using per-file mtime. That is a writer-config drift, not a content drift.

  Entry order. Neither order is lexicographic by path. Linux: css, ios, android, json. macOS: json, css, ios, android. These reflect OS file-iteration order at archive-write time, not a stable manifest. Any reproducibility contract that depends on archive hash has to remove iteration order from the equation.

  Extra fields / permissions. The reported modes are 0644 on both sides and content hashes match, so xattrs and Unix extras are not the visible cause here, but they are a latent risk on macOS (resource forks, ._ files) and need to be excluded by rule, not by hope.

Recommended rule for the next CI run — deterministic and fail-closed:

  Packaging side, identical on both runners:
    1. Pin SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH to the canonical `@northpier/tokens` schema-3 release commit timestamp (or another release-pinned value) and export TZ=UTC for both jobs. The pinned epoch is the only timestamp any entry may carry.
    2. Build a stable entry list before opening the archive: sort by lowercase, forward-slash path. The generator should emit this manifest; the packager must not rely on directory walk order.
    3. Write entries in manifest order. Force file mode to 0644 for all four outputs. Strip extended attributes and any non-DOS extra fields (Info-ZIP `-X -D`, or equivalent in the zipfile-based writer).
    4. Use one writer path on both runners. If the team is currently shelling out to system zip on macOS and a Python `zipfile` on Linux, collapse to one — preferably the Python writer with explicit deterministic flags, so behavior is identical.
    5. Treat the timestamp on each entry as `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`, never the generator's mtime.

  Comparison side, two gates, both required to pass:
    Gate A — canonical content record. For each archive, build `{sorted_path: (sha256(content), mode)}`. Compare Linux vs macOS records. Mismatch = real drift in generator output = block and investigate the generator. This is the drift check the team actually cares about.
    Gate B — raw archive SHA256. Compare Linux vs macOS archive hashes on identical inputs. Mismatch with Gate A passing = packaging nondeterminism = block as a packaging-pipeline defect. Do not green this on the grounds that "contents match." Reproducibility is part of the schema-3 / generator-0.9.0 deliverable, and the lock cannot be honored by hash if the writer is non-deterministic.

  Promotion rule. Publication is green only when Gate A and Gate B both pass on the same canonical inputs. Either gate failing blocks publication. Gate B failure is a writer bug to fix in the same change as the rerun, not a finding to defer.

What this changes for the current block:
  Right now the team is being held by a hash gate that is measuring non-determinism in the writer, not in the content. The right first action is to acknowledge that content is equivalent under canonicalization and that the remaining gap is pipeline-side, then land the packaging fix above (pinned epoch, sorted entries, stripped extras, single writer) before rerunning CI. Once the writer is normalized, the raw hashes will agree across Linux and macOS by construction, and the Gate A canonical record comparison becomes the durable drift check for future schema or generator bumps.

Two teaspoons on the sill during a humid first long cycle is most likely normal rear-drain condensate that has tracked back under the chassis lip or been wind-blown in at a hairline seam — but verify before resuming. Use the 5/22 baseline (filler bolted through accordion frame, foam as seal, no daylight, sash + restraint seated, cord clears pinch) as your reference state; nothing in this inspection touches the bracket or requires a new drain path.

Inspection order, with stop conditions. Walk through in sequence; stop the moment any stop condition triggers.

Phase 1 — locate the water (no tools, no contact with the unit)

  1. Where exactly is the water? A single puddle centered under the front lip suggests condensate tracking back from the drain pan. A puddle offset to one side, or a drip trail on the wall, points to a seam at that side admitting humid outdoor air that condenses on cold surfaces inside the airstream.

  2. If you can see the outside of the unit safely (different window, balcony, or by going out a door), check whether it is dripping steadily from the rear or rear-corner of the chassis onto the exterior ledge. Steady rear drip is normal in humid weather; what you want to know is whether outside drip is happening at all.

  Stop if: water is visibly coming from the front face of the unit indoors, or the wall above/beside the unit shows staining. Both indicate indoor condensate or chronic infiltration, not normal rear drainage.

Phase 2 — seal integrity (visual only, no bracket, no disassembly)

  3. Rigid side filler still flush against sash and accordion frame on both sides, in the same position as 5/22?

  4. Foam seal along the accordion panels and along the seam where the top of the unit meets the lower sash — any new daylight visible? Any compression loss or pull-away from the frame?

  5. Lower sash position unchanged from the verified position? The sash restraints should have prevented droppage, but verify.

  6. Cord still clears the sash pinch point with no scuffing, and the plug is dry and cool at the wall outlet.

  Stop if: filler has shifted from 5/22, foam shows a new daylight gap, or sash has dropped. Seal needs re-seating before any further cooling. The bracket itself is unlikely to have moved, but the seal stack on top of it can shift independently.

Phase 3 — internal inspection (grille + filter off, no bracket)

  7. Remove the front grille and the air filter. Note the filter condition — a dirty filter restricts airflow, ices the coil, and produces a sudden melt-drip exactly like what you're describing.

  8. With a flashlight, look at the evaporator coil and the front-accessible portion of the drain pan. Look for: ice on the coil or fins; standing water pooled in the pan on the indoor side; any drip point on the underside of the coil housing above the indoor section.

  9. Run the flashlight along the underside of the chassis just behind the front lip. Any wet point or drip on the indoor side of the chassis?

  Stop if: visible ice on the coil (let it melt fully; do not resume until the cause — usually the filter — is fixed and the coil is clear); standing water in the indoor-accessible pan; or a drip point on the indoor side of the chassis. Any of these means the unit is not draining to the rear as designed.

Phase 4 — drain observation with unit off

  10. Leave the unit off and unplugged. After 30 to 60 minutes, is the sill still dry, or is new water appearing?

  Stop if: water continues to appear with the unit off. That is an active indoor-side leak, not a condensate event.

Resume criteria — all five must hold before you run cooling again

  Outside drip from the rear or rear-corner of the chassis is occurring (or, if you couldn't see the outside safely, no front-drip and no pan water indoors).
  Filler, foam, sash, and cord match the 5/22 baseline — no new daylight, no shift.
  No ice on the coil; filter reasonably clean (wash or replace if it was loaded).
  Sill stays dry for the full 30–60 min observation window with the unit off.
  Cord and plug dry and cool at restart.

If all five hold, the most likely explanation is normal rear-drain condensate that tracked back a small amount under the chassis lip, or wind-blown humid air condensing at a marginal seam during an unusually long humid run. Resume with a short test — 15 to 30 minutes, then re-check the sill — before any extended cycle.

If the same 2 tsp recurs on the next humid long cycle, the cause is a marginal seal or marginal tilt, and the next step is to address that without touching the bracket (reseat foam, shim the front of the unit slightly to restore outside-down tilt). Do not pre-emptively do either now.

What this procedure avoids

  No contact with the approved bracket at any step.
  No drilling a drain hole — indoors that just moves the problem into the wall framing.
  No power applied until Phases 1–3 are complete and the Phase 4 observation window has elapsed dry.

CROSS-SERVICE INVARIANT REVIEW

Claimed invariant: a window's first-pass rollup commits only when every partition assigned to the completing worker has seen watermark >= window.end + 90s, with rollup and checkpoint written in one transaction, and the new owner of an assignment re-derives eligibility from its own current watermarks before evaluating.

Gaps the invariant leaves open — each is approval-blocking until addressed by the patch or by a pinned contract test:

1. The transaction spans two writes. If rollup lands in the metrics store and checkpoint lands in the metadata DB, "one transaction" requires co-location, 2PC, or an outbox. The patch is silent. No observable state must exist where rollup is visible without its checkpoint or vice versa.

2. The new owner's eligibility re-derivation must use CURRENT watermarks for the NEW assignment's partition set, not the checkpoint's effective_watermark (which was computed under the prior assignment). The patch says "before evaluating eligibility" but does not say "from the new assignment's partitions."

3. min() across assigned partitions is correct only if every input partition feeding the rollup is assigned to exactly one worker at completion time. If a partition is unassigned during the eligibility window (rebalance gap), its watermark is invisible and min() can prematurely complete.

4. "Records arriving after completion are retained for the next correction pass" does not name the retention store or the retention window. If retention is bounded and the correction pass is delayed, late records can be lost between first-pass commit and second-pass consumption.

5. Downstream reads must not see a mutated first-pass. This requires either a fixed compaction_id per first-pass with versioned reads, or downstream pinned to the first committed compaction_id. The patch does not name the read-side rule.

FOCUSED BOUNDARY TESTS

B1 — exactly at the allowance
  setup: assigned partitions all at watermark = window.end + 90s
  action: trigger eligibility evaluation
  expected: completes (the >= rule)
  gates: the >= vs > off-by-one

B2 — one tick before the allowance
  setup: one partition at window.end + 89.999s, others past
  action: trigger eligibility check
  expected: does NOT complete; rolls into next evaluation
  gates: the prior +31s bug does not regress

B3 — empty window
  setup: window with zero records across all assigned partitions; watermarks at or past window.end + 90s
  action: trigger eligibility
  expected: no rollup row committed, no checkpoint written, OR a documented empty-rollup sentinel — not a silent positive completion

North Pier — Windows ZIP hash drift, rerun after timestamp normalization

Recommendation

1. Diagnosis. This is the same class of writer-config drift you already closed on Linux/macOS (per-file local mtimes there), now showing up as the NTFS extra field (0x000a, 36 B/entry) on Windows. The "extracted files equal, entry order equal, normalized timestamps equal" findings rule out content or ordering drift — the bytes that differ are Windows writer metadata, not artifact content. That means Gate A's canonical content hash will agree across all three runners once the writer is normalized; you do not need a new drift check, you need to keep Gate A's "must agree across all rebuilds" invariant intact.

2. Artifact contract (two-tier, unchanged in spirit).
   - Gate A — canonical content hash. Deterministic over normalized artifact payload (file set + per-entry timestamps in UTC, sorted). This is the durable drift check; it survives future schema or generator bumps. Linux/macOS already match here after the rerun; Windows will match too once its writer is normalized.
   - Gate B — canonical envelope hash. Hash of the ZIP produced by the one shared writer, written to a strict template (no extra fields, deterministic ordering, deterministic UTC timestamps). Must agree across all three runners by construction.
   - Transport hash — the raw archive hash each runner emits is metadata about the byte stream that runner produced. It is useful only for forensics and for the GitHub Actions artifact upload. It is NOT part of the contract and MUST NOT be compared across runners.

3. Cross-platform packaging approach.
   - Single writer on all three runners. Pick one implementation (Python `zipfile` in deterministic mode is the natural fit since you're already using it) and run it identically on Linux, macOS, and Windows. This is the same fix you applied to the Linux/macOS pair — extend it to Windows, don't branch it.
   - Explicitly strip / disable the Windows NTFS extra field (0x000a) in the writer. Configure the writer to emit only the minimum extra fields the spec requires; do not let the runtime or toolchain inject platform-native metadata.
   - Environment hardening on Windows, same shape as the macOS fix: `TZ=UTC`, deterministic locale, no user-specific paths, no resource fork / NTFS stream leakage. Set `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` to a fixed build epoch on all three runners — that is the timestamp model, not "current time" or per-file mtimes.
   - Pin the writer version. Record the writer commit SHA in the build log so future Gate A investigations can correlate a divergence to a specific code change.

4. Drift detection policy. Keep Gate A fail-closed. Do not add a platform-keyed allowlist, do not downgrade Gate A to "warn on Windows," and do not treat the Windows raw hash as a separate signal. A real artifact change would still move Gate A on at least one runner; adding a Windows exception would mask that. The rule is: Gate A must agree across all rebuilds from the same inputs, full stop. Gate B agreement is a build-pipeline integrity check, not a substitute.

5. Release gate. Block publication until a third rerun shows Gate A hash equal across Linux/macOS/Windows, Gate B hash equal across the three, and the Windows archive contains no 0x000a NTFS extra field. Once those three hold, the raw transport hashes can be recorded but ignored for the go/no-go decision.

Short version: same fix that closed the Linux/macOS drift — one shared writer, deterministic UTC timestamps, no platform extra fields — extended to Windows. Two-tier contract unchanged, fail-closed, no platform exception.

Runbook `rb_1789267973607` ("shard-keeper: verify lease convergence after failover") sets the bar. Process readiness is not the exit condition — replacement replicas reporting ready only proves the processes are up. The three required exit checks, all of which must pass before reentry, are:

1. Single owner per partition. Each shard partition has exactly one lease owner; no split or competing owners. Duplicate or missing ownership is a hard failure.
2. Monotonic lease epochs. Epoch numbers increase without gaps or rollbacks across the partition set after the event. Any non-monotonic epoch means a fencing or renewal failure.
3. No stale-owner messages for two full lease-renewal intervals after readiness. A single stale-owner notification inside that window fails the check.

If any of those fail, keep the failover open and page the shard-keeper owner (you). Do not close on a partial pass.

Given your evidence — wired and 2.4 GHz stable, no WAN drops, one reboot restored 5 GHz for only ~20 minutes before drops returned, modem clean — the working hypothesis is a 5 GHz radio problem on the router itself, not your ISP line. Most likely cause is a DFS radar-detection event forcing the router to vacate its channel, with a failing radio / thermal issue as the secondary candidate. Treat the steps below as one sequence; only escalate to the next stage if the current one gives you a clean signal.

1. Snapshot everything before you change a thing
   - Log into the router admin page. Note (or photograph): router model, firmware version, current 5 GHz channel, channel width (20/40/80 MHz), transmit power, any "Smart Connect" / "Auto channel" / band-steering toggle, SSID(s), security mode, DHCP range, static leases, port forwards, parental controls, DNS settings.
   - Use the router's "Backup configuration" or "Save settings to file" feature if it has one. This is your rollback.
   - Do not factory-reset. Reboots and config edits are fine; a reset wipes everything above and is not warranted yet.

2. Pull the event log / syslog first (cheapest signal you'll get)
   - Open System Tools → Logs (or equivalent). Screenshot everything from the last 24 hours.
   - Grep your eyes for: "radar", "DFS", "channel switch", "CSA", "channel availability", "wlan0" / "wlan1" up/down, "radio reset", "5G", "watchdog", "thermal", "assert", "firmware crash".
   - If your router supports exporting syslog to a USB stick or LAN host, turn that on and leave it — it costs nothing and gives you timestamps you can correlate.

3. Lock 5 GHz to a fixed non-DFS channel
   - Disable "Auto channel" and "Smart Connect" / band steering. Keep 2.4 GHz on auto for now.
   - In the US, safe fixed non-DFS channels are: 36, 40, 44, 48 (UNII-1) and 149, 153, 157, 161, 165 (UNII-3). Avoid 52–64 and 100–144 (DFS).
   - Start with channel 36 or 149, width 40 MHz, standard (not "turbo") transmit power. If your neighborhood is dense, 149 is often quieter than 36.
   - Save. Wait 24 hours with normal use.

4. How to test channel width
   - Hold the channel fixed and only change the width.
   - Run 80 MHz for ~24 hours. If you see new drops on a non-DFS channel at 80 MHz, drop to 40 MHz — 80 is more sensitive to interference and to client driver bugs.
   - Run 40 MHz for another ~24 hours.
   - If you want to keep throughput, 80 MHz on UNII-1 (ch 36–48) is usually the cleanest 80-wide block in a typical apartment; UNII-3 has restrictions on some clients.

5. Distinguishing interference / DFS from a failing 5 GHz radio
   - Signs pointing to DFS or interference:
       - Drop events in the log say "radar detected" or "channel switch".
       - Drops correlate with weather-radar sweeps (often every 5–10 minutes, depending on your nearest NEXRAD and what the router considers a hit) or with airport / military radar if you're near those.
       - Drops disappear once you lock a non-DFS channel.
       - RSSI on the client is steady right up to the moment of disconnect (DFS vacates in <200 ms; clients see the link just vanish).
   - Signs pointing to a failing 5 GHz radio or thermal:
       - Drops persist on a locked, non-DFS channel, with no DFS events in the log.
       - RSSI on the client degrades before the drop, or throughput collapses before the disconnect.
       - Router logs show "radio reset", "wlan down/up", "firmware crash", or thermal warnings.
       - The "good window" after each reboot gets shorter over time (20 min → 12 min → 5 min). That is the smoking gun for a degrading radio.
       - Case temperature is clearly higher during/after drops than during quiet periods.
   - One clean test that separates the two: put the laptop within ~1 m of the router, fixed non-DFS channel, fixed width, disable the laptop's Wi-Fi power-saving (Windows Device Manager → Wi-Fi adapter → Power Management → uncheck "Allow the computer to turn off this device..."; on macOS, no equivalent but check Energy settings). If it still drops at point-blank range, it is not path/interference — it is radio or client NIC.
   - Swap the suspect: if only one client drops, try another 5 GHz-capable device at the same spot on the same fixed channel. If only one device drops, the router is innocent and that client's Wi-Fi card or driver is.

6. Stop-reboot triggers
   - Two reboots in 24 hours is plenty for diagnosis. After the second reboot without a config change, you've learned nothing new from a third.
   - Especially stop if the "good window" is shrinking. That pattern means each power-on is making the situation worse, not better.

7. Contact-the-ISP triggers
   - You don't need to call them yet. The evidence is Wi-Fi-side: wired TV is fine, modem shows no WAN disconnects, 2.4 GHz is fine.
   - Call only if, after steps 3–5, the wired side also starts misbehaving, or modem line stats (downstream SNR, upstream power, correctable/uncorrectable errors) drift out of spec over a day. Most ISP techs will not troubleshoot your Wi-Fi; they will only verify the handoff to the modem.

8. Replace-the-router triggers
   - Drops persist on a fixed non-DFS channel at fixed 40 MHz, with no DFS events in the log.
   - "Good window" after reboot is shrinking across days.
   - Router is 4–5+ years old, or its firmware hasn't received a security update in 12+ months (check vendor support page).
   - Multiple different clients all drop in the same pattern at close range.
   - Replacement note: get one with explicit DFS-disable and per-band controls; mesh kits from the major vendors are fine for an apartment and avoid this exact class of bug because they typically pick UNII-1 by default and stay there.

Iris is right. An explicit `unknown` value carries no freshness claim — the value is unknown, so we cannot say "checked at T and the answer is nothing." The attached timestamp is the last successful source poll, which is a transport/liveness signal about the pipeline, not about the value. Conflating them invents data: a viewer would reasonably read the timestamp as evidence that the unknown reflects a recent, real check, when unknown can mean anything (permissioned gap, partial poll, schema miss, staging-only stub) and we cannot assert which.

Correct semantics for the fixture:

    Unknown value
    +----------------------------------------------+
    |  Value: unknown                              |
    |  No freshness claim is made about the value. |
    +----------------------------------------------+

The poll timestamp, if shown at all, is metadata about the source connection having been polled — not metadata about the incident-load value. Two acceptable renders under the preview contract:

  1. Omit the timestamp when the value is `unknown`. Cleanest. Removes any
     possibility of conflation.
  2. If shown, label it explicitly as source-connectivity metadata
     ("source last reached at T", "last successful poll at T"), position
     it as a separate pipeline-health field, and never phrase it as
     "incident-load last updated", "as of", or any value-freshness
     construction.

What is NOT acceptable: rendering the poll timestamp adjacent to the value in a way a viewer can read as freshness for the `unknown`. That is exactly the read Iris flagged, and it would tell an internal viewer "we just checked and there's nothing," which the value does not support.

Two consistency notes:

  - The fixture's no-raw-text / no-internal-IDs property is not the issue
    here. Even with a fully scrubbed fixture, the semantic conflation
    persists — unknown means we don't know, not "recently checked,
    empty."
  - This stays consistent with the v0 rule you set earlier: the surface
    may say there is no permissioned incident-load summary, but the copy
    must avoid implying raw incident text exists behind it. Same
    principle — don't let pipeline metadata imply value content we don't
    have.

So: for an explicit `unknown`, drop the value's freshness implication entirely. The poll timestamp, if kept, is pipeline-health metadata only, and the copy must say so.

For a shallow skin flap at the base of the finger, with normal sensation/movement, no deep cut, no nail involvement, and bleeding already stopped:

Cleaning (do this now at the gym or once home):
- Rinse gently under clean running water for 1–2 minutes. Mild soap around the wound is fine; do not let soap sit in the wound bed.
- Skip hydrogen peroxide and iodine — they damage healing tissue and slow reattachment of the flap.
- Pat dry with clean gauze. Do not rub or peel anything loose.

Flap — preserve, don't trim:
- A flap that's still attached and pink/red (not gray, black, or leathery) acts as a natural biologic dressing and will often re-adhere. Leave it in place.
- Only trim if it is clearly non-viable (dusky/black, shriveled, or obviously contaminated beyond simple cleaning) — in which case a routine clinic visit, not tonight, is the right place to do that.
- Don't pull, fold it back, or "tuck" it under.

Covering for the evening:
- Apply a thin layer of plain petrolatum or antibiotic ointment (bacitracin/polysporin) if you have it and no known allergy.
- Cover with a non-adherent pad (Telfa) or a petrolatum-impregnated gauze so the dressing doesn't stick to the flap; then a soft gauze square; tape loosely. The flap should stay slightly moist, not dry out or crust hard.
- Re-dress once in the evening, then daily. Change sooner if it gets wet or soiled.

Activity limits tonight and next few days:
- No more climbing today. No gripping-heavy tasks (heavy bags, opening jars) until the flap is stable.
- Keep it dry in the shower (cling-film wrap or a finger condom). No swimming, hot tub, or dish-soaking until fully closed.
- Avoid bending the finger forcefully into a crimp. Buddy-tape to the adjacent finger if the flap catches on things, but keep it loose so circulation isn't compressed.

Urgent care (ER or urgent care today/tonight) if any of these appear:
- Bleeding that restarts and won't stop with 10–15 minutes of direct pressure.
- Spreading redness, red streaks up the finger/hand, increasing warmth, throbbing pain, pus, or fever — early flexor tenosynovitis or cellulitis.
- New loss of sensation, inability to bend or straighten the finger through full range against resistance, or pain on passive straightening — tendon involvement.
- The flap turns rapidly black, the wound gapes open, or you can see bone/joint — needs closure.

Routine (primary care, walk-in clinic, or a dermatologist within 1–2 days) if:
- The flap turns dusky/dark but there's no spreading redness or pain.
- Mild increasing tenderness without the urgent signs above.
- It hasn't closed in 5–7 days, or the area becomes persistently tender, swollen, or develops a small lump.

Given your history with climbing tweaks (forearm twinge pattern, calf/ankle protocols), this one is in the minor-bump category: clean, preserve, occlude, rest the grip, and watch for the red-flag list above.

The wound sounds like it's in good shape, but it's only a day old. Honest assessment, then coverage and stopping criteria.

IS PLAYING REASONABLE

Borderline. A skin flap in the first 24-48 hours is genuinely vulnerable to shearing and direct impact — which is exactly what bracing or a fall onto the hand delivers. Many people would skip the next one or two games and return around day 3-5, when the flap is more anchored.

That said, you're not goalkeeper and you're not planning to dive for the ball with that hand. The realistic exposure is an意外 fall. Reasonable to play IF you're willing to accept that a fall or hand impact could reopen or shear off the flap. If you want the safer call, wait one more game. This isn't a clear yes or no — it's a judgment call on your risk tolerance.

COVERAGE WITHOUT CONSTRICTION

The hard constraint: no tight circumferential wrap. As your finger swells with exercise, a snug ring of bandage acts like a tourniquet.

Two workable approaches:

1. Non-stick pad, taped only on top and bottom
   - Non-stick gauze (Telfa, or plain gauze with a thin smear of petrolatum) over the wound
   - Two short strips of tape on the dorsal (back) and palmar (front) of the finger
   - Sides of the finger left unbandaged so it can swell and you can check color

2. "Donut" cut-out
   - Cut a piece of moleskin or thick adhesive pad with a hole slightly larger than the wound
   - Stick around the wound so the wound sits recessed in the hole, shielded from direct pressure
   - Tape only on uninjured skin on either side

Either way:
- Keep the wound slightly moist under the dressing (don't let it dry to a hard crust)
- You should be able to fully bend and straighten the finger inside the bandage
- After applying, press the fingertip — color should return within ~2 seconds
- Finger should feel warm, not cold or tingly

Redress with a clean, dry dressing after the game. Sweat and field dirt are not what a fresh flap wants.

WHAT SHOULD MAKE YOU STOP

On the field, stop immediately if:
- Direct ball impact on the finger (even through padding)
- Any fall onto that hand
- Bleeding restarts through the bandage
- Pain increases during play beyond your baseline minimal tenderness
- Bandage gets saturated, displaced, or torn

During and after, treat these as urgent (stop play, loosen, or seek care):
- Bleeding that doesn't stop with 10-15 minutes of direct pressure
- Finger becomes cold, pale, dusky, numb, or tingly distal to the bandage — that's constriction, loosen right away
- Inability to bend or straighten the finger against resistance, or pain on passive straightening — possible tendon involvement
- Wound reopens, flap lifts/shears off, or you see anything that isn't clean pink/red tissue
- Increasing redness, warmth, swelling, drainage, or pus over the next 24-48 hours

If none of those happen, the wound is tolerating the activity. Clean it, redress, and watch it the same way you would have without playing.

Yes — short and easy is reasonable given the picture you describe (closed, dry, pink, no tenderness, no infection signs, no pain on grip or light hang). The new skin is fragile for several weeks even when it looks healed, so the goal today is friction control and load management, not stress-testing.

(I'm not a clinician. If anything unexpected shows up, defer to your usual care.)

1) TAPING WITHOUT CONSTRICTION

The finger itself isn't injured — the new epidermis is. Your job is a protective barrier over it, not a structural splint.

- Use breathable climbing finger tape (cloth, slightly stretchy). Avoid rigid athletic tape and avoid Leukotape directly on the wound — it adheres to new skin and tears it on removal.
- Put a thin layer of plain petroleum jelly on the pink area, then a single non-adherent pad (Telfa, or a small piece of hydrogel dressing) trimmed to just cover the new skin. This keeps tape off the new skin and prevents shearing when you remove it later.
- Anchor with an H-tape or loose spiral: two light anchor strips around the finger just above and below the wound (loose enough that you can fit a fingertip between tape and skin), then 1–2 thin bridge strips running longitudinally over the pad. Do NOT use a single tight circumferential strip — that's what causes constriction.
- Tension check after taping: press the nail bed — color returns in under 2 seconds, taped finger feels the same temperature as its neighbors. Tingling, throbbing, pallor, or coolness = redo looser.
- Re-check at the 15–20 min mark. Sweat + load tightens tape that felt fine at rest.

2) HOW TO PROGRESS

Today (short, easy):
- 30–40 min cap. Stop at the cap regardless of how you feel.
- Juggy, large positive holds only. No crimps, no slopers, no pinches that roll skin.
- Open-hand grip only. No half-crimp, definitely no full crimp.
- No dynos, no campus moves. Big moves on big holds are fine if skin feels nothing.

Next 1–2 weeks (if today stays clean):
- Hold size can shrink gradually toward moderate edges; still avoid sharp crimps.
- Half-crimp on edges you can hang comfortably; full crimp stays off.
- Volume climbs slowly, sessions still under an hour.

Weeks 2–3:
- Full crimp returns last, and only on edges that don't load the healing area directly.
- Slopers / high-friction holds back near the end of this window.
- Treat the new skin like a blister that never blistered — its tensile strength is well below baseline for ~4–6 weeks even though the surface looks normal.

3) WHAT ENDS THE SESSION — BEFORE THE SKIN REOPENS

Stop on any of these; they precede reopening:

- Stinging, burning, or a "pulling" sensation localized to the healing area during a pull. This is the most common early signal.
- A hot spot developing under the tape.
- Tape wrinkling, bunching, or rolling under load — that concentrates force on one spot.
- A pink dot or any moisture showing through the pad — the surface has opened, even microscopically.
- Taped finger going paler, cooler, or developing pins-and-needles — tape is too tight, and prolonged constriction itself damages skin.
- Sharp pain at the site (different from normal muscle/tendon effort).
- Tape dislodging, soaked with sweat, or peeling back to expose the wound.

Also stop at the planned cap (30–40 min) regardless. Fresh skin doesn't give much warning before it gives, and "one more problem" is how most climbing setbacks happen.

If the skin actually opens — even a hairline — clean it, cover it, and take a few more days before the next session. Don't climb through a reopened flap.
