Recommendation: keep the Arris S33 + your existing router.

Comparison on the dimensions that matter:

  Install-day mechanics
    Owned (S33 + your router): same appointment window; the ISP confirmed
    line-activation support covers customer-owned modems.
    Rental ($15/mo gateway): same appointment window; ISP owns the whole
    stack.
    -> Tie. The provider pre-empted the usual objection here.

  Equipment-failure exposure
    Owned: you absorb failure cost. S33 is current and well-supported;
    a replacement runs ~$100-150 if it dies.
    Rental: ISP swaps it.
    -> Slight edge to rental, but only matters in a tail scenario.

  Security / firmware control
    Owned: you schedule firmware; no provider remote management.
    Rental: provider pushes firmware automatically — good for patches,
    less good if you want stable config.
    -> Wash.

  Long-term cost
    Owned: $0/mo. Pays back vs rental in ~7-10 months.
    Rental: $15/mo = $180/yr.
    -> Clear edge to owned.

  Day-1 configuration complexity
    Owned: two boxes, two power bricks — but you already run your own
    router, so this is nothing new.
    Rental: one box, but your existing router becomes redundant unless
    you double-NAT or demote it to AP mode.
    -> Edge to owned (fewer migration steps for gear you already use).

  Lock-in
    Owned: modem is yours; portable across ISPs or resellable.
    Rental: return on cancel; missing return = fee.
    -> Edge to owned.

Install-day pre-flight — the only real risk vector:
  - Confirm the S33's MAC is registered on the ISP account before Sept 24
    so activation isn't held up at provisioning.
  - WAN on your router stays DHCP (cable hand-out is DHCP, not PPPoE).
  - Power the S33 up once before the appointment to clear any stale
    provisioning state if it's been in storage.

Why this is the lower-risk choice overall: the provider's own statement
already neutralized the install-day objection — same window, same line-
activation support. After that, the owned path wins on cost, lock-in, and
not introducing a migration step for your existing router. The rental's
only real advantage (failure-replacement) is a thin tail, and the cost of
self-insuring against it is ~$100-150 once vs $180/yr forever.

What the bounded observation does not answer

The bound being clean tells you ingest-client#87 was well-behaved during a controlled sixty-minute window. It does not tell you how it will behave at hour six, hour twenty-four, or under sustained load drift, because the sixty-minute window is too short to characterize steady state for this surface. The release decision is a separate decision

Removing the time bound is a governance decision, not an observation outcome. Three things must be explicit before the bound comes off, and none of them is settled by the clean numbers:

2. Replacement stop condition. With no time stop, something else has to fire when numbers move. Pick one and write it down before the release: a numerical stop re-armed at the existing threshold, an SLO or error-budget breach, or a p99/error-rate rollback trigger. 3. Provenance on the release record. Repacking sequence (books)

Goal: every box under 35 lb, apartment stays walkable, the frequently-used row stays on the shelf, towels/linens used as fill rather than as extra weight.

1. Stage the 6 smalls flat in the packing zone. Drop a folded towel in the bottom of each (cushion + light fill credit).
2. Leave the designated frequently-used row untouched. Don't even slide books on it.
3. Pull from the 8 mediums heaviest-first (textbooks and large hardcovers before paperbacks). Take ~8-12 lb out of each medium until it reads under 35 lb on the scale. Close, tape, and set aside each medium as soon as it passes — don't reopen.
4. Distribute the pulled books into the smalls by size, not by source box. Layer: a few oversized or art books flat at the bottom with a towel on top, then paperbacks and standard hardcovers upright. Stop each small at roughly 3/4 full by volume so the lid closes without crushing spines.
5. Tuck a folded towel or linen into any small that has visible slack, both for fill and to keep the load from shifting when the mover tilts the box.
6. Weigh each closed small. Anything over 35 lb: pull one more handful and rebalance it into a medium that still has headroom (a medium sitting at 30 lb can absorb another 4 lb safely).
7. Final pass: re-weigh all 14 boxes, confirm lids taped, confirm books are spine-down or flat so they don't migrate under load.

Expected outcome: 8 mediums at roughly 33-34 lb, 6 smalls at roughly 20-28 lb, walkways clear, one shelf row fully usable.

Drywall-anchor patch sequence (paint later)

Assumes the common self-drilling threaded anchor. For a different anchor type the only step that changes is removal.

1. Unscrew the screw from each anchor.
2. Back the anchor itself out of the wall with the same screwdriver, turning counter-clockwise. If it just spins free, ignore the anchor body and go to step 4 — the empty hole patches the same way.
3. If the anchor is the push-through kind and won't back out, tap it gently into the wall cavity with a screwdriver tip and one light hammer tap. You're left with a clean round hole at the surface.
4. Lightly sand about an inch around each hole with fine sandpaper so the spackle has a scuffed surface to grip.
5. Press lightweight spackle into each hole with a putty knife, slightly overfilled. A small bump is fine — overfill sands flush easily, underfill is annoying to build up later.
6. Wipe the surrounding paint with a damp cloth so any smeared spackle doesn't dry on the wall.
7. Let dry per the spackle label (about 30 min for fast-set, 1-2 hr for standard).
8. Put a small piece of painter's tape on each patch labeled "paint later" so the handoff walkthrough sees them and so you don't lose the spots before you come back with a brush.

That's it — no paint today, no special tools, and the patches sand and paint cleanly whenever you're ready.

LOW-STRESS PACKING SETUP FOR KIBO

What you're already seeing (following, pacing when boxes move, settling only when bed is in place) is mild place-attachment vigilance, not distress. The negatives you listed (eating, drinking, taking treats, walking normally, no panting/vomiting/diarrhea/trembling/destruction) match that read. The job now is to keep him in that band.

ANCHORS — do not move until the final block
- Bed and food/water station stay in their current corner.
- Build the safe area around them; never build the safe area and then move the anchors into it.

SAFE AREA
- One room, door closed or baby-gated. Small and den-like beats large and exposed when a dog is mildly stressed.
- Add: a worn unwashed shirt or blanket with your scent, one long-lasting chew item (Kong/frozen topper), water within reach.
- Sound: low-volume familiar music or a white-noise source to dampen tape, tape-gun, and box noise.
- Light: dimmer than the packing rooms; avoid flickering stacks of lights nearby.
- Visual access to a person, if that's what calms him. If he fixates on movement, gate him out of sightline instead.

ACTIVITY TIMING AROUND EACH BLOCK
- 20-30 min pre-block: sniffy walk or yard play. Goal = a tired dog, not a wired one.
- During the block: one person stays with him in the safe area, or he goes to a trusted friend's place for the duration. Do not rotate him between rooms while packing is live.
- Post-block: 20-30 min quiet decompression before any stimulation. Skip high-arousal play right after.
- Hold meal times exactly — feeding predictability is a strong anchor.
- Keep his normal walk schedule intact through moving day.

PACKING RULES TO LOWER HIS LOAD
- One room in flux per block. Never multiple rooms at once.
- Stage boxes in one non-safe-area stack; no boxes entering or leaving the safe area.
- Low voices during transitions; no door slams near his room.
- Don't bathe him on a packing day — familiar scent matters more than usual right now.

RED FLAGS — CALL THE VET IF ANY OF THESE APPEAR
- Refuses food >24h, or water >12h
- Vomiting or diarrhea (any blood)
- Panting at rest with no heat/exercise cause
- Trembling/shaking that doesn't resolve within ~1h of returning to safe area
- Pacing that won't stop even with bed in place and a person present
- House-soiling from a previously trained dog
- Destructive behavior at doors/windows (escape attempts)
- Hiding and refusing to come out for >1h
- Sudden guarding or aggression not previously shown
- Reluctance to walk, lameness, or posture change

A note on aids: if you ever want to add a pheromone diffuser, compression wrap, or calming chew/treat beyond the behavior setup above, run it by your vet first — especially given his paw history and any other meds. Nothing in this plan requires sedation, and the plan is designed to keep it that way.

Stopping point first, since that's the decision that protects the bookcase:

  STOP and brace for the mover if any of these is true:
  - The hex socket deforms further (rounds out more, edges start to crumble)
  - The wood around the joint creaks, splits, or the panel starts to flex
  - You have to use two hands / body weight on any tool to make it turn
  - The fastener begins to cam upward out of the wood instead of rotating
  - You've spent ~5 minutes total on attempts 1–3 with no movement
  The rule is simple: if it isn't turning with firm hand pressure, it's done for today. The assembled remainder fits through the doors, so a braced partly-assembled bookcase is strictly better than a cracked one.

  SAFEST ATTEMPT ORDER (try in sequence, stop the moment the first one bites or any stop condition hits):

  1. Rubber band in the socket. Fold a wide rubber band into a small pad, press it firmly into the stripped hex socket, then seat your original hex bit into the pad and turn slowly with steady inward pressure. The rubber fills the gap between the bit and the rounded walls. Lowest risk, often enough on lightly-stripped sockets.

  2. Painter's tape instead of (or under) the rubber band, two or three layers packed into the socket before inserting the bit. Same idea, slightly different fill behavior; sometimes one works where the other doesn't. Still essentially zero risk to the wood.

  3. Next-size-up hex bit, used by hand only — no driver, no ratchet, just fingers and slow steady torque. The oversize bit wedges into what remains of the socket walls. Use a folded piece of cardboard as a shim between your knuckles and the wood so any slip can't dent or scratch the panel. If the bit walks out of the socket rather than turning the fastener, stop — that's the camming-out stop condition above.

  4. Last resort before bracing: locking pliers on whatever is left of the fastener head — usually the exposed rim where it sits above the wood surface, not down inside the stripped socket. Pad the plier jaws with cardboard so they don't mar the wood, clamp with the minimum force needed to bite, and try to turn. The instant you feel the head deform or the pliers want to slip, release and back off. This is the step most likely to ruin the fastener for future disassembly, so it's also the most natural place to commit to "we're done, brace it."

  Skip the manual screwdriver for this. It's the wrong profile for a hex socket and the slip risk to the wood is higher than anything above.

  BRACING THE PARTLY-ASSEMBLED BOOKCASE FOR THE MOVER (do this once you call it):

  - Leave the fastener exactly as it is — don't try to back it partway out, don't add Loctite, don't cut it. A stopped fastener is recoverable; a mangled one isn't.
  - Wrap a few layers of painter's tape tightly around the joint where the side panel meets the frame, overlapping onto both pieces, to add shear resistance and keep the panel from drifting.
  - Lay a piece of cardboard over the outside of that joint and tape it down as a splint — this also protects the wood from strap pressure on moving day.
  - Mark the panel with a small piece of tape and a Sharpie note ("stripped fastener, do not tighten, lift from frame side") so the mover doesn't try to "fix" it by torquing the joint and cracking the wood.
  - When the mover arrives, tell them in person that this bookcase is braced, not fully assembled, and should be carried flat / on its long edge rather than stood upright and tilted — upright carrying puts bending load on the braced joint, flat carrying puts only compression on it.

  That's the whole plan: four attempts in order, a stop rule you can apply by feel, and a brace-and-label path that keeps the bookcase movable and the fastener recoverable for a proper extractor later.

First-night plan for Kibo at S. Slope

The pattern you describe is mild adjustment vigilance, not distress: he's checking the door but self-recovers to the bed when you sit nearby, and he's eating/drinking/taking treats. The job tonight is to keep that ratio (bed wins, door doesn't).

Setup (do once, before settling in for the night)
  - Park his familiar bed away from the entry, ideally in a corner near where you'll sit. Water next to the bed, not by the door. Dim lighting.
  - Sound masking on: a fan, white noise, or low music. Given the 9/23 bike scare, hallway sounds are likely the trigger; reducing the stimulus matters more than reassurance.
  - Have one long-lasting chew or stuffed Kong available at the bed, not at the door.
  - Essentials from today's handoff should already be in place (familiar bed, water). If you have a worn t-shirt or blanket with your/your household's scent, drape it near the bed.

Door protocol (the part that actually shapes tomorrow night)
  - When he goes to the door: no talking, no "it's ok," no follow, no treat at the door, no eye contact. Sit back down.
  - If he barks: silent, calm, return to your seat. Do not come to him at the door. Do not pick him up from the door.
  - When he returns to the bed on his own — which he's already doing once you sit nearby — that's the moment for calm praise and a treat delivered at the bed.
  - Outings: leash (Y-harness per the 10/24 rule), shorter leash at the building entry, walk straight out and straight back, no hallway scanning. Businesslike, not exploratory.
  - Your own arousal is the thermostat. Sit, read, laptop. No hovering, no repeated check-ins.

What not to do
  - No punishment for the barks. He isn't being defiant; he's alerting. The barks will fade fastest if the door has zero payoff.
  - No medication. Unnecessary for this picture, and sedative-style products can blunt the very self-settling he's already showing.
  - No new crate or new bedtime routine tonight. Defer any training changes until nights 3-4 if needed.

Signs that warrant veterinary advice

Same-night / emergency vet
  - Non-productive retching or repeated unproductive attempts to vomit (GDV/bloat risk — pacing + tight abdomen is the classic combo)
  - Restlessness that escalates over hours rather than tapering
  - Trembling that intensifies beyond a startle response, or panting at rest that doesn't abate in a cool/quiet room
  - Whimpering/crying that doesn't respond to your presence at the bed
  - Refusing water across several hours, or vomiting water
  - Blood in stool or vomit; black tarry stool
  - Any collapse, weakness, ataxia, or pale gums
  - Breathing difficulty, or reverse sneezing that doesn't break

Call the vet tomorrow (document tonight)
  - Treat refusal that persists past morning on 9/28
  - Appetite not back to normal by midday 9/28
  - Loose stool more than twice, or any stool change paired with low energy
  - Door-monitoring that isn't tapering by night 2-3 — that's when a behavior call becomes useful, not tonight
  - Escalating lip-licking, yawning, or whale-eye — these can mask pain or nausea in stoic dogs
  - Per the standing paw rule: any swelling/discharge/odor/bleeding/limping. New building, new walks, new surfaces — check paws at the morning outing.

Expectation-setting: one mildly alert night is normal. The benchmark isn't silence tonight; it's a shorter return-to-bed delay than last night, repeated across the next two or three. If that trajectory doesn't show by night 3, that's the trigger for a behavior-consult conversation, not a vet one — absent any of the red flags above.

This pattern — generalized bilateral soreness across large muscle groups after two days of unaccustomed heavy work, worse with stairs, eased by warmth, and no focal pain, swelling, weakness, numbness, or systemic symptoms — reads as typical exertional muscle soreness. Nothing in your description points to a tear, nerve involvement, or rhabdomyolysis right now. That said, I'm not a clinician; Devika's call on no more lifting is the one that matters, and you should run anything below by her before acting on it.

Evening recovery plan
  Stop lifting. Done for tonight.
  Warm shower or warm compress on the worst areas — heat is the right modality for this kind of soreness, and you've already confirmed it helps.
  Hydrate well. Two move days of sweat plus under-drinking is the usual setup for next-day cramps and worse soreness. Water is fine; add a little extra salt/food if you've been sweating heavily.
  Eat a real dinner with protein. Overnight repair is the main thing happening; protein matters more than any supplement here.
  Acetaminophen or ibuprofen per the bottle label if soreness limits sleep. Ibuprofen with a small snack to protect the stomach.
  Gentle movement only — a short easy walk, slow stair climb if needed. Prolonged sitting makes tomorrow worse, not better.
  Stretching: very gentle, hold-to-comfort only. No aggressive pulls on sore shoulders or thighs. If a stretch reproduces sharp pain, stop.
  Skip alcohol tonight. It fragments sleep and masks soreness, so you'll misjudge readiness tomorrow.
  Sleep at a normal hour. Recovery is mostly sleep-driven.

Sunday pickup soccer — recommendation: sit it out.
  Reasoning: with bilateral shoulder and thigh soreness still bad enough to bother you on stairs, your legs are almost certainly still strength- and proprioception-impaired. Pickup soccer on sore, guarded legs is a high setup for a hamstring, groin, or calf strain. One session isn't worth a soft-tissue injury that costs you weeks.
  If you really want to play, gate it on a morning self-check: stairs feel normal, you can jog and decelerate without guarding, and a few minutes of cutting feel smooth. If any of those are off, skip and play the following weekend. A lighter alternative tomorrow — easy bike, walk, easy hike — is fine if you're moving comfortably.

Warning signs that should prompt medical evaluation
  Urine changes: dark brown or tea-colored urine, or noticeably reduced urination. Rhabdo is the concern after heavy unaccustomed exertion, and today's clear urine doesn't rule out a delayed picture.
  Focal swelling that's increasing, especially in one calf, with tenderness or warmth — DVT concern.
  Pain that becomes focal, sharp, or knotted rather than diffuse, or a sudden snap or pop — possible muscle tear.
  New numbness, tingling, or weakness in an arm or leg, or pain that radiates down a limb.
  Inability to bear weight, a joint that locks or gives way, or a joint that looks deformed.
  Fever, chills, or spreading redness and heat over a muscle area.
  Chest pain, shortness of breath, lightheadedness, or coughing up blood — 911 / ER, not urgent care.
  Soreness that's still severe and not trending better 72 hours after the heaviest day, or that suddenly worsens after seeming to improve.

If anything on that list shows up tonight or tomorrow, flag Devika first — she's the clinician in the house and can tell you what's urgent versus what can wait for Monday.

For the next 1-2 weeks, default to the side-street loop. Six minutes is a cheap trade during the settling-in window — a new apartment, new street smells, and trucks he hasn't habituated to is a lot of stacked novelty for a dog who had a bike scare a month ago. Keep the Y-harness on; shorten the leash specifically through the noisy block when you do use it, so the line stays calm and predictable rather than taut.

For gentle exposure to the noisier block, three small rules:
  - Walk it on the opposite side of the street from the freezing intersection, at off-peak times (mid-morning, after lunch, weekends when commercial truck traffic is naturally lighter).
  - Cross at the next intersection over rather than the one where he freezes — let him pass it without needing to "decide" anything at the corner itself.
  - Skip the block entirely on garbage day, school-letout, or any day with sustained construction noise.

Quick bathroom breaks: use the nearest calm side street, not the noisy block. The shortest block isn't actually shorter if it produces a frozen dog who then has to decompress for twenty minutes once he's back inside. Save the noisier block for outings where you have time to take it slow.

A few things that would prompt me to revisit — not now, just watch-for:
  - Freezing starts spreading to other intersections, or to indoor sounds (garbage trucks from the apartment, sirens on TV)
  - He begins refusing walks or hiding when the leash comes out
  - Appetite or sleep regresses past the first week
  - Any reactivity (lunging, barking) at the noise instead of shutdown

If any of those show up, that's when a vet-behaviorist consult makes sense. For now the move is: calm route as default, low-dose exposure on his terms, no drills at the intersection. Treating it as not-a-big-deal is exactly the right framing.

Your situation matches the standard low-battery chirp pattern: single short chirp ~once a minute, "LOW BATTERY" on the display, no symptoms, and your separate plug-in CO monitor reads 0. That is consistent with a battery alert, not an active alarm — but treat it as a fix-it-tonight item, not a deal-with-it-later item.

IMMEDIATE SAFE RESPONSE (tonight)

  - Replace the battery now, or first thing tomorrow morning if you don't have the right battery on hand. The battery type is printed on the side/back of the unit — most combination alarms take a 9V; some newer ones take AAs; some are sealed 10-year lithium with no compartment at all.
  - If it is a sealed unit (no battery door), the chirp means end-of-service-life. You cannot swap a battery in it; replace the whole alarm.
  - Use a fresh name-brand alkaline battery. Rechargeables and cheap batteries shorten service life and can cause false chirps.
  - After the swap, hold the TEST button for ~5 seconds. You should hear the full alarm pattern briefly — that confirms the speaker, sensor, and electronics all work. If you don't get a test sound, replace the whole unit.
  - Check the manufacture date stamped on the back. Combination smoke/CO alarms are rated for 10 years from that date, not from purchase. If it's 10+ years old, replace the entire alarm regardless of battery state.

HOW TO DISTINGUISH A CHIRP FROM AN ACTIVE ALARM

  - Low-battery / end-of-life chirp: one short beep every 30-60 seconds, "LOW BATTERY" or "LB" or a battery icon on the display, lower volume, single beep at a time. Annoying, not designed to wake you.
  - Smoke alarm (active): three loud beeps in a row, repeating continuously — BEEP BEEP BEEP, pause, BEEP BEEP BEEP — full alarm volume.
  - CO alarm (active): four short beeps, pause, repeat — BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP, pause, BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP — this is the urgent pattern. Many units also show a CO ppm number on the display when this fires.
  - Test-button press: a brief sample of the full alarm pattern. Doesn't mean there's an emergency; it just confirms the speaker works.
  - Any actual CO ppm reading on the display (e.g., "37 PPM") is a real detection, not a low-battery state.

LEAVE / CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES INSTEAD OF TROUBLESHOOTING IF ANY OF THESE IS TRUE

  - The alarm is sounding its full alarm pattern (3 beeps for smoke, 4 beeps for CO), not a single chirp — even briefly, even if it then stops. CO can be intermittent.
  - Anyone has symptoms: headache, dizziness, nausea, drowsiness, confusion, flu-like feelings without a fever, chest pain, or loss of consciousness. CO poisoning often mimics the flu.
  - Your plug-in CO monitor shows any sustained ppm reading above 0. Even a low reading with symptoms is real concern.
  - You smell gas (rotten-egg smell is natural gas / LPG — different from CO but also a leave-and-call situation). Call your gas utility or 911.
  - You can't tell why the unit is chirping or alarming.
  - Anyone is hard to rouse, or Kibo is acting unusual (lethargy, stumbling, vomiting).

If any of the above apply: get everyone (humans + Kibo) out, open doors/windows on the way out if you can do it safely, do not stop to silence the alarm, and call 911 from outside. In NYC that's 911 — fire/EMS will respond with CO meters. Don't re-enter until the fire department or a qualified technician clears the home.

ONE QUICK HOUSEKEEPING NOTE

  - CO is colorless and odorless, so the plug-in monitor you already have is doing real work. Confirm it has power and check its own manufacture date — plug-in CO sensors also have a service life, typically 5-10 years depending on model.
  - The hallway is the right placement for a combination smoke/CO alarm — between sleeping and living areas. Keep it there when you replace the unit.

FIRST-PASS INTERPRETATION

The signal isolates cleanly: latency inflation is scoped to one client and one payload-size band, with no error/duplicate/retry/accounting anomalies and no drift in the other client classes. That shape is inconsistent with a general ingest-edge regression — a general regression would normally pull the cross-class baseline with it (it is within 7%) and would not be confined to requests above 8,000 points. The current evidence is therefore most consistent with a client-side change in batch size: that one client is now sending enough oversized payloads (>8K points) to dominate the global p99 in the alert window, even though their overall request volume may be unchanged. Error-rate flatness and the zero accounting/duplicate/retry gaps argue the latency is volume/queue-shaped, not correctness-shaped.

WHY THE EXISTING SIGNAL ALREADY FAVORS ONE HYPOTHESIS

Cross-class latency near baseline is the strongest in-hand discriminator. If ingest-edge itself had regressed (deploy, GC, shard hot-spot, downstream capacity), the same tail increase would show up across other high-volume clients, not just one. Combined with the >8K-point concentration, the working prior is: client behavior, not ingest-edge code.

SMALLEST EVIDENCE REQUEST

One query, payload-size distribution for the affected client_id, alert window (08:31–now) vs the same hour-of-day baseline over the prior 7 days. Specifically: median, p90, and fraction-of-requests above 8,000 points for that client, now vs baseline.

Why this is the smallest decisive ask:
- It directly tests the proposed mechanism (the >8K-point concentration already visible in the alert).
- If the client's median point-count and >8K fraction are both elevated vs baseline, hypothesis 1 is confirmed and ingest-edge can be set aside for this incident. From there the follow-up is a client conversation plus a temporary guardrail decision (rate-limit on >8K payloads or per-client concurrency cap), not a rollback.
- If the client's payload-size distribution is flat against baseline while only their latency is elevated, hypothesis 1 is weakened and the search pivots to per-client-specific ingest-edge behavior (shard affinity, per-client serialization, downstream partition skew for that client's tenant).

One secondary check worth running in parallel because it is cheap and rules out the remaining confound: any ingest-edge deploy or config change in the 24h before 08:31. If yes, it does not by itself prove causation, but it shifts the prior; if no, the client-batch prior hardens. No rollback or guardrail should be decided on the current evidence — only on the result of that one distribution query.

Operational steps:

  2. Apply the revert; verify the next flush window shows p99 back to baseline.

  4. Capture the incident + replay results for the postmortem.

Why not an ingest-edge change this weekend: the replay isolates cause to client config. Widening ingest-edge behavior over the weekend expands scope beyond what the evidence supports and adds blast radius for every other client.

EVIDENCE NEEDED BEFORE A PERMANENT GUARDRAIL

The replay proves causation at one point on the curve. A guardrail decision needs the curve, the cluster state, and the client trade-off — not just one replay.

1. Knee of the latency curve. Replay at intermediate batch sizes (2k, 5k) with proportional flush intervals to find where p99 actually bends. A guardrail below the knee is wasted headroom; above it doesn't protect.

2. Ingest-edge resource state during 08:30-09:00. CPU, memory, queue depth, per-batch processing time per shard. Was this client a meaningful fraction of total load? Headroom present means latency growth is intrinsic to batch processing; saturation means capacity may be the real fix, not a cap.

3. Downstream effect. shard-keeper queue depth and metrics-router p99 in the same window. Did the 10k batch cause pressure past ingest-edge, or did it buffer and absorb?

4. Other-client latency in the window. If only this client moved, a client-side cap is the right place to enforce. If others moved too, ingest-edge is the enforcement point.

5. Client intent and tolerance. Why did they raise the batch — lower request volume, cost reduction, something else? Is sub-second p99 a hard SLA, or is 2.69s acceptable to them? If they tolerate the new latency, we may not need a guardrail at all; we may need a different conversation.

6. Failure modes at the new size. Replay showed no accounting loss, which is good. Real-traffic data still needed on: memory pressure at 10k, timeout/retry behavior under deeper buffering, backpressure mechanics (does the client queue indefinitely or back off?).

7. Recovery characteristics. When the revert lands, how fast does p99 return? Validates the containment and tells us whether residual queue depth or connection state needs to drain.

8. Request-rate trade-off. The 10x lower request rate presumably saves the client something. A batch cap forces ~10x more requests back through. Capacity and cost model must absorb that, or the guardrail just shifts the problem onto another resource.

9. Pattern across clients. One-off misconfiguration or recurring pressure? A repeat offender points at server-side enforcement; a single client points at a client-side cap.

GUARDRAIL DESIGN (once evidence is in)

  Client-side cap: relies on client compliance; doesn't protect ingest-edge from misconfiguration.
  Server-side cap on ingest-edge: uniform protection; a behavior change visible to every client.
  Hybrid: server-side hard cap + client-side warning when approaching the cap.

  The choice follows from items 4 and 9 above. Don't pre-decide the design before the evidence is in.

REASSEMBLY ORDER (keeps both tall side panels supported on the floor the whole time — no racking force on them until the case is fully closed):

1. Clear a flat, soft area big enough to lay both side panels flat with the top, bottom, and fixed shelves between them. A blanket or cardboard on the floor protects the faces and lets the panels slide without scuffing.

2. Dry-fit everything first. Set the new connector next to the originals and confirm it matches: same bore depth, same thread/clip, same orientation. Lay every panel in position without engaging any connector so you know the layout cold before anything is under load.

3. Lay both side panels flat on the floor, inner faces up, parallel, with their top and bottom edges aligned. They are now supported along their full length — they cannot twist in this position. This is the single most important rule: do not stand the partial case up until step 6 is done.

4. Seat the dowels. Insert dowels into the pre-drilled holes in the side panels (or the horizontal panels, whichever the design calls for). Press the top, bottom, and any fixed shelves down between the two side panels. If a dowel doesn't slide home with light hand pressure, the panel isn't aligned — back off and re-seat, do not force.

5. Engage all connectors, including the replacement. Drive each one to the same resistance the surrounding connectors show — snug, not crushing. Wood is the soft member here; over-torque is what strips connectors in the first place.

6. With the case still flat on the floor, press down at all four corners and along the front edges. Anything that shifts now means a connector isn't fully seated — fix it before the case is lifted.

7. With a helper, lift the case from the bottom (not by the top edge) and stand it upright in its final position against the wall.

8. Reattach the back panel fully — every fastener back in its original hole. The back panel is what actually squares the case; an under-fastened back is the most common cause of racking once shelves are loaded.

ALIGNMENT CHECKS (run before any shelf goes in):

- Diagonals: measure both diagonals of the case interior, top corner to opposite bottom corner. They must match within ~1/8 in (3 mm). Mismatch means the case is racked — recheck connector seating before going further.
- Width: measure interior width at the top and at the bottom. They should be equal.
- Plumb: hold a level against each side panel's front edge. If out of plumb, shim under the low corner — do not pull the case level by tightening the back panel.
- Joints: every dowel you can see should sit flush or below the panel surface. Run a finger around each hole at a joint — any movement means the connector isn't fully home.

STABILITY CHECKS (before loading):

- Racking test: with the case still empty, push firmly at the top-front corner diagonally toward the opposite bottom-rear. The case should not rack, shift on the floor, or creak. If it does, the back panel is under-fastened or a connector is half-seated.
- Connector audit: walk every joint. Each lock fully rotated/closed, none spun free, no daylight gap between mating panels.
- Anti-tip: a tall bookcase with loaded shelves needs a wall anchor or strap. With the back still accessible and the shelves empty, this is the easiest moment to install one. If you don't have one, get it before the shelves go in — leverage from a few feet of loaded shelves is enough to topple the case in a stumble, and that risk goes up if a pet or a child is in the room.

LOADING RULE: heaviest items on the bottom fixed shelves, lightest on top. Stay within each shelf's rated load — fixed shelves higher than adjustable ones usually.

If you want, send a photo of the connector and the panel layout and I can flag anything that doesn't match the standard sequence before you start.

Decision rule first
  USDA guidance: perishable food held above 40°F for more than 2 hours should be discarded, regardless of smell or appearance. Pathogens that cause foodborne illness generally do not produce off-odors or visible changes, so "looks fine" is not a reliable test. Your fridge was at 50°F and the food has been in the danger zone (40-140°F) for ~2h40m, so the 2-hour clock has been exceeded.

Per-item guidance

  Milk, 48°F → discard
    Pour it out. Liquid dairy is one of the highest-risk perishable categories once it has been in the danger zone for >2 hours.

  Cooked chicken, 49°F → discard
    Cooked poultry is especially high-risk (Salmonella, Staphylococcus aureus toxin that is not destroyed by re-heating). Do not salvage by reheating — toxins formed by some bacteria are heat-stable.

  Yogurt, 47°F → discard
    Same rationale as milk. Cultured dairy still supports pathogen growth in the danger zone.

  Eggs, 48°F → discard
    Raw in shell, hard-boiled, or liquid/pasteurized — all are covered by the same 2-hour rule once they have been above 40°F. If these are raw in shell and you want to cook them immediately into a fully-hot dish you intend to eat right away, that is a reasonable personal call, but the conservative food-safety guidance is discard.

  Sealed hard cheese, 44°F → keep
    Hard and semi-hard cheeses (cheddar, parmesan, swiss, gouda, manchego, etc.) have low water activity and tolerate brief excursions above 40°F better than other perishables. A sealed block at 44°F is well within what most food-safety authorities consider safe to keep. Refrigerate normally; if any mold shows up later, cut at least 1 inch around and below the spot and the rest is fine.

  Soft or semi-soft cheeses (brie, ricotta, cream cheese, fresh mozzarella), deli meats, cooked rice, leftovers, raw fish, raw ground meat — if any of these are also in the fridge, treat them under the same rule: discard.

Immediate steps to bring the refrigerator back to a safe temperature

  1. Confirm the door is fully closed and the gasket is actually sealing all the way around. A door that "looks closed" but isn't sealing is the most common cause of this scenario.
  2. Turn the thermostat to its coldest setting for the next several hours to speed recovery.
  3. Do not open the door any more than necessary for the next 3-4 hours — every opening slows recovery and adds to danger-zone time for whatever food is still inside.
  4. Verify with an appliance thermometer placed on the middle shelf, not the built-in display. Built-in displays can be off by several degrees and are slow to update. Wait until the thermometer reads 40°F or below before restocking perishable food.
  5. Once the thermometer confirms 40°F or below, return the thermostat to its normal setting (usually around 37-38°F).
  6. Clean any spills from the discarded items now, while the fridge is warming up and before you put new food in.

If the gasket looks damaged, the door does not stay closed on its own, or the fridge does not return to 40°F within a few hours, that is a separate issue worth a service call before you restock.

One caveat: this is general USDA-aligned guidance, not a substitute for your local health department or a food-safety authority if anything about the situation is unusual.

Bottom line: run Option A first. It is the lower-risk way to gather decision-quality evidence by Monday, and it does not foreclose Option B as a follow-on if A's evidence says the cap is too tight or the problem persists above it.

Why A is lower risk

  Blast radius is local. A changes one client (cap at 2000 + 1s flush). B changes ingest-edge, which is shared infrastructure you own and that the active metrics migration currently flows through. Anything B touches has to be observed across every caller, not just the affected one.

  No new code path at a shared layer. B introduces a soft rejection mode above 8000. That is a new behavior with new accounting. Given the prior label_map / fake-clean-cutover concern on shard-keeper and the rollup-is-structural / fail-closed posture from earlier this year, the cost of adding a new rejection class at ingest-edge right now is not just "does it work" — it is "did we instrument it correctly end-to-end, and is anything downstream quietly misinterpreting it." A does not create that surface.

  Evidence is cleaner. A isolates one variable: what does this client look like at <=2000 points/batch with 1s flush. Accepted/rejected accounting is degenerate (everything accepted, possibly with overflow handling) and duplicate-request-id behavior is observable at the client with no contamination from other tenants. B's evidence is conflated by the 8000 boundary — points just over vs. just under behave differently, p99 near the threshold is noisy, and you cannot tell whether a regression is from the new rejection path or from another caller reacting to it.

  Faster to start, faster to reverse. A is effectively a config + client knob change. B needs to ride the normal deploy/rollout cadence for a shared component, which is exactly the kind of window Hema's team may want to reorder if prod forces it. A's lead time is shorter, which is what matters for a Monday decision.

  Failure modes favor A. If A is wrong, the worst case is "this client legitimately needs more than 2000 points" — visible immediately in p99 / dropped-signal complaints, recoverable by raising the cap or reverting. If B is wrong, the worst case is a misbehaving reject path on ingest-edge affecting non-target traffic — the same shape of risk that made the shard-keeper cutover worrying.

What you actually learn from A in 7 days

  - Whether the client can operate cleanly at 2000/batch with 1s flush (i.e., is 2000 a real ceiling or did it just mask the symptom)
  - Affected-class p99 under the cap — does latency profile improve, hold, or get worse
  - Whether the cap produces duplicate request IDs (it will, if overflow handling re-sends rather than drops — worth specifying explicitly before the run)
  - Whether overall error rate moves at all on the shared path (it should not, which is itself useful evidence)

If A's seven-day picture shows the client genuinely cannot live at 2000 (p99 regresses, signal loss, or the oversized-batch condition reappears above the cap), that is the evidence that justifies B as the next experiment — now with a known client peak and a known ingest-edge baseline, which B currently does not have.

What would change my recommendation

  - If you already have a validated, deployed soft-rejection path at ingest-edge from prior work (e.g., the malformed/arbitrary pre-pub reject posture documented in August) and the new 8000 threshold slots cleanly into existing accounting with no new code, B's incremental risk drops and A vs B becomes closer to a wash.
  - If the affected client's natural batch size is materially above 8000 (not just "occasionally spiky"), A's cap creates an artificial ceiling and its evidence does not generalize — in that case B is the only one of the two that tests the real condition, and A would be wasted days.
  - If Monday is hard and the deploy window for ingest-edge is open this week, B's lead-time argument weakens.

One thing to pin down before either run starts: define "cap at 2000" and "soft reject above 8000" as either drop-excess or split-and-resend, and instrument duplicate request IDs in both modes. Without that, the dup-ID signal the owner wants to observe is not comparable across the two experiments.

Suggested order: A this week, with a written go/no-go gate on Friday on (a) can the client run at 2000 and (b) is the oversized-batch signature still present above the cap. Use that to decide Monday whether B is the next step or the cap number simply moves.

This email has multiple high-confidence phishing indicators. Treat it as malicious.

Indicators:
  - Pressure tactic: "30 minutes" + immediate lockout threat, designed to skip verification.
  - Generic greeting ("Dear Sphere User") rather than your name or username.
  - Sender domain sphere-login.example uses a "login" subdomain that real corporate IT rarely uses for outbound security mail.
  - Link domain sphere-access.example does not match the sender domain — a legitimate renewal flow typically lives on the same domain the notice comes from.
  - Both domains use the .example TLD, which is reserved/documentation-only; production corporate infrastructure virtually never resolves there. A real attacker would use a look-alike (e.g., sphere-secure.com or sphere-login.net); .example here is consistent with a sandbox/test artifact or a deliberately fake lure in your environment.
  - Asks you to "verify credentials" via an external link. Legitimate certificate renewal is handled by the VPN client or an internal SSO page you reach by typing the URL yourself.
  - No context match: nothing in your known environment (metrics-router, ingest-edge, shard-keeper, internal tooling) suggests "Sphere" is a real vendor or internal service you use. From your side, this name appearing is itself a tell.
  - Classic credential-harvesting shape: urgency + threat + external link + credential prompt.

Safe handling — do these, in this order:
  1. Do not click the link. Do not hover over it either if your mail client previews URLs on hover (some clients fetch the target).
  2. Do not reply to the message, even to "unsubscribe."
  3. Do not forward to colleagues from this email; that spreads the lure.
  4. Verify independently out-of-band. Open a browser and type your real VPN portal address yourself, or contact your IT/security team through a channel you already trust (Slack, phone, known email). Do not use any contact info inside the suspicious email.
  5. Preserve the artifact before deleting: full message including headers. In most clients: View > Show Original / Show Source, then save the raw file. This is what security needs for blocklists and forensics.
  6. After preservation, delete from inbox and trash so a future accidental click on another device cannot reach it.

Reporting steps:
  1. Forward the preserved message as an attachment (not inline) to your internal security/phishing reporting address — e.g., phish@yourcompany or whatever your runbook specifies. Attaching preserves headers; inline forwarding strips them.
  2. If your mail client has a "Report Phishing" button, use that in addition — it usually pipes to the same backend with metadata your gateway needs.
  3. If you have a security ticket/IR queue (e.g., the incident tools available here), file a ticket with: subject line, sender, recipient, sending IP if visible in headers, the URL, and a one-line note that no interaction occurred.
  4. If your org uses an external mail provider (Mimecast, Proofpoint, Google/Microsoft report-add-ins), report through that channel too so the gateway can add a rule.
  5. If "Sphere" is a real vendor you actually do business with (it is not, from your context, but if it were), also notify that vendor's real security contact — found via their legitimate website, not the email — so they can warn other targets.

If at any point you realize you did click or typed credentials, treat it as a credential compromise: rotate the VPN/SSO password immediately from a device known clean, revoke active sessions via your IdP, and notify security as an active incident rather than a phish report.

Bottom line: classic urgency + credential-link lure on a non-matching, non-production domain. Preserve, report, delete, do not engage.

A "once-per-revolution" pattern points more strongly at the rotor than the caliper (constant drag would be the caliper), but the two can coexist, so do the cheap reversible checks first.

DIAGNOSTIC ORDER

1. Wheel-out visual: lift the front, spin slowly by hand, watch the rotor edge-on between the pads. Any visible lateral hop = bent rotor. Note the high spot; mark it with a tape flag or grease pencil. If the hop repeats at the same spot every spin, it's the rotor, not the caliper.

2. Pad-gap feel: with the bike still on the ground or in a stand, squeeze the brake lever firmly a few times. If the rub lessens each time and then stabilizes, the pistons were uneven — your caliper is miscentered (or the pistons need to be reset; for hydraulics see step 5).

3. Caliper recentering (the standard fix): loosen the caliper mounting bolts just enough that the caliper body can float. Squeeze and hold the brake lever firmly (or clamp the lever against the bar with a strap). While holding, retighten the caliper bolts evenly. Release the lever. Spin the wheel.
   - Rub gone or dramatically reduced → it was a miscentered caliper.
   - Rub unchanged but still localized to one rotor position → bent rotor.

4. Rotor wobble measurement: hold a Sharpie tip near (not touching) the rotor and spin. Lateral deflection under ~0.2-0.3 mm is within usable spec for most road rotors; ~0.5 mm+ is worth truing. Use a rotor truing tool (e.g., Park DT-2, Shimano TL-FB11) and bend only the high spot — small corrections, several attempts, never bend a hot rotor.

5. Hydraulic-only check (if applicable): confirm the brake lever was never pulled while the wheel was out. If it was, the pistons over-extended; the pads won't retract and you'll have constant rub plus a mushy lever. Fix: push the pistons back with a plastic tire lever or piston tool, then re-bed. If braking feels firm and lever bite is normal, skip this.

6. Pad/rotor contamination check: look at the rotor face under a light. Oil/chain lube on the rotor causes light scrape plus reduced braking. Clean with isopropyl alcohol and a lint-free wipe; if pads are contaminated (dark glossy film), replace them — contaminated pads won't recover.

DO NOT RIDE IF

- You can see a crack anywhere on the rotor, or a deep gouge at the braking surface.
- The rotor rubs harshly (not a faint tick) and braking power drops or feels gritty.
- The lever bottoms out against the bar, or you have to pump it to get pressure.
- After step 3 (recenter), the rotor still shows a clear high spot AND lateral hop you can see at arm's length — that's a rotor that needs truing or replacement before you load it under braking.
- Rotor has blue/purple heat tint, or you smell hot metal — pads have been dragging under load; stop and inspect.
- Any pulsing, vibration, or "hopping" sensation through the bars or fork during braking, even at low speed.
- A rim wobble reappears under load (loose spokes or an unseated axle masquerading as brake rub).

A faint, consistent tick once per revolution that survives the recenter step and shows no visible rotor hop is usually a slightly warped rotor that can be slowly hand-trued. Anything that matches the do-not-ride list above: fix it before you roll out of the hallway.

General first-aid guidance, not a substitute for in-person evaluation if anything below changes.

Care for the next 5-10 days:
  Clean once daily with soap and water, pat dry.
  Apply a thin layer of plain petroleum jelly or bacitracin to keep it moist.
  Cover with a non-stick pad, or better, a hydrocolloid patch cut to size. Change daily, or sooner if it lifts or gets wet.
  At 48 hours you can leave it uncovered at home if it's not oozing. Keep it covered for climbing.

The loose flap:
  Snip only what is clearly devascularized — white, shriveled, lifts with no sensation — flush, with clean fine scissors wiped with alcohol.
  Leave anything that still covers the raw wound bed or is pink and firmly adherent; that tissue is acting as a biologic dressing and will integrate or shed on its own.
  Reasoning: a flapping edge will catch on holds and re-tear; a well-attached flap protects and reduces contact pain. If in doubt, wait 24 hours and reassess — the truly loose portion announces itself.

Red flags — get evaluated:
  Spreading redness, warmth, swelling, pus, foul odor, or red streaking — infection.
  Bleeding that won't stop with 20 minutes of direct pressure.
  New numbness, tingling, or coldness in the fingertip.
  Inability to fully bend or straighten the finger.
  Deep gap with visible deeper tissue, or any nail involvement (subungual blood, nail lifting).
  Embedded grit you can't rinse free.
  Tetanus not current (booster >5 years for a dirty-wound source, >10 for clean).
  Diabetes, immunosuppression, or vascular disease affecting healing.

Return to climbing:
  Wait until fully re-epithelialized — new skin, not a wet or easily-oozing scab. Usually 5-10 days for a 6mm split.
  Quick test: press firmly on the area; no pain and nothing lifting means you're close.
  First sessions back: cover with a hydrocolloid or Tegaderm film plus one wrap of climbing tape; re-tape between attempts.
  Favor open-hand and slopers; avoid full crimps and pockets compressing the wound for at least a week past closure.
  Stop and re-cover if you see fresh bleeding, the scab lifts, or you feel a sharp catch.

One side note: distal-pad flappers are the classic bouldering overuse injury. If the surrounding callus is dry or overbuilt, a light file on the edges and a skin balm at night reduces the chance of the next one.

Order of operations, in the order I'd actually do it:

1. Full unload first.
   You already pulled the top half; clear the lower shelves too before any shimming. A partially loaded case torques when you lift a corner to slide a shim under, can rack joints, and makes the case hard to slide flush. Set books on the floor sorted by shelf position so reload order is obvious later.

2. Find studs while the case is still pulled out.
   Stud-find and mark the centerline of the nearest stud (ideally two if the case spans more than one bay — typical 16" or 24" centers). Pencil the centerline at the height the strap will sit. This is the one step that's painful after the case is in final position.

3. Level by shimming the feet, not the body.
   Goal: plumb the case in both planes, not "level to the floor" — the floor is the problem.
   - Work corner by corner. Use a short level on the case top or on a shelf, both axes.
   - Stack composite shims under the low-side foot. Pair them face-to-face alternating direction (like brickwork) so they grip and don't shoot out when you set the case down. Tap in gradually; recheck after each pair.
   - If the unit has adjustable feet, wind them up first and shim only the remaining gap. Don't shim under a fully extended adjustable foot.
   - Brace the case while lifting corners — partially shimmed cases love to slide forward or tip toward you.

4. Verify stability before reloading or strapping.
   - Push test: firm lateral pressure at the top, ~10 lb. No sway, no rock, no creak at the back joint.
   - Lift test: rock each corner; every foot must bear. A rocking corner means a floating shim.
   - Recheck plumb on both axes. Slightly out-of-plumb reads as "leaning" once loaded.
   - Push forward at the top — the case should resist from friction + shims, not just gravity.

5. Attach the anti-tip strap — high, into stud.
   - Position: as high on the case as the manufacturer allows. Tipping moment is largest at the top; mid-case is the wrong place.
   - Wall side: two screws into stud centerline. No drywall anchors for a loaded tall unit.
   - Case side: into the back rail or top rail is best. Screws into a thin back panel are acceptable only if the panel is solid (not a 3mm hardboard).
   - Snug, not tensioned. The strap prevents forward tip; the shims carry weight. They are not interchangeable.
   - Recheck plumb after tightening — the strap shouldn't pull the case out of true.

6. Reload in the right order.
   - Heaviest on the LOWER shelves, and preferentially over the low/shimmed corner of the unit. Top weight over a shimmed corner amplifies any future shim compression.
   - Avoid loading the top shelf if you can. Tall + top-heavy is the failure mode anti-tip straps exist to prevent.
   - Respect the per-shelf rating. "Not overloaded" empty can become overloaded the moment a row of oversized hardcovers goes on.
   - Re-sort: reference/heavy low, paperbacks mid, decorative/light up top.

7. Final stability check with load.
   Push test again at the top. A solid-empty case can shimmy once loaded if a shim wasn't fully seated. Walk the base and look for daylight between any foot and its shim stack.

- 1/4" slope is meaningful. If the slope runs parallel to the case, you may only shim two feet on one side — easy. If it runs the other way, all four feet need work. Confirm before you start so you know whether it's a two-corner or four-corner job.

OBSERVATIONS TO RECORD OVER THE NEXT CYCLE

Run a full cold-to-thermostat cycle deliberately. Log as you go.

- Start conditions: time, outdoor temp, thermostat setpoint, whether the radiator had been off all day or had residual warmth.
- Sound timing: seconds from when you first hear flow in the pipes to first sound; how many distinct sounds; duration of each; interval between them; total duration of the noisy period.
- Sound location: top of radiator, bottom near the valve, supply pipe entering the wall, return pipe, baseboard behind, ceiling above, or radiator body itself. Get close and put your hand on the suspected spot — feel a faint vibration confirms location.
- Sound character: knock (metallic, single, sharp), tick (lighter, single), creak (longer, lower), hiss (air/gas), rattle (loose bracket), bang (loud, deep — different from a knock).
- Heat pattern after 20-30 minutes: top vs bottom vs near-valve vs far end. Uniform = good. Cold section = air pocket (hot-water) or sludge, both building issues.
- Supply vs return pipe temps: supply should feel clearly hotter than return. Similar temp on both = no flow through that radiator.
- Cool-down: any sounds on the way down, and when they start.
- Visual: under the radiator, behind it, around the valve stem, both pipe joints, the wall behind, the floor for any damp spot. Use a flashlight and a dry paper towel pressed to suspect seams — damp shows on the towel even when the floor looks dry.
- Air and smell: any metallic, sweet (ethylene glycol), musty, or burning odor.
- Other rooms: are other apartment radiators quiet or making their own noises. Whole-building ticking on first cold cycle = normal; only yours = worth flagging.
- Was the valve position changed by anyone between cycles.

Save the notes with date and outdoor temp. Patterns across 2-3 cycles matter more than any single one.

HARMLESS EXPANSION NOISE — WHAT IT SOUNDS LIKE

What you described is consistent with normal thermal expansion and is the most common cause of first-cycle knocking in cast-iron or steel column radiators:

- Single or a few metallic ticks or pings during the first few minutes of warm-up, then silence. This is cast-iron sections and pipe joints expanding at slightly different rates.
- A short creak or low groan as the supply pipe shifts in its bracket — especially the first cold cycle of the season after a long idle.
- One or two faint "gurgle-ticks" as a small air bubble moves through (hot-water system). Persistent gurgling is not harmless.
- Tapping or clicking on cool-down as everything contracts.

These are louder in older buildings with rigid iron piping and on the first cold cycle of the heating season — both true at a 9/27 move-in. They do not predict failure on their own.

SIGNS THAT WARRANT A ROUTINE MAINTENANCE REQUEST

Report these to the building/super during business hours, no shutdown needed:

- Cold spots in the radiator after 30+ minutes of running.
- Radiator heats but room does not reach setpoint while others do.
- Valve stem weeps or shows crusty white/green residue.
- Visible rust flaking, paint bubbling, or wall discoloration behind or under the radiator.
- Repeated knocking every cycle that does not fade, especially if it sounds deep or pipe-borne rather than from the radiator body.
- Sweet smell (glycol leak) or persistent musty smell.
- Boiler cycling rapidly, never shutting off, or making new noises — that is the building's responsibility, but worth flagging.
- Any other apartment radiator leaking or not heating — suggests system-wide issue.

SIGNS THAT WARRANT IMMEDIATE SHUTDOWN AND EMERGENCY CALL

Do these without waiting:

- Active drip, flow, or puddle from the radiator, valve, pipe joint, or wall — turn the radiator's valve clockwise to close it. If it does not stop, shut the apartment supply if you have one, and call the super/emergency line now.
- Steam discharge from a radiator on what is otherwise a hot-water system (system overheating) — leave the room, call emergency.
- Loud, deep bangs or violent shaking (water hammer), especially at startup — close the valve, call immediately; sustained water hammer can rupture pipes.
- Radiator visibly shifted off its brackets or supports, or leaning — do not use it; it can fall.
- Bulge, crack, or wet rust streak on the radiator body.
- Burning smell, scorch marks, or smoke.
- Radiator full of hot water but cold to the touch on one whole side with gurgling — possible internal failure.
- On a steam system: radiator won't shut off, valve hisses continuously, whistling from the vent, or loud banging inside the unit.

PRACTICAL CAUTION

- Do not bleed the radiator, do not open the valve further, do not tighten the valve packing nut. All three are building scope and small mistakes on a pressurized system cause leaks.
- Do not set anything on top of the radiator — blocks convection and can scorch finishes.
- Do not hang laundry on it — accelerates internal rust.
- If you ever do need to close the valve in an emergency, turn clockwise gently until it stops; do not force.

Based on what you described — three sharp knocks, then quiet, even heat, dry everywhere, thermostat reached — this is most consistent with first-cycle thermal expansion on a freshly commissioned heating season. Worth one or two more observed cycles to confirm the pattern, and the damp-towel check after each. If anything in the "warrant" lists above shows up, escalate.

The "absent source returns existing explicit unknown" unit covers step 5, but not the post-delete state of the cache for the same key.

  d. Boundary fixture I'd require. Provenance timestamp exactly at the freshness limit, and provenance timestamp fresh but underlying source known to have drifted (provenance lies). CLASSIFICATION

What the 20 controlled runs support — narrowly:

1. In controlled lease transfers, new-holder cache prefetch completes warmup in 1.1–1.8 s and total transfer in 1.5–2.4 s. Both fit comfortably inside any reasonable holder-budget and are well under what the blocked 7 s timeout change would have guaranteed.

3. Prefetch is a credible alternative to the timeout reduction for the specific failure modes the timeout was intended to paper over, in the controlled regime tested.

What the 20 runs do NOT support:

- Production-wide behavior. n=20 with controlled transfers is not a fleet-level statement about shard-keeper under realistic traffic, shard distribution, or cache-state mix.
- Failure modes not exercised by the harness. Specifically: prefetch partial-failure, prefetch returning after the gate-close window, cold/evicted keys outside the prefetch set, network jitter between gate-close and later routing, concurrent transfers on adjacent shards.
- Tail behavior. n=20 cannot reject rare-event hypotheses (e.g., a 1-in-50 dual-holder window); it can only show none occurred in this sample.
- That prefetch alone removes the underlying timeout tightness. If the original 7 s proposal was driven by observed p99 pressure, controlled warmup pmax of 2.4 s does not refute that pressure — it only shows prefetch shifts the distribution.
- Any conclusion about interaction with the metrics-router cutover path (Hema's lane). Controlled transfers don't traverse it.

In short: these results support "prefetch is viable in controlled conditions as a substitute for the blocked timeout change." They do not support "prefetch is safe to ship."

NEXT EVIDENCE STEP

The relevant gap is environmental realism, not sample size. A "longer measurement run" of the same controlled kind narrows variance; it does not close the controlled→production gap. The next step needs to address at least one of: failure-mode coverage or traffic/cache-state realism.

Two bounded options, scoped for Cyrus's team to choose between:

Option A — Bounded mixed-state controlled run (cheaper, precursor):
- Same controlled harness, ~20 transfers, but with explicit injection: cold key (prefetch miss), partial prefetch (prefetch returns success but warmup incomplete at gate-close), prefetch failure (timeout / error returned to caller).

Option B — Bounded staging canary (closes more of the gap):
- Limited to one or two staging shards for a defined window (suggest 24–48 h).
- Synthetic load that traverses the actual metrics-router routing path under realistic concurrency.
- Active measurement of: gate-close ordering, dual-holder window, stale-serve rate, prefetch-success-rate vs warmup-time distribution.
- Pre-committed rollback criteria (any dual-holder; stale-serve above defined threshold; warmup p99 above defined bound) and an automatic revert path.
- Bounded by: shard scope, time window, traffic envelope, and stop conditions.

Either is bounded. A is the cheaper way to retire the failure-mode hypothesis before exposing the change to anything traffic-shaped; B is the way to retire the traffic-shape hypothesis before any prod exposure. A is a sensible prerequisite to B; B is not warranted until A passes.

Three questions, in order:

1. Is this consistent with overload?

Yes. The load math lines up: 1,500W + 750W = 2,250W, which is about 18.75A at 120V. A typical NYC bathroom circuit is 15A (1,800W capacity); even a 20A circuit (2,400W) would run near its limit, and a GFCI receptacle is thermally rated to its circuit ampacity, so it can self-trip on sustained overload before the upstream breaker does. Supporting signs that point to overload rather than a wiring or ground fault:

- Trip happened only under simultaneous high load, not under light load.
- Reset is clean, and the GFCI then holds and runs the phone charger normally.
- Outlet face, plugs, cord insulation: cool, no odor, no discoloration, no buzzing, no moisture.
- No recent water event, physical damage, or electrical work on the circuit.

So the trip reads as a thermal/capacity event, not as a fault signature. The unknowns are the actual breaker rating and whether the receptacle is on a dedicated bathroom branch or shared — worth checking the panel label, but the safe-use guidance below is the same either way.

2. What is safe to use on that circuit now?

Safe:

- Phone charger, electric toothbrush, LED bulb, exhaust fan — individually or together.
- Single high-load device used alone, briefly: hair dryer (1,500W) or space heater (750W) by itself is fine; the heater in particular is well under capacity.
- Any normal-use appliance run for a normal duration.

Not safe on this circuit:

- Both high-load devices at the same time (the trigger that just tripped it).
- Hair dryer plus anything else drawing meaningful current on the same circuit (a curling iron, another heater, a vacuum if it shares the branch).
- Daisy-chained power strips or extension cords to the receptacle.
- Any device with a warm plug, damaged cord, or intermittent behavior.

Practical rule for the bathroom: one high-draw appliance at a time, nothing else on the same circuit while it's running. If you're unsure what else is on that branch (some bathrooms share with a hallway or adjacent room), treat the dryer as the only thing running anywhere on the circuit until you know.

3. Recurrences that mean leave the circuit unused pending management or an electrician:

- GFCI trips with a single device on the circuit, even briefly (heater alone, hair dryer alone, or any appliance under ~1,000W).
- GFCI trips under light load (charger plus light, or even just the light/exhaust fan).
- GFCI trips with nothing plugged into it.
- GFCI will not reset, or resets but will not hold.
- Any trip accompanied by a warm outlet face, odor, discoloration, buzzing, crackling, scorch marks, melted plastic, or moisture in or near the box.
- A trip after any water event near the outlet, physical damage to the cover/face, or recent electrical work anywhere on the circuit.
- Repeated nuisance trips even with conservative single-device use — that suggests an undersized branch or a failing GFCI and warrants inspection regardless of load pattern.

Until the circuit's actual rating and what else shares the branch are known, the conservative operating rule above (one high-load device at a time, no stacking) is the right one. If you'd like, I can also draft a short note to your management company documenting tonight's event in plain language so there's a written record on file before any recurrence.

Closed and asymptomatic at six days is a good sign — full epithelialization typically finishes inside a week, but the new skin is still structurally immature. It won't reach normal strength for another two to three weeks, and the first week back on the wall is the most common reopening window. The progression below assumes boulder-only for now and assumes you want to keep that finger out of trouble.

Before any wall
  - Test the fingertip off the wall first — a doorframe edge, a table corner, the lip of a heavy mug. You're checking for pinpoint tenderness at the split line, any "giving way" sensation, or sharp pain on lateral pressure. If any of those fire, don't go to the wall yet.
  - Visual check: the line should be flat, dry, and pale. Not raised, puckered, shiny, or pink-red. If there's any scab, blister, or moist seam, give it another 3–5 days.

Taping — yes, protect it
  - Standard climbing finger tape (Leukotape, Metolius, or similar) cut into a thin strip placed directly over the healed line, then a light circumferential wrap to anchor it. The point is to take shear off the new skin, not to splint the joint.
  - Don't tape tight enough to feel cold or throbby. Color should look normal.
  - Re-tape between burns. Sweaty or lifted tape is worse than no tape — it peels the new skin when removed.
  - Cyanoacrylate liquid skin (New-Skin and similar) under tape is an option if the line is fully sealed. Test a small area first; on a fingertip it can crack and lift.

Session 1 — first wall day
  - Warm up off the wall thoroughly. Warm fingers are pliable; cold fingers re-split.
  - Open-hand grip only. No full or half crimp on the affected finger if you can avoid it.
  - Large positive holds. Slopers and pinches are NOT friendly here — slopers peel the skin, pinches load the pad hard. Jugs and big edges.
  - Two to three grades below your normal warm-up. Three to five easy problems. Total session 30–45 minutes.
  - Follow the stop rules below.

Sessions 2–3 — over the next week
  - Keep taping.
  - Move from open-hand jugs to open-hand on good edges, slightly smaller. Begin to allow some half-crimp on holds where the injured finger isn't the primary loader.
  - One grade below your normal flash level. Still short sessions.

Sessions 4+ — weeks 2–3
  - Drop the tape once you can half-crimp a moderate edge (around 20mm) with no sensation at the split site.
  - Reintroduce full crimp gradually. Pocket pulls last — pockets concentrate load on the distal pad and are the most common re-tear position.
  - Slopers stay risky until you've logged several clean sessions.

Avoid for the first two weeks
  - Full crimp on small or sharp holds.
  - Pockets and pinches.
  - Cold gyms or outdoor cold sessions (cold + dry = re-split).
  - Long sessions. Fatigue drives re-grip forces up.
  - Removing tape aggressively — peel slowly, parallel to the skin, in the direction of the crack line.

Stop the session immediately if any of these happen
  - Sharp or pinpoint pain at the healed line during a move.
  - Sensation of skin "lifting," peeling, or "giving way."
  - Bleeding, wetness, or visible separation.
  - New skin looking shiny, raised, or pale after a burn — that's a friction warning.
  - Pain that lingers after you come off the wall.

If any of those fire, stop, clean gently, leave the finger alone for 48 hours, then back the progression down one step on the next attempt. Two consecutive reopens means a longer pause (10–14 days off the wall for that finger) and a clinical check.

When to flag it to a clinician rather than self-manage
  - Reopens more than once.
  - Any redness, warmth, swelling, drainage, or throbbing — infection signs you want caught early even though they aren't present now.
  - Loss of sensation, or persistent tenderness away from the split line (pulp or nerve, not just skin).
  - The joint above becomes stiff, swollen, or painful — that's a different problem from the skin.

The conservative line: until you've done three or four taped sessions with no sensation at the site and can half-crimp a moderate edge without tape, treat the finger as still healing. Most climbers who re-split do it in the first week back by going one grade too hard too soon.

General guidance, not a substitute for clinical advice. Devika is the right person to ask if anything in the red-flag list above shows up.
