Your instinct to skip the supplied wood screw into apparent metal framing is the right call. A wood screw's threads strip light-gauge steel under load, and anti-tip restraint is exactly the application where that failure mode shows up: a forward tip puts the fastener in shear along the wall, which is the direction a stripped sheet-metal thread gives up first.

Confirming what you're actually hitting

A stud finder plus a magnet that clings usually means steel stud, but the magnet can also be reading a nail plate, conduit, fire-blocking, or a screw/nail in a wood stud. Before you drill anything: metal studs are typically 16" or 24" on center. Find a reference point (an outlet or switch box is usually nailed to one side of a stud), measure over, and see if the next hit lands at that interval. A second confirmed stud lets you compare readings and gives you a redundant anchor point.

Safe attachment options, in rough order of preference

1. Fine-thread self-tapping screw into the stud. Use a Type A or Type AB point, #8 or #10, with a pre-drilled clearance hole sized to the screw's root diameter rather than its outer thread — roughly 7/64" for #8, 9/64" or 1/8" for #10. Drive it through the strap, the drywall, and into the stud. For anti-tip service in 20–25 gauge steel this is the standard fix and holds well; the load is shear, which a properly seated self-tapper resists.

2. Backing cleat if the bookcase is tall or the climber risk is real (Kibo counts). Cut a piece of plywood or a steel strap, run it horizontally across two studs, fasten the cleat to each stud with multiple self-tappers, then fasten the anti-tip strap into the cleat. This spreads load and gives you redundancy if one fastener ever works loose.

3. Through-bolt to blocking if you can confirm wood blocking exists between the studs behind the drywall. Drill through the stud into the blocking and use a bolt-and-nut assembly. Strongest option, but you usually can't verify blocking without a scope or an outlet-box peek.

4. Toggle or snap-toggle bolts into the cavity. Acceptable for the strap end only if you genuinely can't land on a stud. Toggles resist pull-out well but are weaker in shear along the wall, which is the dominant force in a tip event — so don't treat them as equivalent to a stud hit.

5. What to avoid: the supplied wood screw, drywall-only anchors (no stud engagement), and any "just drive it harder" improvisation. All three fail the same way under tip loading.

When to stop and involve building management or a contractor

- The wall is a fire-rated assembly. Penetrations in rated multi-family walls often have to be sealed with intumescent caulk, and some buildings prohibit tenant penetrations altogether.
- You feel resistance while drilling that isn't the stud itself. That can mean conduit, plumbing, or a sprinkler line — push through and you've just made a much bigger problem.
- Your lease or house rules restrict wall modifications, which is common in rentals, and the restriction explicitly or practically covers metal framing.
- The bookcase is tall enough that a tip would actually hurt someone, and you aren't confident your chosen fastener will hold its rated load over time. If you have any doubt, paying a handyman for ten minutes of work is cheaper than a vet visit or a drywall repair.
- You can't find a second stud, can't confirm backing, and can't tell whether the cavity is clear.

A useful question to put to building management, in one ask: "I want to install the manufacturer's anti-tip strap on a wall my stud finder and magnet both indicate is metal framing. The strap instructions only cover wood studs and drywall anchors. Can you tell me whether the wall is fire-rated, whether there's wood blocking between the studs, and whether your rules allow tenant-installed fasteners in metal studs or require building staff to do it?" Those three answers decide everything else.

Two things worth flagging for a cat household specifically: don't plan around "top half unloaded" as a long-term state — cats will jump on the case the moment access opens, and a tall narrow case still tips from a load landing near the top. And when you check the install after a few weeks, tug the strap's wall end, not just the bookcase end — most anti-tip failures in the field are the wall fastener working loose, not the strap or the case attachment.

A 1/rev pulse under braking after a recent caliper recenter is a real signal on the front brake — do not ride it until the cause is identified. Two things are most likely given your sequence: a caliper that was visually centered but not held under load while the bolts were re-torqued, or a rotor that shifted (bolt loosen or seat slip) when you re-seated the wheel. Both are 10-minute, no-part fixes. Below is the safe order to walk down, then the threshold.

DIAGNOSTIC ORDER — stop at the first cause you find and confirm

1.  Mark and track (zero tools)
    Spin the wheel with the bike off the ground while lightly braking. When the pulse hits, stop the wheel and mark the rotor at the caliper slot with a sharpie. Spin again.
    - If the pulse happens at the same rotor position every time → cause lives on the rotor (warp, loose bolt, contamination hot spot).
    - If the pulse position wanders → cause lives in the hub / bearing / axle / caliper mount, not the rotor.

2.  Rotor bolts (Allen key, torque to maker spec)
    Loosen and re-tighten each bolt in a star pattern to the rotor manufacturer's torque (look it up on the rotor maker's page — do not guess; common ranges are 6–7 Nm for most 6-bolt systems, but it varies). This is the single highest-yield step after any wheel-out / re-seat event and the one most often missed. If the pulse tracks the mark from step 1, this is often the whole fix.

3.  Caliper re-alignment by squeeze-and-tighten (Allen key, optional zip-tie)
    - Loosen the two caliper mounting bolts just enough that the caliper body floats.
    - Squeeze and HOLD the brake lever firmly. If you don't have a helper, ratchetstrap or zip-tie the lever to the bar and leave it tied.
    - While the lever is held, tighten the caliper bolts to spec in a star pattern.
    - Release the lever. This centers the caliper under load, not by eye. A visual re-center that wasn't held under load is the most common cause of "I just centered it and now there's a pulse."

4.  Visual rotor runout check (zero tools)
    Spin the wheel slowly and watch the rotor sweep past each pad. If you can see the rotor wobble side-to-side, or a single high spot passing one pad, it's too much. Skim past a true dial indicator for this step; if you can't see anything, go to step 7 later.

5.  Free-spin with brake released (zero tools)
    Pull the caliper off the mounts (or back the pad retention so pads don't contact) and free-spin the wheel. Listen and feel for any rhythmic resistance, click, or grit indexing once per revolution.
    - Present → hub bearings (cones too tight, pitted, or dry).
    - Silent → brake-side cause, not hub. Go back to step 1–4.

6.  Hub bearing check (zero tools, then cone wrench)
    Wheel in frame, no rider weight. Grip the fork and try to rock the wheel fore-aft and side-to-side — any clunk or shift is play. Then lift the bike, spin, and grab the rim hard mid-spin — a gritty or shuddering stop means pitted cones; a long, quiet spin means bearings are OK. If bearings are suspect, overhaul before riding.

7.  Rotor measurement and truability (dial indicator or rotor truing fork)
    Only needed if steps 1–6 all pass and the pulse still tracks the rotor mark. Use a proper truing fork (Park DT-2 or equivalent) — not pliers. If measured runout is small enough to true (~0.2 mm and under) and you're practiced, true it. If it's bigger, or you can't measure, replace the rotor. Do not ride on a visibly warped rotor under front-brake duty.

8.  Pad inspection
    Look at the pad face under the pulse-marked rotor spot. A glazed/contaminated patch on the pad that lines up with the rotor high spot can mimic warp. If glazed, deglaze with fine sandpaper on a flat surface or replace.

RIDE-VS-REPAIR THRESHOLD

Do not ride (this is where you are):
- Pulse at moderate effort, low speed. On the front brake this is non-negotiable.
- Lever feel has changed (pulls farther, spongier, approaches the bar).
- New noise: grinding, ticking, metallic scrape.
- Visible rotor damage: crack, deep groove, blue or black heat discoloration, lip.
- Hub develops any play or grittiness.
- Pulse intensity increases across repeated test spins.

OK to ride (short, low-speed, no traffic, no downhills, no passengers, brakes tested before each outing):
- Cause is fully identified and fixed (bolt torqued, caliper re-aligned by squeeze-and-tighten, hub confirmed smooth).
- Re-test on the same low-speed traffic-free loop shows the pulse is gone or fully imperceptible below your normal braking effort.
- Lever feel is unchanged and the wheel free-spins quietly with no brake.

Hard rule for the front brake:
- If you have not found and fixed the cause, do not ride it in traffic. A 1/rev pulse at low speed and low effort means the same pulse at high speed and high effort, and the failure modes there are lever fade, judder, or sudden lockup — all of which on the front brake end with you going over the bars.

Most-likely actual cause in your case: I'd bet on either a rotor bolt that wasn't re-torqued after re-seating the wheel, or a caliper that was visually centered but not load-centered when the bolts went back down. Steps 2 and 3 in that order, then re-test.

Interpretation of the seven-day oversized-batch client experiment — what it supports and does not support, before owners choose the permanent disposition.

What the run supports
- Operational stability of the temporary configuration (2,000-pt client max, 1 s flush, unchanged ingest-edge admission) for this one client, against this workload, over this window.
- Point-accounting invariants held end-to-end: zero unexplained accepted/rejected discrepancy and zero duplicate request identifiers. Batch-boundary changes are exactly where dedup and partial-write bugs hide, so a clean count across the full window is a meaningful signal, not a cosmetic one.
- No new aggregate error surface: overall error rate 0.18% matches the surrounding baseline, so the temp config did not introduce a detectable error mode at the platform level during the run.
- Affected-class p99 of 0.94 s is an observed value for this client. Whether that is acceptable is a separate judgment against the latency budget the owner already has on file — the measurement itself is sound, the acceptability is not.

What the run does not support
- Generalization to a platform-wide batch policy. One client, one workload shape, 7 days, with the prior configuration as implicit control is not a basis for changing the platform default.
- Any change to ingest-edge admission behavior. The experiment explicitly held admission unchanged; the run says nothing about alternate admission policies and was not designed to.
- Behavior under conditions it did not exercise: concurrent oversized-batch clients, partition/failover, rolling deploys mid-window, the long tail past 7 days, or a workload mix materially different from this client's.
- A characterization of headroom. Stability of the listed numbers does not imply resource, queue-depth, or backpressure headroom; those weren't measured here.
- Rollback safety of the temp config as a default starting point. The configuration was put in place directly and observed in steady state; a real cutover path was not exercised.
- Treating 0.94 s as a policy ceiling. It is one observed p99 on one client, not an SLO.

Before owners choose disposition
- The data supports a "stable for this client, under this configuration, over these 7 days" finding. It does not support a "ready to ship as platform default" finding.
- Permanent disposition — revert, keep as a client-specific exception, or expand with explicit controls — is an owner call. It should require the actual owner's sign-off, not a unilateral promotion from this run.
- The temporary configuration should stay temporary until that call is made and any resulting change has gone through normal review. A single-client experiment is not an approved platform policy.

  - Stale provenance → entry deleted on read → returned UNKNOWN_STALE_SOURCE → 0 renders after stale determination. This is the 2024-10-11 ordering fix executed correctly: freshness evaluated before render eligibility, stale → invalidate + explicit unknown (not a cached value, not a render-eligible state).

Remaining exposure

The public OTLP gateway already enforces two limits — TLS termination, gzip termination, and a 4 MiB cap on the compressed request body. It does not, per the current documents, enforce any post-decompression byte limit. That leaves a classic zip-bomb shape at the ingress: a single request that fits under the 4 MiB compressed cap can decompress to a payload many orders of magnitude larger. Because the gateway terminates gzip and holds or forwards the decompressed body, both the gateway's own in-memory footprint and the size of what is forwarded to the private collector scale with the decompressed size, not with the 4 MiB input. Worst-case gateway memory and forwarder payload are therefore ratio-dependent, not bounded.

The collector-version guidance makes the gap explicit: it tells you not to lean on collector-side limits as the public-ingress control. So whatever cap exists on the private collector is not a substitute for a gateway-side bound. The private collector is reached only via the gateway's internal forward path — it is not directly internet-exposed — but it is still a reachable internal target for resource exhaustion when the gateway hands it an oversized decompressed body. None of this is evidence of exploitation; it is a residual control gap that follows from the documented boundaries.

Smallest bounded mitigation

Add one new limit at the existing termination point: a hard post-decompression byte cap on the request body, enforced at the gateway after gzip decode and before forwarding. Concretely:

- Pick a fixed upper bound on the decompressed body, on the order of tens of MiB (a small multiple of the 4 MiB compressed cap, or a value sized to realistic OTLP payloads). The exact number is a policy choice; what matters is that it is hard, not ratio-derived.
- Reject any request whose decompressed body exceeds the cap — return a 4xx (413 is the conventional fit) and do not forward a partial body.
- Apply the check at the same inspection point that already enforces the 4 MiB compressed cap, so the bound is colocated with the existing gzip termination and cannot be bypassed by a later code path.

That single additional bound converts the worst case from "ratio-dependent, effectively unbounded" to a fixed ceiling on the decompressed payload the gateway will hold, parse, or forward. It is the smallest change that produces a bounded outcome, and it satisfies the collector-version guidance because the control lives at the public ingress rather than on the collector.

Optional, only if you want a second layer beyond the hard cap: a decompression-ratio tripwire (e.g., reject when decompressed exceeds N times compressed) as a cheap early signal against mid-range bombs, applied alongside — not instead of — the hard byte cap. The hard cap is the one that actually bounds the worst case; the ratio check is purely defense in depth.

What this evidence supports

Correctness of prefetch-based lease transfer under the observed workload:
  - Ordering invariant held in every trace: old gate closed before later routing opened. No window in which two holders could simultaneously accept reads/writes.
  - Single-holder invariant held throughout: exactly one holder served for the full 24h. No dual-serve, no split-brain.
  - Freshness: no stale responses recorded across 1,200 transfers. Cache content at the new holder matched what the old holder was serving at the cutover.
  - No data-loss indicators.

Bounded warmup cost at the observed rate (~50 transfers/hour average):
  - p99 warmup 2.2s, max 3.4s; total transfer cap 4.1s.
  - 3/1,200 = 0.25% temporary 503 rate, all isolated to the warmup window. No 503s post-warmup.

So prefetch, as observed, satisfies the correctness invariants the prior timeout-reduction proposal could not, at the cost of a short warmup window with a small bounded 503 rate. That is the headline: a working structural mechanism with measurable but contained warmup cost.

What this evidence does not support

  - Behavior above the observed rate: peak bursts, simultaneous expirations, cold-start storms.
  - Behavior beyond 24h — no signal on memory growth, connection-pool drift, GC, cache decay, or interaction with deploy/restart cycles.
  - Failure modes: prefetch timeout, partial prefetch (warmup completes but cache incomplete at gate flip), downstream slowness during warmup, lease reassignment during prefetch (TOCTOU between prefetch and gate flip), prefetch service restart mid-warmup.
  - Interaction with the metrics pipeline (metrics-router / ingest-edge / shard-keeper). Prefetch changes lease-handoff timing the metrics path depends on; this run did not surface that signal.
  - Multi-holder or cross-region transfer paths, if applicable.
  - The 0.25% 503 rate is bounded, but the variance is unknown — 3 in a day is fine, 30 in an hour would not be.

Gap to flag: 24h is half the 48h obs-clean bar that has been standing precedent for structural rollup-class changes. Not disqualifying on its own, but worth acknowledging in the release-review.

Safeguards needed for a guarded rollout (data platform team owns, no ownership change)

These have to be enforceable from outside the data platform team's change boundary:

  1. Ordering guard: per-transfer trace assertion that old-gate-closed precedes later-routing-opened. Page on any violation or any gap narrower than expected.
  2. Single-holder guard: assertion that exactly one holder serves at every instant across the transfer window. Page on any two-holder window.
  3. Freshness guard: no-stale-response carried into production as a release gate, not just an observation. Same shape as the Lantern freshness-before-render rule.
  4. Warmup-latency SLO with bounded 503 budget: p99 ≤ ~2.5s, warmup-window 503 rate ≤ 0.5%, hard ceiling on warmup max. Auto-trip on breach.
  5. Automatic fallback: if warmup exceeds threshold or 503 rate exceeds budget, fall back to the old path without requiring data-platform intervention.
  6. Independent rollback path: revert must be executable by the depending team, not gated on the data platform team's deploy pipeline.
  7. Canary / staged rollout: start at a low % of transfers, ramp only on metric gates passing. No all-at-once flip.
  8. Structural-rollup treatment in the release-review: cache state crosses the holder boundary, so the structural rule applies by analogy — snapshot fully loaded + in-window partitions == in-scope; partial via logs/metrics/retry/secondary-writes is still partial. Commit-time guard alone is insufficient.
  9. Owner-map clarity in the release-review record: data platform owner of the prefetch change named, depending-team rollback contact named, no blank fields.

Remaining evidence needed before authorization

  1. Multi-day observation at the same traffic level — minimum 7d, ideally 14d — to clear the 48h bar. Capture memory/connection/GC signals, not just latency and 503 rate.
  2. Peak/burst characterization: explicit test of simultaneous lease expirations (cold-start storm), not just average-rate transfers.
  3. Failure-mode tests covering: prefetch timeout, partial prefetch, lease reassignment during prefetch, prefetch service restart mid-warmup.
  4. Metrics-pipeline interaction: confirm metrics-router / ingest-edge / shard-keeper timing is unaffected by the lease-handoff change. This is your scope.
  5. Sustained 503 budget across the longer window — current 0.25% over 24h must hold over 7–14d including peak hours.
  6. Explicit confirmation that prefetch is not a covert re-introduction of the unsupported timeout-reduction mechanism — enumerate the failure modes the original proposal carried and show they do not apply to prefetch.

Once (1)–(3) and (6) are in hand and (4) is signed off by the metrics-pipeline owner, the guarded rollout under safeguards (1)–(9) is supportable without changing service ownership. The structural framing matters here: prefetch moves lease-handoff state across a holder boundary, so it should clear the same bar as other structural rollups, not the lighter bar for in-place behavior changes.

Conservative home plan for Kibo after this morning's single grass-vomit episode

Context: the episode looked benign — grass plus a small amount of breakfast, no blood, alert, drinking, soft non-tender abdomen, no other signs. Treat the next 24-48 hours as a watch window. If anything below trips, contact the vet. Most items below are same-day calls; the urgent list is ER-now.

WATER
- Next 2-4 hours: ice cubes or ~1-2 tbsp of room-temp water at a time, every 15-30 min. No full bowl, no gulping.
- If he holds water without vomiting, gradually increase volume over the rest of the day back toward normal.
- If he vomits water back: fast 1-2 hours, restart with ice chips only. Vomiting water a second time = vet call.

FEEDING
- Hold food for 6-12 hours if he is settled and drinking OK. (Skip the hold if he is clearly hungry after several hours — a small bland meal is fine.)
- Bland reintroduction: boiled skinless chicken or lean ground turkey (no skin, fat, or seasoning) plus plain white rice or plain cooked sweet potato. Roughly 70% carb / 30% protein.
- First meal: a few tablespoon-sized portions scaled to his size. Wait 30-60 min. If no vomiting, offer a little more.
- Day 1: 3-4 small bland meals.
- Day 2: 2-3 larger bland meals if stools and energy look normal.
- Day 3: mix his regular food back in (25/75, then 50/50, then 75/25 bland-to-regular across meals).
- Skip: treats, table scraps, fatty food, dairy, sudden new foods, rich chews.

MONITORING (next 24-48 hours)
- Energy and engagement vs his baseline. Mildly quiet is fine; withdrawn or hiding is not.
- Appetite returning within 12-24 hours.
- Gums: pink and moist. Lift a lip to check.
- Stool: formed, no blood, no mucus, no black or tarry appearance. Soft stool for a day is acceptable.
- Abdomen: soft and non-tender. He should let you touch it without flinching.
- Watch for repeat grass-eating — some dogs cycle into it. Interrupt calmly and redirect to a walk or an appropriate chew.

SAME-DAY VET SIGNS (call your regular clinic)
- A second vomiting episode.
- Diarrhea, especially more than once, or with blood or mucus.
- Appetite still off past 24 hours.
- Energy still low past 24 hours.
- Mild abdominal tenderness or a posture change.
- Repeated or compulsive grass-eating.

URGENT / ER-NOW SIGNS
- Repeated vomiting (2+ episodes) or vomiting that will not stop.
- Blood in the vomit, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds (dark brown, granular).
- Bloody stool, black tarry stool, or persistent diarrhea.
- Hard, distended, or painful abdomen, or "praying position" (front down, rear up, belly stretched) — possible bloat or GDV; time-critical in deep-chested dogs.
- Repeated retching or dry heaving with nothing coming up — possible obstruction.
- Severe lethargy, collapse, weakness, or inability to stand.
- Pale, white, yellow, or tacky/dry gums.
- Resting breathing rate above ~40/min, labored breathing, blue or purple gums or tongue.
- Restlessness, pacing, inability to settle — pain or bloat until proven otherwise.
- Trembling or shaking that is not cold-related.
- No urine for 12+ hours, or straining to urinate.
- Temperature above ~103.5°F or below ~99°F (if you can take it rectally).
- Any reason to suspect the grass was treated (fertilizer, pesticide, mushrooms, cocoa mulch) — bring the package if you have it.
- Known or suspected ingestion of a foreign object, bone, toy piece, sock, toxic food, etc.

Practical notes
- Grass eating itself is common and usually not the cause of illness. The pattern is what matters — a repeat of this morning's picture, even without escalation, is worth a vet visit.
- If a second episode happens, expect the vet to want an exam plus bloodwork, and imaging if symptoms continue.
- Trust your read of him. If something feels off even if it isn't on a list, call. A "false alarm" is always better than a missed bloat or obstruction.

Yes — leave it unused. Do not mount it, do not load it, and do not try to "test" the clamp. Don't attempt any repair (JB Weld, epoxy, etc.) — unsafe on a structural load-bearing clamp and it voids the defect claim.

Why, even though 14.2 lb is well under the 22 lb rating:

- Cast-metal clamp bodies (usually aluminum or zinc die-cast) are notch-sensitive. A crack is a stress concentrator that grows under the cyclic load of arm adjustments, desk bumps, and the clamp bolt's own preload.
- The crack is in the anchorage, not the arm. Failure here drops the arm and the monitor.
- You can't NDT it at home. A surface hairline can be deeper, or it can be the visible tip of a subsurface crack.
- Rated capacity assumes defect-free material. Using a part you know is cracked shifts liability to you if it fails.

Evidence to include in the return request:

1. Photos you already have: crack, model label, serial number, packaging.
2. Add:
   - Crack photo with a ruler in frame showing the ~18 mm length. Scale beats any written description.

Here's a bounded checklist that produces evidence without modifying the wall or the seal joint.

What makes the evidence useful: same points, same meter, same time-of-day, time-stamped photos, and a log that correlates interior readings with what the exterior is actually doing. The point is to let you and any contractor see whether the elevated reading moves with rain — and if so, with rain from which direction.


BEFORE THE NEXT RAIN (do once)

  1. Photograph the current state, all date-stamped:
     - Interior: the painter's-tape outline and the lower-left window return
       (try to include the meter reading in the shot)
     - Exterior: the seal-joint gap from the same angle the inspector used
  2. Record baseline meter readings at fixed points:
     - The elevated spot at the window return
     - The same unaffected control area the inspector used
     - Two or three other reference points (upper corners, opposite wall)
     Note indoor temp and outdoor temp if you have them.
  3. Set up a one-page log with columns:
     Time | Interior visual | Meter at window return | Meter at control |
     Outdoor conditions | Wind direction | Notes
  4. Watch the forecast. A sustained rain or a wind-driven rain hitting the
     affected facade is far more informative than a light drizzle on the
     other side of the building — note start time and direction.


DURING THE RAIN (only when rain is hitting the affected facade)

  1. Readings at 30–60 minute intervals at the same fixed points.
  2. Photograph the meter at the window return each time — same angle,
     same lighting — so the number on screen is visible.
  3. Note any new visual change: darkening, sheen, drip, expanding stain.
  4. From the window (do not lean out, no ladder), observe whether rain is
     visibly entering the gap and from which direction the wind is driving
     it. Log wind direction each reading.
  5. If the rain isn't reaching that facade, skip and wait for a better
     event — don't manufacture observations.


WITHIN 24–48 HOURS AFTER THE RAIN

  1. Repeat meter readings at the same fixed points.
  2. Repeat interior photos at the same angles.
  3. Note the drying pattern: does the elevated reading drop back, hold,
     or climb relative to baseline?
  4. Re-photograph the exterior gap — same angle — and compare to the
     before-rain shot (opening wider? debris displacement? new staining
     on surrounding trim?).
  5. Send management the log plus paired before/after photos, with a
     specific ask: an assessment date from the exterior contractor, or
     escalation if the data point toward this gap being the source.


URGENT MANAGEMENT ESCALATION — contact management immediately if ANY of
these appear, regardless of whether a contractor date has been set:

  - Active dripping, pooling, or running water inside
  - Moisture, staining, or elevated meter readings near any electrical
    fixture, outlet, switch, or wiring
  - Plaster or drywall becoming soft, spongy, bubbling, or deforming
  - Wet area expanding beyond the current painter's-tape outline
  - Musty odor developing, or visible mold/discoloration appearing
  - Water reaching the floor, baseboards, or spreading to another room
  - Meter readings at the window return spiking well above baseline
    during or immediately after rain

The first two and the last one are the most time-sensitive — they
change the building's risk profile before the contractor appointment
matters.

This is a client-interpretation problem, not accounting loss.

Why it is not accounting loss

  - Sphere's counters reconcile exactly: accepted (11,760) + rejected (240) = attempted (12,000). Every point the client submitted is accounted for on the server side.
  - There are no duplicate request identifiers and no retries, so no double-counting or replay that could inflate or deflate either side.
  - The rejection reason is "invalid attributes" — a client-side schema issue, not a server drop. The 240 points were refused at ingestion because they failed validation, not because they were lost in transit.

The OTLP partial-success contract

  OTLP defines an ExportPartialSuccess response that carries:
    - rejected: the count of items the server refused (here, 240; the field is rejected_data_points for metrics, rejected_spans / rejected_log_records for the other signals)
    - error_message: human-readable reason (here, invalid attributes)
  The accepted count is NOT a separate field. The client is expected to derive it:
    accepted = attempted - rejected
  So 12,000 attempted, 240 rejected, and 11,760 accepted is the canonical reading of this response — the three numbers are consistent, they just have to be drawn from two places (the client's submit counter and the server's rejected counter) and combined correctly.

How the client should represent the three counts

  The dashboard should track three separate counters, not one:

    Attempted:  12,000  — points the SDK submitted in the batch
    Accepted:   11,760  — derived from the partial-success response
                              (attempted minus rejected)
    Rejected:     240   — read from partial_success.rejected_data_points

  The current bug is conflating "attempted to send" with "successfully accepted." A single "sent" counter treats rejected and accepted points the same, which is wrong against the OTLP contract — partial success explicitly means some points were not accepted by the server.

Operational follow-up

  - Surface partial_success.error_message (and any per-item rejection details if the exporter exposes them) so the invalid attributes can be fixed upstream. That is the actual cause of the 240-point gap; fixing it removes the gap permanently.
  - Until the attribute issue is fixed, the three counters will continue to sum to 12,000 with a stable 2% rejection rate, which is the expected shape of a partial-success stream, not a leak.

Run it over two sessions. Session A as soon as practical (today or tomorrow, fully rested). Session B Saturday or ~60-90 min before Sunday kickoff. Each step must be clean before progressing to the next.

Session A — push the ceiling:

  1.  5-10 min easy cycle or brisk walk warm-up.
  2.  Slow single-leg calf raises ×25 each side (you've cleared 10; 25 at slow tempo is the next gate).
  3.  Fast single-leg calf raises ×25 each side, full height, controlled descent.
  4.  Double-leg pogo hops ×20.
  5.  Single-leg hops in place ×10 each side — note symmetry.
  6.  Forward bounds (single-leg landings) ×5 each leg.
  7.  Lateral bound-and-stick (single-leg landing, side-to-side) ×5 each direction.
  8.  30 m easy jog ×4, 90 s rest.
  9.  30 m stride (~75%) ×4, full rest.
  10. 30 m near-sprint (~95%) ×4, full recovery.
  11. Reactive 5-10-5 shuttle (acceleration + deceleration + change of direction).
  12. 10 repeated maximal vertical jumps or small box drops.
  13. 5 min easy cool-down spin or walk.

Session B — confirm reproducibility:

  Repeat steps 4-12 under the same conditions. Compare right vs left on every test.

DECISION CRITERIA

Full play (normal):

  - All steps clean across both sessions.
  - Zero pain, tightness, cramping, heaviness, or power loss on the right.
  - Performance within ~10% of left on every test.
  - Right calf feels the same as left 2 h after Session A and again the next morning.
  - No swelling, warmth, color change, or focal tenderness at any point.

Modify (limited minutes / reduced role):

  - Mild tightness or "awareness" that doesn't worsen through the test and resolves with brief rest.
  - Asymmetry 10-20%.
  - Hold yourself under ~70% intensity, avoid max sprints and hard right-footed cuts/pivots, sub out at the first right-calf sensation. Skip headers if jumping reproduced tightness.

Stop — do not play Sunday:

  - Any pain during the test (sharp, grabbing, cramping, or "something is wrong").
  - Tightness that builds across reps or doesn't fully resolve within 2-3 min rest.
  - Calf cramping, sudden loss of push-off power, or a guarded gait at any point.
  - Performance drop >20% vs left on any test.
  - Any swelling, warmth, or color change in the right calf during or after the test.
  - Next-morning symptoms after Session A that localize to the right calf. General DOMS is normal; calf-specific soreness at 24-48 h is a signal, not noise.

Seek medical evaluation before playing — these are not graded-return questions:

  - Unilateral right-calf swelling, warmth, or redness.
  - Pain reproduced by dorsiflexion (toes pulled up) or any palpable deep tenderness.
  - Cramping that doesn't fit a strain pattern, or heaviness that worsens with standing.
  - Any symptom that recurs or worsens across the two sessions instead of improving.

A note on the original event: two weeks of unilateral tightness that has not progressed is reassuring, but a one-time unilateral calf complaint always warrants keeping DVT in the differential in the back of your mind. The bar for raising it to Devika is low — localized swelling, warmth, color change, or pain with dorsiflexion. Don't sit on those to "see if it passes."

Practical sequencing. Run Session A today or tomorrow. If anything reads amber or red, do not play Sunday: the Devika afternoon is the higher-stakes commitment, and being sore or hurt for it costs more than one missed pickup. If Session A is fully green, use Session B as the Sunday pre-kickoff warm-up and apply the same criteria in real time on the field.

Why the pattern points at microwave leakage, not the line:
  Consumer microwaves run near 2.45 GHz, dead-center in the 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi
  band. When the door seal or magnetron lets RF leak, the radio in the work
  room sees its signal crushed under the noise while 5 GHz (far from 2.45 GHz)
  and wired Ethernet (no radio at all) are untouched. The modem and ISP path
  are fine, which matches what your provider page shows. The collapse-and-
  recover timing while the microwave is actually running is the giveaway.

Low-effort verification, using only what is already in the apartment:

  1. Start a continuous ping from the work laptop to the router's gateway
     (commonly 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1; the address is on the router
     sticker). macOS / Linux: ping 192.168.1.1. Windows PowerShell:
     ping -t 192.168.1.1. Leave it running.
  2. Have someone run the microwave for 30 to 60 seconds.
  3. On 2.4 GHz you should see sharp latency spikes and "request timed out"
     lines that stop the moment the microwave stops. Repeat on 5 GHz or
     wired and the ping stays flat. That contrast is the concrete proof,
     and you do not need any new gear to capture it.
  4. Optionally confirm what the laptop is actually attached to:
       macOS: hold Option and click the Wi-Fi icon (shows band, channel,
             RSSI, noise).
       Windows: netsh wlan show interfaces in PowerShell (shows Radio
             type: 802.11n/ac and channel).
       Linux: iw dev wlan0 link (shows freq and channel).
     If the laptop is on 2.4 GHz while the microwave runs, the band reading
     itself is part of the verification.

Choosing the stable setup without moving the modem or buying anything yet:

  First choice - move the work laptop to 5 GHz for daily use. You already
  noted 5 GHz is stable, so the signal reaches the work room. Two ways
  without new hardware:
    - If the router exposes separate SSIDs (often named like "Home" and
      "Home_5G", or "Home" and "Home_5GHz"), connect the laptop to the
      5 GHz one and leave it there.
    - If both bands share one SSID, log into the router (typically
      http://192.168.1.1, credentials on the sticker) and either enable
      band steering / "prefer 5 GHz", or split the SSIDs so you can pick
      the 5 GHz one explicitly. This is a setting change, not equipment.

  Second choice - wired Ethernet to the work room, only if you already
  have a cable that reaches. A flat Ethernet cable run along a baseboard
  or under a rug is sufficient. Use it as the fallback for video calls or
  large transfers. If no cable is already on hand, defer buying one until
  you have confirmed 5 GHz alone is not workable for the work room.

  Small, free follow-up - if 2.4 GHz still matters for something else
  (older devices, a far corner of the apartment), log into the router and
  change the 2.4 GHz channel. Channel 1 sits furthest from the 2.45 GHz
  microwave center, so it usually survives a bit better than channels 6
  or 11. This rarely fixes the issue outright but can shrink the blast
  radius for other devices.

Things to defer until the pattern is actually reproduced and confirmed:

  - Buying a new router, access point, mesh node, or powerline adapter.
  - Moving the modem or router.
  - Contacting the ISP or building (the line is fine; this is local RF
    in your apartment).
  - Replacing the microwave (worth considering only if the leak is
    strong enough to bother other electronics or people, but unrelated
    to getting the laptop online today).

Short version: the symptom pattern is the verification. Put the work laptop
on 5 GHz (or wired if a cable is already within reach) and you have a
stable path without buying or relocating anything. Only escalate to a
new channel, new cable, or new hardware after that, if anything still
bothers you.

The safer ordinary option is to **spoil the ballot and take a clean replacement**. That's the standard New York path (Election Law § 9-112): the poll worker voids your current ballot, marks it spoiled, and you get a fresh one to mark and feed through the scanner. You're allowed up to two replacements, so you still have room if a second ballot also trips the scanner. The "emergency-ballot" / affidavit envelope path is a provisional ballot — it gets sealed with your identity, set aside for the board of elections to review later, and is meaningfully more likely to be rejected for procedural reasons and not counted. Take the replacement unless a poll worker gives you a concrete, specific reason it won't work at your site.

For the actual marking, the things that most often trigger an "ambiguous mark" warning on the optical scanner are: ovals not filled completely (you should see solid ink with no white inside the oval), stray marks or stray pen strokes anywhere on the ballot, marks that cross into another contest's area, and using anything other than the provided pen. A slow, deliberate fill of each oval is usually enough.

On ballot secrecy while asking for help:

- The ballot itself is anonymous — nothing on it links it back to you. Poll workers are prohibited from observing how you vote, and they know that.
- Keep the ballot covered or face-down on the table when you're not actively marking it. Don't unfold it in a way that exposes selections to anyone behind you.
- When you ask the poll worker for help, ask **procedural** questions, not content ones. Good ones: "Can you show me on a sample ballot how dark the ovals need to be?" "Is there a pen here I should use?" "The scanner rejected mine twice — is there a known issue with the marking today?" All of those are about the machine and the process, not your choices.
- If a poll worker starts to look at your ballot to "see what went wrong," stop them and ask them to look at a sample ballot instead. They can demo on the posted specimen.
- If you need physical assistance marking for any reason, New York lets you name a person of your choice (other than your employer or union rep) to help — but that only applies if you genuinely need help; for a mechanical question, the poll worker answers at the table without seeing your marks.

One practical sequencing tip: before you leave the table with the replacement, ask the poll worker to point you to a good spot with a flat surface and good lighting so the second pass goes through cleanly the first time.

So with the cap in place, oversized batches do not appear to be silently double-admitted, dropped, or misclassified as a side effect of the cap.
- The cap is functioning as a clean admission boundary, not as a hidden retry trigger. If oversized batches were being rejected and retried aggressively, you would expect retry storms or duplicate-id pressure; neither appeared.

What the queue event supports (and what it does not)

- Client 3's 11-minute interval at 82% local send-queue utilization absorbed the burst, drained on its own, dropped zero points, and produced no retry storm. That is consistent with queue behavior that is pressured but not breached for this client, this workload shape, and this cap.
- The same interval is the most plausible explanation for client 3's higher p99 (1.02s vs 0.91 / 0.95). Tail-latency elevation tracks queue pressure, even at "only" 82% — so 82% is not a free zone; it is a zone where p99 is already visibly affected but the system still self-recovers.
- It does not support generalizing "82% is safe under all conditions." This is a 3-client run with one observed burst on one client. It does not test what 88%, 92%, or 95% looks like, it does not test concurrent bursts across clients, and it does not test burst duration beyond ~11 minutes.

Bounded permanent-policy choices still requiring owner review

1. The per-batch point maximum itself. The evidence supports "2,000 is operable for these three clients over 14 days." It does not support picking any specific permanent number — 2,000, a higher number, or a tenant-class-tiered number. The choice of permanent cap is a policy call, not something this run settles.

2. Whether the cap stays as a hard reject, becomes an admit-and-queue, or becomes admit-with-defer. The run measured only the hard-reject path; the alternative admission shapes are not evidenced here.

3. Queue-utilization thresholds for alerting and shedding. 82% self-recovered in this run; the run does not bound the threshold at which self-recovery stops. Owner-owned: where to alarm, where to shed, what to publish externally versus keep internal.

4. Scope of the cap. Per-client (current) versus per-tenant-class versus aggregate. Three clients is too narrow to justify an aggregate-shaped policy; it is also too narrow to justify removing per-client protection.

5. Whether the 14-day window is sufficient to convert any of the above into permanent policy, or whether a longer internal shadow (or staged external shadow) is required first. The evidence does not answer this; it only constrains the answer.

6. What is publishable to clients and what stays internal. Per your standing rule, queue-internal signals do not surface as customer-facing load signals; that still applies and is not altered by this run.

Items (1) through (4) are the policy calls. Item (5) is the gating decision on whether (1)–(4) can be made yet. Item (6) is a constraint on how the answer is communicated, not on what the answer is. **Blocking — `go-otlp-client#88`: OTLP partial-success not handled; delivered counter overcounts rejected points.**

The current completion logic treats HTTP 200 as full success and increments `metrics.delivered` by the full batch size:

```
if response.status == 200 {
    metrics.delivered += batch.len();
    return nil
}
```

This is incorrect against the OTLP exporter contract. OTLP returns 200 OK on **partial** accepts; rejected points are surfaced in `ExportMetricsPartialSuccess.rejected_data_points`, not via HTTP status. The attached replay confirms the failure mode:

- Attempted: 12,000
- Accepted: 11,760
- `partial_success.rejected_data_points`: 240 (reason: invalid attributes)
- Client-reported delivered: **12,000** ← wrong by 240, i.e. 2% overcount

Required before this can merge:

1. **Inspect `partial_success` on every 200 response.** Do not return `nil` purely on HTTP status; check `rejected_data_points` (and the analogous fields on logs/traces partial-success responses).
2. **Account for the three counts separately.** Maintain distinct counters for attempted, accepted, and rejected data points — do not collapse them into a single `delivered`.
3. **Never attribute rejected points to delivered.** Only the accepted subset increments delivered; rejected points increment a separate rejection counter (tagged by the partial-success reason string) and must surface in logs/metrics so they are visible to operators, not silently absorbed.
4. **Treat `error` responses separately.** A non-2xx (or a partial-success with no accepted points) should not advance the batch as delivered; retry semantics belong in the retry layer, not silently flattened into delivered counts.

Silent overcount on a metrics client is a load-bearing failure: it corrupts delivered-rate SLOs, masks ingest drops at the server, and breaks any downstream billing/usage model that trusts `delivered`. This needs to be fixed before cutover.

VERDICT: Drop the `unless`. It collapses two independent failure modes into one and silently kills the rollup backlog signal under exactly the conditions where you most need it. Treat upstream health as context (separate alert + runbook cross-reference), not as a suppression condition.

WHY IT'S BROKEN

1. Independent failure modes, conflated. A rollup backlog is structurally actionable — per the rollup STRUCTURAL rule (snapshot fully loaded + in-window partitions in scope; commit-tx guard insufficient), partition drift degrades data correctness regardless of metrics-router's health. A metrics-router scrape outage is a separate, infra-owned problem. Coupling them via `unless` means one failure hides the other.

2. The PromQL doesn't do what the annotation claims. `unless` is a vector set operation, not a causal guard. `A unless B` keeps LHS series whose `on(...)`-projected label set has no match in RHS. With `on()` empty here, both sides project to the empty label set, so every LHS series is matched against every RHS series. Concretely: if `up{job="metrics-router"} == 0` is true for ANY instance, the entire rollup backlog alert is suppressed globally — not "suppress when this scrape is missing," but "silence the whole backlog view whenever metrics-router has a single down target." That's the opposite of the stated intent.

3. Worst-case is the failure mode the alert creates. Metrics-router down + rollup drift happening at the same time → zero signal on the drift, because the `up==0` series from the down instance suppresses everything. That's also the exact moment a structural backlog is most likely to develop (no ingest signal reaching rollup), and it's the moment this alert goes quiet.

SAFER FORMULATIONS

Option A (preferred — two alerts, clean ownership):
  - Data platform owns:
        max_over_time(rollup_queue_age_seconds[5m]) > 300
    annotation: "Rollup queue age >5m. If co-firing with Infra's metrics-router availability alert, treat backlog as possibly stale — but do not assume upstream is the cause. Page data platform."
  - Infra owns (already exists):
        up{job="metrics-router"} == 0
    annotation: "If data-platform's rollup-queue-backlog alert is also firing, investigate ingest path before assuming queue depth is the root cause."

Option B (single expression, no suppression):
  - Drop the `unless` entirely:
        max_over_time(rollup_queue_age_seconds[5m]) > 300
  - Handle the stale-scrape concern in the runbook, not in the query: "if upstream scrape issues are suspected, cross-check Infra's metrics-router availability alert before paging on a fresh backlog reading." The staleness window is bounded by the scrape interval — that is precisely what the separate `up==0` alert is for.

Option C (single expression, staleness gate owned by rollup-service):
  - Replace `unless` with `and` against a staleness predicate drawn from rollup-service's own metric space, e.g.:
        max_over_time(rollup_queue_age_seconds[5m]) > 300
        and on() rate(rollup_queue_age_seconds[1m]) > -1
  - Suppression now means "rollup isn't reporting," not "upstream infra is down." Keep the predicate inside rollup-service's own emit heartbeat; do not lean on `up` to decide rollup's alertability.

OWNERSHIP

In all three options, data platform stays the owner of the rollup backlog alert. Infra continues to own the metrics-router `up` signal and any derivative alerts; the only Infra-side ask is that the existing `up==0` runbook cross-reference the rollup backlog alert so on-call doesn't have to chase the link themselves. Recommend Option A to Cyrus; it is the only one where the two failure modes are independently visible and independently paged.

When the structural-rollup work surfaced partial-snapshot paths the commit-time guard didn't catch, his team owned the rollback of the compaction-worker flag rather than routing around it — the correct read of where the blast radius actually sat. On the shard-keeper 503 guard, he paused rollout at the moment the guard fired instead of papering over it with a config tweak, which kept the cutover honest about what was actually verified. Pushing for a narrow Infra boundary check rather than shifting incident ownership was the right call too — kept the response scoped to the service that owned the behavior.

Likely cause first: localized hot-only pressure loss right after building plumbing work is almost always sediment or debris dislodged during the work and lodged in either the under-sink hot shut-off valve, the spout aerator, or (on a single-handle faucet) the cartridge's hot inlet. Bathroom fixtures are unaffected because they sit on separate branches and were not in use during the work, or their own screens were already clear.

Diagnostic sequence (no supply-line disconnection):

1. Verify and exercise the under-sink hot shut-off.
   - The hot-side stop is on the left supply line under the cabinet.
   - Turn the oval handle or stem slot fully counterclockwise until it stops. If it was partly closed, full flow may return immediately.
   - Cycle gently closed -> open -> closed -> open a few times to flush debris from the valve seat. Slow and even - do not force.
   - Run the kitchen faucet full-hot for 30 seconds, then back to off. Recheck pressure.

2. Remove and clean the spout aerator.
   - The aerator is the small threaded insert at the very tip of the spout.
   - Unscrew by hand, or with pliers wrapped in a cloth/rag to avoid scratching the finish. It unthreads counterclockwise as viewed from the spout end.
   - Take it apart: housing, screen, and sometimes a flow-restrictor disc. Rinse each piece under the cold tap and pick out any grit.
   - Run the kitchen hot side without the aerator for ~15 seconds into a bucket or bowl. If grit streams out, let it finish flushing. Cold side is fine, so a shared aerator is unlikely to be the sole cause - but cleaning it rules it out and improves the post-restoration flow.
   - Reassemble and retest.

3. Flush the faucet through full travel.
   - Sweep the handle fully cold -> hot -> cold several times, then leave fully open on hot for 2 minutes. This can clear loose debris in the cartridge's hot inlet without any disassembly.
   - Repeat the cold/hot sweep 2-3 more times over the next 30 minutes, since debris can re-lodge as flow settles.

4. Only if 1-3 fail and you know the faucet brand/model: shut the under-sink hot stop off (clockwise to snug, do not force), open the kitchen faucet to relieve line pressure, then remove the handle and cartridge per the brand's instructions and rinse grit from the inlet ports. Re-seat. This is closing a stop, not disconnecting supply lines - but only attempt it if you have the right tool and confidence. Otherwise this step belongs to maintenance.

Stop and contact management when any of the following is true:

- Steps 1-3 do not restore normal hot pressure after a few minutes of flushing.
- A new symptom appears during any step: dripping at the shut-off, moisture in the cabinet, water hammer, discolored water, or any drop in hot pressure at the bathroom sink or shower.
- The under-sink shut-off will not turn, leaks when moved, or is corroded/immobile. Do not force it.
- You are not comfortable with step 4, or the faucet brand/model is unknown.
- Building plumbing work was done today and has not been logged by management regardless of outcome - other units may be affected, and the cause may sit on the building side (riser strainer, recirculation balancing, partially closed manifold). A single-unit hot-only loss immediately after building work is a reasonable basis for a same-day maintenance request rather than waiting to see if it resolves.

If hot pressure drops at other fixtures overnight, escalate as a building-wide event rather than a kitchen-local one.

10:05 AM → 10:45 AM (setup before sleep)

  Light: dim now. No screens if avoidable. Bedroom fully darkened — curtains drawn plus a towel under the door if light leaks in.
  Temperature: cooler is better, aim 65–68°F if you can swing it.

10:45 AM → 3:30 PM (the 5-hour block)

Yes — wet-only squeal on a disc brake, especially on a freshly installed rotor, is normal behavior and not a safety concern in itself. Here is why it happened, the sequence to run before the next ride, and the signs that mean you should stop.

WHY WET-ONLY SQUEAL HAPPENS

A thin film of water on the rotor lowers local friction just enough to let the pads micro-slip and re-grip, which excites a resonant frequency in the pad/rotor/caliper system. The result is a high-pitched squeal that lasts until the water is wiped off by braking heat and pad contact. Two things in your case make it more likely rather than less:

  - The rotor is new. Fresh rotors have not yet transferred a uniform pad layer onto the braking surface, so the friction interface is less stable until bedding is complete.
  - Light rain plus a short ride means the rotor did not get hot enough, or stay hot long enough, to dry during braking — so you heard it on the first stops only.

The indicators you listed — firm lever, straight stopping, no pulse, no scraping, no discoloration, no debris — all confirm the brake is mechanically sound. The noise is environmental, not a fault.

CLEANING AND TEST SEQUENCE BEFORE THE NEXT RIDE

Do these in order. Each step has a purpose.

  1. Remove the front wheel. Lay the bike so the caliper opening faces up or cover it; do not squeeze the lever with no rotor in place — pistons can over-extend.
  2. Clean the rotor with 90% or higher isopropyl alcohol or a dedicated bicycle brake cleaner. Spray onto a clean lint-free cloth, then wipe the rotor — do not spray directly into the caliper.
  3. Use a fresh section of cloth for each pass. Reusing a contaminated cloth is the single most common way to re-contaminate a clean rotor.
  4. Inspect the rotor for: the minimum thickness marking (stamped near the spider), deep circumferential grooves, scoring, blueing, or cracks. A light grey sheen is normal bedding transfer; a dark patchy layer is not.
  5. Inspect the pads if visible: minimum material thickness, even wear front-to-rear and inner-to-outer, no oily film, no embedded metal. If anything looks off, replace the pads — cleaning a contaminated pad is unreliable.
  6. Refit the wheel and confirm the rotor sits cleanly between the pads with no rub when you spin it.
  7. Before riding, pump the lever a few times at standstill to re-seat the pads.

RIDE TEST

Pick a flat, low-traffic area. Walk the bike first to listen for rub. Then progressive stops:

  - Walking pace, light front brake only. Confirm firm lever, no rub.
  - 10 to 12 km/h, moderate front brake. Confirm straight stop.
  - 20 to 25 km/h, firm front brake. Confirm straight, no pulse, full lever reserve, predictable.
  - Repeat one or two harder stops to continue bedding if the rotor is still new — progressively harder stops across 20 to 30 total stops is the standard bedding routine.

If everything feels normal, the rotor should be bedded and dry-condition squeal should not recur. Wet-condition squeal may still happen in future rain; that is expected and benign if the criteria below stay clean.

SIGNS THAT MEAN STOP RIDING

  - Squeal continues after the rotor dries — pad contamination or glazing.
  - Lever becomes spongy, sinks to the bar, or loses firmness under load — air in the hydraulic line, leak, or severely worn pads.
  - Stopping pulls to one side — uneven pad wear, contaminated pad, or caliper misalignment.
  - Pulsing through the lever under braking — rotor thickness variation, warp, or a loose caliper mount.
  - Loud grinding or metallic scraping that does not stop — pad material worn through, debris in the caliper, or pad dragging.
  - Visible blueing, deep scoring, or cracks on the rotor — heat damage or mechanical failure in progress.
  - Reduced stopping power that worsens with repeated braking — fade, contamination, or fluid boiling (rare but possible on long descents).
  - Any hydraulic fluid on the rotor, caliper, or lever area — leak; do not ride until located and fixed.
  - Burning smell with reduced power — sustained overheating; stop and let everything cool before assessing.

In short, what you experienced is the textbook wet-disc-brake squeal pattern on a not-yet-bedded rotor. A clean, inspect, progressive-test routine will confirm the system is sound, and the list above gives you the thresholds to act on.

Water back after the valve replacement. Quick read of what you described: 20 s of light brown at the kitchen cold that cleared, bathroom cold cleared faster, no sewage odor, no ongoing sediment, no leak, no advisory in hand. That is consistent with routine sediment disturbance from flow/pressure changes at the main when the valve is reopened — generally flushable, not an emergency. But "generally flushable" is conditional on the flush going well and on nothing below being on the list. Treat the sequence and the stop-list as a single protocol: run the sequence; the moment you hit any stop-list finding, stop and call management instead of pushing on.

A caveat before the protocol: I do not have a live CDC or EPA feed in this session, so this is general public-health and plumbing guidance (CDC after-a-main-break guidance, EPA building-water guidance, AWWA, residential water-heater manufacturer flushing guidance), not a verbatim current directive. Before you start, glance at any building notice, email, or portal entry from management and any local utility advisory. If either side has issued a "do not drink" or "boil water" notice, that overrides the routine flush below — the right move in that case is to call management first and not drink or use the water for any purpose until cleared. If your hot system has been stagnant more than a few days rather than hours, the Legionella-side calculus gets stricter and a management call is the right first move regardless of how the cold flush looks.

================================
SAFE FIXTURE-FLUSHING SEQUENCE
================================

Order matters: cold before hot, fixtures closest to where water enters the building first, working outward. Flow moderate — high enough to move sediment, low enough not to aerosolize or hammer the lines.

  1. Identify the cold fixture closest to your service entry / meter / boiler. Usually the kitchen sink if the riser comes up there.
  2. Remove the aerator from that fixture. Sediment lodges in the screen and will keep discoloring water even after the line is clear. Set the aerator aside.
  3. Run cold at a moderate stream for several minutes — until it has been clear and quiet for at least 1–2 minutes straight. Don't shut off and recheck; let it run.
  4. While it runs, watch for particles, smell, foam, or film.
  5. Rinse and reinstall the aerator. Move to the next-closest cold fixture. Repeat per fixture until every cold fixture flushes clear.
  6. Flush the toilet 2–3 times to clear the cold fill line.
  7. Now hot. If you have a tank water heater, you want enough hot running to turn over the tank. Run all hot fixtures simultaneously at moderate flow for roughly 15 minutes (rule of thumb for a residential tank). Alternatively, if the heater drain valve is accessible, drain a few gallons from the tank bottom to flush settled sediment — that is more effective than just running fixtures. If you have a tankless / on-demand heater, just run each hot fixture for several minutes.
  8. Shower last. Run hot for several minutes. Keep the bathroom door open and the exhaust fan on — the point is to ventilate aerosolized droplets. Hot-side stagnation is the Legionella risk that drives the order: cold flush first, hot flush second, shower last.
  9. Appliances, only after hot is fully flushed:
       - Dishwasher: empty cycle on the hottest / sanitary setting. No detergent for the first cycle — the goal is to flush the inlet hose and the machine interior.
       - Washing machine: empty hot cycle, no clothes. A rinse/spin first, then a hot cycle with no detergent, is a common variation.

Drinking-water filters — replace the cartridges. Activated-carbon refrigerator filters, pitcher filters, undersink carbon stages, and RO membranes that were in service during the outage are not safe to trust afterward. Stagnant water sitting in the housing during the disturbance can grow bacteria, and the carbon can release trapped material when flow resumes. Manufacturer guidance for the major residential lines (PUR, Brita, GE, Whirlpool, iSpring, Pentair) after a main disturbance is replace the cartridge. If you have an undersink RO, replace the membrane and all post-filters per the maker's outage guidance. Don't drink from those until they are swapped. Ice maker: throw out the first full bin of ice and let it make two more full bins before using.

================================
FINDINGS THAT MEAN STOP AND CALL MANAGEMENT
================================

Any one of these during the flush changes the answer — do not push on and "see if it clears":

  - Cold water does not run clear at any fixture after roughly 5 minutes of flushing at that fixture.
  - Discoloration returns after it had cleared.
  - Solid particles or grit are visible after the initial clearing.
  - Sulfur / rotten-egg smell. Distinct from a faint metallic smell (metallic is normal after disturbance). Sulfur points to sewage influence or sulfate-reducing bacteria.
  - Chemical, solvent, fuel, or plastic smell.
  - Oily film, foam, or persistent cloudiness that does not resolve.
  - A boil-water or do-not-use notice issued by management or the utility. If one is in place, do not drink or use the water for any purpose until cleared, and the flush sequence above is not the right move on its own.
  - Symptoms in any household member in the next 24–48 hours: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps. Save any leftover tap water for testing if practical, and tell the clinician it was post-outage.
  - Any leak that shows up during flushing, or pressure that does not return to normal (no water, very low pressure, or hammering that doesn't settle).

If none of those fire during the flush, the sequence above should bring everything back to normal use — hot drinks, coffee maker, ice maker all fine once hot is flushed and filters are replaced. The two checks that earn their weight afterward: (a) taste and smell at the kitchen cold after the flush — should be neutral, no metallic bite beyond a faint trace; (b) the aerator screen when you pull it — should be clean, not caked with orange/brown sediment. If either is off, that is a stop-list finding too.

What the evidence supports
  - The cache-ready-visibility-before-admission invariant held on every sampled trace across 26,400 holder transfers. That is the core correctness claim of the patch, and it is directly verified rather than inferred.

What the evidence does not prove
  - 5% traffic almost certainly does not cover every label_map read site. The shard-keeper touch matrix includes routing plus admin/validation paths; a 5% slice of holder transfers will skew heavily toward the routing path. A fake-clean cutover from a missed read site is the named risk and remains open.
  - The cache-readiness check at 5% is mostly exercised on warm/hot paths. Tail behavior under cache-cold restart, partition pressure, or contention is not in this sample.
  - p99 stability does not scale linearly. Freshness evaluation moves to a hotter path as scale grows, and the +0.1s headroom may compress.

Safeguards to keep at the larger canary
  - 5-503s-in-10-min rollback guard: armed, unchanged, and not relaxed as a confidence gesture. Zero fires is not the same as unnecessary.
  - Per-cohort cache-ready-visibility metric, not sampled traces. The "preceded admission" invariant must stay continuously observable at the larger cohort — sampled traces stop being load-bearing evidence past the smallest canary.
  - Bounded by cohort, not just by traffic percentage. Define the cohort explicitly so blast radius stays isolatable.
  - Touch-matrix coverage check before scaling further: pre-commit to demonstrating the larger canary exercises admin/validation read sites, not just routing. If those sites are not naturally exercised, route synthetic traffic through them.
  - Fail-closed posture for cache unreadability. If the cache layer becomes unreadable mid-canary, the contract must degrade to "not ready / unknown," not admit. State this explicitly in the runbook rather than assuming it.
  - Partial-signal monitoring on top of the guard. Per the structural-rollup rule, the rollback guard alone is insufficient — partial indicators via logs, metrics, retry counts, and secondary writes need continuous visibility.
  - Decision ownership stays with Cyrus's team. Canary success should not drift the rollout decision right by default; the next-step call is still theirs.
  - Pre-defined halt conditions for the larger canary that would not have surfaced at 5%: cache-cold restart behavior, admin-path errors, freshness-eval latency under load, retry-rate spikes.

Bottom line: the canary results justify a larger bounded canary. They do not justify skipping one. The patch's behavior on the transfer path looks correct; the open risk is coverage of the rest of the touch matrix — which is exactly what a bounded expansion is supposed to test.

Three participating clients, one burst tail, three different load-handling choices. The distribution tells us where the load is concentrated; it does not tell us why, what triggers the previously reproduced latency, or how each client behaves under rejection. Comparing them honestly on failure modes and on what we still don't know:

OPTION A: HARD 2,000-POINT CAP
Failure mode. The 0.4% burst band (2,001-9,600) gets refused. The "preserves point accounting" property holds only if the client treats the refusal as authoritative and does not silently truncate. The 88% peak queue utilization for the burstiest client is the real concern: 12% headroom is consumed by ordinary variance (scheduling jitter, retries, GC), so any compounding — the burstiest client retrying aggressively, or its burst coinciding with a smaller surge from another client — pushes the queue into backpressure within the same minute. Detection is fast (queue depth, ingest-edge latency), but the failure is a self-inflicted retry storm rather than an external fault.
Evidence gaps. "Peak" is undefined — p99, max over the 30 days, or steady-state under a specific retry policy? We don't know the burstiest client's retry semantics (immediate, exponential, batched). We don't know whether the 88% is from one retry-multiplied burst or from sustained load. "Preserves point accounting" is asserted, not verified end-to-end — is there a reconciliation check that confirms refused batches are resubmitted in full and not silently dropped? What is the SLO for refused batches; if clients must retry within seconds, queue load compounds; if within hours, the data is stale on arrival.

OPTION B: DOCUMENTATION-ONLY
Failure mode. The previously reproduced latency path remains possible. We know it has been reproduced at least once, which means the trigger conditions still exist in the wild. The burstiest client continues to send up to 9,600 points, and whatever combination of batch size, frequency, and ingest-edge state caused the original spike can recur. The dominant risk is not new; it is the same incident, awaiting its next trigger. Detection depends on whether the latency path has a runbook signature; root cause is harder to attribute without enforcement telemetry, since we cannot distinguish "client out of guidance" from "client in guidance but unlucky."
Evidence gaps. What is the actual signature of the reproduced latency path — duration, blast radius, time-to-detect, time-to-mitigate? Is the trigger a single large batch, sustained bursts, or correlated bursts across clients? Which of the three clients are currently compliant versus chronic over-senders? The 30-day window may exclude known incidents, in which case the 0.4% figure understates true burst rate. There is no enforcement signal in metrics, so any future regression analysis has to reconstruct client behavior post-hoc.

OPTION C: SOFT REJECTION ABOVE 8,000
Failure mode. 0.03% of recorded requests rejected — extremely low in aggregate, but with only three clients, this could be effectively all of one client's tail. "Soft" rejection is the risk: clients without partial-delivery plus retry semantics will silently lose points above 8,000, turning a small rejection rate into a small data-loss rate. The 2,001-8,000 band is unmitigated, so if the latency trigger sits below 8,000 — say at 4,000 or 5,000 — this option does not prevent the reproduced path. Immediate handling for Kibo's pothos exposure

Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) contains insoluble calcium oxalate crystals. When chewed, the crystals mechanically irritate and inflame the oral mucosa — burning, hypersalivation, lip-licking — and rarely cause enough pharyngeal swelling to threaten the airway. The plant isn't well absorbed systemically in dogs, so the main concern is local tissue injury and, in severe cases, airway compromise.

What you're seeing right now (lip-lick, no vomiting, no oral pawing, normal breathing, no visible swelling) is consistent with mild-to-moderate local exposure. Your decisions so far — removing the plant, keeping the piece, not inducing vomiting, no human meds — are all correct.

Do now (next 30-60 minutes):

  - Rinse his mouth with cool water if he'll tolerate it: gently flush the cheek surfaces, gums, and tongue for 30-60 seconds using a cup or low-pressure spray. If he resists, skip and just let him drink.
  - Offer water freely. A tablespoon of milk or plain yogurt can also help bind residual crystals and soothe the mucosa.
  - Withhold food for 30-60 minutes if he shows oral discomfort, then offer a bland meal (plain boiled chicken and rice) if he wants it.
  - Do NOT induce vomiting — re-exposing the esophagus to the crystals causes worse injury.
  - Do NOT give Pepto, Imodium, Benadryl, or any other medication without veterinary direction.

Observation window: 2-6 hours. Watch for any of:

  - Increasing drooling, or repeated lip-licking, face-rubbing, or pawing at the mouth
  - Visible swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat (lift the lip, check under the tongue, watch the external throat)
  - Voice change — bark going hoarse or quieter is an early pharyngeal sign
  - Any breathing change: faster rate, louder effort, panting at rest, extended neck posture, reluctance to lie down
  - Repeated vomiting, vomiting with blood, or sustained retching
  - Difficulty or refusal to swallow water across multiple attempts
  - Lethargy past the first hour, or collapse

Call animal poison control NOW if you see:

  - Any visible or suspected oral, facial, or throat swelling (even subtle)
  - Voice change
  - Breathing changes of any kind
  - Repeated vomiting or retching that won't stop
  - Inability to swallow water after several attempts
  - Persistent pawing at the mouth beyond 30-60 minutes

Go directly to an emergency vet (skip the phone call) if:

  - Stridor, gasping, blue or pale gums, or any airway compromise
  - Collapse, severe lethargy, or unresponsiveness
  - Profuse drooling with retching and visible distress
  - Palpable or visible swelling of the tongue or throat

Two poison control lines, both staffed 24/7 by veterinary toxicologists (consultation fee applies, typically $85-95):

  - ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: 888-426-4435
  - Pet Poison Helpline: 855-764-7661

About the leaf piece: good that you kept it. When you call, the more useful info than species ID is roughly how big the piece was relative to his muzzle and what fraction looks chewed versus dropped intact — they'll calibrate against his weight.

Worth making the call right now? Given he's currently stable, calling either line now is reasonable and removes some guesswork about whether the observation window above is sufficient or whether proactive care is warranted. If you'd rather wait and watch, the triggers above are your threshold; if anything on the "call now" list shows up, call regardless of time of day.

Expected course if no triggers fire: most mild pothos exposures self-resolve in 12-24 hours, oral discomfort fading first. Some dogs have residual lip-smacking or soft-food preference for a day or two. If he's eating, drinking, behaving normally, and shows no oral pain by morning, he likely came through it. If anything subtle shows up tomorrow — dropping food, preferring soft food, low-grade lip-licking — a same-day vet check is reasonable but not emergent.

64°F is uncomfortable, not dangerous on its own. The actual hazard is sustained cold through sleep and a continued fall overnight. Goal: slow the drop, hold one warm retreat room until the boiler is back.

Set up one retreat room now:
- Smallest exterior-wall exposure, door you can close. Bedroom usually wins.
- Hang a blanket over the window — that is your biggest single leak. Roll a towel at the door base to block drafts.
- Close interior doors to unused rooms. Pull Kibo in with you.
- Elevate Kibo's bed off the cold floor (cushion on a chair is fine). Floor pulls heat fast.

Keep warm:
- Layers including a hat or hood — head and neck account for most of the perceived cold.
- For Kibo: coat or sweater if you have one; otherwise a light layer under a blanket. Body contact helps, even a little.
- Use the hot water — tea, broth, warm water. Internal warming plus humidity helps how cold it feels.
- Light movement before bed (stretching, pacing the room). Stillness during sleep lets core temp drift down.

Things you already have right (don't change):
- No oven for heat — combustion products, and the room cools again as soon as you turn it off.
- No improvised heaters or daisy-chains on the work-room outlets. A single, modern, tip-protected space heater plugged directly into a living-area wall outlet is a fine stopgap later — only while you're awake and present, never overnight unattended.

Stronger-escalation triggers (call management back, push for a firm ETA, ask about alternate heat):
- Retreat-room temp hits 60°F.
- Two hours pass with no technician update.
- Anyone — adult or Kibo — is shivering and cannot stop within about 10 minutes of rewarming.

Leave / go elsewhere for the night if:
- Retreat-room temp hits 55°F — sleep becomes the real risk below this.
- Tech ETA slips past roughly midnight with no working heat restored.
- Cold-stress signs appear: uncontrolled shivering, confusion, slurred speech, stiff fingers or toes; for Kibo, lethargy plus ongoing shivering.

Sleep-window note: the most important variable is whether heat is back before you sleep. If by about 22:30 the apartment is still dropping and management cannot give you a firm restore time, treat that as a leave trigger even at 58°F. Sustained cold through sleep is the actual hazard, more than any single number in the moment. If you do leave, take Kibo's harness and a blanket for the car.

Honor the shape she asked for:

  - Shower ready and warm; towel and clean clothes where she can reach them without asking. Then the quiet hour as parallel presence — you on the couch or the other side of the room, doing something low-effort, within earshot but not in her face. The work-room setup is built for exactly this; use it.
  - Something easy to eat available without announcement — tea, toast, soup. Don't comment on how much or how little she has.
  - Pets handled so nothing pulls on her: Kibo walked (short leash near the park entry), Paw fed and watered. Phones quiet, no one else invited over tonight.

After the hour, if she opens the door, listen. No clinical follow-ups. No "have you thought about talking to someone." Silence is fine, and if she cries, that's not a problem to fix. If she doesn't open the door, the closed door is also fine — sleep when her body is ready, no performance of being okay required.

What to leave out:

  - "Are you okay?" on repeat. "Do you want to talk?" every twenty minutes.
  - Minimizers: "at least they aren't suffering," "you did everything you could," "they're in a better place."
  - Clinical-detail questions. She drew that line; respect it.
