The math here is straightforward enough to do by hand carefully and show every step — and the framing matters more than the arithmetic. Here is how to tell the two effects apart, the comparisons to make, and which numbers to pull from the bill before contacting the utility.

================================================================
1. ACTUAL READ vs. ESTIMATED READ — WHY IT MATTERS
================================================================

The single biggest red flag in your excerpt is this line:

    Ending meter reading: actual, December 12.
    Prior period: ... ending reading estimated November 11.

The utility billed the November period on an ESTIMATE, then on December 12 sent an actual reader. That is the moment of truth, because the December bill is almost certainly doing one of two things:

  (a) Correcting the estimate — using real kWh instead of estimated kWh, which can produce a one-time swing that has nothing to do with what you actually used in this 31-day period, or
  (b) Reflecting real higher use.

You cannot tell which one it is from the dollar totals alone. You need the underlying numbers.

Two readings matter most:

  • The ENDING meter reading printed on the December bill (the actual read taken Dec 12).
  • The STARTING meter reading printed on the December bill (this is the utility's "opening" meter number for the period — it should equal the ending read from the November bill, which was an estimate).

The math:  kWh billed this period = Ending meter read − Starting meter read.

If that subtraction reproduces the 286 kWh on the bill, the usage is grounded in real meter turns and the estimate-vs-actual issue is settled — any difference is genuine consumption. If the subtraction does NOT reproduce 286 kWh, the bill is mixing estimated and actual data and you have a basis to dispute.

Also worth pulling:

  • Prior bill's ESTIMATED ending read. The utility may print the prior "estimate" number next to the new actual. The gap between estimated and actual is the true true-up — and if the estimate was LOW (as it often is in shoulder-season bills), the true-up inflates this bill's "usage" line.
  • History of "actual" vs "estimated" flags. If November is the only recent estimate, that is itself information — the reader cycle may have skipped you.

================================================================
2. NORMALIZE FOR THE EXTRA DAY (31 vs 30)
================================================================

Before comparing anything, neutralize the period-length difference:

    Current: 286 kWh / 31 days = 9.23 kWh/day
    Prior:   252 kWh / 30 days = 8.40 kWh/day

    Difference: +0.83 kWh/day  (+9.9%)

The extra day alone, at the prior rate of use, accounts for roughly 8.40 kWh. So out of the 34 kWh nominal increase (286 − 252):

    ~8 kWh  → "free" attribution to the longer billing cycle
    ~26 kWh → genuine higher daily consumption, weather, behavior, or estimate true-up

If you do nothing else, do this: ask whether the 9.9% daily-use bump is plausible for the time of year (lighting, heating, appliances, guests). In early December at the South Slope, modest heating load kicking in is the most likely benign explanation for ~10%.

================================================================
3. THE TWO RATES THAT MATTER
================================================================

Your bill splits charges into two components, and the per-kWh rates are the cleanest way to spot a rate change hiding inside a usage change:

    Supply:    $34.32 / 286 kWh = $0.1200/kWh
    Delivery:  $56.20 / 286 kWh = $0.19650/kWh
    Blended:   $90.52 / 286 kWh = $0.31650/kWh

The blended rate looks unusually high because this appears to be a Con Ed residential bill, where the "delivery" portion is large and includes fixed customer charges, demand/grid charges, and other pass-throughs that don't scale linearly with kWh — but the rates above are correct for this bill as stated.

What to compare against the prior bill:

  • Supply ¢/kWh — should be nearly identical period-to-period. If prior was $0.12 and current is $0.12, you are clean. If prior was, say, $0.085 and current is $0.12, the supplier changed and rates moved — that explains a chunk of the dollar jump with no usage change at all.
  • Delivery ¢/kWh — small variations are normal (rate cases, fuel adjustment, riders). Large jumps (>10–15%) warrant a call.
  • Fixed monthly charges — both supply and delivery usually carry a non-kWh customer charge. If the prior bill was 30 days and current is 31 days, prorated fixed charges can add ~3% by themselves.

The cleanest comparison is:

    (Current bill ¢/kWh) vs. (Prior bill ¢/kWh)

If rates are flat, all the dollar increase is usage (+ the extra day). If rates moved, you need to separate "more kWh" from "more expensive kWh."

================================================================
4. PUTTING IT TOGETHER — BEFORE YOU CALL
================================================================

Compute these four things and write them down before contacting the utility:

  1. Daily-use delta:    9.23 vs 8.40 kWh/day  (+9.9%). Plausible for early-Dec heating load?
  2. Per-kWh rate delta: compare supply and delivery ¢/kWh to the prior bill line-for-line. Flag anything > ~5%.
  3. Estimate true-up:   starting-meter-read − prior-bill-ending-read (should = 0 if the estimate was perfect; any non-zero is the true-up hidden in this bill).
  4. Fixed-charge prorating: 31/30 = +3.3% baseline drift that is not "use."

If (1) is plausible, (2) is flat, (3) is small, and (4) accounts for ~3% — the bill is real, the use is real, the dollar increase is just normal December.

If (3) is large — i.e. the prior estimate was significantly off — you can ask the utility to spread the true-up over future bills rather than absorb it in one period. Most will.

If (2) shows a rate change you weren't notified about, that's the dispute: ask for the bill to be recalculated at the prior period's rates, or at minimum an explanation of the rate change with effective date.

Bottom line: the layered proposal is defensible as a permanent answer, but it isn't a decision yet — it has unresolved failure modes and several "evidence first" gaps that the alternative options (discard / quarantine / hold / partial) interact with differently. Below is the assessment, then the comparison, then the evidence I'd want before signing off.

  Decomposing the proposal (so we can argue about each layer):
    Layer 1 — SDK pre-transmit reject at >8,000 points, caller instructed to split.
    Layer 2 — ingest-edge HTTP 413, accepted=0, rejected=submitted, oversized_batch metric.
    Layer 3 (implicit) — older client rides Layer 2 indefinitely; no stated retirement path.

  Failure modes specific to the layered proposal:

    a. "Split" pushes chunking semantics onto callers without a contract.
       Who owns ordering, idempotency, partial-failure handling? If a caller splits
       50K into 7×7K and one sub-batch fails for an unrelated reason, the caller
       has no defined behavior. You trade a server-side hard reject for a client-
       side soft contract that nobody has specified.

    b. The 8,000 threshold is presented as a fact, but no rationale was given.
       Points vs. bytes vs. cardinality vs. wall-clock cost are different limits.
       If the actual OOM trigger is bytes (8K small ints vs. 8K histograms are
       very different), the SDK rule is miscalibrated and the server backstop
       carries the real load. Layered looks clean while hiding the wrong knob.

    c. Counter divergence between SDK-rejected (caller-side, never observed by
       ingest-edge) and server-rejected (ingest-edge counter). accepted=0 +
       rejected=submitted only sees what reaches the wire. A new "sdk_rejected"
       signal is implied but not stated. Without it, you cannot tell whether the
       server backstop is doing 1% or 60% of the work.

    d. The older client has no stated migration path. "Initially relies on the
       server backstop" reads as permanent unless there's a deprecation
       timeline. That means the 413 path is forever-code, and "permanent
       disposition" is really "permanent with a permanent escape hatch."

    e. Symmetry gap: no floor. If callers learn to split, you'll eventually see
       traffic shaped into many tiny batches where per-batch overhead
       (auth/schema/validation) dominates and throughput collapses. The
       proposal adds a ceiling without addressing the floor.

    f. Failure mode under SDK miss: if a caller emits a "small" batch that
       expands post-encode (cardinality explosion, label blow-up), the SDK
       passes it and the server still has to handle it. That's actually a
       reason to keep Layer 2 — but the proposal doesn't acknowledge this
       explicitly, so the server-side cost is being hidden inside "backstop."

    g. Migration ordering cost with Hema. The proposal constrains the cutover:
       SDK changes have to ship in lockstep with whatever else is moving. If
       prod forces Hema to reorder, this design becomes the bottleneck rather
       than a decision.

    h. Operational follow-through on oversized_batch. A permanent metric with
       no runbook entry, no alert, no per-client breakdown, and no on-call path
       is the same fake-clean shape as the shard-keeper label_map worry —
       looks quiet in dashboards while the underlying behavior is unchanged.

  How the alternatives compare:

    Discard (drop oversized batch silently):
       - vs. proposal: loses observability entirely. Caller has no signal, no
         lever, no way to detect their own misbehavior.
       - When it wins: when oversized batches are sampling/analytics where
         loss is tolerable AND the caller is untrusted enough that 413 will
         just be ignored.
       - When it loses: anywhere data is billing, audit, alerting, or
         correctness-relevant. You trade 413-with-trace for data corruption.

    Quarantine (hold in side buffer for inspection/replay):
       - vs. proposal: preserves the data; defers the decision. Costs a TTL,
         a max size, a reader interface, a retention story, and a backpressure
         plan when the buffer fills.
       - When it wins: oversized rate is non-trivial AND the batches are
         valuable enough that dropping or rejecting them is unacceptable.
       - When it loses: oversized rate is low AND the batches are
         discardable. Quarantine's storage bill and operational surface
         exceed its value. Most metrics pipelines land here.

    Hold (429 / block caller until path frees):
       - vs. proposal: graded behavior, not binary. Requires its own capacity
         guarantee, otherwise it's a renamed queue with no upper bound.
       - When it wins: oversized data is genuinely worth waiting for and
         the caller is patient (e.g., async control plane, batch job).
       - When it loses: caller-facing synchronous ingest where Hold becomes
         a retry-storm generator and head-of-line blocker.

    Partial (accept first N, reject the rest):
       - vs. proposal: breaks all-or-nothing semantics. Requires 207-style
         multi-status responses, which most HTTP clients don't handle
         natively, AND requires domain knowledge of what "first N points"
         means analytically. For most metric shapes (windows, histograms,
         per-shard rollouts) "first N" destroys meaning.
       - When it wins: almost nowhere in metrics. Only if the SDK can
         identify a self-contained prefix that is analytically meaningful
         (rare).
       - When it loses: everywhere else. Partial usually degrades into the
         proposal in practice — SDK rejects oversized inputs outright
         because "first N" can't be defined safely.

  Net of the comparison: discard loses on observability; quarantine and hold
  add operational surface that's only justified if oversized data has
  non-trivial value; partial almost always collapses into the proposal. The
  layered design isn't competing against four peers — it's competing against
  one viable alternative per axis (discard if you don't care, quarantine if
  you really need the data). That's why the proposal feels like a front-
  runner. But "viable" ≠ "evidence-backed."

  Evidence I'd want before committing to the layered design as permanent:

    1. Empirical batch-size distribution per client: p50/p95/p99/p99.9 of
       points and bytes. Is 8,000 a real breakpoint or a guess? Is the
       server backstop actually catching 8,001-point batches, or is it
       catching something the threshold missed entirely (bytes)?

    2. Per-client oversized rate from the v2 metric. If the older client is
       99% of the source, the proposal is mostly a one-offender
       accommodation dressed as architecture.

    3. Caller behavior under 413 today. Does the older client retry the
       same batch (storm), drop silently (data loss), or split (which we
       haven't asked it to do)?

    4. SDK adoption cost. Two clients adopting is two integrations; what
       are they, who owns them, what's the rollout shape? Per-client opt-in
       or coordinated cutover?

    5. The "split" contract. Ordered? Idempotent? At-least-once or
       at-most-once across sub-batches? How is partial sub-batch failure
       surfaced? This must be written down before the SDK change ships,
       not after.

    6. Counter coverage. Where is "sdk_rejected" recorded? If the answer
       is "nowhere," you cannot tell whether Layer 2 is doing 1% or 60%
       of the work, which means you cannot retire it.

    7. Retirement path for Layer 2. What has to be true before the server
       413 path can be deleted? Is the older client on a real deprecation
       timeline, or is "initial" actually "forever"?

    8. Floor / batching hygiene. What's the minimum batch size we'd accept?
       If callers learn to split, what's the per-batch overhead and how
       does it interact with auth/schema validation cost?

    9. Hema's cutover sequence. Does this design force her ordering? If
       yes, what does that cost if prod forces a reorder? Memory note:
       she may reorder if prod forces it — so this is a real constraint.

    10. Runbook for oversized_batch. Who pages, on what threshold, with
        what runbook? Without this, the metric is decorative.

    11. Rollout discipline. Per the established pattern: SDK owners sign
        off on SDK changes; ingest-edge owner verifies server behavior
        independently. Same here — vendors don't get to mark this
        "done."

  What would actually decide it:

    - If oversized batches are uniformly low value AND the older client's
      misbehavior is the only real source, the layered design is right
      and the missing work is just items 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10.

    - If oversized batches contain data we genuinely cannot lose
      (audit/billing/correctness), quarantine beats reject, and the
      proposal is the wrong frame.

    - If the older client is staying forever and not adopting, the
      proposal is really "permanent server-side reject" with an SDK
      sugar-coating — say so and design accordingly.

    - If the 8,000 threshold isn't load-tested against byte size and
      cardinality, the proposal is a guess with a backstop. Don't
      commit until that's grounded.

  I'd push back on the framing of "permanent" until items 1, 2, 5, 6, 7,
  and 10 have evidence. The proposal is the most defensible of the
  options, but its current statement dodges the hard parts (threshold
  rationale, counter coverage, retirement path, caller chunking
  contract) and that's exactly where post-hoc regret lives.

OVERALL: Compatibility evidence is solid for the layered candidate. The only finding is one SDK's sparse error text, and it should be fixed but should NOT gate the disposition decision.

COMPATIBILITY EVIDENCE — STRONG
- Local pre-transmission rejection in both current SDKs → bounded server load, no wasted round-trips above 8000 points.
- Server-side 413 path verified via the older client (10,000 attempts, every one handled correctly, all recovered via split) → the network-boundary layer holds.
- Splitting produces complete accepted-point accounting → no data loss in the documented recovery path.
- Programmatic error codes correct across all tested clients → automation is safe.
- "No unchanged retry" preserved → clients don't loop on the same oversized payload.

ONE SOFT FINDING
- One SDK language's local error text is just `batch too large` and omits the 8000-point threshold. The programmatic error code is correct, so this is purely a developer-UX gap, not a contract gap.

ON SEQUENCING (text fix vs. disposition choice)
Fix the text. Don't let it gate the disposition.

- The text is orthogonal to the disposition. Discard / quarantine / hold / partial are all about server-side handling of an oversized payload; the client-side error string is unchanged by any of them and remains accurate under each.
- The fix is a string change in one SDK with no protocol or counter implications. Programmatic contracts are already correct, so this is purely a readability improvement for anyone staring at a log line.
- Gating the disposition on a UX string would conflate two unrelated decisions and risk slowing down the larger architectural call.

Recommendation: choose the permanent disposition on its own merits from the v2 telemetry, and land the text correction in parallel or in the same release window — not as a precondition.

CAVEATS WORTH FLAGGING TO THE OWNERS
- "Local pre-transmission rejection" evidence only covers the two current SDKs. Third-party SDKs and hand-rolled clients still rely on the 413 path, so the older-client 10,000-attempt result is the more durable signal that the layered design holds at the network boundary. Don't overweight the local-rejection numbers when extrapolating.
- "No unchanged retry" depends on the 413 + client-no-retry pairing. If the chosen disposition changes how an oversized result is represented on the wire (e.g., a hold disposition could re-shape the response), re-verify the no-retry contract against the new response shape before declaring it stable.

Safe unplugged jam-removal and inspection sequence. Stop at any point that fails a check.

PRE-CHECKS (still unplugged, cool-down period)
- Cord cool at both ends and outlet face. If warm at any point: leave out of service, do not plug in again.
- Hot-electrical smell from a stalled motor is normal for a few minutes as windings dissipate heat. Sniff again at 10-15 min. Persistent or sharp smell = insulation/winding damage, leave out of service.
- Do not open the motor housing. Do not lubricate. Do not pry between burrs with metal tools.

ACCESS
- Remove hopper. Empty it. Inspect the bean batch and hopper for additional stones or debris — sieving the rest of the bag once is worth it, this is rarely a one-off.
- Shine a flashlight down into the burr chamber. Note exactly where the stone sits relative to the outer burr teeth and whether it is wedged in the grinding gap or sitting on top of the burrs.

REMOVAL
- Goal: walk the stone back up the way it entered, not through the burr gap.
- Tool: wooden chopstick, bamboo skewer, or plastic spudger. Avoid metal against the burr teeth.
- Technique options, in order of preference:
    1. If your grinder has a back-burr / manual reverse mode, run it briefly with the hopper removed so you can watch — the stone usually walks upward and out.
    2. If the burr carrier can be rotated by hand with hopper removed (some designs), turn it backwards in short arcs to walk the stone up.
    3. Tap the grinder body gently while applying light lateral pressure on the stone with the chopstick to nudge it toward the upper opening.
- Do not force the burrs forward against the jam — risk of chipping a tooth.
- Once out, keep the stone. Note its size and whether it fractured; fragments left behind cause repeat stalls.

POST-REMOVAL INSPECTION
- Flashlight both burrs: any chipped, bent, flared, or missing tooth? Any metal swarf or shiny dust? Even one damaged tooth means leave out of service — running on a chipped burr contaminates grounds with metal and ruins the burr set quickly.
- Rotate the lower burr / drive by hand with chamber empty. Should be smooth with light, even resistance. Red flags: notching, scraping, gritty feel, binding at one position, or any new axial/radial play.
- Sniff again. Smell should be neutral or fading. New or stronger hot smell = leave out.
- Housing: any brown or tan smear around vents or seams = sustained overheat, leave out.

GATE 1 — single test run is permitted only if ALL are true:
  - Stone removed whole or only as a few clean fragments, all out of chamber
  - Burr teeth visually intact
  - Burrs rotate smoothly by hand, no new play
  - No persistent hot-electrical smell after cool-down
  - No discoloration on housing
  - Cord and plug cool and undamaged
  - Outlet face cool

GATE 2 — leave out of service if ANY of these are true (pre-test or during test):
  - Any burr tooth damage (chip, bend, missing, flare)
  - Stone cannot be removed cleanly or fragments remain
  - Burrs bind, notch, or scrape by hand
  - Hot-electrical smell returns or persists beyond ~15 min cool-down
  - Any brown/tan discoloration on plastic housing or vents
  - Cord, plug, or outlet shows heat damage (discoloration, deformation, warm to touch)
  - Breaker/GFCI tripped at any point during the original stall
  - During test: smoke, smell, scraping/clicking, motor housing gets hot within seconds, breaker trips, or output contains visible metal specks

SINGLE TEST PROTOCOL (only if Gate 1 passes)
- Plug in with hopper empty or with only a few beans. Run 5-10 seconds, then stop and unplug.
- During: listen for scraping or clicking, watch for smoke at vents.
- Immediately after: sniff at the burr chamber and vents, touch the motor housing. Should be barely warm at most.
- If clean, repeat with a slightly larger bean load for another 10 seconds.
- If still clean, run a normal dose. Inspect the grounds for any metallic glints — a tell for chipped teeth.

AFTER
- If everything passed: monitor over the next several doses. Recurring thermal smell, intermittent stalls, or any noise you didn't have before means take it out of service and have the burrs and motor inspected.
- If Gate 2 triggers at any point: do not run again. The likely failure modes from a stalled burr contact are chipped tooth, shock-loaded bearing, degraded thermal fuse, or weakened winding insulation — all of which get worse, not better, with continued use.

Path summary: remove stone cleanly, inspect burrs and bearings by hand and nose, gate on those plus the cord/outlet, do one short loaded test, gate again on heat/smell/sound. Anything off at any step = out of service until a burr set and/or motor inspection.

Pattern read

The undercling reproduces the pain and ordinary grip does not = flexor-loaded
issue (finger/wrist flexor tendons or their muscle-tendon junction, possibly
common flexor origin near the medial epicondyle). Undercling is the most
eccentrically provocative grip for that system, which is why open-hand felt
fine. The absence of swelling, bruising, neurovascular signs, focal bony
tenderness, and motion loss, plus full ordinary grip, makes a strain-grade
tendon/myofascial irritation the most likely thing — not a tear, fracture,
or nerve compression. That fits a conservative loading-pause approach.

Phase 0 — Loading pause (next 5 to 7 days)

  Stop: climbing, undercling work, crimping, pull-ups, heavy grip carries,
         deadlifts/grip-heavy lifts, prolonged forceful gripping.
  Keep:  ordinary daily use (mug, door handle, laptop, bag handles are fine).
  Allow: pain-free wrist/finger ROM (circles, prayer stretch, extensor
         stretch); isometric ball or towel squeezes at sub-max only.
  Cold:   10-15 min after anything that reproduces symptoms; not required
         if symptom-free.
  Meds:   short-course oral NSAID is reasonable if daily-life pain >=3/10;
         skip if pain-free in ordinary use (NSAIDs can blunt tendon repair).
  Sleep:  avoid sleeping on the right wrist/fist curled.

Phase 1 — Return criteria (all must hold before Phase 2)

  - 5 to 7 consecutive days of pain-free ordinary use
  - Pain-free full wrist and finger ROM, both directions
  - Resisted wrist flexion / pronation at moderate load = no pain
  - Sub-max sustained grip (5-10s hard ball squeeze) = no pain
  - No symptoms at rest or overnight

Phase 2 — Climbing return (tiered by grip, ~4 weeks)

  Wk 1  Jugs and open-hand only, easy boulders or top-rope, <=30 min,
        RPE forearm <=4/10. No undercling, no crimp.
  Wk 2  Add large slopers and pinches, easy crimps on big holds. Still no
        undercling unless 3+ sessions symptom-free at <=2/10.
  Wk 3  Re-introduce undercling on progressively smaller holds. Crimp on
        good holds allowed.
  Wk 4  Full return if warmup is <=1/10 and post-session soreness clears
        within 24h.

  Rules across all weeks:
    Warmup is mandatory (5-10 min easy traversing, open-hand only).
    Stop the session if any warmup grip hits >=3/10.
    Regress one tier for 48-72h if next-day pain >2/10 or lasts >24h.

Escalate to sports medicine or PT if any of these appear

  - No improvement after 10-14 days of strict Phase 0
  - Pain recurs at the same or lower load on Phase 2 return
  - Pain shifts to the medial epicondyle, forearm muscle belly, or wrist joint
  - Focal bony tenderness, swelling, bruising, clicking/snapping, or visible
    deformity at any point
  - Numbness, tingling, or grip weakness that doesn't resolve within 48h
  - Pain during ordinary use (not just climbing) or pain that wakes you
  - Reproducible pain on resisted wrist flexion or pronation that persists
    into the next day

Practical note

  Given Devika is in-house, a 60-second screen — resisted wrist flexion,
  resisted pronation, palpation of the medial epicondyle and forearm flexor
  belly — would catch the most common culprits. PT (with climbing-specific
  return programming) is higher yield than a sports-med visit if the picture
  stays stable; sports med first if any red flag above appears.

The cleanest move is to take the already-done thin section off the heat first so it stops coasting, then finish the thick sections at high heat so you hit 145°F before the thin piece has time to dry out.

1. Thin section (already at 145°F): move it to the serving plate now and tent tightly with foil. It'll coast another 3-5°F during rest — accept that as the cost of food safety and keep it away from any further heat. A spoon of warm butter or oil over the top after tenting helps with the slight dryness.

2. Thick sections (126°F and 133°F): pick by time.

   - Fastest (1-2 min): slice each thick piece horizontally to halve its thickness, then sear the cut sides in a hot oiled/buttered pan, about 45-60 seconds per side. Pull at 145°F instant-read. Carryover will take it to roughly 148-150°F, which is fine.
   
   - Gentlest (3-5 min): put the thick pieces on a small sheet pan in a 425°F oven (or low broiler) until the probe in the center reads 145°F. Tent and rest.
   
   Start the 126°F piece first; pull the 133°F piece ~30 seconds earlier since it's already closer.

3. Vegetables (done, short delay):
   
   Off the heat, covered with a lid or foil. They'll hold well for 5-10 minutes with minimal further softening. If you expect more than about 10 minutes, slide them into a 200°F oven on the serving plate. Skip the microwave — uneven reheating.

One tip: probe the thick sections from the side, not the top. A 126°F reading from the top of a thick fillet usually means the core is colder than that, which is exactly why the thinner part finished first.

First-pass classification

Provisional: BOUNDED HANDOVER FLAP, not an incident — pending the checks below. Rationale from the observed facts: 12/480 shards saw two generations for 22s during a planned node swap, all 480 converged, zero write errors logged, no stale-write sentinel fired, client latency flat. In a lease-based system, a brief generation overlap on the *outgoing* holder during a planned replacement is the expected shape of lease expiry + new lease grant. What makes it bounded (and not a split-brain) is whether the OLD generation was already fenced out of serving writes before clients could route to it. The 22s window is plausible lease TTL + drain, but plausibility is not proof — verify the fencing held.

What would flip this from bounded to incident:
 - OLD generation accepted any write during the window (real concurrent authority).
 - Post-convergence state on the 12 shards diverges from pre-flap state beyond expected handover artifacts.
 - Any downstream site (router, admin, validation, metrics label) is still serving the OLD generation past t+22s — the label_map leak shape from your memory.

Checks before treating as bounded convergence

A. Authority discipline during the 22s window (most important)
 1. For each of the 12 shards, pull lease-grant + lease-revoke lines from node logs. Confirm: lease-revoke(G_old) timestamp < lease-grant(G_new) timestamp < first-observed-G_new-in-client-traffic.
 2. Confirm G_old rejected every write attempt during the overlap (look for explicit "lease expired / fenced / not leader" lines, not just absence of writes).
 3. Fencing-token check: if your writes carry a fencing token or monotonic stamp, confirm every accepted write in the window carries G_new's stamp.

B. State equivalence on the 12 shards
 4. Compare shard state t0 (pre-flap snapshot) vs t1 (post-converge): manifest/version vector / latest-applied-op-id. Should match exactly or only differ by the expected handover artifact (one empty no-op or one lease-renewal record — pick the one your system uses).
 5. Run repair/audit on just the 12 shards. Zero divergence required.
 6. Pull stale-write detector counters for those 12 shards across the alert interval and the surrounding ±5 min. Even if the detector didn't fire, the raw counts should be inspected.

C. Generation-observation site coverage (label_map leak guard)
 7. Enumerate every site that observed the dual-generation: routing, admin read, validation read, repair, audit, metrics-label. For each, confirm it observed G_new by t+22s and not later. This is the touch matrix from your memory — a "fake-clean" cutover is exactly a missed site.
 8. Sample client routing decisions during the window. Any decision served with G_old as the live generation? If yes, real breach regardless of write outcomes.

D. Cause / selection of the 12
 9. Why these 12? Check whether they shared a property — same previous lease holder (the replaced node), same epoch, same partition, larger-than-typical lease TTL, recently rebalanced. A predictable selection (e.g., "all 12 were lease-owner on the replaced node") supports handover. An unexplained selection supports a separate fault.
 10. Cross-reference the replaced node's shutdown sequence: clean drain vs. abrupt termination. Abrupt termination widens the bounded-convergence hypothesis.

E. Observability coverage
 11. Was the 22s alert the full window, or a sampled detection? If sampled, you cannot rule out other shards also flapping silently — pull the raw dual-generation counter (if it exists) across all 480 for ±5 min around the event.
 12. Confirm the stale-write detector's coverage actually includes writes during the 22s window, not just steady-state. A detector that doesn't sample the window gives a false-clean signal.

F. Downstream / client side
 13. Client retry behavior in the window: any retries that landed on a different generation? Idempotency keys intact?
 14. Any acks in the window issued under G_old? If yes, that's the smoking gun for concurrent authority.

Decision rule once checks return
 - All A, B, C clean → bounded convergence. File the 12-shard list + old/new generations as a known-shape handover, set an SLO on the handover window, add per-shard dual-generation counter if absent.
 - Any A check fails → real concurrent-authority window. Escalate to incident even though no write errors surfaced, because the next flap may not be as forgiving.
 - C fails but A+B clean → label_map leak on a non-authority site. Lower urgency than A, but still an incident class — fix the missed site before the next planned replacement.
 - D shows unexplained selection → open a separate hypothesis (network partition, clock skew, lease-TTL regression) and don't close the loop until explained.

Artifacts you already have cover most of A and D. The gap is C (site coverage) and E2 (detector coverage during the window) — those are the two that decide bounded vs. not.

CHRISTMAS EVE PLAN — 6:30 PM SERVICE
4-lb whole chicken, unstuffed, refrigerated. Separate roast potatoes. Short-sauté green beans.

PRIMARY APPROACH
  Oven: 400°F, middle rack (with a second rack above for the potato pan later).
  Target roast: 1h 15m. Plan to pull at 165°F in BOTH the thickest breast and the thickest thigh (no bone contact). 15-min rest before carving.
  Why 165°F, not 180°F: that is the USDA safe minimum for whole poultry; carryover during the 15-min rest pushes it ~5°F higher, juices redistribute, breast stays moist.

TIMELINE (working backward from 6:30 PM)

  4:00 PM  Pull chicken from fridge. Pat very dry inside and out. Salt generously with kosher salt — cavity, under skin if you can, all over. Leave uncovered on a rack or plate. Drops the chill, dries the skin for better browning, shortens cook by ~10 min.

  4:40 PM  Preheat oven to 400°F. Set one rack lower-middle (chicken) and one upper-middle (potatoes).

  4:50 PM  Cut potatoes to ~1.25-1.5" pieces. Toss with oil and salt. Hold.

  5:00 PM  CHICKEN IN. Breast-up on a rack in a roasting pan or sheet pan. No lid, no stuffing, no trussing unless you want neater carving.

  5:45 PM  POTATOES IN. Spread in a single layer on a separate sheet pan, mostly cut-side down. Slide onto the upper rack directly above the chicken. Both cook together for 30 min — no need to rearrange.

  ~6:00 PM  Begin probing the chicken (see temp procedure below). Don't open the oven more than once every 5-7 min — each peek costs 5-10°F.

  6:15 PM  CHICKEN OUT, ideally. Goal: both breast and thigh at 165°F. If at temp, move to a board/cutting board and tent LOOSELY with foil (loose = skin stays crisp). If 155-160°F, give it 5-8 more min. If under 150°F, see contingency below.

  6:15-6:30 PM  CHICKEN RESTS on the counter. Carryover brings it to ~170°F internally.

  6:20 PM  Wash and trim green beans. Optional: blanch 90 seconds in salted water, drain. Skip the blanch if you like a snappier bean — it just buys you insurance against undercooked crisp beans.

  6:24 PM  GREEN BEANS ON HEAT. Hot pan, oil or butter, beans, salt, minced garlic if using. Toss 4-6 min over high heat until bright green and just tender. Off-heat: squeeze of lemon or splash of vinegar.

  6:28 PM  PULL POTATOES. Toss with butter, herbs, salt. Cover loosely with a clean towel or foil to hold heat for 2 min.

  6:30 PM  CARVE and PLATE. Carve the rested chicken (breast off the bone, thighs separated), plate alongside potatoes and beans. Potatoes are 2 min out, beans are ~0 min out — both fully hot.

TEMPERATURE-CHECKING PROCEDURE (the safety-critical part)

  Tool: instant-read thermometer, calibrated. (Ice-water check should read 32°F / 0°C. If it's off by more than 2°F, adjust mentally or replace the battery.)

  BREAST: Insert into the deepest part of the larger lobe, angled so the tip sits in the muscle bulk and does NOT touch the breastbone or ribcage. Bone conducts heat and reads false-high.

  THIGH: Pull the thigh slightly away from the body. Slide the probe parallel to the drumstick bone so the tip sits in the meatiest part of the thigh, NOT touching bone. Aim from the outside in, just past the joint.

  If you only get one clean probe: check the thigh. Thigh is the slowest-heating part and the safety anchor — breast will already be done by the time thigh is at 165°F.

  For highest confidence (with time): check both lobes of the breast and both thighs. The LOWEST reading must be 165°F.

  Pull trigger: 165°F in both sites. Pull a touch earlier (162-163°F) if you want extra insurance, since carryover adds heat. Don't pull much below 162°F and hope — the math stops working in your favor.

CONTINGENCIES

  Chicken ahead of schedule (165°F at 6:00-6:05): pull early. It can rest up to ~25 min on the counter in a draft-free spot, tented loosely. Skin is at its crispiest right after pulling — re-crisp for 60-90 seconds under the broiler at the very end if it softened.

  Chicken behind schedule (only 150-155°F at 6:15 PM): raise oven to 425°F, leave chicken uncovered. Check every 4-5 min. Potatoes can hold at 200°F in a foil-covered pan if needed.

  Something catastrophic (oven trouble, etc.): USDA-safe hold for a cooked chicken is 1-2 hours at room temp covered, or longer if you move it to the fridge and reheat — but quality drops fast past 30 min. Pull it earlier than you'd like, wrap in foil + a towel in a cooler if you have one, and call it a day.

VEGETABLE-HOT MATH (why this plan doesn't strand them)

  Potatoes: 45 min at 400°F from raw, 1.25-1.5" pieces. Pull at 6:28 PM, plate at 6:30 — they lose maybe 5°F, which is fine.
  Green beans: 6 min over high heat. Starting at 6:24 PM lands them on the plate at full heat.
  The hot-vegetable trap is holding them for an hour. The fix is sequencing the START of vegetable cooking to match service, not cooking them early.

OPTIONAL UPGRADES (only if you have prep time and want to)
  - Spatchcock the chicken (remove backbone, press flat). Cuts cook time to ~50-60 min at 425°F, more even doneness, crispier skin. But you must commit at the start — don't try to spatchcock after it's been roasting 30 min.
  - Compound herb butter under the breast skin. Adds flavor, doesn't change timing.
  - Salt potatoes the night before or at least 30 min ahead for crisper outsides.</mm:think>Let me know when the season shifts — I can re-tune this if you cook at altitude, switch to convection (drop temp ~25°F), or move to a larger bird.

EVIDENCE CLASSIFICATION

The headline pattern is consistent with bounded input-spike backlog: consumers healthy, errors zero, self-resolving when input normalizes, upstream (metrics-router, ingest-edge) at baseline, queue age came back down on its own. That is what a bounded backlog looks like from the outside. The one asymmetry that makes Cyrus's second-look request correct is that consumer throughput stayed FLAT rather than rising to a new plateau. A truly capacity-bound consumer under +31% input would normally show one of two signatures: (a) throughput climbing to its ceiling with per-batch latency stable, or (b) throughput flat at ceiling with per-batch latency rising. Flat items/sec at rising input can also mean nominal item/sec is unchanged but each item now demands more hidden work — retries, secondary writes, snapshot reload, batch reassembly. Closing as bounded capacity requires ruling out that hidden-work interpretation before declaring "consumer was just doing its best."

CHECKS BEFORE CLOSE

1. Retry and secondary-write counters during the burst window (per-item retry count, DLQ depth, secondary-write success rate). Per the 6/4 structural note on rollup: commit-tx guard is insufficient; partial completion is observable only through logs/metrics/retry/secondary-writes. Error=0 plus flat throughput is not enough — these counters are the only way to confirm no hidden work was added.

2. Per-batch latency / work-per-item distribution. Did +31% accepted points translate to longer per-batch processing time at the same items/sec? Look for processing-time p50/p95 shift, not just items/sec. If bytes/sec rose and per-batch latency rose proportionally, "flat throughput" is misleading and the consumers were actually working harder.

3. Snapshot / cold-load events in window. A snapshot reload during the burst absorbs consumer capacity without changing items/sec. Known Data Platform concern, not Infra.

4. Provenance / pipeline_run_id completeness on items processed during the burst — fail-closed per the 6/10 pattern: no event means missing, not assumed-ok. Any items with missing or partial provenance silently inflating queue age without progressing.

5. Whether nominal consumer throughput is actually at a documented ceiling. If no ceiling has been measured and published, "bounded capacity backlog" is currently unfalsifiable from metrics alone — that is itself a finding even if checks 1–4 come back clean.

DATA PLATFORM FOLLOW-UP (rollup owner — Cyrus)

- Measure and document steady-state consumer capacity (items/sec AND bytes/sec). Absence is why this alert was hard to classify.
- Add alerting on retry rate and secondary-write success rate, alongside the existing error-rate and queue-age alerts. Error=0 is necessary, not sufficient.
- Guard / alert on snapshot reload happening during burst window.
- Review batch-sizing policy under burst — whether items/sec is the honest throughput signal, or whether bytes/sec + per-batch latency is needed.
- Partition-scope check: confirm the +31% mapped to in-window partitions only. Carryover or out-of-window items would inflate queue age without representing real in-scope work.

INFRA CONCERN (separate track, ownership unchanged)

- Confirm metrics-router label_map integrity on the rollup ingest path. Per the shard-keeper label_map note: the worry is fake-clean cutover via a missed site. This is a due-diligence check — if mis-routing is found, the fix belongs to the metrics-router owner; rollup remains downstream of Cyrus.
- Confirm shard-keeper touch-matrix covers rollup routing / admin / validation sites for the burst window.
- Ingest-edge buffer and batch metrics at burst-window granularity, not just the baseline summary that already checked clean.

Recommend not closing the alert as bounded capacity until checks 1–4 come back clean. The flat-throughput signature is the one feature that keeps this from being obvious, and it is precisely the signature that the 6/4 commit-tx / partial-via-retry note was written to catch.

The math makes the trip expected, not a mystery.

Load calculation (120 V nominal):

- Kettle alone: 1,500 W ÷ 120 V = 12.5 A (83% of a 15 A breaker)
- Toaster alone: 1,450 W ÷ 120 V ≈ 12.08 A (81%)
- Combined: 2,950 W ÷ 120 V ≈ 24.6 A — about 164% of the breaker's 15 A rating

A standard 15 A breaker uses an inverse-time curve: roughly, 135% of rating trips in 1–3 hours, 150% trips in minutes, 200% trips in seconds. At ~165%, an immediate trip on both appliances running together is exactly what the breaker is designed to do. The breaker is doing its job, not failing.

Why your reuse plan matters

You already followed the right first step: unplug before reset, which prevents a second trip the moment you re-engage the breaker. The breaker held normally on reset with no load, and there is no heat, odor, discoloration, buzzing, or loose receptacle — those are the specific signs that would point at the wiring rather than the load. So the current evidence points at overload, not a fault.

How to reuse the two appliances safely

- Never run the kettle and toaster on the same 15 A circuit at the same time. Run them sequentially: one finishes (unplug or switch off) before the other starts. This is the simplest, lowest-risk change.
- Do not "share" the circuit with other kitchen loads while either is running. Coffee maker, microwave, toaster oven, slow cooker, Instant Pot, hair dryer, etc., add up fast. The microwave is usually on its own circuit, but verify yours.
- Treat the kettle and toaster as short-duration loads. They are not subject to the NEC 80% continuous-load rule in the strict sense, but it is a useful benchmark: 15 A × 120 V × 0.8 = 1,440 W continuous. Anything that pulls more than ~1,500 W on this circuit is at or above its design limit by itself, so never pair it.
- Keep the appliances plugged directly into the wall receptacle, not into a power strip, extension cord, or tap. High-wattage resistive loads through extra junctions are a common overheating source.
- If you want to use both back-to-back, unplug or power off the first before starting the second — do not rely on the breaker's tolerance.

If the circuit is labeled 20 A

A 20 A kitchen small-appliance circuit (common under NEC 210.11(C)(1) and 210.52(B)) would carry 16.7 A at 2,950 W combined — still overloaded, but a 20 A breaker will tolerate a 15 A draw better. The labels on your breaker panel are what count; trust the label, not the outlet count.

When to involve the landlord / property management

Contact management (not an electrician yet) if any of the following:

- The kitchen has only one 15 A small-appliance circuit. NEC requires at least two 20 A small-appliance circuits serving the kitchen countertop, and many older kitchens don't comply. This is a code/landlord issue, not a personal-equipment issue.
- The breaker trips again with only one appliance running (i.e., kettle alone trips a 15 A breaker, or toaster alone trips it). That means the appliance is drawing more than the circuit can supply, or the breaker is weak/sensitive — both worth reporting.
- The breaker trips repeatedly even after you switch to sequential use, suggesting a borderline load or a failing breaker.
- You notice any receptacle that is loose, warm, discolored, buzzing, or has a burning smell — at that point, stop using the outlet and notify management immediately, since that's a wiring/receptacle concern.

When to involve a licensed electrician

- Any of the above signs management escalates (loose, warm, discolored, buzzing, or sparking receptacle).
- Repeated nuisance trips after you've corrected usage — points to a failing breaker, undersized wiring, or a shared neutral issue.
- Lights dimming or flicker on the same circuit when the kettle or toaster kicks on — indicates voltage drop on possibly shared or undersized wiring.
- A breaker that will not reset, or that trips again with nothing plugged in — that's a fault, not an overload, and needs an electrician urgently.

If you live in a rental, the right sequence is: report the trip and what you observed to management in writing, let them decide whether to send an electrician, and keep using the appliances sequentially until they respond. Don't reset and walk away from a breaker that won't hold, and don't open the panel yourself.

Quick context read on Wes's solo scope and the metrics-router canary noise history, then I have what I need.

The signal shape you describe — 7/500s on 420 decisions, neighbors at zero, all sharing one internal synthetic request id, ~holiday evening idle traffic — is a textbook low-volume artifact, not a regression. It is the canonical reason pure error-rate panels page on idle traffic. Here is how I'd interpret it, what to verify, and a safer formulation.

Interpret the threshold crossing
- 1% on 420 decisions is 4.2 errors. The alert saw 7, so it fired. On 40,000 decisions per five minutes (your typical band) 7 errors is 0.0175% — nowhere near 1%. The crossing is purely a small-denominator artifact: low traffic amplifies tiny blips into a "high" ratio.
- Adjacent intervals at zero + shared synthetic request id point to a single transient failure on the synthetic probe itself, not a population-level incident. (OTel collector batch jitter, a probe auth token nearing rotation, a flaky dependency path the synthetic exercises more aggressively than real traffic, etc.)
- Latency and egress reconciliation normal means there is no signal that real customers are affected. The four user-visible signals in the canary runbook (p99 band, error rate, dropped writes, rollup-service lag) are the gating set; only the ratio panel moved, and only on the synthetic.
- This matches the pattern in rb_metrics_router_canary (2023-08-16 note, 2023-09-07 / 2023-09-27 warmup notes): treat a canary-class page that isolates to a specific traffic source or warmup window as evidence to investigate, not as an automatic rollback.

Immediate evidence checks (in this order)
1. Confirm the seven failures share the synthetic request id and that id is the only one failing in the window. If other request ids are also failing, the classification changes and you reopen as a real incident.
2. Pull p99, dropped writes, and rollup-service lag for the same five-minute window. If any of the four user-visible signals has moved off baseline, treat as a regression; do not rely on the ratio panel alone.
3. Check whether a scheduled synthetic-probe job was running at exactly that window (OTel collector batch window, probe auth-token rotation, a probe target that runs only on a schedule). If yes, the source is the probe — pause the probe, do not touch metrics-router.
4. Cross-check the deploy path: any config push or canary in flight on metrics-router in the last hour? If yes, follow rb_metrics_router_canary's three-step response (OTel collector batch window → p99 vs baseline → rollback via pipeline only if regression confirmed). If no, there is no deploy to roll back.
5. Confirm egress reconciliation stayed clean for the same window. If reconciliation drifted, the question is no longer the synthetic — it is a route-divergence question and the rollback set in the canary runbook applies.
6. Capture the synthetic request id and the failure timestamps in the canary note; this is exactly the kind of one-line addendum the runbook has been accumulating.

Safer alert formulation
The fix is to add a minimum-volume floor so the ratio only triggers when there is enough traffic for the ratio to mean something, and to add an absolute-count companion so a small fleet that is genuinely failing still pages. Two formulations; pick based on what your alerting layer supports:

Formulation A — dual-condition (recommended for most stacks):

  alert: MetricsRouterRouteErrorRateHigh
  for: 5m
  expr: |
    (
      sum(rate(metrics_router_route_decisions_total{status="500"}[5m])) /
      sum(rate(metrics_router_route_decisions_total[5m]))
      > 0.01
    )
    and
    (
      sum(rate(metrics_router_route_decisions_total[5m])) > 100
      or
      sum(rate(metrics_router_route_decisions_total{status="500"}[5m])) > 5
    )

  Read: the 1% ratio fires only when there are more than 100 route decisions in the 5m window OR more than 5 absolute 500s in the same window. The first clause protects against idle-traffic paging (your current case); the second clause protects against a small fleet that is genuinely failing (e.g. 4/50 = 8% on a canary pod still trips even though the ratio denominator is below 100). 5 is a starting point — tune against your typical absolute error band during non-quiet windows.

Formulation B — stacked windows (for noisier environments):

  expr: |
    (
      sum(rate(metrics_router_route_decisions_total{status="500"}[5m])) /
      sum(rate(metrics_router_route_decisions_total[5m]))
      > 0.01
    )
    and on() (
      sum(rate(metrics_router_route_decisions_total[5m])) > 100
      or
      sum_over_time(metrics_router_route_decisions_total{status="500"}[15m]) > 15
    )

  The 15-minute absolute count window catches persistent low-rate failure that the 5-minute ratio wouldn't surface if traffic is intermittent.

Tuning notes tied to your setup
- 100 decisions / 5m is conservative for a holiday evening but loose for normal business hours; if your typical 5-minute volume sits in the tens of thousands, raising the floor to 500 won't lose sensitivity on real incidents. The point is "above the synthetic-probe noise floor," not a fixed number.
- Keep the 1% ratio as the sensitivity floor for real-failure detection; don't relax it. The fix is the denominator gate and the absolute-count companion, not a looser ratio.
- Make sure the synthetic probe is labeled separately (`synth=true` or a `probe_id` label) so future formulations can suppress it explicitly. Cardinality Guardrails first-cut guidance keeps bounded classification labels in metrics and pushes raw probe identifiers to logs — the same shape applies here: a `probe_class=internal_synthetic` label is bounded and cheap; the raw request id stays in logs. This also lets the alert exclude the probe without affecting real-traffic sensitivity, which is cleaner than the dual-condition approach.
- The canary runbook's rollback set (active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, dropped series off baseline, reload failure, restart) is unchanged — this alert work does not relax any of those gates, and the deploy-pipeline-only rollback rule still applies. If the evidence checks above reopen as a regression, follow rb_metrics_router_canary, not this alert.

Bottom line: this evening's page is a small-denominator artifact on a single synthetic probe, and the right answer is to tune the alert — not to chase a regression that isn't there. # Right-forearm conservative graded-loading plan (2024-12-28)

Given that undercling simulation is now reproducing symptoms for the second time, I read this as residual irritability of the common flexor origin / flexor-pronator mass near the medial epicondyle — not a tear, fracture, or nerve compression. The plan below respects that the issue isn't healed enough to undercling, while still moving you forward on everything else.

Throughout: "session pain" = the highest number you record during or immediately after the load. "Next-day pain" = pain at rest the morning after. Pain scale is 0–10.

## Daily baseline self-check (start each day before any load)

  - Resting pain at neutral wrist (0/10 expected).
  - 30-second lengthened flexor stretch (elbow straight, wrist extended, palm up).
  - 10 light towel squeezes (no resistance).
  - 10 light resisted wrist flexions (≤1 kg, no elbow bend).
  - 10–15 second deadhang on a large jug.
  - Easy movement for 5 minutes, then re-check resting pain.

All items must be 0–1/10 and free of any red-flag symptom before you proceed with that day's planned phase.

## Phase 1 — Tendon loading + unload (days 1–7, no climbing)

Goal: build tendon tolerance with isometric / slow-eccentric wrist flexion, prove undercling sim drops to ≤1/10.

  - Daily: 3 sets × 10 slow-eccentric wrist flexions with a light dumbbell (≤1–2 kg), 3-second descent. Elbow supported on a table, neutral forearm.
  - Daily: 3 × 30-second sub-maximal isometric wrist flexions at ~30% effort against the other hand.
  - 3 × per week: isometric deadhang on a large jug, 3 × 20 sec, body weight only.
  - 1 × per week: the undercling simulation (palm up, fingers in a half-crimp against a table edge or doorframe, gentle 5–10 sec load) — record the number. Target: ≤1/10 by day 7.

Pain during Phase 1 should stay ≤2/10 and resolve within minutes. If undercling sim isn't ≤1/10 by end of Phase 1, hold at Phase 1 and arrange eval.

## Phase 2 — Open-hand hangboard (every other day, days 8–14, still no climbing)

Only enter Phase 2 if Phase 1 criteria are met and the day-of self-check is clean.

  - 20mm or 30mm jugs, open-hand only, no crimp, no half-crimp.
  - 3 rounds × 4 hangs × 7 sec on / 53 sec off.
  - Add weight in 2.5 kg increments only if previous session stayed 0–1/10 with no next-day pain.

Still simulate undercling (load only, no climbing move) every ~3 days to confirm trend continues down.

## Phase 3 — Easy climbing reintroduction (2× per week, days 15–21)

  - Limit volume: 4–6 easy routes per session, well below max grade, bouldering or top-rope.
  - Footwork-first mindset, open-hand grip default, avoid full crimp and avoid any undercling, side-pinch, or compression hold.
  - Cap sessions at 45 minutes, stop on the first session pain ≥3/10.
  - No climbing on consecutive days during this phase.

## Phase 4 — Undercling-specific exposure (only after eval, days 22+)

Hold this phase until you've had a sports-med or PT consult, because this is the second recurrence and the pattern itself is the problem.

  - Resume the actual undercling pattern on a steep, large-hold problem, body-weight only, 3–5 short efforts per session.
  - Load progression: body weight → +2.5 kg → +5 kg, only if previous session was 0/10 at the time and 0/10 next morning.
  - Full undercling sessions integrated only when you can do 3 successive body-weight efforts at 0/10 in-session and 0/10 the next morning.

## Delay progression if any of these appear

  - Session pain reaches 3/10 or higher.
  - Undercling sim rises by ≥1 point from your baseline.
  - Next-day resting pain >0/10.
  - Ache lingers >24 hours after a session.
  - Stiffness that doesn't warm out in the first 10 minutes of easy movement.
  - Return of any ordinary-use pain, waking pain, or any red-flag symptom.

If any of the above appear, drop back one phase and stay there until two clean sessions in a row.

## Arrange sports-medicine or physical-therapy evaluation if

  - Undercling sim has not dropped to ≤1/10 by end of Phase 1 (10 days).
  - Any hangboard load reproduces symptoms (you should be sub-clinical at Phase 2).
  - The pain location shifts from the diffuse forearm flexor pattern to the medial epicondyle itself, the forearm muscle belly, or the wrist joint.
  - Any red flag appears: swelling, bruising, numbness, tingling, grip weakness, clicking/snapping, deformity, or persistent next-day pain with resisted flexion or pronation.
  - Waking pain at rest returns.
  - A third recurrence of the undercling pattern.

Prefer a sports-medicine physician or a physical therapist with climbing-injury / tendinopathy experience, and tell them: second recurrence of undercling-provoked forearm pain, 1 week of full rest with incomplete resolution, current 0/10 at rest, 2/10 on undercling sim, normal neurovascular exam by self-check.

## Practical adjustments for this plan

  - Keep climbing journal entries that note session pain, next-day pain, and any undercling exposure — even a sim.
  - Don't warm up into underclings before the eval has cleared the pattern.
  - If you start a bouldering session and feel the forearm "talk" in the first 30 minutes, end the session there.

Pre-update checklist, install sequence, first-restart verification, and recovery path. Use in order; do not skip verification steps because each one narrows the recovery options if something goes wrong.

==============================================================
PRE-UPDATE CHECKLIST  (verify EVERY line before launching)
==============================================================

Final state confirmation:
  [ ] 41 GB free  vs  28 GB required  →  ~13 GB headroom (acceptable)
  [ ] External backup: not just "last successful" — open the backup
        tool and run VERIFY on the destination. Time Machine does this
        automatically on the backup drive; third-party tools have an
        explicit Verify.
  [ ] AC connected, no sleep/power timers, lid will stay open
  [ ] No other pending installs or reboots queued
  [ ] Workshop recording, slides, source tree, and Application Support
        folders still present and openable

Record current state (so you can prove nothing silently changed):
  [ ] OS build + version (System Settings → General → About)
  [ ] Machine serial, Apple ID account in use, FileVault status
  [ ] Time Machine destination name + free space on that drive
  [ ] Critical apps list — note license/activation state for anything
        not in the App Store (Adobe, MS 365, IDE, audio plugins)

Recovery media — this is the "preserve a recovery path" work:
  [ ] Boot into Recovery once (Cmd+R on Intel; hold power button on
        Apple Silicon). Confirm "Restore from Time Machine" is offered
        AND your backup drive is listed. Restart back to normal boot.
  [ ] If you have a bootable clone (Carbon Copy Cloner / SuperDuper),
        confirm it boots: hold Option at startup, select the clone
        volume, log in, shut down.
  [ ] Confirm 2FA device is at hand and charged (Apple ID, Google,
        password manager, anything that may re-prompt on first boot).

Pre-flight hygiene:
  [ ] Quit filesystem-hooking software: Backblaze / CrashPlan / other
        backup agents, antivirus, VPN clients with kernel extensions,
        disk-cleanup / sync daemons you do not need during the install.
  [ ] Eject non-essential external drives.
  [ ] Note log location: /var/log/install.log (you'll read it after).

==============================================================
INSTALLATION SEQUENCE
==============================================================

1. Save and close everything.
2. Launch from System Settings → Software Update, or run the downloaded
   package. Confirm the target build and required-space number one
   more time — if the updater now asks for MORE than 28 GB, stop and
   free more space.
3. If asked "Install now" vs "Install later" — choose Install now so
   the staged reboot is explicit and you are present for it.
4. Do not interact with the machine during the prepare and write
   phases. Order of operations the installer runs:
       a. Prepare  (reversible file staging)
       b. Write new system files
       c. Prompt for restart — confirm
       d. Post-restart "completing installation" with 1–3 auto-restarts
5. Keep AC connected throughout. Do not close the lid.
6. Do not sign in to iCloud or open heavy apps until the verification
   section confirms the build is healthy.

==============================================================
FIRST-RESTART VERIFICATION  (in this order)
==============================================================

1. Boot lands on login screen → log in normally.
2. System Settings → General → About → new build string matches what
   the updater advertised.
3. Console.app → search "install" → confirm the install.log ends with
   "Install completed successfully" and contains no "failed" / "error"
   / "aborted" lines for this build.
4. Disk Utility → select internal volume → First Aid → Run → "OK".
5. Terminal:  diskutil info /  → look for a recent APFS sealed-system
   snapshot. macOS keeps a pre-update snapshot specifically so you can
   revert; confirm one exists for this install.
6. Launch critical apps ONE AT A TIME, quitting between each:
       - Workshop recording app
       - Slides app
       - Source / IDE
       - Browser (then trigger a 2FA prompt deliberately to confirm
         the device works)
7. Open Time Machine → "Back Up Now" → let it complete. This is your
   post-update snapshot in the backup system.
8. Confirm /Library/Application Support and ~/Library/Application
   Support folders you listed earlier still exist and the owning apps
   launch cleanly.
9. Activity Monitor → CPU tab: after 10 minutes idle, nothing pegged
   at 100% sustained. Spotlight indexing and Photos analysis are normal
   for a while; high sustained CPU is not.

If all nine pass, the install is healthy. If any fail, go to Recovery.

==============================================================
RECOVERY PATH  (escalate top-down; do not stack fixes)
==============================================================

A. App-level only (build is healthy, one app broken):
   Update that app; if vendor-current, send the install.log excerpt.
   Do not roll back the OS for a single broken app.

B. OS feature broken but boots:
   - Disk Utility First Aid on the volume.
   - Safe boot (hold Shift at startup) to clear caches, then reboot
     normally.
   - If still broken: boot to Recovery → "Restore From Time Machine
     Backup" → pick the snapshot taken just before this install.
     On Apple Silicon, "Reinstall macOS" from Recovery preserves data
     and is often the cleaner option when the issue is system-level.

C. Won't boot / kernel panic / progress bar stuck > 2 hrs with zero
   disk activity:
   1. Force-shutdown. Power on into Recovery
      (Cmd+R on Intel / hold power on Apple Silicon).
   2. Disk Utility → First Aid on internal volume.
   3. If First Aid fails → restart into Internet Recovery
      (Cmd+Opt+R on Intel / keep holding power on Silicon).
   4. Recovery → "Restore From Time Machine Backup" using the
      verified external backup you ran pre-install.
   5. If the backup is unavailable or fails mid-restore: boot your
      clone (Option / hold power on Silicon), then Migration
      Assistant → transfer user data into a clean install performed
      from Recovery.

D. Data-only concern (install otherwise fine):
   Boot to Recovery, open Terminal, mount the data volume read-only,
   and copy what you need to an external drive. Or Target Disk Mode
   (Intel) for full read/write access from another machine.

Decision rule: if the failure is fixable from inside the running OS,
fix it there. If not, you have three independent restore paths —
verified Time Machine backup, sealed-system snapshot, and (if
prepared) bootable clone — pick one, do not combine them.

==============================================================
DO NOT DO DURING INSTALL
==============================================================
  - Close the lid or unplug AC.
  - Force-shutdown unless the installer is hung > 2 hrs with zero
    disk activity (verify via Console / Activity Monitor first).
  - Run Disk Utility First Aid on the system volume while the
    installer is mid-write — it will conflict.
  - Reset NVRAM / SMC mid-install — those are recovery actions,
    not pre-install actions.

A 2 mm case split is real swelling — gas has built up inside, so treat it as a thermal-runaway risk even though it's quiet now. Plain-text outline below.

ISOLATE IN THE APARTMENT (do these now)
  1. Leave it unpowered and don't try to reseat the case. Don't charge, don't test the button, don't drop it.
  2. Move it to the least-flammable spot you have: a tile floor, concrete patio, inside a metal pot/pan/ammo can, or set it on a ceramic plate/tray. A metal bucket partly filled with clean dry sand, kitty litter, or vermiculite is the best at-home containment — sand smothers and soaks heat if it vents.
  3. Keep it away from: paper, fabrics, upholstered furniture, beds, curtains, gas range, radiator, direct sun, window with afternoon sun. Out of reach of Kibo and kids.
  4. Don't seal it in an airtight box, ziplock, or airtight bucket — if it vents, pressure can build or moisture trap. A loose-fitting metal container with a slightly cracked lid is fine.
  5. If it's currently on a wood shelf, desk, or near anything flammable, move it now. The time to act is while it's still cool.
  6. Tape over the USB ports with a strip of electrical tape (no bare metal touching metal during carry).
  7. Open a window in that room for ventilation; don't sleep with it in the bedroom.
  8. Plan to remove it from the apartment within 24–48 hours — don't store it indefinitely indoors.

HANDLE AND TRANSPORT
  - Carry in the metal pot/bucket with sand around it, or a rigid plastic tub (ammo can, small toolbox) lined so it can't shift. The goal: no loose battery rattling, no pressure on the swollen side.
  - Don't put it in a backpack, purse, or pocket. Don't wrap it in a towel and hold it — a towel soaked in solvent off-gas is a wick.
  - Drive it in the trunk, not the cabin, on a non-flammable surface (metal tray, tile, sand-filled container). Don't leave the car closed in the sun.
  - Take the most direct route. Don't leave it in a parked car while you shop.
  - Do not fly with it, and do not put it in checked luggage — swollen cells are explicitly excluded.
  - Keep your phone within reach; if it vents in the car, stop, exit, and call 911 from outside.

DISPOSAL (not household trash, not curbside recycling)
  - Best: a Call2Recycle drop-off. https://call2recycle.org/locator — enter ZIP; most Home Depot, Lowe's, Best Buy, Staples, and many Apple/Verizon stores accept loose lithium power banks for free. Call ahead to confirm "damaged/swollen OK."
  - Next: your municipal Household Hazardous Waste (HHW) facility or a scheduled HHW pickup day. Many accept swollen cells specifically because regular streams won't.
  - Earth911.com is a good backup search by "lithium-ion batteries."
  - Some local fire stations accept — call first, not all do.
  - Mail-back: Call2Recycle and a few vendors (Battery Solutions, Big Green Box) sell pre-labeled UN-rated mailers; this is the right path if no drop-off is nearby, but expect shipping cost and lead time.
  - Before handoff: tape over ports, keep it in the sand-filled rigid container for the trip, hand it directly to staff and tell them it's swollen so they can route it as damaged goods.
  - Do not put it in regular trash, recycling, or e-waste bins — compactor and sorting fires are the most common downstream cause.

EMERGENCY SIGNS — CHANGE THE RESPONSE TO: EVACUATE, CLOSE THE DOOR, CALL 911
  - Any hissing, popping, crackling, whistling, or bubbling sound
  - Any odor: sweet/solvent/ether/glue-like, acrid, or "chemical" smell — don't wait to identify it
  - Any smoke or visible vapor: white, gray, yellow, or black
  - Sudden heat — warm or hot to the touch — or the sand/contents feeling warm
  - Swelling visibly increasing (case gap widening, surface bulging) over minutes
  - Discoloration, soot, charring, melted plastic, liquid leak
  - Sparks, arcing, flame, or glowing spots
  - The unit being moved or bumped and then behaving abnormally within the next hour

If any of those happen:
  1. Get people and pets out of the room/ apartment. Close the door behind you to slow the fire.
  2. Call 911 and say "lithium-ion battery fire" — they bring different extinguishers and need to know not to expect a normal electrical fire.
  3. Don't try to grab it once it's venting or flaming. If the fire is small and you have a Class D extinguisher or a large amount of sand, you can smother from a safe distance; otherwise let it burn in the contained area and evacuate.
  4. Consumer lithium-ion fires can be cooled with lots of water (unlike lithium-metal), but the priority is evacuation over firefighting. Don't breathe the smoke — the off-gases (HF, CO, etc.) are toxic.
  5. After the event, ventilate the room for hours before re-entering, and tell the responders exactly what the device was and where it had been stored.

Quiet today doesn't mean safe later — a swollen 18650/21700 cell can vent spontaneously or from a small jolt. The isolation + 24-hour removal plan is the right move.

Plan assumes the most likely cause is mild dietary GI upset from the fat load, with pancreatitis as a secondary possibility worth watching for over the next 24-72 hours. Two loose stools without vomiting, blood, lethargy, or pain is the right setting for watchful home care, not the ER.

FEEDING (next 24-48 hours)
  - Skip the regular breakfast. Hold regular food entirely until stool firms up.
  - Bland diet only: boiled skinless, boneless chicken breast (rinsed, no oil/salt/fat) + plain white rice. Roughly 1 part chicken to 2-3 parts rice.
  - Portion smaller than a normal meal. Split into 3-4 small offerings over the day rather than one or two large ones; an irritated gut handles small volumes better.
  - No treats, no table scraps, no dairy, no fat, no bones, no rich food. If you want a probiotic, a canine-specific one is fine; skip the yogurt unless you already know he tolerates dairy.
  - Reintroduce regular food only after stool is formed for ~24 hours. Transition over 2-3 days: 75% bland / 25% regular, then 50/50, then 25/75, then full regular.

HYDRATION
  - Fresh water available at all times, but offer small frequent sips rather than a full bowl at once. A large bolus on an irritated stomach can trigger vomiting and lose you the hydration gain.
  - Watch intake: drinking normally is reassuring; refusing water or drinking very little is a concern.
  - Quick dehydration check you can do at home: lift the lip - gums should be pink and slick, not tacky or pale. Pinch a bit of skin over the shoulders; it should snap back in under 2 seconds.

MONITORING - WHAT'S REASSURING
  - Stool firms up over 24-48 hours, frequency returns to his baseline.
  - Energy and alertness stay normal; he wants to walk and engage.
  - Appetite returns by the next normal mealtime.
  - Gums pink, posture normal, no belly-guarding when you lift or gently press the abdomen.

CALL THE VET, SAME-DAY (not ER, but don't wait)
  - Loose stool persists past 48 hours or is getting more frequent (more than 4-5 episodes in 24 hours).
  - Any blood in stool: fresh red streaks or, more concerning, black/tarry/melena.
  - Mucus in stool becomes prominent.
  - Vomiting starts, even once or twice.
  - He refuses food entirely for more than 24 hours.
  - Mild lethargy beyond just being a bit quiet - sleeping more than usual, less interested in you or his routine.
  - Mild tenderness when you gently press his belly, or a slight hunched posture.

GO TO URGENT CARE / ER NOW (any one of these)
  - Repeated vomiting that won't stop, especially unproductive retching (heaving with nothing coming up) - this is the bloat/GDV pattern and is always an emergency regardless of cause.
  - Abdomen looks visibly swollen, feels tight, or is painful to touch.
  - Pale, white, yellow, or tacky/sticky gums.
  - Collapse, weakness, wobbliness, disorientation, or sudden restlessness he can't settle from.
  - Large amount of blood in stool, or black tarry stool.
  - Signs of severe dehydration: gums dry, skin tent stays up, eyes look sunken.
  - Shaking/trembling, panting at rest, or vocalizing when picked up - any of these mean significant pain.
  - You later realize he got into something else (bones are the big one - cooked bones can perforate and may not show signs for hours).

WHEN YOU CALL OR GO IN, HAVE THIS READY
  - Time and number of loose stools, color, any blood or mucus.
  - Last normal stool, when he last ate normally, what he ate.
  - Whether he has vomited at all and how many times.
  - Water intake estimate.
  - Gum color and his energy right now.
  - Rectal temperature if you can take it safely (normal dog: 101-102.5 F).

The single biggest signal that this is "fine, keep watching" is steady improvement over 24-48 hours: stools firming, energy normal, appetite back, no new symptoms. The single biggest signal to escalate is any new symptom appearing - especially vomiting, blood, belly pain, or behavior change - because two mild signs often become obvious in retrospect when a third one shows up.

CLASSIFICATION: Bounded maintenance behavior — snapshot lag during active compaction, currently self-recovering. The evidence fits the maintenance pattern; it is not yet signed off as bounded.

Why this reads as bounded maintenance:

  - Snapshot age breach (19-21m vs 15m warning) is brief and self-resolving (declining).
  - Scope is narrow: 3 of 480 shards (~0.6%).
  - Co-occurs with active compaction workers, which legitimately compete for I/O and slow snapshot progress.
  - Integrity invariants hold: lease convergence complete, no stale-write, no split-generation.
  - Downstream signals clean: 0 read/write errors, client latency at baseline.
  - Disk headroom present (<61%).

VERIFICATION CONDITIONS — must all hold to keep the classification as bounded:

  V1. Self-heal completes within a bounded window. Snapshot age returns to ≤15m warning line within 2× the normal snapshot interval. Need to confirm what the normal snapshot interval is for this fleet.
  V2. Scope stays bounded. Lagging shard count does not grow beyond ~5 (1%). Growth = pattern, not blip.
  V3. Compaction is genuinely progressing, not merely labeled "active." last_compaction_timestamp advancing, compaction_queue_depth draining, files merged. An "active" worker that is stuck is a different signal entirely.
  V4. Integrity invariants remain intact across the next observation window:
        - stale_write_detected = false
        - split_generation_detected = false
        - lease holders stable, no term bumps on any of the three shards
  V5. Downstream signals stay clean for one full snapshot interval after recovery: read error rate = 0, write error rate = 0, p99 client latency ≤ baseline.
  V6. Disk utilization stays <70% and not climbing. 61% is fine; the question is trajectory, not level.
  V7. Read amplification unchanged. No spike in concurrent snapshot-holding readers — that would extend retention beyond expected and is its own failure mode.
  V8. No correlated degradation on secondary shard-keeper surfaces (routing, admin/validation read sites). Per the earlier label_map leak concern: a clean primary surface with a degraded secondary is the fake-clean pattern to watch for.

ESCALATION CONDITIONS — any one of these flips to incident immediately, do not wait for a second signal:

  E1. Snapshot age crosses the hard SLO line. Need the value (typically 30m or 2× warning).
  E2. Snapshot age >15m persists longer than 2× the snapshot interval without continuing to decline.
  E3. Lagging shard count grows beyond 5, or the lag spreads across distinct compaction groups / leaders / hosts / disk pools. Clustering weakens the bounded reading.
  E4. Any integrity signal appears: stale_write_detected true, split_generation_detected true, lease holder change, term bump.
  E5. Read errors, write errors, or p99 latency drift above baseline — even small.
  E6. Compaction workers not making forward progress despite the "active" label (queue depth stuck, no merge activity, last_compaction_timestamp frozen).
  E7. Disk utilization crosses 75% or I/O saturation climbs (await/io trending up).
  E8. Snapshot age "declining" but the rate is too slow or stalls before crossing back under the warning line.

GAPS IN THE ALERT — things not stated that should be confirmed before signing off, because absence of a signal in the alert is not the same as absence of the signal in the system:

  - The hard SLO line value (15m is the warning; the error/hard threshold is missing).
  - Normal snapshot interval (needed to define "brief").
  - Compaction progress rate, not just active/idle status.
  - Read amplification / concurrent snapshot-holding readers.
  - Whether the three shards share a compaction group, leader, host, or disk pool.
  - Whether stale-write / split-generation are actively checked by the alert, or just absent from it. The instrumentation-gap risk is the same one that surfaced with the label_map leak.

Decision rule: if V1-V8 hold and E1-E8 stay false for one full snapshot interval past recovery, treat as bounded maintenance and close out. If any single E condition fires, escalate now. If any of the GAPS cannot be filled, that itself is a soft escalation — sign-off requires the surfaces the alert does not cover to be confirmed clean by independent read.

Annual premium         $204                    $186                   -$18 (savings)
