DOES $18 COMPENSATE? (the math)

On the deductible alone:
  Extra out-of-pocket per claim: $500
  Annual savings: $18
  If you file one claim this year: net is -$482 ($18 saved - $500 extra out of pocket)
  Break-even on the deductible change requires ~28 years of zero claims to offset a single $500 extra payment.

On loss of use:
  $4,000 less coverage for temporary housing and meals if displaced.
  At $200/night hotel plus meals: $12,000 covers ~60 days; $8,000 covers ~40 days.
  At $150/night: $12,000 covers ~80 days; $8,000 covers ~53 days.
  Anything past those thresholds comes out of pocket on the competing quote.

Combined worst case (one claim + displacement over 40 days):
  Net protection reduction: $500 + $4,000 = $4,500
  Annual savings: $18
  Ratio: ~250x worse than the savings.

Realistic 5-year view:
  Zero claims, no displacement: +$90 in your pocket (savings win, but you've given up coverage for nothing you used).
  One claim, <40 day displacement: net -$482.
  One claim, >40 day displacement: net ~-$4,482.
  Expected value of the additional coverage on the renewal (lower deductible + more loss-of-use + likely water backup) is almost certainly far above $18/year for a typical renter.

EXACT COVERAGE QUESTIONS TO RESOLVE BEFORE DECIDING

On the current renewal (pull the full declarations page; the items below are not visible from your summary):
  1. Personal property basis: replacement cost or actual cash value (ACV)? ACV can pay 30-60% less than replacement on older electronics, furniture, and gear.
  2. Water backup / sump pump failure: included, limited, or excluded? Many policies exclude by default; if the renewal excludes it, that's the same posture as the competing quote on this one line.
  3. Off-premises theft coverage for bicycles and gear: what sublimit? Default is often $1,000, which is low for a year-round rider.
  4. Electronics / computer / camera / phone sublimit: what cap inside the $40,000 personal-property limit?
  5. Jewelry, watch, firearm, collectibles sublimits.
  6. Pet liability and pet-damage coverage (relevant given Kibo — dog-bite exposure on a $300k liability policy is the single most likely large claim in your household).
  7. Medical payments to others and identity-theft coverage (often free add-ons).
  8. Inflation guard / automatic annual coverage increases built in.
  9. All discounts applied: claims-free, security system, paperless, autopay, bundle. The $204 may already include them; the $186 may not.
 10. Liability structure: $300k per occurrence or aggregate? Any umbrella eligibility?

On the competing quote (request a full declarations page or binder before signing):

  2. Confirm water backup is excluded; ask the carrier what the endorsement costs to add it back.
  3. Confirm off-premises bike-theft sublimit (often $1,000 default) and whether it can be raised.

  6. Inflation guard included.

  8. Whether loss-of-use can be raised from $8,000 to $12,000 and what that costs (likely $5-$15/year, which would erase most of the $18 savings and make the comparison clean).

  - If the renewal fails two or more of the above checks, use those gaps to negotiate the renewal down toward (or past) the competitor's price, or add endorsements, rather than switching to a quote that's weaker on the items you can already see.
  - Switch only if the renewal is materially worse on the items the competing quote did state (it currently isn't on premium, property limit, or liability) AND the endorsements to fix the renewal would cost more than $18/year plus the $4,000 loss-of-use gap.

Quick read: Kibo is showing classic noise anxiety but is currently stable — responsive, taking treats, breathing normally between bangs, no danger signs. The closet he's choosing is actually a good sign; he's self-selecting a den-like space. Work with that, don't move him.

SAFE RETREAT — DO NOW (next 15 min)
- Let him have the bedroom closet. Put his bed in there if it isn't already.
- Close the closet door (or hang a thick blanket over the opening) to darken and muffle.
- Move the white-noise machine in with him; set it loud enough to mask mid-range bangs (fireworks are mostly mid-frequency).
- Add a worn t-shirt or small unwashed blanket of yours in with him — familiar scent calms more than a clean bed.
- If you have an Adaptil diffuser, plug it in near the closet now (takes ~30 min to build up). If not, skip — don't run out to buy.
- Thundershirt / anxiety wrap: only if you already own one and he's worn it before. Do NOT introduce one cold tonight.
- Close all interior doors so he can't bolt through the apartment if a loud one hits.
- Move any breakables or sharp-edged items off the floor of wherever he's pacing.
- Charge your phone, keep it on you, and save your nearest 24-hour emergency vet number now (not the regular vet — the ER). Many cities have specific NYE surges and ERs fill fast.

YOUR ENERGY
- Act boring. No soothing cooing, no "it's okay baby," no eye contact when he's stressed. Just sit quietly in the room with him, scroll your phone, occasionally drop a treat near him without fanfare. Calm + boring = faster down-regulation.

FOOD & WATER
- Offer a light meal in the next hour — not a full dinner. A stressed dog with a full stomach on a noisy night is a vomiting risk. Small portion of his normal food, or skip dinner entirely and just use treats for distraction.
- Keep water available in the closet, but don't push him to drink. He can rehydrate after the noise dies down.
- No new foods, no table scraps, no rich treats tonight.

BATHROOM TRIPS
- One short walk, on Y-harness + short leash, before the big crescendo (most US cities peak ~midnight).
- Pick the quietest block available. Avoid the park entrance and any wide-open intersection.
- Go out for business only — pee/poop, straight back in. No loitering, no sniffing tours, no "letting him work it off."
- If he refuses to walk or freezes, do not drag. Carry a small towel under your arm so you can scoop him up and bring him back inside if needed (only if he's small/medium — you know his size).
- After ~11 PM, skip walks unless he absolutely insists. He can hold it; the risk of him bolting at a bang outside is worse than one missed walk.
- If he does potty inside from stress, no correction — clean it silently and move on. Stress urination is not a behavior problem.

DISTRESS RED FLAGS — CALL ER VET NOW
- Gums: pale, white, blue, gray, or bright brick red (lift his lip and check now while he's calm, so you know his baseline color)
- Collapse, wobbling, or sudden inability to stand
- Non-productive retching or dry heaving (especially in a deep-chested dog — bloat/GDV risk)
- Repeated vomiting, or any blood in vomit or stool
- Seizure (paddling, loss of consciousness, loss of bladder/bowel)
- Unresponsive to you or to his name when normally responsive
- Bloated, hard, or distended abdomen
- Bleeding from anywhere
- Body feels hot to the touch (rectal temp >103°F if you can check) AND he's panting hard with no cooling
- Excessive drooling + extreme restlessness + retching together = ER

DISTRESS YELLOW FLAGS — CALL REGULAR VET TOMORROW
- Won't eat or drink for 12+ hours after the noise ends
- Hides and won't come out for 4+ hours after the last bang
- Persistent shaking that doesn't resolve within an hour of quiet
- Indoor accidents continuing into the daytime
- Limping, lethargy, or appetite loss tomorrow

DURING DEVIKA'S ABSENCE (7 PM onward)
- Stay in or near the bedroom. Don't run a bath, don't cook something loud, don't vacuum — anything that adds noise you can control.
- Text her a quick "Kibo anxious, handling it, ER number saved, will update if anything changes" so she isn't checking in worried. Keep it short.
- If a red flag hits: call ER first, then text Devika. Don't drive solo with a seizing or collapsing dog if you can avoid it — many ERs will send guidance by phone while someone else drives.

AFTER THE NOISE ENDS (past midnight)
- Don't immediately re-engage him. Let him come out on his own.
- Once he's calm and the bangs have stopped for 30+ min, offer a small meal and a quiet walk.
- Tomorrow morning: call your regular vet and ask about prescribing an anxiety med for next NYE / thunderstorms. Sileo (dexmedetomidine oral) or trazodone are common options; getting it on file now means you're ready next time.

North Pier token-workflow context confirmed from memory: Anya owns the lane; canonical is pinned in CI; generator is pinned in the shared CI manifest; compatibility table pairs schema-2 ↔ 0.8.x generator, schema-3 ↔ 0.9.x+; drift check blocks hand-edits; iOS is one platform target alongside web/CSS/Android/docs.

Below is the smallest discriminating sequence. No manual edits to the generated iOS file at any stage; every step pushes the diagnosis upstream of the artifact.

================================================================
Stage 1 — Stale generated output (cheapest; run first)
================================================================
Goal: verify the iOS artifact was actually rewritten by the run Anya calls "clean."

  a. Hash + mtime the iOS artifact in generated/. Same for the web artifact. Compare both to the run's start timestamp.
  b. Run the generator with its verbose / target-list mode and confirm "iOS" appears in the emitted-targets list for this invocation.
  c. Confirm the iOS output path the generator writes to is the same path the consumer (or drift check) reads from. North Pier's known shape: tokens.css is copied into generated/ before platform JSON is validated; the iOS target path should be in that same generated/ tree.

Reads:
  - iOS mtime/hash predates the run, OR iOS not in emitted list, OR write-path ≠ read-path  →  STALE OUTPUT. The "clean run" did not actually rewrite the iOS artifact (build-pipeline cache, target skipped, output dir mismatch).
  - iOS mtime/hash is from this run AND path matches  →  rule out stale; proceed.

================================================================
Stage 2 — Generator-version drift
================================================================
Goal: confirm the generator version actually invoked is the one pinned and is compatible with the canonical's schema line.

  a. Record the generator version the run actually resolved to — from the lockfile the run consumed, not from a local checkout. (Anya's pin in the shared CI manifest is what should govern.)
  b. Compare that resolved version to the pin in the shared CI manifest. Mismatch = manifest drift.
  c. Cross-check the resolved version against the North Pier compatibility table:
       schema-2 canonical  ↔  generator 0.8.x (^0.8.4 <0.9.0)
       schema-3 canonical  ↔  generator 0.9.x+
     If the canonical's schema line and the resolved generator's line disagree, the iOS platform adapter may be reading a transform schema that silently drops or mis-resolves the spacing token.

Reads:
  - resolved ≠ manifest pin, OR schema lines disagree  →  GENERATOR-VERSION DRIFT. The iOS transform is the layer that doesn't see the new value, even though web does.
  - resolved = pin and schema lines agree  →  rule out drift; proceed.

================================================================
Stage 3 — Canonical-package problem (deepest)
================================================================
Goal: determine whether the canonical's iOS-visible surface actually carries the new spacing value. "Canonical looks right" can still be true for web and false for iOS if the canonical has platform-specific scoping, alias targets, or overrides that the iOS transform honors differently.

  a. Run the generator in a resolve / inspect mode for the iOS platform only. Have it print the post-alias-resolution, post-iOS-transform view of the spacing token (canonical name → iOS name → resolved value).
  b. Run the same resolve for the web platform; print the analogous view.
  c. Compare the iOS-resolved value to the canonical's spacing value, and to the web-resolved value.

Reads:
  - web-resolved = new value, iOS-resolved = old value (or spacing token absent from the iOS view)  →  CANONICAL-PACKAGE PROBLEM. The spacing token's placement, alias target, or platform scoping diverges between iOS and web reads — e.g., the token is keyed under a category the iOS adapter filters out, or an iOS-specific override in the canonical still points to the old value.
  - iOS-resolved = new value AND the on-disk iOS file still shows old value  →  none of the three. Generator's write path for iOS is broken; separate triage as a generator bug, not drift and not canonical.

================================================================
Decision rule
================================================================
  Stage 1 fail                                  → stale generated output
  Stage 1 pass + Stage 2 fail                   → generator-version drift
  Stage 1 pass + Stage 2 pass + iOS-resolved old → canonical-package problem
  Stage 1 pass + Stage 2 pass + iOS-resolved new, file old → generator write-path bug (escalate, not in scope here)

================================================================
Anchors each stage records (so Anya can hand the result back without re-running)
================================================================
  - iOS artifact path + sha256 + mtime
  - canonical package version + schema line
  - generator version (lockfile-resolved) + manifest pin
  - verbose/resolve-mode output for web and iOS spacing token

That's the bounded sanity check: three stages, each independently conclusive, no manual edits to the iOS file, and the artifact on disk is only consulted as evidence — never as the fix surface.

Off-bike inspection sequence. Tools that help: chain wear gauge (Park CC-3.2 or similar), cassette lockring tool for your freehub standard (Shimano HG = TL-LR11 / FR-5 + pin spanner; XD/XDR = specific tools). Without them, the visual checks still get you most of the way.

1. Wheel security (do this first - it's the only one that's a ride-or-don't-ride safety call before you touch anything else)
   - Try to rock the wheel laterally in the dropouts. Any movement = loose axle. Re-seat and torque to spec, then re-check.
   - On QR bikes: confirm the QR is fully clamped (lever should leave a clear imprint in your palm when closed). On thru-axle: torque to frame spec.
   - Grab each spoke near the hub and gently rock the wheel - any click or grind = loose spoke or bearing issue (different problem, but worth noting).
   - With the wheel off, check that the cassette does not rotate independently on the freehub body. Hold the cassette and try to turn it counter-clockwise against the freehub. Any play = lockring loose or stripped splines. If it moves: do not ride until a shop re-installs or replaces the cassette/freehub. This is one of your hard "leave it parked" outcomes.

2. Cassette wear (cog-by-cog, light from behind the teeth)
   - Look at each cog's teeth from directly above and from behind. Worn teeth are asymmetric - the trailing edge curves into a hook or shark-fin, the leading edge stays straight. Compare across the cassette.
   - Focus on the smallest cog. On bikes that spend a lot of time in the small ring under load, the small cog wears first even though you'd expect the middle to. A hooked small cog + skip only there under hard pedaling is a textbook match.
   - Run a fingernail across the tooth tip perpendicular to the chain direction. If it catches on a hooked edge, that cog is past service.

3. Chain wear
   - Chain checker: 0.5% = replace chain. 0.75% = replace chain and inspect cassette; if any cog is hooked, replace cassette with the chain.
   - No gauge: the 12T-pull-12-inch method. 12 full rivets (pin to pin) on a new chain measure 12.00". 12 1/16" (= 12.0625") = ~0.5%. 12 1/8" (= 12.125") = ~1%, replace and inspect cassette.

4. Stiff link
   - With chain fitted, slowly back-pedal and watch the chain pass over the upper and lower derailleur pulleys. A stiff link will appear to "kink" - it does not lie flat against the pulley as it passes.
   - Off the bike: bend a section of chain into a tight U with your thumbs. Every link should flex freely. Any link that resists or feels stiff is the candidate. It's almost always at the master link or a recently cleaned/oiled joint.
   - Fix attempt only if you've confirmed a stiff link: flex the link side-to-side repeatedly (not against the pin direction) and re-lube. If it doesn't free up in a few cycles, that link is replaced by cutting and re-joining or a shop visit.

5. Indexing (cable tension + limit screws)
   - Shift into the smallest cog. Turn the cranks by hand. The derailleur should align the chain perfectly on the cog with no tick or rub.
   - If the chain hesitates shifting into the small cog: turn the barrel adjuster 1/4 turn counter-clockwise (more cable tension). If it overshoots / tries to go past the small cog: 1/4 turn clockwise.
   - Shift up and down the cassette, both directions, under no load. Hesitation, noise, or a slow shift = cable stretch or housing drag, fixable at the barrel. If a gear won't be reached at all: high or low limit screw.
   - Caveat: a worn cable or contaminated housing can mimic a hanger or indexing problem. If the cable hasn't been changed in years and shifting is sluggish, factor that in.

6. Hanger alignment (only if 1-5 don't isolate it)
   - Lay a straight edge along the upper derailleur cage and the lower pulley. The cage should sit parallel to the smallest cog. A visible kink or twist in the hanger itself = bent hanger.
   - Precise check needs a hanger alignment gauge (Park DAG-2.2, etc.). Without one: if steps 1-5 don't explain the skip and the hanger has any history of impact, take it to a shop for a gauge check before riding under load.

Distinguishing cues (what each failure mode looks like):

- Skip only under hard pedaling, only in the smallest cog, no other symptoms: most likely indexing drift on that one shift position, OR wear concentrated on the small cog (small-cog wear is common on road bikes that ride in the big ring/small cog).
- Skip repeats at the same crank angle each revolution: stiff link (it binds at the same chain position).
- Skip coincides with the wheel visibly shifting in the dropout: loose axle. Stop now.
- Skip with a metallic clunk or the bike lurching under hard pedaling: loose cassette on freehub. Stop now.
- Skip across multiple cogs under hard load, not in one specific position: chain stretch, almost always with visible cog wear. Chain gauge decides it.
- Skip started right after a recent shift, or after the cable was adjusted: indexing. Fix at the barrel.

Leave the bike parked and take it to a shop if any of these are true:

- Cassette moves on the freehub or you can see lockring damage.
- Chain is at or past 0.75% AND any cog shows hooked teeth.
- Hanger is visibly bent or you have no gauge and any of the other steps didn't isolate it.
- You found a stiff link that did not free up with flex + lube.
- You found lateral wheel play in the dropouts that didn't resolve with proper re-seating.
- Any of the above combined with skip under hard load - skip under hard load means a real tooth/joint failure is plausible, and small cog failures can lock the chain suddenly.

What you can fix in a stand and ride: indexing drift confined to one shift position, a freed stiff link, a re-seated wheel that is now solid, or a chain that came in under 0.5% with no cog wear. Anything else, the bike stays parked.

One note since you mentioned no visible damage and you stopped the ride: the absence of a crash, bent hanger, broken tooth, or wheel movement doesn't rule out a partly worn small cog or a partly stretched chain - those are wear patterns, not damage, and they're invisible until you load them. The reason the small-cog-only + hard-pedal pattern is the textbook presentation is that the small cog has the smallest tooth and the chain wrap is shortest, so it's the first place a marginal chain or marginal tooth loses mesh under torque.
Done.

What you observed is the classic signature of a marginal Ethernet run between modem and router: 1000BASE-T needs all four twisted pairs clean, and 100BASE-TX only needs two, so a single degraded pair drops the autoneg result to 100 Mbps. The fact that mechanical reseating restored gigabit suggests oxidation or a near-open contact rather than a hard break, which means the underlying conductor is still flaky and will most likely recur. Treat the reseating as buying you time, not as a fix.

PHASE 0 — CAPTURE STATE (zero disruption, do this first)
  • Screenshot the router's current WAN link page: speed, duplex, uptime.
  • Export or scroll back the router syslog / event log for the time window when Devika's charting and your browsing stalled. Look for lines like "WAN link down", "WAN link up", "link speed changed 1000→100", or "cable diagnostics" failures.
  • If your modem's admin UI is reachable (often 192.168.100.1), grab the downstream/upstream SNR, transmit power, and event log. Even though the optical light was normal, the modem-side counters matter later.
  • Note the timestamp pattern. Simultaneous stalls on wired + 5 GHz during light use is consistent with WAN-side loss; if it were radio interference, only Wi-Fi would have stalled.
  • If the router supports remote syslog or has a link-watch / health-check page, enable it now so you have continuous evidence if it happens again.

PHASE 1 — CABLE SUBSTITUTION (prime suspect, lowest risk)
  • Replace the short modem↔router patch with a known-good Cat5e or Cat6 cable of the same or shorter length. The short run means cheap cable is fine; what matters is that all four pairs are spec-compliant and the crimps are clean.
  • Avoid re-using the suspect cable on any other link, even temporarily — its margin is the question you're testing.
  • Verify the router reports 1000 Mbps / full duplex on the WAN port right after the swap. If it renegotiates to 100 Mbps with the new cable, the cable wasn't the cause and you can skip straight to Phase 2.
  • Leave the new cable in place for 48–72 hours of normal use. Recheck the WAN link page once or twice a day. You want to see 1000 Mbps held continuously with no down/up or speed-change entries.

PHASE 2 — PORT AND CONNECTOR CHECKS (only if Phase 1 doesn't hold)
  • Inspect both RJ45 ends of the original cable under a magnifier or phone camera: straight pins, intact gold plating, no crushed jacket near the boot, no kink in the run.
  • Reseat the new cable at both ends firmly; feel for a positive click on the retention tab. A loose jack can mimic a bad cable.
  • If the router has a configurable WAN/LAN port, try moving the WAN side to another Ethernet port. If the modem has more than one Ethernet jack, try the spare (uncommon, but some ONTs/cable modems have two).
  • Run the router's built-in Ethernet cable diagnostic if it has one (most do under "tools" or "admin"). It will report per-pair opens, shorts, and length — pair failures point unambiguously at the cable, not the port.
  • If a different port holds 1 Gbps stably, the original port is damaged and the router itself is suspect.

PHASE 3 — LOG ANALYSIS WHILE IT RUNS
  • Watch for WAN link up/down events. Single-digit per day during quiet hours is noise; clusters during use or after the cable was touched point at a marginal mechanical connection.
  • Correlate the 5 GHz stalls with WAN down events. If they don't correlate, you may have a second, unrelated issue (Wi-Fi band steering or channel contention) and should not let that confuse the diagnosis.
  • Note any T3 / T4 timeouts, sync loss, or uncorrectable codewords on the modem side. Their absence is also evidence: it confirms the ISP-side physical layer is healthy and the problem is in your short patch.

EVIDENCE THAT JUSTIFIES CONTACTING THE ISP
  • Cable swap did not hold 1 Gbps, AND
  • Port swap on the router did not resolve it, AND
  • Modem event log shows upstream/downstream SNR trending toward the failure threshold, rising uncorrectables, T3/T4 timeouts, or repeated DHCP/auth renewals during the stall windows.
  • Optical light normal is not, by itself, proof of a clean ISP link. ONTs and cable modems can hold optical/ coax sync while the data-plane side is degraded. Bring the captured modem counters and your timeline when you call — that turns the call from "intermittent" into actionable.
  • If the only thing you can show is that the WAN port on the modem drops to 100 Mbps with two known-good cables and two known-good router ports, the modem itself is the suspect and the ISP will swap it.

TIMING / LEAST-DISRUPTIVE NOTES
  • Do the cable swap during a window when neither of you is mid-task. Reseating got you through the immediate incident, so this does not need to be tonight — schedule it before Devika's next charting shift rather than during it.
  • The 48–72 hour soak in Phase 1 is intentionally longer than feels necessary. Most marginal cables fail within a day of moderate use; a clean multi-day run at gigabit is strong evidence the issue is resolved.
  • Don't power-cycle the modem as part of this. A power-cycle clears modem-side counters you may still need, and it doesn't tell you anything the cable swap won't already tell you.

Bottom line: 1G→100M renegotiation after a reseat is almost always the patch cable, not the ISP. Substitute the cable first, give it a few days, and only escalate to the ISP with modem-side counters in hand if a known-good cable on a known-good port still won't hold gigabit.

What you're seeing is almost certainly BitLocker (or the equivalent full-disk encryption Sphere enables on managed devices) asking for the recovery key because last night's firmware update changed the TPM-measured boot chain. This is the encryption doing its job, not a compromise of the device — it's a routine, expected prompt after BIOS/firmware or TPM firmware updates, and after certain hardware changes.

Three things worth holding onto while you wait:

- Don't enter personal account credentials on a screen you didn't navigate to yourself, and don't use any "recovery key finder" site from search results. The prompt you're already looking at is fine to act on; unsolicited sites/calls are the actual threat vector here.
- For a Sphere-managed device, the recovery key is held by Sphere IT / your org's endpoint management console — not by you personally. You typically can't pull it from a personal Microsoft account for a corporate-joined machine.
- There's no meaningful "bypass." Trying one is exactly the path that locks the device permanently or signals tampering.

Action: contact Sphere IT through a channel you already trust — the support number on the asset-tag sticker, the helpdesk contact from your onboarding docs, or your manager walking you in. Tell them:

  - Asset tag: SPH-LT-4431
  - State: stuck at disk recovery-key screen
  - Trigger: overnight firmware update
  - Nothing entered, no resets, no bypass attempts

If your team has access to a self-service portal or the MDM console (Intune/Sphere admin), pulling the key there is usually faster than opening a ticket. If not, the helpdesk can typically push the key or remote into the recovery flow within minutes.

One operational note: avoid repeated power-cycles until IT confirms it's safe. Some firmware updates leave the device in a half-flashed state, and a reboot loop can turn a routine recovery into a re-image.

PROPORTIONATE ACCOUNT-CONTAINMENT SEQUENCE

Assumed starting signal: password is unique to this account, MFA is on, and there are no unfamiliar orders, payment changes, recovery-email changes, or active sessions. That signal set points to credential exposure, not confirmed account compromise — so the actions below stay inside the account unless an escalation trigger fires.

PHASE 1 — INDEPENDENT SIGN-IN
  - Type the retailer's URL directly from a bookmark or known address. Do not use any link from the alert, notification, or email, even if it looks legitimate.
  - Sign in with current credentials to confirm access is intact.
  - Open the account's security / login activity / recent activity page and review every entry. Screenshot or export the log before making changes so you have a baseline if escalation becomes necessary.
  - Note anything unfamiliar: timestamp, IP, device, location, or app.

PHASE 2 — PASSWORD REPLACEMENT
  - Generate a new strong unique password in the password manager.
  - Change it from inside Account Security / Change Password — not from a "reset" link in an email or notification.
  - Confirm the password manager records the new entry and updates the breach flag on the old one.
  - If the retailer offers a "password last changed" timestamp or email confirmation, verify it.

PHASE 3 — SESSION AND DEVICE REVOCATION
  - Use "Sign out of all devices" / "Manage devices" if available.
  - Remove any device, app, or OAuth token you do not recognize.
  - Revoke connected apps the retailer does not need (e.g., a social login you no longer use).
  - After the password change you will be signed out of the current session anyway; this step covers anything an attacker may have left persistent.

PHASE 4 — MFA AND RECOVERY CHECKS
  - Verify primary MFA factors (authenticator app, hardware key). Re-register anything that looks altered.
  - Remove any MFA factor, backup phone, or trusted device you did not add.
  - Invalidate existing backup codes and generate a fresh set; store them in the password manager or a printed secure location.
  - Confirm recovery email is correct and is one you actively control.
  - Confirm recovery phone is correct.
  - Clear any "remember this browser" / trusted device list.
  - If MFA is SMS-based, move to an authenticator app or hardware key — SMS has SIM-swap risk that MFA alone does not neutralize.

PHASE 5 — SAVED-PAYMENT AND PROFILE REVIEW
  - List stored payment methods. Verify each (brand, last 4, expiry). Remove anything unfamiliar.
  - Check the default payment method on any subscription, saved cart, or one-click purchasing setting.
  - Review full order history: recent orders, pre-orders, digital orders, gift cards, store credit, refunds.
  - Review shipping address(es) and account profile (name, phone, email) for unauthorized changes.
  - Review notification and communication preferences — an attacker sometimes adds a forwarding email or SMS to suppress future alerts.
  - Review loyalty points, gift-card balance, or store credit for unexplained activity.

PHASE 6 — POST-CONTAINMENT MONITORING (NEXT 30 DAYS)
  - Watch bank and card statements for charges from this retailer, especially small "card-testing" amounts.
  - Watch for password-reset emails you did not request (signal of phishing on the email address itself, not the retailer).
  - Re-check the account's login activity weekly.

ESCALATION TRIGGERS — BROADER ACTION JUSTIFIED ONLY IF
  - Any unfamiliar order, payment method, address, MFA factor, recovery email or phone, active session, or connected app appears at any point → treat as confirmed compromise, not just credential exposure.
  - The breach scope is explicitly payment-data inclusive (not just credentials) → consider card replacement even without anomalies.
  - A small unfamiliar charge appears on a saved card (card-testing signal) → replace the card with the issuer immediately and report as fraud.
  - The recovery email account itself shows compromise indicators → secure the email account first, then return to the retailer.
  - The retailer offers breach-specific remediation (forced reset, fraud credit, account freeze) → accept it.
  - MFA is SMS-based and you have any reason to suspect SIM-swap exposure → move off SMS regardless.

CARD-ACTION DECISION RULE (PROPORTIONATE)
  - No anomalies AND breach is credential-only → do NOT cancel the card. Only the password was exposed; the card data was not. Replacing the card churns recurring charges, auto-pay, and merchant whitelists with no compensating security gain.
  - Any anomaly OR a payment-scope breach → replace the card with the issuer, monitor the old number for 30 days post-cancellation, and update any other merchants holding the same card on file.

ONE-LINE SUMMARY
  Unique password + MFA on + no order/payment/recovery/session anomaly → in-account containment only, no card action, no email rotation, no other-account rotation. Broader action is triggered only by the specific signals above.

PRESERVATION-FIRST SEQUENCE — Encrypted Local iPhone Backup

The principle: do not touch cloud allocation or backup scope until a verified, restorable encrypted backup exists on local disk.

---

STEP 0 — Preconditions (verify before plugging in)

- Confirm free space on the computer: roughly 1.5x the cloud usage (~75 GB free to be safe; iCloud says 49.7 GB used).
- Update iTunes/Finder first so the backup format is current.
- Use a known-good cable directly into the machine (rear port on a desktop preferred over a hub).
- Confirm you know the Apple ID password and the device passcode — both will be required.
- Note: iCloud Photos is current, so the local backup does not need to carry full-resolution photo originals. The goal is messages + device settings + keychain, which is exactly what the encrypted backup covers.

---

STEP 1 — Initiate the encrypted backup

macOS (Finder, 10.15+):
  1. Connect iPhone via cable, tap Trust, enter passcode.
  2. Open Finder, select the iPhone in the sidebar.
  3. Under "Backups," choose "Back up all of the data on your iPhone to this Mac."
  4. CHECK "Encrypt local backup."
  5. Set a strong password. Store it in your password manager and/or a sealed offline copy. iOS does not store this password anywhere; loss = unrecoverable backup.
  6. Click "Back Up Now."

Windows (iTunes):
  1. Connect, trust, passcode.
  2. Select the device icon.
  3. Summary > Backups > "This Computer" + check "Encrypt local backup" + set password.
  4. Click "Back Up Now."

Keep the iPhone unlocked and connected for the full duration. If the screen auto-locks, the backup pauses silently — temporarily set Settings > Display & Brightness > Auto-Lock > Never for the duration.

Expected time: 30–90 minutes for ~50 GB on USB 3.

---

STEP 2 — Verify BEFORE touching cloud (this is the preservation gate)

A. Primary — device list check:
   - macOS: in Finder, click "Manage Backups…" — confirm an entry dated today with a lock icon (encrypted).
   - Windows: in iTunes, Edit > Preferences > Devices — confirm dated today with the encrypted indicator.

B. Filesystem check — confirm files actually exist:
   - macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup/
   - Windows: %USERPROFILE%\Apple\MobileSync\Backup\
   - Look for a subfolder with today's modification time and a size in the expected range (40–60 GB; may be smaller if iCloud Photos is optimizing).

C. Spot-check (stronger) — confirm the right data is inside:
   - Inside the backup folder, open Manifest.db with sqlite3 (macOS Terminal) or DB Browser for SQLite.
   - Run: SELECT DISTINCT domain FROM Files;
   - Confirm expected domains appear: Library/SMS, Library/Preferences, Keychain, Health, etc. SMS domain is the load-bearing one for your stated need.

D. Optional strongest — restore test on a spare device or spare Mac/PC (only if you have one).

If A and B pass, you have a real encrypted backup. C raises confidence dramatically without a restore. D is the only true end-to-end proof.

---

STEP 3 — Record and protect

- Write down: backup date/time, device UDID (shown in Finder/iTunes), size, and encryption password location.
- Optionally rsync/robocopy the backup folder to a second drive for redundancy.

---

STEP 4 — Only now touch cloud

With a verified encrypted local backup in hand, it is safe to:
  - Free iCloud storage (manage other devices' backups, large mail attachments, etc.).
  - Reduce iCloud Backup scope (e.g., disable apps that don't need cloud backup now that you have a full local copy).
  - Delete the stale Dec 26 backup if desired.

Re-run a local encrypted backup after any major device change (iOS update, restore, major data migration).

---

FAILURE MODES TO WATCH FOR

- "Not enough disk space" — free more on the computer; the backup needs ~50 GB of working room.
- Backup appears to "hang" — usually the phone locked; re-unlock and resume.
- "Backup corrupt" error — erase iPhone backup folder and retry; if it recurs, check disk health (Disk Utility First Aid / chkdsk).
- Forgot encryption password — the backup is permanently unrecoverable; iOS holds no copy.

If any verification step fails, do not proceed to Step 4. Re-run from Step 1 with a different cable/port or after freeing more disk space.

LOCK THE CARD NOW. The $1.00 authorization is the textbook shape of card-testing: someone holding a card number (usually exposed in a breach, a phishing capture, or a merchant database) is verifying it works before attempting a larger charge. Your other signals line up with that reading — physical card in hand, login and MFA still working, no phishing interaction, single small pending, no other unfamiliar activity. Locking is the proportionate move because the cost of locking is small inconvenience and the upside (blocking the follow-up attempt this pattern is designed to precede) is large. Locking does not delete the pending $1.00; it only blocks new authorizations. That asymmetry is what makes it proportionate.

1. IMMEDIATE CONTAINMENT (next 5 minutes)
   - Lock or freeze the card in your issuer's app. Most issuers call this "Lock card" or "Freeze card." Reversible; no impact on pending authorizations.
   - Do not also cancel yet if your issuer's flow keeps lock and cancel distinct — lock first, cancel/replace after the issuer confirms the path.
   - Check any digital wallet (Apple Pay / Google Pay / Garmin Pay / etc.). If the card is tokenized, remove the token from any device you did not personally add.
   - Do not call any phone number from a text, email, or push notification. Use the number printed on the back of the physical card or the in-app support flow.

2. INDEPENDENT ISSUER CONTACT (within the next hour)
   - Reach the issuer via the number on the back of your card or via a prior paper statement. Verify the app/website URL independently — do not follow links from emails.
   - Tell them, in this order: "I have a $1.00 pending authorization from NORTHSTAR DIGITAL at 8:41 PM on Jan 17 that I do not recognize. The card is in my possession, account login and MFA still work, no other activity looks wrong, and I have not responded to any phone, text, or email prompts. I would like this reviewed as a possible unauthorized authorization and the card replaced."
   - Ask specifically:
     - Is "NORTHSTAR DIGITAL" known to your fraud team, and can you describe the transaction (channel, MCC, terminal ID)?
     - Does my profile show any other pending activity or recent login/device change?
     - Did this authorization originate card-not-present (online/phone/app) versus a physical dip or tap? CNP strongly implies card-number compromise rather than a skimmer at a terminal, and the response is the same in either case but the framing matters.
     - Will replacing the card issue a new number, expiry, and CVV, and will the old number be closed (not just marked lost)?
     - Can recurring billers I want to keep be transferred to the new card, and unrecognized ones removed?
     - Will you open a fraud claim and give me a reference number for my records?
   - I cannot identify "NORTHSTAR DIGITAL" with any certainty from here — treat the merchant as unknown until your issuer describes it. Common legitimate sources of small authorizations are gas pumps, transit, rentals, and subscription trials, but the merchant string "NORTHSTAR DIGITAL" does not match the patterns I can verify.

3. EVIDENCE TO PRESERVE
   Capture now, before the pending auth drops or the app refreshes:
   - Screenshot of the pending $1.00 authorization: full *** exact merchant string ("NORTHSTAR DIGITAL"), date and time (8:41 PM, Jan 17), masked card number (last four), authorization status, and any reference or transaction ID shown.
   - Screenshot of the full pending activity list showing no other unfamiliar items.
   - Screenshot of the posted transactions as of now.
   - Note the date and time you first observed the authorization and the date and time you locked the card.
   - Save (do not delete) any push, SMS, or email alert the issuer sent about the charge.
   - If you call the issuer, record: date, time, the number you dialed (the one on the back of the card, not a link), agent name or ID, and the claim/reference number they give you.
   - Keep the screenshot file in a folder you can find later — issuer disputes sometimes request the original artifact weeks after the event.

4. CRITERIA FOR REPLACING THE CARD
   Replace (new number, new expiry, new CVV) if any of the following is true:
   - The issuer confirms the $1.00 is unauthorized.
   - The authorization came in card-not-present form. Possessing the physical card does not protect against a card number that leaked from a breach, a website you used, or a saved-card database — the durable fix is a new number.
   - You have any residual doubt after the issuer's review. The cost of a replacement is low; the cost of a successful follow-up is not.
   Do not replace solely on the basis of a $1.00 auth if the issuer can independently confirm it is a legitimate pre-auth hold from a merchant you actually use (gas pump, transit, rental, subscription trial you signed up for) and you can identify the merchant yourself. In that case: lock briefly, observe, then unlock.
   When you replace, confirm the issuer closes the old number rather than merely marking it lost, transfer the billers you want to keep, and add the new card to any digital wallet only on devices you control.

ON WHETHER TO LOCK WHILE THE PENDING AUTH IS PENDING — direct answer: yes. The pending authorization will resolve one of three ways:
   - It drops on its own (most common with card-testing) — no cost to you, and the lock prevented the real attempt.
   - It posts and you dispute — issuer reverses it under the fraud claim, and the new card still goes out.
   - It turns out to be a legitimate hold you forgot about — you unlock, no harm done.
   The lock does not affect the $1.00's lifecycle; it only blocks new authorizations. That is the asymmetry that makes locking the proportionate move rather than a panicked one.

Two things you have already done correctly and that you should keep doing: not calling a number from a text or email, and not treating the absence of other unfamiliar activity as a reason to ignore the one item that does not match. Card-testing is recognizable precisely because everything else looks normal until the follow-up.

A second window requires a separate fresh opening decision, available only after the first push's full observation window has closed and the full health set has returned to baseline. No. Silently mapping QA -> staging breaks the contract. Don't do it.

Why this is the wrong fix:

  1. The bounded contract lists qa as rejected, not as an alias. Adding a silent remap makes the reject list a lie. Every release owner reading "qa is rejected" would be wrong about what the system actually does, and every downstream consumer loses the ability to reason about what was published.

  2. Fail-closed is the point. The path published zero series and held error/latency at baseline precisely because the input fell outside the contract. That is the correct outcome for a malformed value. The release owner sees the rejection and fixes the input; silent coercion hides the bug and lets the next malformed value through unchecked.

Downstream consumers comparing "staging" series cannot tell whether they came from a release that tagged itself staging or from one that tagged itself QA and got rewritten. That breaks every "what was running when" investigation.

  4. Case is part of the value. QA and qa are different tokens. If the contract is lowercase, an uppercase submission either meant an accepted value (and the owner should fix the case) or meant something outside the contract (and should be rejected). Either way, the answer is not to guess.

  - Surface the rejection where the release owner will see it, so QA-tagged releases stop getting quietly dropped.

Retired generations at 3 and full-health-set-to-baseline do not change the classification — the same rule that put the 103 ms September push into stopped-window territory applies at 102 ms. Stop was automatic on the observation; no judgement was involved, and no further push may land inside this window for any reason.

Pause and rollback are different actions. This is a window stop, not a rollback signal. The rollback set (active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, dropped series, reload failure, restart) did not fire, so no rollback via the deploy pipeline is required and none is warranted by this event.

Authorization sequence required before any recovery push or later window:

  1. Recovery prerequisites (all must hold, none are optional):
     - Retired generations drain back to 4 or fewer.
     - Cleanup pauses back at or below 100 ms.
     - Full health set back to baseline: active-generation consistency across pods, route parity against the previous-generation table, dropped series clean against the pre-canary baseline, reload failures at or below the pre-canary rate, restarts at or below the pre-canary rate.
     - Per the 2024-06-17 infra-review boundary still in force: prerequisites hold continuously for 10 minutes; identical active-generation sets across all canary pods; cleanup-pause p99 strictly below 100 ms.

  2. Once those prerequisites hold, a fresh opening decision becomes AVAILABLE. It is not granted. No recovery push is authorized until you make that decision in writing.

  3. Your fresh opening decision permits exactly one fully observed recovery push. "Fully observed" means p99, heap, active-generation count, retired-generation count, cleanup-pause duration, active-generation consistency across pods, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, and restarts are all monitored across the entire push window and the post-push drain. Mapped operators execute; you own the decision.

  4. The recovery push does NOT reopen a multi-push window. No second push may be launched inside that fresh window until the observation window closes cleanly and the full health set returns to baseline again.

  5. A subsequent window requires a SEPARATE fresh opening decision from you, available only after the recovery push's full observation window closes and the full health set is back at baseline.

The full cycle that governs from here: threshold stop (already fired at 102 ms) → recovery prerequisites holding → fresh decision from you → exactly one fully observed recovery push → full health set back to baseline → fresh decision from you → next window. The cycle does not compress, does not skip steps, and does not carry the prior window forward. Baseline recovery, on its own, has not authorized another push and will not. The next move is yours to decide.

A few things to flag before answering the three questions.

The STOP signal. Your standing protocol lists lick as a stop signal, and Kibo has now licked the same paw twice in five days. That doesn't override the "otherwise normal" picture, but it does mean the walk that prompted the lick should have been cut, not finished — even on a short route, if any treated section was crossed.

The rough patch. A 4 mm shallow rough area with no split, swelling, heat, discharge, odor, bleeding, or pain-on-handling is not on the same-day vet list (burn/blister, won't bear weight, persistent limp, swelling/discharge/odor/bleed, drool/vomit/lethargy). It is most consistent with epithelialization over the original salt injury extending onto the pad surface, or a mild salt microabrasion. Worth watching, not urgent on its own.

To your three questions:

1. Rinsing plus a short route — yes, but with caveats. Lukewarm rinse, towel-press dry between toes, inspect, re-balm remains the right routine. Short route is fine only if it genuinely avoids every treated section; the quiet route still has scattered treatment, so any contact is still a chemical-exposure walk, not just a friction walk. Pre-walk balm 5–10 minutes ahead (CaCl2 is exothermic on contact — the balm buffer matters) and boots for any segment where you cannot visually confirm a section is dry/untreated would be a stronger posture than route-shortening alone, given two licks in five days on the same paw.

2. Dog-safe paw balm — appropriate. Apply only after rinse and full dry, on pads and between toes. Verify the ingredient list against ingestion risk, since Kibo is licking: avoid zinc oxide, miconazole, and concentrated tea tree; petrolatum, lanolin, shea, beeswax, and vitamin E are the safer carriers. A thin layer is enough; thick goop traps moisture and slows drying between toes, which is the opposite of what you want.

3. Persistence thresholds for the vet call. The explicit same-day criteria stand as written. Beyond those, reasonable escalation points:

  - Licking continues or recurs on the next 1–2 walked days despite avoidance, pre-balm, and post-rinse re-balm — the behavior is telling you the exposure is still above tolerance on that paw.
  - The rough patch enlarges, deepens, fissures, or starts to bleed.
  - New finding between toes (the pinkness had resolved; re-emergence is a different signal).
  - Any of the same-day list items appears, even mildly — limp that lasts past the first few steps at home, swelling you can feel, warmth relative to the other pads, any discharge or odor.
  - Behavior change off the walks: off food, low energy, resting the paw when standing.

Practical next step. I'd treat the next 24–48 hours as a test: skip walked exposure entirely if you can substitute a sniff outing on untreated ground (dirt path, untreated sidewalk after a dry day), keep rinse-dry-inspect-re-balm on any contact walk, and if Kibo licks again on a genuinely low-exposure walk, that is the persistence signal to book a vet visit rather than another cycle of rinsing.

One thing to keep separate: a vet visit here is not because the rough patch is alarming in isolation — it is because recurrent licking on the same paw after the original injury has healed between the pads means the pad-side healing or pad-side irritation is the part that isn't yet resolved, and a clinician can distinguish healing scab from chemical fissure from early callus, which you cannot reliably do at 4 mm by inspection alone.

Safe immediate assessment: no active hazard. No smoke, spark, odor, heat, moisture, or discoloration — none of the signs that would mean call 911 or vacate the room. You isolated it correctly (both lamps unplugged, receptacle left empty). What you almost certainly have is a fault on that receptacle or its branch circuit, not on the lamps — the first lamp works in another room and a second known-good low-power lamp fails the same way at the same outlet. The two most common causes, in order:

1. A tripped breaker that does not visibly look tripped. Bedroom circuits are typically AFCI-protected under modern code, and AFCI handles can sit in a position that looks "on" even when tripped. Some breakers show a small flag or color window between ON and OFF that is easy to miss. An arc event from a marginal cord, plug, or receptacle connection is exactly the kind of thing AFCI breakers are designed to catch.
2. A failed receptacle itself — most often a loose backstab connection, worn internal contacts that no longer grip the prongs, or a neutral that has worked loose at the splice. The face can look perfectly fine while the back of the device is the problem.

Permitted reset — yes, one deliberate check of the breaker is reasonable, with the receptacle empty:

- Go to the panel and identify the breaker for that circuit (bedroom circuits are often shared with an adjacent room or hallway; if it isn't labeled, that's worth noting for management). Look at the handle position carefully — is it firmly ON, sitting in a middle position, or showing a small flag/window? On an AFCI breaker the trip indicator is subtle.
- If it appears tripped, one firm reset (full OFF, then ON) is permissible, with nothing plugged into the receptacle.
- After resetting, do not plug a lamp back in yet. The receptacle should sit unused until the breaker holds cleanly and an electrician has had a look.
- If the breaker is not obviously tripped, do not toggle it off and on repeatedly — that accomplishes nothing and can mask a real fault.
- If, after a single reset, the breaker trips the moment anything is plugged into that receptacle, leave it off. That confirms a real circuit fault and tells the electrician exactly where to look.

Reporting — yes, report to building management and do not open or replace the receptacle yourself. This is the right call whether you rent or own in a managed building, because the work needs a licensed electrician: replacement of the receptacle and re-termination of the conductors properly (pigtailed to the side screws, not the original backstab holes). It is a small job, but a failing backstab or loose neutral under load is the classic precursor to arcing and heat, so the fix should not be deferred and the outlet should not be put back into service on a guess.

What to watch for while it's open — any of these means stop using the circuit and escalate (call management / an electrician immediately, fire department if you see or smell active burning):

- Any smell of warm plastic or ozone from the plate or wall near it
- Buzzing, crackling, or sizzling
- The faceplate becoming warm
- Flickering or loss spreading to other outlets or lights in the room
- A breaker that trips as soon as a load is plugged into that receptacle

None of those are happening now, so you are not in an emergency — just a fault to clear on a normal timeline.

Practical until it's fixed: use the other bedroom outlets (you've already confirmed they work). If you need a bedside light temporarily, a cord from a working outlet is fine, but don't daisy-chain power strips and don't run cords under rugs or across a walking path. A small piece of tape over the dead receptacle so a guest (or you, half-asleep) doesn't try to use it is worth doing.

Yes — retire the shorter leash now, and don't trim or tape it. Here's the reasoning and the longer-leash handling notes.

Retire, don't tape or trim:
- The damage is in load-bearing webbing near the handle stitching, which is exactly where force concentrates when you brace on the leash (lunge, tangle, sudden stop). Several visibly cut fibers at a stitch line means the threads the stitching passes through are also compromised, even though the stitches themselves still look intact.
- Tape is cosmetic only — it doesn't restore any tensile strength. The webbing still has its weak section hidden underneath.
- Trimming isn't viable here. The fray is at the handle attachment; cutting it out would either remove the handle or leave a too-short, hand-burning stub. There isn't enough slack on a typical fixed-length leash to re-stitch a new handle cleanly at home.
- A leash is a single-point-of-failure safety device: failure under load is unpredictable and usually happens at the worst possible moment. With Kibo, that moment looks like a squirrel at a park entrance, a dog greeting, or a bike swerve — exactly the conditions you're about to walk into.

So: shorter leash goes in the trash (or the repair-shop bin if you want to send it to a leather/canvas shop out of principle, but don't walk it). Replace with a new one of the same length; until then, use the longer leash with managed length.

Longer leash near the Prospect Park entrances:
- Shorten the effective length, don't rely on the full extent. Loop or coil the excess webbing in your non-dominant hand, or wrap once around your wrist, so Kibo is working with roughly the same radius you're used to. Let the slack out only when you've cleared the entrance threshold and have open path.
- Grip closer to the clip end on the busy stretches. Hold the leash a foot or two below the clip rather than at the handle, so a lunge's force meets your whole arm instead of the full length of webbing. This also keeps your hand out of any bike-handlebar zone if someone passes close.
- Watch the bike corridors specifically. The Southwest-corner and Prospect Park West entrances see heavy two-way bike and scooter traffic; even riders going the right way can come up fast behind a stroller or dog. Audible + visual check before stepping off the curb in either direction.
- Mind the tripping line. Excess leash trailing on the ground is a real hazard — cyclists can catch it, pedestrians can step on it (and you'll feel a yank you didn't see coming). If you can't keep the slack fully coiled, at least keep it off the pavement on the bike-lane side.
- Cross the entrance at a clean gap, not in the middle of a flow. Kibo knows the routine; he'll get the "let's go" cue and you want to be through the high-traffic zone in a straight line before letting the full length out.
- Park side, once you're past the entrance and on a less dense path, you can let the longer leash do its job — more sniff range, fewer pedestrians. Re-shorten before you exit.

The 316 SS bolt-snap you keep as the clasp backup is unrelated here (that's for a clasp auto-closure failure, which you've ruled out — the clasp is fine). For the leash-substitute period, length management is the whole game.

Premise check (do this first, before any reads):
  - Confirm the migration script's write target is the canonical package and not a generated-outputs directory. If a write has already begun, halt further writes and snapshot the current state (git status, HEAD hash) before anything else mutates it.
  - Confirm with the three owning teams that the canonical package is still the accepted source. Don't proceed on assumption.

Verification sequence (bounded, with stop conditions):

1. Generator version
   - Identify the generator version that produced the iOS token file under question: build metadata, generation timestamp on the file, generator binary hash, or pinned version in the build config.
   - Confirm that version is the one the canonical package expects (manifest/lockfile).
   - Stop: generator version is the expected one AND it matches the most recent successful generation run.
   - What it rules out: wrong toolchain, partial upgrade. What it doesn't prove: that any value is correct.

2. Package commit
   - Capture the canonical package HEAD at the time the iOS file was generated (git log, tag, build manifest).
   - Read the canonical token definitions at that commit from the SOURCE files, not from generated output.
   - List commits since that HEAD that touch iOS-relevant token values; review each for in-flight changes.
   - Stop: a known-good canonical commit is identified and its source values are recorded as the baseline.

3. Generation logs
   - Locate the generation run(s) that produced the iOS token file in the relevant window.
   - Confirm: run completed, no fallback path, no warning about unknown tokens or missing fields, no partial regeneration, no retry.
   - Cross-check: the file's generation timestamp matches a successful run, not an aborted or retried one.
   - Stop: a successful, non-fallback run is tied to the file under question.

4. Drift check
   - Regenerate the iOS file from current canonical HEAD into a scratch path. Diff against the file the migration script wants to read from.
   - Classify any drift:
     (a) generator-only — generator version/transform differs but canonical is unchanged,
     (b) canonical — canonical changed since the file was generated,
     (c) manual — file edited outside the generation pipeline.
   - Stop: drift is classified and the canonical-side values are known to be right or wrong by source-level evidence, not by timestamp.

Decision at the end of the sequence:
  - Canonical is right: do not writeback. The newer-looking timestamps are generation timestamps; the generator will (or already did) catch up.
  - Canonical is wrong: the fix is a reviewed commit/PR in the canonical package authored by a human reviewer of the token definitions, not a writeback of generated output.
  - Only proceed with the migration script's writeback if drift check = (a) AND there is independent source-level evidence (spec change, reviewed ticket, owner sign-off). Even then, fix it at the source — don't overwrite canonical with generated bytes.

Why generated iOS output should not be written back into the canonical package without source-level evidence:

1. Direction of derivation is one-way. The generator goes canonical -> output. Reversing it makes the generator's bytes authoritative and the canonical package a downstream artifact. That inverts the architecture the three teams signed off on.

2. Timestamps are not authority. Newer-looking timestamps on the generated file are generation timestamps (when the generator ran). They tell you the file was regenerated; they do not tell you that any value changed or that any value is wrong.

3. Loss of structure and intent. Generated output is a flat/serialized form. Writing it back loses source-level structure (naming, comments, grouping, default rationale, conditional logic the generator may not round-trip). The canonical package is where intent lives.

4. Bypasses review on the source of truth. A migration-script writeback lands as an automation-authored commit on the canonical package. The owning teams' review surface for canonical changes is silently bypassed.

5. Three-team blast radius. All three teams consume generated outputs from canonical. If the writeback bakes in a generator bug, a transform loss, or a stale default, every team gets the wrong value simultaneously and silently, and every future regeneration reproduces the bug as if it were canonical.

6. Wrong debugging surface. If canonical was actually wrong, overwriting it with generated output hides the bug in the generator instead of fixing it at the source. The next canonical edit re-introduces the disagreement.

7. Audit trail. A generated->canonical writeback looks in git history like "migration script" changed the token definitions. From the diff, the owning team can't tell what was actually decided, only what bytes appeared.

Source-level evidence means: a spec change, a reviewed ticket from the owning team, a diff against an upstream source, or a deliberate design decision. None of those is satisfied by newer-looking timestamps on a derived file.

The symptoms point to a local clog at the stopper / pop-up / trap arm — hair and soap scum are the usual culprit, and ninety-second clearance with no other fixtures affected is consistent with that. Here's a safe renter-level sequence and the signs that mean stop and call management.

Cleaning sequence (in order, stop when it clears):

1. Clear what you can see. Pull the stopper (lift and twist, or pop the pivot rod under the sink if it has one — no tools needed). Strip hair and soap off the stopper and the crosshair/strainer directly below it. This alone fixes most slow bathroom sinks.

2. Hot water + dish soap. Squirt a few drops of dish soap down the drain. Heat a kettle until just off the boil (don't pour boiling water onto a cold porcelain basin — thermal shock can crack it). Pour slowly, let sit five minutes, then run hot tap for thirty seconds. This emulsifies residual soap scum.

3. Cup plunger. Use a sink plunger (flat-bottom, not the flanged toilet kind). Block the overflow hole in the basin with a wet rag so pressure builds. Six to eight firm pumps, then test. Skip this if you have a pop-up linkage you can't fully seal.

4. Plastic drain zip / hair snake. A barbed plastic strip (a few dollars at any hardware store) reaches hair 2–6 inches down the tailpiece without scratching pipes. Insert, twist, pull. Better than a wire hanger, which can score porcelain and lodge in the P-trap.

5. Baking soda + vinegar (optional). Half cup baking soda, half cup white vinegar, wait 15–30 minutes, flush with hot tap. Modest help, not a miracle — skip if step 3 or 4 worked.

Skip entirely: chemical drain cleaners (you already know), disassembling the P-trap (renter-iffy, spillage risk, often a lease gray area), boiling water into a cold basin.

Stop and call management if any of these appear:

- More than one fixture affected, or water backing up in the tub, shower, or toilet when this sink drains
- Gurgling from other fixtures while this one drains
- Sewage odor from this drain or anywhere in the bathroom
- Any moisture, staining, drips, warped cabinet floor, or mold under the sink — even a slow one
- Water at the overflow, around the base of the fixture, or seeping at the wall
- No real improvement after steps 1–4
- It clears and then slows again within hours (suggests the blockage is downstream in a shared line, not local)

If you hit the wall after step 3 or 4, that's a reasonable handoff point regardless — management can snake the trap arm or branch without you touching the plumbing.

The dock still delivering power + Ethernet while video is dead — with direct HDMI fine — isolates the failure to the USB-C DisplayPort alt-mode handshake. USB-PD and USB/Ethernet use different wire pairs than DP-alt-mode, so a stale post-sleep renegotiation or a partial cable fault breaks video alone. Sequence to discriminate A/B/C, all non-destructive and touching nothing in device-mgmt:

1. Force a display-stack reset on the existing connection.
   - Win+Ctrl+Shift+B (Windows; flashes screen, reinitializes display drivers / re-runs handshakes).
   - Or Settings -> Display -> Detect.
   - If video returns -> A (stale post-sleep handshake). Done.

2. Hot-unplug the USB-C at the LAPTOP end, count to 10, replug.
   - Distinct from your prior reconnect because it forces the laptop's USB-C controller to redo alt-mode negotiation from scratch, not just reseat the dock side.
   - If video returns -> A (laptop-side alt-mode state).

3. Move to the laptop's other USB-C port (if it has two).
   - Many laptops only enable full DP-alt-mode on one port.
   - If video returns on the second port -> that port's alt-mode path is bad; use the working one until service.

4. Swap the USB-C cable for a known-good one rated for DP-alt-mode (or Thunderbolt-certified).
   - USB-C cables can lose high-speed lanes (the ones DP uses) while keeping USB 2.0 + power functional. Same symptom shape as your failure.
   - If video returns -> C (cable). Retire the old one.

5. Swap the dock, or bypass it with a direct USB-C -> DisplayPort/HDMI adapter.
   - If video returns -> B (dock video path). The dock can still charge and provide Ethernet because those paths are independent of its video output chip.
   - If still nothing after a known-good cable AND a known-good dock, the issue is upstream of the dock (laptop GPU/driver/firmware); at that point contact vendor support with this diagnostic trail.

Order rationale: 1-2 are 30-second software/reseat tests that catch the most common cause (stale post-sleep alt-mode). 3 isolates a specific port. 4 and 5 require spare hardware — skip ahead if you already have it on hand; otherwise stop where video returns and the culprit is identified.

CLASSIFICATION

The asymmetry is the strongest signal. Only one tenant is elevated while accepted-point accounting and dispatch errors are normal, AND that tenant is sitting at 7/8 of its per-tenant slot cap with no empty-tenant bloat visible in the ring. A scheduler fairness failure would either (a) require ring/active-tenant mismatch (you've already looked and don't see it) or (b) pull at least one neighbor tenant's wait up as the rotation slowed — neighbors are normal. The 7/8 cap state is the giveaway: requests are accumulating into the slot pool faster than they're draining. That is the held-open signature — a slot occupied past expected handler time, with new requests piling up behind it.

Most likely: client-side timeout or retry behavior for that single tenant is keeping requests occupying their slots longer than expected. Scheduler fairness is not ruled out by one symptom, but the facts lean away from it. Do not change ingest-edge until the three checks below localize where the 2.6s lives.

THREE CHECKS BEFORE ANY INGEST-EDGE CHANGE

1. TRACE — localize where the 2.6s lives
   For 5 recent slow requests on this tenant, pull the end-to-end span:
     receive -> enqueue -> dequeue -> dispatch_start -> response
   What discriminates:
     - gap between receive and enqueue: held before ingest-edge (client/network side; do not change ingest-edge)
     - gap between enqueue and dequeue: scheduler-side (would imply scheduler skipped this tenant across iterations)
     - gap between dispatch and response, compared to accepted-point p99: handler-side — but accepted-point accounting is normal, so this would imply a sampling/filtering mismatch in your metric
   One slow span is enough to localize. Do not proceed without this.

2. TIMEOUT — per-request open duration vs expected handler latency
   For the 7 currently waiting requests on this tenant:
     - request_open_age_seconds distribution
     - compare each to the tenant's expected handler latency floor (use accepted-point median; p99 if the tenant is uniformly heavy)
     - confirm per-tenant read-deadline and client-side retry/backoff config vs the other tenants
   What discriminates:
     - open_age >> expected handler latency: client/timeout is holding the slot; queue-wait p99 is rising because the queue depth is at cap and slots aren't freeing at the rate new requests arrive
     - open_age ~ expected: slots are not held; the requests are genuinely sitting in the queue, which redirects you to Check 3 as the primary signal

3. QUEUE-AGE — per-tenant queue depth and time-since-last-dequeue
   Per-tenant queue-age histogram for this tenant, plus time-since-last-dequeue-for-this-tenant over the last 5 minutes:
     - ages spread uniformly from 0 to ~2.6s AND the scheduler dequeues this tenant on every pass: fairness is fine; the queue is just deep — consistent with Check 2 finding held-open slots
     - ages skewed old AND time-since-last-dequeue large: scheduler is skipping this tenant — fairness failure; correlate with a ring snapshot (active tenants vs tenants with current demand) to confirm stuck pointer or ring bloat

DECISION RULE

  Check 1 gap = enqueue->dequeue, AND Check 3 shows scheduler not dequeuing
    -> scheduler fairness; investigate ring snapshot and last-iteration pointer
  Check 1 gap = enqueue->dequeue, AND Check 2 shows open_age >> expected latency
    -> scheduler is fine but slots are held by long-lived requests; root cause is
       client-side, not ingest-edge
  Check 1 gap = receive->enqueue
    -> held before ingest-edge; look at client/network for this tenant specifically
  Check 1 gap = dispatch->response despite accepted-point being normal
    -> re-check accepted-point filtering; you may have a sampling mismatch hiding
       the real handler latency

TAKEAWAY

The smallest set is one slow trace (Check 1), the open-age-vs-expected-latency comparison on the 7 waiting requests (Check 2), and the queue-age histogram plus time-since-last-dequeue for this tenant (Check 3). If Check 2 shows held-open requests, the change lives on the client side; ingest-edge should not be modified. Your negative observation on ring bloat plus the 7/8 cap state means the dominant hypothesis is held-open requests, and the right next move is to read those spans before touching anything.

NEW YORK RESIDENCY ALLOCATION

The street address printed on your 1099 does not affect your New York residency allocation. Three points carry this:

  1. NYC residency is determined by actual physical presence, not by the
     address an issuer prints on an information return. NYC personal income
     tax applies to anyone who is either domiciled in NYC or a statutory
     resident (permanent place of abode in NYC plus 183+ days in NYC). You
     lived in NYC for the entire year, so you are a full-year NYC resident
     regardless of which NYC street address the issuer recorded.

  2. The 1099 address is not transcribed onto your return. On Form IT-201
     (NYS) and the NYC component, you enter your current address as the
     taxpayer; the issuer's address line on the 1099 is never carried
     forward. Information-return matching by NYS Department of Taxation
     and Finance and the IRS is keyed on TIN and amounts, not address.

  3. Allocation is not implicated at all. Day-count allocation between
     New York and another jurisdiction only matters when a taxpayer enters
     or leaves NY during the year. Your move stayed within NYC, so 100%
     of your NY-source income is taxed as full-year NYC resident income
     with nothing to split.

ISSUER CORRECTION BEFORE FILING

Legally, no — you are not required to obtain a corrected 1099 before
filing. The 1099 is reportable by TIN and dollar amount; an address
mismatch between a 1099 and your return does not delay, invalidate, or
re-classify the filing. If you cannot get the corrected form in time,
file as-is using the correct TIN and amounts.

Practically, yes — I would still request the corrected 1099 now (a
"Corrected Form 1099" filed with the IRS by the issuer), because:

  - address mismatches between your filed return and information returns
    occasionally trigger identity-verification or fraud-flagging
    correspondence at the state level
  - any future amended forms, replacement 1099s, or notices from the
    issuer will route to the wrong address until the issuer record is
    fixed
  - it keeps your records consistent with the corrected W-2 for the same
    year

BOTTOM LINE

File when ready using the correct TIN and amounts; the Park Slope
address on the 1099 changes neither your NYC residency status nor any
tax owed. Request the corrected 1099 in parallel so your information-
return trail matches the W-2 going forward.

KIBO EAR — POST-BATH MONITORING PLAN
2025-02-08

ASSESSMENT (what you described fits)
- Mild pinna (ear-flap) irritation, most likely from residual moisture or mild self-trauma after scratching. Outer-flap pinkness without discharge, odor, swelling, or canal debris points away from acute otitis externa right now.
- Two head shakes and a few scratches in the morning is below the threshold for an urgent visit, but it's a signal worth watching closely for the next 24–48 hours.

SAFE EAR CARE (do now)
1. Dry the outer ear gently.
   - Use a soft, dry cloth or un-waxed cotton ball on the visible outer flap and the opening of the canal only.
   - Pat, don't rub. Do not insert cotton swabs, fingers, or anything into the ear canal.
2. If the ear still feels damp inside, do a short "towel-and-air" pass.
   - Hold the flap up, place a dry cotton ball loosely at the canal opening (do not push in), let him shake, then remove the cotton.
   - A minute or two of airflow (carry him into a warm dry room) helps.
3. No over-the-counter ear products yet.
   - Skip hydrogen peroxide, rubbing alcohol, vinegar mixes, essential oils, or leftover dog ear meds. Anything placed in the canal before a vet looks can mask findings or worsen irritation.
4. No further bathing of that ear / head for a few days. If you need to clean him up, avoid water near the ears or use a damp cloth only.
5. Continue normal routine; no dietary changes.

WHAT TO TRACK (next 48 hours)
- Scratch count: roughly how many times per hour when awake, and whether it's increasing.
- Head shakes: any cluster of 3+ shakes in a short window, or shakes that recur through the day.
- Pinna color/size: same pink spot, fading, spreading, or new areas.
- Any new moisture, waxy debris, crust, or scab forming.
- Appetite, energy, gait, and willingness to be touched on that ear.

WATCH-AND-WAIT WINDOW
- Reasonable to monitor at home for 24–48 hours while symptoms stay mild and stable.
- If by 48 hours the pinkness has not faded OR scratching/shaking is not clearly trending down, schedule a non-urgent vet visit (ear check + otoscopic exam).
- If anything below turns "yes" before then, move the visit up — same day if severe.

VET — SAME DAY OR SOONER (any one of these)
- Discharge from the canal or on the flap: brown, yellow, black, pus-like, or bloody.
- Odor (sweet, yeasty, or foul) — ear infections often smell before they look bad.
- Swelling of the flap or canal opening; the ear feels hot or thickened.
- Pain: pulling away, yelp, or growl when you touch near the ear or base of ear.
- Head tilt (ear held lower, face turned to one side) or any loss of balance / circling / leaning.
- New or worsening redness that spreads across the flap.
- Repeated head shaking — multiple clusters through the day, or shaking that wakes him.
- Repeated scratching that doesn't pause, or scratching that breaks the skin.
- Lethargy, inappetence, vomiting, or any change in how he carries himself.
- Sudden hearing change (not responding to cues on that side).

VET — ROUTINE (within a few days if none of the above)
- Mild pinkness or mild scratching that hasn't fully resolved by 48 hours.
- Recurrent ear issues (more than 1–2 per year) — worth a baseline exam and discussion of prevention.

PREVENTION GOING FORWARD (post-bath routine)
- After every bath or swim: dry outer ears with cloth + cotton ball at canal opening, then a few minutes of airflow before he goes outside. This is the single biggest reducer of moisture-driven otitis.
- In salt season (active now through ~March), wipe the outer ear/flap gently after walks if slush has splashed up — same logic as paws, no harsh cleaners.
- If he has floppy/heavy ear conformation or a history of ear issues, ask the vet about a routine drying product they recommend for at-home use.

BOTTOM LINE
- Today: gentle drying only, no products in the canal, watch and log.
- Recheck at 24h and 48h.
- Any discharge, odor, swelling, pain, head tilt, balance change, or escalation of scratching/shaking → vet same day.
