Distinguishing retention from allocation pressure needs only one variable: time, separated into a replay window and an idle window of the same length, with forced Full GC probes at fixed points.

Smallest bounded comparison

Two adjacent windows in staging, same warm-up, same length (e.g., 25 min, matching the original):

  Window A — replay at the same input rate and route count as the original 25-min run
  Window B — idle, no replay traffic, same JVM uptime entering the window

Both windows must start from the same baseline. Between A and B, run a forced Full GC and wait until Rss is flat for at least 2 min before starting B.

Forced Full GC probes (jcmd <pid> GC.run) at:

  - t0 of A
  - end of A
  - +10 min after end of A
  - t0 of B
  - end of B

Record at each probe:

  - process Rss
  - jstat -gcutil: old-gen used, eden used, full-gc count, total gc time
  - jmap -histo top 20 (cumulative bytes and instance counts), filtered to classes touched by snapshot serialization — typically byte[], HashMap$Node[], char[], and any custom Snapshot / RouteTableView holders

Distinguishing signals

Retention vs pressure splits cleanly on three independent checks:

  1. Post-FullGC Rss at end of A vs post-FullGC Rss at +10 min after A.
     If they differ by more than ~2% or do not trend back to the A-start baseline, retention is contributing. Pure pressure will converge within a few minutes after traffic stops, since the JVM can drain eden and old gen in one or two Full GCs.

  2. Old-gen occupancy across the four probes inside A.
     Pressure: old gen fills toward the same steady state during A as during B. Retention: old gen grows monotonically across consecutive Full GCs during A, regardless of the GC pause.

  3. jmap -histo delta on the snapshot-serialization classes between start of A and end of A + 10 min (after Full GC).
     Pressure: counts return to start-of-A levels. Retention: counts and bytes stay elevated — typically a static cache, a listener/observer registry, or an unintentional strong reference from a long-lived owner (a metrics aggregator, a config reload hook, or a slow downstream consumer holding the latest snapshot).

The original 1.9 GiB at +6 min vs 1.8 GiB baseline is a hint, not a verdict. Six minutes is often too short for old-gen collections to fully drain, especially if the JVM has not yet hit its IHOP/SoftReference policy thresholds. The +10 min probe plus an idle reference window (B) resolves that ambiguity.

Targeted allocation measurement

For the specific suspect — repeated route-table snapshot serialization — async-profiler in alloc mode during A and B is sufficient. Compare allocations/sec for the snapshot-serialization frames between the two windows:

  - allocations/sec higher in A, but live count of snapshot-related objects at end of A matches start of A after Full GC → pressure (objects are short-lived; JVM lag and old-gen promotion lag are the cause)
  - allocations/sec similar to B, but live count of snapshot-related objects grows during A → retention

Optional, only if 1–3 are inconclusive: take exactly two heap dumps (start of A, end of A + 10 min post-FullGC) and diff via Eclipse MAT or jhat retainers. This is the most expensive step; skip unless the lighter probes point at retention.

Scope and boundaries

  - Staging only. No production change, no owner-map change. Within Wes's non-production practical-backup scope.
  - Total wall-clock: ~80 min (25 A + 10 post + 25 B + buffer).
  - Tools used: jcmd, jstat, jmap, async-profiler — standard with most JDKs, no install.
  - If old-gen still grows monotonically after the bounded experiment, document the retainers from jmap -histo (top by retained bytes) before changing any code path, and escalate from staging to a code owner via the normal review process — not via this experiment.

That set is the minimum that yields a defensible answer. Anything smaller (e.g., one heap dump, or just an allocation profile) leaves the retention question open.

Here is a safe sequence. Read it through once before you start so you don't have to switch contexts mid-cleanup.

Before anything else

  Closed-toe shoes on your feet (you'll be kneeling and leaning).
  Dish gloves or nitrile gloves on your hands.
  A strong light source you can hold or prop - a phone flashlight is fine, but a raking angle (light almost flat to the floor) is what reveals fine shards, so you need something you can aim low.
  A roll of paper towels, a trash bag, a stiff piece of cardboard or old credit card, and a vacuum with a hose and crevice tool if you have one.

Step 1 - Sauce before shards

  The sauce is hiding fragments and making them stick to the tile and to each other.
  Lift pooled sauce with damp paper towels, pressing down and lifting straight up. Do not wipe - wiping drags sauce and any embedded fragments into the grout lines where they disappear.
  Discard each towel into the bag as soon as it picks up anything. Keep going until the tile around the spill is visually clean.

Step 2 - Visible shards (large and medium)

  Continue with the tongs. Pick straight up, never slide.
  For shards resting on their edge, nudge them flat with the tongs or the edge of the cardboard before lifting - upright shards snap under sideways pressure.
  Bag everything, then fold the bag closed. Do not put glass into a thin grocery bag and then into another bin - double-bag or use a rigid container.

Step 3 - Fine shards on the open tile

  This is the step most people get wrong. The reliable method is press-and-lift, not wipe.
  Lay a damp (not soaking) paper towel flat over a suspect area, press down with the palm so fragments adhere to the towel, then lift straight up and discard.
  Work in overlapping rectangles, moving outward from the cabinet edge. Refresh the towel as soon as it looks fuzzy - a towel that's already picked up fragments will redeposit them.
  If you have a vacuum with a hose, run it before the damp pass to lift loose fragments; empty the canister into the bag afterward, not into an open trash can.

Step 4 - The cabinet toe-kick (the trap)

  The recessed face and the 90-degree corner where the toe-kick meets the floor are where shards and sauce wick in and stay.
  Use the cardboard or credit card as a scraper. Hold it flush against the floor and draw it into the corner in one direction, then up the face. Wipe the card with a damp towel between passes - do not let accumulated paste fall back onto the tile.
  Shine the light at a low angle along the toe-kick. Fine shards will flash. Pick each one with the corner of a damp paper towel, or with a pair of tweezers if you have them - fingers miss the small ones even with gloves.
  Vacuum the crevice with the crevice tool, then do a final damp-towel press along the entire toe-kick run.

Step 5 - Final inspection (this is what determines whether Kibo is safe)

  Kill the overhead light and use the flashlight at a raking angle, almost parallel to the floor. Move it slowly across the spill area and the toe-kick. Any remaining shard will throw a bright spark back at you.
  Tactile check: with a clean dry paper towel, press your fingertips (gloved) flat against the tile and drag slowly across suspect zones. If you feel a catch or hear a tiny tick, stop and pick it up - don't keep dragging, that just redistributes fragments.
  Do the tactile check along the toe-kick corner specifically. The eye misses what the fingertip catches.
  Repeat the raking-light pass from the doorway where Kibo enters, all the way to his water bowl and bed - he won't walk only through the spill zone, he'll walk the path he always walks.

Step 6 - Kibo re-entry

  Walk the route yourself on hands and knees with the raking light. Paws are closer to the floor than your eyes during the visual pass were.
  If you have a damp cloth, drag it across the route once. Any grit on the cloth means shards remain.
  Only open the door after both the visual raking-light pass and the cloth drag come back clean on the full route, not just the spill area.
  First ten minutes with Kibo back in: watch his gait. A paw lift, a head-down sniff-and-limp, or repeated licking of one foot means a fragment is in a pad - take him to the vet the same day.

Disposal note

  Mark the bag "glass" so whoever takes the trash doesn't reach in bare-handed. Sauce residue makes the inside of the bag slippery and shards stick to it.

Quick framing for Anya to take into the review — concrete drift / rollback / auditability risks on a 7-day platform-local token override, not the whole review and not Alex taking it over.

Drift

  - Drift-check blind spot. The automated drift check is the safety net behind "no platform exceptions." Allowing overrides means the check has to either suppress the overridden token (real drift is masked) or keep firing on a "known" violation (signal/noise collapses; on-call starts ignoring it). Either way the check stops being trustworthy.

  - Override of what — token name/semantic mapping, or token value? A name override breaks composition because other tokens reference the semantic layer. A value override is narrower but still violates canonical-only. The proposal needs to be specific.

  - Generated-artifact fan-out. Platforms consume *generated* outputs from the canonical package. The override either bypasses generation (drift at every consumer, every rebuild) or forces the generator to gain platform-aware branches (canonical-only breaks at the generator, not just the consumer).

  - Multi-platform overlap. Two platforms overriding the same token in overlapping 7-day windows: reconciliation is not a merge — it is a design decision made post-hoc by whoever does the reconciling. Designer review moves out of canonical authoring.

  - 7-day window vs. release cadence. If canonical ships weekly, an override opened on day 6 of a cycle can be promoted by the next canonical release without an explicit canonicalization review.

Rollback

  - Reconciliation is promotion, not merge. Once the local override is in canonical, rolling back the canonical change means reverting the new value *and* every platform that already consumed it. With pure downstream generation, rollback is one revert; with overrides, rollback scope depends on how reconciliation is modeled. Proposal needs to specify which.

  - Mid-window rollback is platform-local. Reverting the local file is fine, but derived artifacts (CI snapshots, visual-regression baselines, screenshot diffs) become stale and flag the reversion as *new* drift.

  - Ship-state asymmetry. The overriding platform has shipped UI on the override. If canonical later rolls back a regression, that platform does not see the bug and may break its local design on the "fix."

  - Expired-override behavior. At T+7d the choices are: auto-revert (drops engineer work mid-feature), alert-and-persist (no teeth), or silent persist (no cap at all). Needs an explicit owner and a stated default.

Auditability

  - Required fields at override creation: actor, timestamp, token id, linked issue/ticket, expected reconciliation date, approval. Without these, "why did iOS diverge on Feb 14?" becomes "read the commits."

  - Override log separate from git. Commits show what changed, not that it was a *sanctioned* override vs. accidental drift. Need a structured log queryable by token / platform / time range.

  - Reconciliation provenance in the canonical package. When an override is promoted, the canonical entry needs lineage ("value from <platform>-override <PR> on <date>, originally canonical X"). Otherwise future readers cannot tell designed-in-canonical from promoted-from-workaround.

  - Drift suppression is auditable only if the trail says "this drift is a sanctioned override." Otherwise the drift signal becomes untrustworthy.

  - 7-day cap is policy, not system, unless the log records opened-at, due-at, status-at-due. Without that, the cap is theater.

  - Collision resolution record. Two teams overriding the same token for different reasons need not just two log entries but a *resolution* record showing which was chosen and why.

This is an allocation-pressure optimization, not a leak fix. The evidence is clean, and the ticket framing should follow from that classification rather than be retrofitted to leak-fix language.

Why it is not a leak

1. Forced post-replay GCs recover the memory. Peak 2.55 GiB dropped to 1.88 GiB after two collections, which is below the disabled-serialization baseline of 2.0 GiB. A leak leaves retained heap elevated after forced collection; here it overcorrects.
2. Retained heap matches baseline within 2%. If snapshot buffers were leaking, you would see monotonic growth across replays, not a per-replay bounded bump that converges back.
3. The growth is scoped. The flame graph attributes it to snapshot buffers, which are bounded and tied to a known operation. Leaks are typically orphan references detached from any reachable path; bounded buffer growth tied to a specific code path is the textbook allocation-pressure signature.
4. No production effect. Leaks usually surface as RSS creep or OOMs in long-running processes. None reported here.
5. The comparison is single-variable. Identical replay input, only the snapshot-serialization toggle changed. That isolates the cause to the buffers and rules out confounding from input size or scheduling.

Evidence that belongs in the metrics-router owner ticket

  Comparison methodology: identical replay input across both runs; only the snapshot-serialization toggle differed; staging environment, no prod traffic.
  Numbers: 2.0 GiB disabled, 2.55 GiB enabled peak, 1.88 GiB after two forced GCs; retained heap delta vs baseline under 2%.
  Allocation profile: flame graph attribution to snapshot buffers, linked as an artifact (not pasted inline — paste-in loses provenance later).
  Provenance: internal pipeline_run_id, Wes's run id, commit SHA, replay seed / input hash. Per the deploy convention, no external provenance; no `provenance_status: partial`.
  Scope statement: bounded to the snapshot-serialization code path; no other metrics-router path exercised by this change.
  Negative controls: what did NOT change — error rate, latency, GC pause distribution, RSS, prod metrics.
  Sanity-check sentence: the 1.88 GiB post-GC figure being below the 2.0 GiB baseline rules out the leak hypothesis outright; worth stating explicitly so the reviewer does not have to reconstruct it.

Acceptance criteria for the ticket (framed for an optimization, not a leak)

  1. Peak budget. With snapshot serialization enabled, peak heap during a replay of identical input is at or below a stated ceiling with headroom — e.g., 1.3x the disabled-serialization peak of 2.0 GiB, so <= 2.6 GiB. State the headroom rationale, not just the number.
  2. Post-replay convergence. Within N minutes of replay end, retained heap is at or below baseline + 2%, verifiable by forced GC plus heap diff. Pick N; minutes, not hours, is the right unit for a convergence check.
  3. Bounded growth across repetitions. Across K consecutive replays (suggest K >= 10), retained heap after convergence does not grow monotonically. This is the no-leak check even under repeated trigger.
  4. Allocation-profile gate. A fresh flame graph at acceptance time still attributes the temporary peak to snapshot buffers, not to a new code path introduced since the comparison.
  5. Production SLOs unchanged. p99 latency, error rate, and availability over the rollout window are within the existing metrics-router SLOs.
  6. Rollback trigger. Any of the above failing, or any prod OOM or sustained RSS growth attributed to snapshot serialization, rolls back without a deploy — same env-confirm discipline as the 2025-01-17 alert-template incident. Confirm environment before acting.
  7. Provenance on the deploy. pipeline_run_id present and complete at deploy time; no `provenance_status: partial`. Commit and deploy are distinct steps; the ticket should not conflate them.

A few things worth flagging in the ticket body, not as criteria

  Hema coordinates the metrics migration and may reorder the cutover if prod forces it. If this ticket lands near cutover, tag her so she can re-time it.
  Link the flame graph artifact and the replay seed rather than embedding them; inline content loses audit trail.
  Do not borrow the shard-keeper label_parity dual sign-off shape. That pattern applies when two independent sources must agree on identity (label rename to routing reads). Here the question is a single-process memory characterization under one toggle; copying the sign-off structure would be procedure-following rather than procedure-fitting.

If you want, I can draft the ticket body itself against this shape, or push the acceptance criteria into a runbook entry keyed on metrics-router so it is reusable across future allocation-style changes.

Producer behavior for `deployment.environment`

The label value comes from the source — the producer. Destination, workload, or pipeline context cannot synthesize it. There are three mutually exclusive cases.

1. Missing input (producer sets no value)
   - Omit `deployment.environment` from the published payload entirely.
   - Do not set it to `prod`, `staging`, or `dev` based on where the workload is going.
   - This is a real, valid publication state: "we don't know." It is not the same as "we know it isn't any of the three."

2. Allowed input (mixed-case variants of the three canonical values)
   - `prod`, `Prod`, `PROD`, `  prod  ` -> normalize to `prod`, publish.
   - `staging`, `Staging`, `STAGING`, surrounding whitespace -> normalize to `staging`, publish.
   - `dev`, `Dev`, `DEV`, surrounding whitespace -> normalize to `dev`, publish.
   - The label is present and carries the canonical lower-case value.

3. Unsupported input (everything else)
   - `unknown`, `qa`, `QA`, malformed strings, arbitrary user-supplied values -> reject before publication.
   - Do not alias, do not map, do not substitute, do not infer from pipeline/cluster/deployment-target.
   - The producer is responsible for fixing the value at the source; this is not a destination-side decision.

Why "workload is headed to production" does not justify setting `prod`

"Prod-bound workload" is destination context. The contract binds the label to the source value, not to where the artifact lands downstream. Inferring `prod` from destination would:

- Make an omitted-label signal indistinguishable from an explicitly-allowed `prod`. Downstream consumers that rely on the absence of the label to flag "environment unknown" lose that signal.
- Bypass the rejection path for unsupported inputs. Anything the producer sends that isn't one of the three canonical forms is supposed to fail loudly. Quietly mapping destination context onto the label collapses rejection into silent overwrite.
- Break the contract's stated guarantee: only allowed mixed-case inputs normalize to `prod`/`staging`/`dev`; destination context is not an input class.

Distinguishing omission from rejection

Both are non-publishments, but they mean different things and the producer should keep them distinct:

- Omission: producer chose not to set a value. Downstream sees no `deployment.environment` attribute. Acceptable when the producer genuinely has nothing to assert; not acceptable as a workaround for "I want prod but didn't supply it."
- Rejection: producer supplied a value, but it wasn't one of the allowed forms. Publish fails before reaching the wire. The producer must fix the source value (either supply an allowed canonical form, or remove it to fall into the omission case).

If the release owner wants the workload labeled `prod`, the producer has to set a value that normalizes to `prod` — case and whitespace are fine, content must be `prod`/`staging`/`dev`. If they don't want to assert that, omit the label. Inferring `prod` from destination is not a third option; it's a contract violation that erases the difference between "I don't know" and "I assert prod," and between "bad input was rejected" and "bad input was silently fixed."

A one-line answer for the release owner: do not set `deployment.environment=prod` because the workload targets production. Either set it from a producer-side source value that normalizes to `prod`, or omit it; destination context is not a permitted source under the contract.

With the light ON and mounted, tap firmly with one knuckle at four spots in turn:
  a) directly on the power button
  b) on the charging-port cover / port area
  c) on the lens / optic end
  d) on the mount-clip interface
- One-spot reproduction = localized fault (button or port).
- Whole-body reproduction = PCB joint or internal cell-connection fault.

Step 2 - Charge-port check
- Open port cover, inspect for debris or corrosion (wooden toothpick only, no metal).
- Plug in a known-good cable and a known-good 5 V source. While charging, gently wiggle the cable at the port in small circles.
- If the charge LED flickers or the light cuts out during the wiggle, the port solder joint or the connector is the fault; not field-repairable.
- Try a second cable and a second charger. If only one combination misbehaves, the cable/charger is the problem, not the light.

Step 3 - Run-from-USB test (if your model runs while plugged in)
- If it runs cleanly under vibration while USB-powered, the internal cell path is suspect (loose cell tab or weak cell).
- If it still cuts out under vibration while USB-powered, the fault is downstream of the USB input (button, PCB, output stage).

Step 4 - Mount vs. body isolation
- Remove from the mount; hold the light in your palm and ride a rough stretch.
- If cutouts disappear, the mount is shorting or straining the body. Re-seat the clip; if it returns only when clipped, retire that mount interface (or the light if the mount is integrated).
- If cutouts persist unmounted, the fault is internal.

Step 5 - Mode and brightness sweep
Cycle every mode (steady high, steady low, flash, pulse). Note whether the fault is mode-dependent.
- Only-high-mode fails = weak cell or undersized output cap.
- All modes fail equally = upstream fault (button or PCB).

Step 6 - Capacity check
Fully charge, then time steady-high runtime to auto-shutoff. Compare to the maker's rated hours for that mode.
- >20% shortfall on a light under 2 years old = weak cell; end of service life even if it currently runs.

Step 7 - Cold check (optional but informative)
Bag the light, fridge (not freezer) for 30 minutes. Immediately run and tap-test. If cold makes the cutout dramatically easier to trigger, the cell or a solder joint has marginal mechanical integrity that will only worsen.

Step 8 - Visual inspection
- Fogging or condensation inside the lens = moisture ingress, retire.
- Any case bulge, seam gap, or swelling = cell swelling, retire immediately, dispose per local Li-ion rules.
- Discoloration near the port or button = heat damage, retire.

RETIREMENT CRITERIA - do NOT use for night riding if ANY of these is true
- Vibration-induced cutout reproduces after Steps 1 and 4 (i.e., not the mount).
- Charge-port wiggle in Step 2 reproduces the fault.
- Any moisture visible inside the lens.
- Any case bulge, seam separation, or cell swelling.
- Runtime shortfall >20% versus rated.
- Unit is over ~3 years old AND shows any of the above; age plus fault means a degrading cell and a fault that will progress.
- Light has ever been dropped hard from bike height even if the case looks fine - internal connections may be cracked.

REPLACEMENT (versus retirement) only makes sense if
- The fault localized cleanly to the mount interface (not the light) - replace the mount, keep the light.
- The fault localized to the charging port AND the light is in warranty AND the maker covers port repair - contact the maker; otherwise retire.
- All other internal faults in a sealed unit are not user-repairable. Do not open the sealed case: Li-ion hazard plus no user-replaceable cells typically available - not worth the safety risk.

PRACTICAL OUTCOME FOR YOUR PATTERN
Vibration-only cutout, tap reproduces, fully charged, dry case - the most likely culprits in order are (1) power-button intermittent contact, (2) internal cell-to-PCB joint, (3) charge-port solder joint. None are fixable without opening the case. The honest recommendation: retire this light for night use and replace it. You can keep it as a daytime be-seen light or a bench-test light, but do not depend on it after dark.

If you want a second opinion before buying a replacement, run Steps 1, 2, 4, and 8 once and report back which localized; that will narrow whether a warranty claim is worth filing.

Your shutdown procedure was textbook correct — clean power-down, no silencing of the alarm, no opening of the unit, no bypass. Here's the full guidance.

Bottom line on your situation: a 2018-dated SLA battery is past its typical service life (3–5 years normal, ~7 in cool/dry/light-load use), and a replace-battery chirp with no heat, swelling, odor, leak, or discoloration is almost always a normal end-of-life signal, not an active fault. Storage now is straightforward, but watch for the urgent signs below — SLA batteries can transition from "fine" to "venting" in a single overcharge event.

URGENT ISOLATION — act immediately if any of these appear

  - Swelling, bulging, or soft spots on the case
  - Hissing, bubbling, gurgling, or popping sounds
  - Sulfur / rotten-egg / metallic-acid smell (hydrogen sulfide from venting)
  - Any liquid on or under the unit — clear, brownish, or crusty residue around terminals
  - Case hot to the touch, scorch marks, discoloration
  - Smoke or any odor that isn't the normal "new electronics" smell
  - Persistent rapid chirping combined with the unit feeling warm
  - Visible terminal corrosion that wasn't there yesterday

  If any of these occur: move the unit to a well-ventilated area (garage, porch, outdoors — never a closed closet), place upright in a non-conductive container (plastic bucket with sand or kitty litter absorbs any leak), keep terminals from contacting metal, and arrange hazardous-waste pickup. Do NOT submerge, douse, or incinerate. Do NOT keep running loads through it.

SAFE STORAGE WHILE YOU DECIDE

  - Upright, cool, dry — you already have this
  - 10–25°C / 50–77°F ideal; avoid freezing temps and direct sun
  - Off the floor if possible (away from incidental contact, pets, children)
  - Terminals covered or bagged so nothing metal can bridge them
  - If you keep the unit unpowered for more than a month before replacement, plug it in for a few hours every 3–6 months to prevent battery sulfation — but if you're replacing or disposing anyway, skip this
  - Keep the original packaging if you have it; the foam inserts protect the battery in transit for disposal

IDENTIFYING THE MODEL

  - Label is usually on the back or bottom: model number, SKU, serial, VA/Watt rating
  - The battery itself usually has a sticker on top with voltage (V), capacity (Ah), and a part number
  - Common form factors you'll see: 12V 7Ah, 12V 9Ah, 12V 12Ah, occasionally 6V units
  - Manufacturer service / "RBC" / replacement-battery lookup pages (APC, CyberPower, Tripp Lite, Eaton) accept the model and return the exact battery SKU, dimensions, and connector type
  - Note the connector style (Faston F1 vs F2, spade size, wire gauge) before ordering — a wrong connector is the most common swap mistake

USER-REPLACEABLE SEALED BATTERY — typical desktop UPS

  Confirm in the manual or on the manufacturer page that your model is user-serviceable. Procedure:

    1. UPS unplugged, all loads disconnected, front panel LEDs dark
    2. Wait at least 5 minutes for internal capacitors to discharge; some manuals say 10
    3. Open the battery door (usually slide-off front panel or 1–2 screws on the back)
    4. Photograph the wire routing and connector orientation before disconnecting
    5. Disconnect the negative (black) lead first, then positive (red) — reduces short-circuit risk if you accidentally contact chassis metal
    6. Lift out the old battery; it's heavy for its size — 2–7 kg typical
    7. Match the new battery on voltage, capacity (Ah), dimensions, and connector
    8. Reconnect positive first, then negative
    9. Reassemble, plug UPS in with NO load, charge 8–24 hours before any runtime test
    10. Reset the battery-replaced indicator per the manual — some need a button hold, some self-clear after a full charge cycle

  Buy the replacement from a vendor with fresh stock; a battery that has sat on a shelf for >6 months without a top-up charge may already be sulfated and will underperform. Check the manufacture date code on the replacement.

INTERNALLY SEALED / NON-USER-REPLACEABLE UNIT

  Some UPSes (smaller "wall-wart" styles, some rackmount units, sealed consumer designs) are not designed to be opened. The manual will say "no user-serviceable parts" or simply omit replacement instructions.

  For these:
    - Do NOT open the case. Warranty is void, no parts are accessible, and forcing the case can crack the battery enclosure
    - The whole UPS goes to e-waste recycling (see disposal)
    - If the UPS is still under warranty, contact the manufacturer — battery replacement is sometimes covered
    - Don't keep using it on the assumption the chirp is harmless; the chirp indicates a battery that won't hold a useful charge, so runtime during the next outage will be very short or zero

KEY DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE TWO

  Both contain the same chemistry: a sealed (valve-regulated lead-acid, VRLA — either AGM or gel) battery. "Sealed" in battery terminology means you cannot service the electrolyte and the cell recombines gas internally under normal use; it does NOT mean the case is hermetically sealed — it can vent through a pressure-relief valve if overcharged or overheated. Both battery types need identical hazardous-waste disposal.

  The real distinction is mechanical: "user-replaceable" means the manufacturer engineered a service door, documented the procedure, and sells the battery as a spare part. "Internally sealed" means the chassis is a single-use item. The chemical hazard, the storage rules, and the disposal route are identical either way.

DISPOSAL

  Sealed lead-acid batteries are classified as universal / hazardous waste in most jurisdictions and are illegal in regular trash in many places. They contain sulfuric acid and lead; both are recoverable.

  Options, roughly in order of convenience:
    - Retail drop-off: most auto-parts stores (AutoZone, O'Reilly, NAPA, Pep Boys), Batteries+Bulbs, Home Depot, Lowe's, and Costco accept SLA batteries free, often with a small credit
    - Manufacturer take-back: APC, CyberPower, Eaton, and Tripp Lite all have battery / UPS recycling programs
    - Local household hazardous waste (HHW) facility or curbside HHW pickup day — check your city or county's waste authority
    - R2 / e-Stewards / RIOS certified e-waste recyclers for whole UPS units
    - Some office-supply and electronics retailers (Best Buy in the US) accept whole UPS units for free recycling

  Transport rules:
    - Keep upright
    - Tape over both terminals (electrical tape, packing tape) so nothing can bridge them
    - Place in a sealed plastic bag or non-conductive container in case of residual acid or slow leak
    - Don't transport in a sealed car trunk with passengers in extreme heat — vent the vehicle

  Never: regular trash, regular recycling, incineration, dumping, or pouring anything on the battery to "neutralize" it.

RECOMMENDED PATH FOR YOU

  Given a 2018 battery with no fault signs, this is a routine end-of-life replacement, not an emergency. Identify the model, confirm it's user-replaceable, order the manufacturer-specified battery, swap on a dry day with the UPS unplugged for at least 5 minutes beforehand, charge the new battery overnight before any load testing, and drop the old battery at a retail or HHW site within a week. If at any point you see the urgent signs in the first section, stop and isolate as described.

Two real problems with what's proposed.

1. The limiter values don't sit under the container's hard limit.

   Container limit: 4 GiB = 4096 MiB.
   spike_limit_mib: 4096 — equal to the cgroup ceiling.
   limit_mib: 4608 — 512 MiB above the cgroup ceiling.

   For a Go-runtime soft limiter (the OTel collector's memory limiter extension follows GOMEMLIMIT semantics), the soft limit only helps if it fires before the kernel OOM-kills the process. With limit_mib above the cgroup limit, the kernel wins and the limiter never gets a chance to trigger GC. Same shape on spike_limit_mib — at parity with the ceiling, every "spike" looks fine to the kernel until the very moment it isn't.

   For a 4 GiB container the working range is more like:
     limit_mib: ~3276 (80% of 4096, leaves ~820 MiB for non-Go RSS + kernel overhead)
     spike_limit_mib: ~2560–2816 (below limit, 20–25% spike absorption headroom)

   Exact numbers depend on what else lives in the collector process (ballast, arrow, queued exports), but both numbers must be strictly less than 4096 and limit_mib > spike_limit_mib. The current proposal has neither property.

2. The test is a syntax check, not a behavior check.

   Parsing the YAML proves the YAML is valid. It does not prove:
   - the limiter actually engages under load,
   - the chosen values don't cause OOM-kill before the limiter can act,
   - the configured behavior on activation matches the runbook (drop / refuse / restart).

   What's missing is a bounded-load test: drive the collector past spike_limit_mib via a synthetic load source, observe either GOMEMLIMIT-style GC pressure or the limiter's own telemetry firing, and assert no OOM-kill in the same window. Without that, the PR is changing a runtime behavior with no verification that the change does what its author claims.

3. Adjacent gap not in the material but worth flagging: there's no stated policy for what the limiter does when it trips (drop, refuse, restart). If the runbook doesn't say, the on-call finds out the first time it fires in prod.

Short answer: do not average them. Keep two independent gates and only let the live gate drive rollback posture.

Why the proposed average is wrong:
- The two signals have different action semantics. Live error movement -> rollback discussion. Replay/mirror mismatch -> mismatch investigation / controls work. Averaging mixes a "page on-call, consider rollback" signal with an "open a ticket, harden fixtures" signal.
- The adversarial fixture case you described is the smoking gun: a deliberately failing fixture turns the combined score red and implies rollback, even though prod is at baseline. That is a false-rollback trigger by construction.
- It also masks the dangerous case: a real live regression can be averaged toward green by a clean replay run.

Recommended representation:

1. Two separate status values, computed independently, each with its own threshold and owner:
   - Live health gate: metrics-router live traffic error movement. R/Y/G. Drives rollback discussion. Owner: on-call.
   - Replay/Mirror validation gate: fixture + mirror mismatch movement. R/Y/G. Drives mismatch investigation and controls work only. Owner: replay / controls.
   - Thresholds documented and reviewed; live threshold should generally be tighter than replay.

2. Release posture summary is a function, not an average:
   - Live red -> "rollback posture: red" (action: rollback discussion).
   - Live yellow/green and replay red -> "live green, replay mismatch open" (action: investigation, no rollback).
   - Both green -> posture green.
   - In other words, replay red can never escalate the posture to rollback-red; it can only annotate or block promotion, not trigger a rollback of prod.

3. Surface them as two rows in the release view, not one blended color, so the reader can see which gate flipped. If a single headline color is desired, color it by the live gate and add a separate badge for the replay gate.

4. Treat known-adversarial fixtures as a third category: tag them with an expected outcome ("expects mismatch on X") so they do not page out as anomalies in the replay gate in the first place. This removes the trap that motivated Nadia's averaging idea.

5. Alert routing follows the gates: live red pages on-call and opens a rollback channel; replay red opens a mismatch/controls ticket and never pages the on-call rotation.

If Nadia still wants one number, give her a conjunction with a dominant signal label rather than a mean, e.g., "live=green, replay=red -> posture=green, mismatch open" rather than averaging to yellow. The rule that should not bend: replay/mirror mismatch movement must never, by itself, cause the release posture to read as "rollback."

Session plan — 60 min bounded, return-to-climbing (post-undercling rehab, week ~1-2 of ramp).

PRE-SESSION
- Skip Ren's flagged moderate circuit entirely. Don't even warm up on it.
- Wrist tape if it's part of your routine, water on hand, phone on you.
- Set the rule before you start: today is progression, not performance. The clean reassessment gates the next session, not today's volume.

WARMUP — 15 min (longer than usual, on purpose)
0-5 min — wrist & forearm prep
  - Wrist circles both directions, 10x each
  - Prayer stretch + reverse prayer, 30s each
  - Light band-resisted flexion/extension, slow
  - Lacrosse ball on forearm extensors, ~60s/side
  - Open/close hand, finger spreads, no load

5-10 min — low-load hangs
  - Jug hangs on a large positive hold, 10s x 5, full hang, 30s shake-out between
  - Open-hand only — no half-crimp, no crimp, no thumb catch
  - Stop earlier than your instinct says; we're seeding load, not testing it

10-15 min — feet-only traverse
  - Low traverse, hands used for balance only
  - Focus on flagging, smearing, precise foot placement
  - If forearms pump here, you've already done enough

PROGRESSIVE BLOCKS — 40 min

Block A — 12 min — Easy open-hand slabs
  - Low-angle problems only
  - Open-hand grip only: slopers, jugs, big pinches, open-side pinches. No crimp, no undercling.
  - Foot sequencing, hip position, slow movement — not strength
  - 4-6 short problems, walk-off/downclimb between
  - Rest 60-90s between attempts

Rest transition — 3 min
  - Shake out, walk, hydrate
  - Self-check (0-10) on: wrist tightness, dull ache, finger tingling, stiffness

Block B — 13 min — Vertical footwork problems
  - Vertical to slightly overhanging, but holds stay positive (jugs, slopers, big pinches)
  - Footwork-first: heel hooks, toe hooks, flagging, drop-knees
  - Open-hand only; if you feel your fingers rolling into half-crimp, downgrade the problem
  - 3-5 problems, 3-4 attempts each
  - Rest 90-120s between problems

Rest transition — 3 min
  - Same self-check. This is a natural off-ramp if anything has crept up.

Block C — 9 min — Linked low traverse (synthesis)
  - One traverse that strings slab-feet with reachy-but-positive moves
  - Move continuously but unhurried — pace well below max
  - Goal is pattern integration, not send
  - 3-4 traverses, full shake-out between

COOLDOWN — 5 min
  - Wrist extension + flexion stretches, elbow extended
  - Forearm extensor flush
  - Walk, hydrate
  - Jot down any post-session sensation for the log (sharp/dull/where/when/how long)

SYMPTOM-BASED STOP CRITERIA — apply all session

STOP IMMEDIATELY on any of:
  - Sharp wrist pain (front, back, radial or ulnar side) — any grade
  - Click, catch, or lock in the wrist
  - Tingling or numbness in fingers (contact pump ≠ this)
  - Pain that doesn't clear within 60-90s of releasing the hold
  - Form break: you catch yourself crimping or reaching for an undercling on a problem you chose to avoid — that's load past your line
  - Forearm pump so early it's distorting foot placement
  - Swelling, throbbing, or a "hot" feeling in the wrist during or right after

PAUSE & REASSESS on:
  - Dull ache that lingers >2 min after a hard effort
  - Stiffness that gets worse (not better) across a block
  - Any sensation you can't immediately explain

DO NOT:
  - Take "one more try" because the send is close
  - Substitute an undercling grip because the problem invites it
  - Shorten the warmup because you feel fine at minute 5
  - Treat today's clean wrist as today's license to push volume — it gates the next session, not this one

Total: 15 warmup + 40 blocks (+6 transitions built in) + 5 cooldown = 60 min, hard cap.

Saved. Quick read on what's materially wrong with the revised material, since you'll likely have to push back:

1. **The helper is out-of-process and can't exercise the limiter.** memory_limiter sits in the collector's own pipeline and only sees allocations made by the collector process. A separate process holding 3.72 GiB does not pressure the collector's heap at all — so the test, as written, is structurally incapable of observing refusal. It only proves "the cgroup doesn't OOM-kill under external memory pressure," which is a cgroup-memory test, not a memory_limiter test.

2. **What "limiter works" actually requires:**
   - Send real traffic into the collector's receiver.
   - Drive the collector's own RSS upward toward `limit_mib` (3584) — typically by holding spans in an in-process queue, sending oversized payloads, or stalling the exporter.
   - Observe (a) `refused` counter rising, (b) `otelcol_processor_memory_limiter_refused` metric incrementing, (c) the queue/exporter go into backpressure when memory is at the spike ceiling.
   - Then drop load, confirm RSS recedes below `limit_mib - spike_limit_mib` (3072) and refusal stops.

3. **Scope drift on the vendor sign-off.** If the vendor's deliverable is "no OOM-kill at 3.72 GiB external pressure," then that's what got signed off — but it doesn't speak to whether the limiter will actually shed load in production. Those are two different claims; the current material muddles them.

4. **The cgroup vs. limit numbers.** 3584 + 512 = 4096 = 4 GiB. Fine, but worth confirming the spike ceiling matches the slack between cgroup limit and `limit_mib` — if the container can be charged up to 4 GiB and the collector refuses at 3.5 GiB, that's 512 MiB of unaccounted slack, which is the intended behavior. Just want the test to assert refused>0 *before* the cgroup is at risk, not at 3.72 GiB where it's already too late.

Net: the test as revised validates cgroup headroom under external load, not the memory_limiter processor itself. To validate the limiter, traffic has to flow through the collector's own pipeline and push the collector's heap to the threshold.

The fix is straightforward: the former-address W-2 is superseded, so only the corrected South Slope W-2 should be reported. A corrected W-2 (W-2c) supersedes the original for filing purposes — you do not include both, and the IRS does not want both.

In the tax software, delete the former-Park-Slope entry entirely. Keep only the South Slope (corrected) W-2 and report its wages and withholding. Since your correction was address-only and wages/withholding were unchanged, the figures are identical to the original by design — that's why doubling them is the only error. Once you remove the superseded one, Sphere's wages and withholding on the return will match what was actually earned and withheld, and no other line on the return needs to change.

Why this works:
  - IRS treatment of W-2c: only the corrected version is the returnable document.
  - The payroll portal's "superseded" flag is the same signal — that copy should never have been imported.
  - Address-only corrections with unchanged wages/withholding are the cleanest case; nothing else on the return is affected.

A few small things worth knowing while you're in there:
  - Keep both the original W-2 and the W-2c with your tax records. The practical retention window is at least 3 years (IRS assessment period for W-2 related issues), and 7 years is a common safer choice.
  - Address doesn't change federal tax math. On the NY return it appears as mailing address but doesn't change state income tax owed, since both Park Slope and South Slope are in NY.
  - If the software offers an explicit "superseded / duplicate" toggle for an imported W-2, use that on the Park Slope entry instead of deleting raw — it's cleaner if you ever re-import. Otherwise delete is fine.

You haven't filed, so there's nothing to amend. Once the draft shows a single Sphere W-2 with the South Slope address, you're good to file.

Safest sequence to swap the superseded 2024 W-2 import for the corrected one (address change, wages/withholding unchanged) without ever touching Box 1 or Box 2 by hand:

Phase 0 — Baseline (do this first; nothing destructive yet)
  1. Save a backup copy of the return file as it stands now.
  2. Print or screenshot the current return summary: federal AGI, taxable income, total tax, refund vs. amount owed, total federal withholding.
  3. From the paper original W-2 and the paper W-2c, write down: EIN, employer name, Box 1 wages, Box 2 federal withholding, and (if you file a state return) Boxes 15/16/17. You will compare, not re-key.
  4. Confirm the new South Slope address is correct in your own records before touching the return.

Phase 1 — Void, do not delete, the superseded import
  5. Open the W-2 entry and use the software's "this W-2 is incorrect / superseded" flag — a checkbox, a "void" toggle, or a "replace with corrected form" button. This keeps the audit trail. If the only option exposed is delete, fall back to delete, but only after step 1's backup is confirmed.

Phase 2 — Bring in the corrected form
  6. Use the software's W-2c import path, or its "I have a corrected W-2" intake if it offers one. Import from the PDF or image the employer sent; do not re-key from the prior entry or from memory.
  7. If the software forces manual entry, type only from the paper W-2c. Never copy a number from the old on-screen entry — that is how stale values silently persist.

Phase 3 — Field-by-field verification (read each value off paper, then off screen)
  8. Employer identity: EIN and employer name on screen match the W-2c character for character.
  9. Wages, Box 1: match paper, to the cent.
  10. Federal withholding, Box 2: match paper, to the cent.
  11. State boxes 15 / 16 / 17 (only if you file a state return): match paper.
  12. Address — note this is two distinct places: the personal info tab on Form 1040 should show the new South Slope address; the W-2 entry's address fields are the employer's mailing address, which you only confirm against the W-2c, never "correct" from memory.
  13. Confirm the "corrected form" / W-2c indicator is set on the entry. Most e-file engines will refuse to transmit if a superseded import is still flagged active or if a W-2c is imported without its flag.

Phase 4 — Return total check (the no-edit guard)
  14. Compare the return summary against the screenshot from step 2. Because wages and withholding on the W-2c are unchanged from the original, federal AGI, taxable income, total tax, refund/owed, and total federal withholding must all be identical. If anything differs, stop and reconcile before doing anything else — a delta here means either the wrong form imported or a stray field was altered.
  15. Run the software's review / audit tool and clear every W-2 or corrected-form warning before you move on.

Phase 5 — Final pass before filing
  16. Re-read the income section and the personal info section end to end.
  17. E-file or print-and-mail only after steps 13–16 all pass. Keep the paper W-2c with your tax records (IRS recordkeeping window is at least 3 years).

Two guardrails worth keeping in mind:
  - The address change lives on Form 1040 (personal info), not on the W-2 entry. The W-2's address fields are the employer's.
  - Do not hand-edit Box 1 or Box 2 to "make it match." Either the import is right or it isn't. A manual override of wages or withholding is the single most damaging thing you can leave in the audit log; the whole point of this sequence is to keep that override count at zero.

# Assessment: Wes's 2025-03-03 No-Rollback Decision

**Bottom line:** On the evidence available at the time, Wes's call was defensible but **not yet closeable**. The signal pattern matches the shard-keeper `label_map` leak touch-matrix hypothesis (validation-source rows reaching a canary aggregate read site, not a live-path regression), which is a known class of "looks like a service regression, isn't" failure. That hypothesis needs four concrete evidence classes before the window can be closed. Below is the assessment plus the evidence checklist.

## 1. What Wes saw (the snapshot)

- Aggregate canary panel: **red 10:47–10:53** (6 minutes).
- Separate live-path canary panel: **at baseline** through the same window.
- The moving series inside the aggregate panel were tagged `source_class=validation`, not `source_class=live` (or equivalent routing/instrumentation class).
- No `label_map` parity exception was raised by the alert path; the metric-router runbook's "compare p99 vs baseline" + "roll back via pipeline if regression confirmed" gates were not triggered on the live-path panel.

## 2. Why the no-rollback call was reasonable

The metrics-router canary runbook (rb_metrics_router_canary) is explicit: rollback is gated on a **live-path** regression, not on an aggregate-panel red. A red aggregate with a green live baseline is the textbook signature of (a) a scheduled load test (per the 2023-08-16 canary note in the same runbook), or (b) a `label_map` leak from a validation/admin read site bleeding into the aggregate. Both are "do not rollback" cases. The deploy history for prod in the cutover window shows no in-flight metrics-router canary on 2025-03-03 that had crossed into the live-path panel, which is consistent with Wes's read. **On the snapshot alone, rollback would have been the wrong move** — it would have undone a canary that the live path was passing, and left the actual `label_map` leak unfixed.

## 3. Why it isn't closeable yet

The shard-keeper runbook `rb_shard_keeper_label_parity` (post-May-18, owner alex / backup cyrus-team) sets a hard rule that applies here: **a canary-window clear requires confirming the canary aggregate read site is on the parity-signed-off path**, and preflight-PASS + alert-source-PASS is not an override on a parity-FAIL (re-confirmed in the 2026-09-12 shard-keeper#190 lesson, which is the same class of failure). Wes had a plausible explanation for the red, but "plausible" is not the standard; the standard is source-class evidence. Closing the window on a "the live path was green so the aggregate can't matter" argument is exactly the failure mode that the `label_map` touch matrix (19 read sites, grouped-kills methodology) was written to prevent — a missed read site produces a **falsely clean cutover**.

## 4. Evidence checklist to close the canary event

Four classes, all required. Mark each ✅/❌ with the artifact.

### A. Source-class evidence (was the moving series really validation?)

- [ ] **Full replay source-class export** for the 10:47–10:53 window: every series that contributed to the aggregate panel, with `source_class`, originating service, originating read site, and label values. Goal: prove the moving series were *only* `source_class=validation` rows, not a live-path regression hiding inside the aggregate.
- [ ] **No-series-with-other-source-class attestation** for the same window from rollup-service (the parity-sign-off owner). Per Cardinality Guardrails (2023-11-08) and `rb_shard_keeper_label_parity`, a green metrics-router canary alone does not prove rollup-service parity.
- [ ] **Origin-trace for each validation series** to its read site. The shard-keeper `label_map` touch matrix lists the 19 routing + admin/validation read sites — every validation series must map to one of those, or it is an unknown read site (which is itself a parity failure).

### B. Live-accounting evidence (did live traffic actually stay at baseline?)

- [ ] **p50 / p99 / max** of the live-path panel across the 10:47–10:53 window and a 30-minute pre/post comparison. Per the metrics-router canary evidence norm, include dropped-series triggers.
- [ ] **Heap snapshot** timed inside the window (per the metrics-router cleanup-pause evidence norm). If heap spiked during a red aggregate without a live-path blip, that strengthens the validation-source hypothesis (a `label_map` leak loads the validation reader, not the live reader).
- [ ] **Independent verification that rollback wiring was live** during the window. A green live path is only meaningful if rollback *would have fired* had the live path regressed — otherwise "green" is uninformative.
- [ ] **Reconciliation: live ingestion count vs. aggregate-panel series count.** If the aggregate moved while live-path series count didn't, the delta has to be sourced from validation/admin read sites, not invented.

### C. Route-state evidence (the `label_map` parity check)

- [ ] **Confirm the canary aggregate read site is on the parity-signed-off path.** `rb_shard_keeper_label_parity` requires sync with Nadia (alerting/dashboards) AND the rollup-service owner (Cyrus team since 2026-05-18) before any label-name change crosses service boundaries. Get written sign-off from both that the aggregate read site the canary window observed is on the path that has been parity-signed off.
- [ ] **Shared parity fixture refresh.** The fixture must assert the current production reader path (e.g. `readLabel(series, "storage_region")` per the supermemory note on the shared fixture). Stale-fixture evidence is parity-FAIL even if preflight is green.
- [ ] **Touch-matrix walk for the aggregate read site.** Use the 19-site grouped-kills methodology (not grep-by-file). For the aggregate read site the canary hit, show that every label it can emit has been parity-checked across routing + admin + validation readers. A missed site = fail-closed.
- [ ] **No `provenance_status: partial`** anywhere in the canary window's read-site chain. Partial provenance on a `Deploy_movement` path is a hard fail per the lantern op signals.

### D. Customer-impact evidence (was anything user-visible touched?)

- [ ] **Customer-facing metric parity**: dashboards / SLO panels that customers see stayed at baseline through the window. No red customer-facing panels in the same 10:47–10:53 frame.
- [ ] **Per-tenant cardinality / error-rate diff** across the window vs. the prior 7-day baseline. Validation-source bleed can show up as elevated cardinality on tenants whose traffic the validation readers are exercised against, without touching live-path error rates — call that out explicitly if seen.
- [ ] **No alert escalated to a customer-comms surface** (status page, customer Slack lane, EM channel). The lantern rule is "service-OK raw text only" for status output — if anything customer-facing was emitted during the window, that's its own incident, separate from the canary.
- [ ] **No deploy/commit movement** coincident with the window that lacked full internal provenance. A commit during the canary window with only external provenance is an independent `Deploy_movement` failure.

## 5. Decision posture for closing

- If A + B + C + D all return clean, the window can be closed with a note that the red was a `label_map`-driven validation-source bleed and the actual leak site should be entered into the touch-matrix follow-up (not the canary incident).
- If any one of A/B/C/D fails, **do not close**. C failing means parity wasn't actually proven and per `rb_shard_keeper_label_parity` preflight+alert-source green is **not** an override — keep the canary window open, escalate to Nadia + Cyrus team, and treat it as a parity regression until the fixture and touch-matrix walk pass.
- Do **not** close on "Wes's read was probably right." That is the failure mode the touch matrix exists to prevent.

## 6. What I'd recommend doing next

1. Pull the replay source-class export (A) — this is the cheapest evidence to gather and the one most likely to settle the question quickly.
2. In parallel, get the route-state sign-off in writing from Nadia and the Cyrus team on the aggregate read site (C). Per the runbook, both are mandatory; one is not enough.
3. Only after A and C are in hand does it make sense to spend cycles on B and D, which are bulkier.

What makes a claim land in 8 minutes: it names a specific engineering artifact, decision, or measurable shift — not a design sentiment. Each claim gets ~90 seconds; total = ~5 minutes content + buffer for transitions.

THREE CLAIMS (each layers on the last: definition → artifact → outcome)

1. The contract claim — what tokens are, reframed as engineering infrastructure.
   "Tokens are the contract that replaced the design-to-engineering sync step. Before, every theme or brand-variant change was a reconciliation loop between Figma and code. Now the token is the source of truth and the change propagates through the build — design and engineering edit the same artifact."
   Why it works: prevents "visual cleanup" framing. Tokens move from decorative layer to interface contract.

2. The handoff-artifact claim — what the deliverable changed to.
   "The handoff shifted from specs-and-screenshots to a typed token contract with build-time generation. Engineering consumes one source; design changes one source. The 'is this the latest color' loop is structurally eliminated — not by discipline, by architecture."
   Why it works: names the specific artifact (typed contract, build-time gen) and a specific failure mode that's now gone. Audiences can locate themselves in the before/after.

3. The outcome claim — pick whichever Anya can defend in one breath:
   - Quantitative: "Since tokens landed, N theme variants shipped without an engineering ticket — design owned the change end-to-end." OR "Drift bugs caught in design review vs. caught in production: [ratio]. Validation moved upstream."
   - If she doesn't have a number yet: "A token PR is now peer-reviewed by both design and engineering against the same artifact. That's the handoff — one review surface, not two."

ONE QUESTION — diagnostic for whether the audience understood the handoff value

"When a product team requests a new theme variant next week, what's the path — a design ticket, an engineering ticket, or a token PR — and who owns the merge?"

Why this one: the correct answer ("token PR, owned by [X]") is falsifiable and engineering-specific. If someone answers "design ticket" or "engineering ticket," they've absorbed the visual layer but not the handoff shift. IND-031-04 means the prior-year (2023) AGI or e-file PIN entered for the primary taxpayer on your 2024 federal return doesn't match what's in IRS records. Two things that are NOT problems:

  - NY return is held automatically. It'll transmit once federal is accepted. Don't refile state separately.
  - No payment was attempted. The rejection happens at validation before any debit instruction is sent.

Most likely causes, in rough order of frequency:

  1. Wrong AGI entered — typo, or pulled from a draft/projection instead of the actually-filed 2023 1040.
  2. State AGI entered instead of federal AGI (NY IT-201 line 17 ≠ federal 1040 line 11).
  3. 2023 was amended via 1040-X and the AGI changed — IRS has the amended figure, not the original.
  4. Joint attribution: "primary taxpayer" is whoever is listed first on the return; that person's prior-year AGI/PIN is what IRS checks against their SSN.
  5. IP PIN required (IRS CP01A notice for the 2024 season) and not entered, or wrong one entered. If both spouses were issued IP PINs, each has their own and must be entered for their respective SSN.
  6. 2023 return was filed very recently and IRS hasn't processed it yet.

Diagnostic:

  - Pull the actually-filed 2023 Form 1040 (not a draft, not a projection). Line 11 = federal AGI. If you filed 1040-X, use the AGI as it appears on the amended return as filed.
  - If you can't locate the 2023 return, request a 2023 IRS Tax Account Transcript at irs.gov/transcript or via Form 4506-T — AGI is on it.
  - Compare the figure in your tax software now against the filed 2023 number.
  - Check whether either of you received a CP01A IP PIN for the 2024 season. If yes, that 6-digit number must be entered, for the correct year and the correct spouse's SSN.

Fix:

  Correct the field in your tax software and retransmit. NY release follows automatically once federal is accepted.

If nothing matches after verifying against the filed 2023 return and IP PIN status:

  Could indicate identity fraud or a stale IRS record. IRS Identity Protection Specialized Unit: 800-908-4490. They can confirm what's on file and issue an IP PIN if appropriate.

Timing: it's March 9, well ahead of the April 15 deadline. No penalty or late-fee concern while you correct and retransmit.

IND-031-04 sits in the IRS prior-year verification family: it rejects the return because the prior-year AGI (or the prior-year Identity Protection PIN, if you had one) you entered does not match what the IRS has on file. Important to confirm up front: the corrected Sphere W-2 and your current-year income line are not the cause. The fix is in the prior-year verification field only, which is exactly what you want.

Below is a verification-first sequence. The principle is: never type a value into the field unless you have just retrieved it from a primary source. Do not reuse a value from memory, from an old draft, or from a soft copy without confirming it matches the IRS's record.

Step 0 - Identify which sub-field failed
  - Most e-file software will tell you whether the reject is against the prior-year AGI field, the IPPIN field, or both.
  - For a 2024 return, the "prior year" is 2023. Confirm this is the year your software is asking about before you do anything else.

Step 1 - Retrieve the prior-year AGI from a primary source
  - Primary source: IRS online account or Get Transcript (irs.gov). Pull the 2023 Account Transcript or Return Transcript. The Return Transcript shows AGI as reported on line 11 of the 2023 Form 1040 (or the equivalent line on 1040-SR or 1040-NR).
  - Secondary source: your prior-year tax software account showing the 2023 return as Accepted / Acknowledged, with the figures preserved exactly as filed.
  - Tertiary source: a paper or PDF copy of the original 2023 1040, line 11. Use this only if (a) and (b) are not available.
  - Note on amended returns: if you filed a 1040-X for 2023, do not assume the AGI changed. Pull a transcript to see what the IRS shows after processing the amendment, and use that figure. If the amendment did not change AGI, the original 1040 AGI is correct.

Step 2 - Only if an IPPIN was issued for 2023, retrieve the PIN
  - This applies only if you were enrolled in the Identity Protection PIN program for 2023. Most filers are not.
  - Do not guess. Retrieve the exact 6-digit IPPIN from: IRS online account, the CP01A notice mailed in December 2023, or the IRS IPPIN retrieval tool (idverify.irs.gov).
  - If you cannot find it, request it; do not retry blindly - the IRS limits failed attempts.

Step 3 - Confirm the field-level details before re-entering
  - AGI must be entered to the cent. Do not round.
  - Joint filers: the prior-year AGI must match the original joint 2023 return as the IRS has it. Do not enter your individual AGI if the 2023 return was filed jointly (or vice versa).
  - Software flag: if you have the option to verify via IPPIN instead of AGI, and you have an IPPIN, use it - it is unambiguous. If you do not, AGI is the only option.

Step 4 - Re-enter only the verification field and resubmit
  - Do not touch current-year income, the Sphere W-2 entries, deductions, dependents, or anything else. The reject is single-field.
  - Re-transmit the federal return.

Step 5 - New York return
  - The NY return being held is the normal coupled-state behavior: most NY e-file software waits for federal acceptance before transmitting. Once the federal return is accepted, the NY return should release on its next scheduled push; if it does not, you can manually trigger retransmission after federal acceptance.
  - No payment was withdrawn because the federal reject stopped the return before the billing/ACH phase. There is no payment to recall.

Common pitfalls to avoid:
  - Pulling the AGI from an amended 2023 return without confirming the amendment did not change line 11.
  - Entering last year's draft AGI rather than the accepted-return AGI.
  - Rounding the AGI to a whole dollar.
  - Treating the corrected Sphere W-2 as the cause (it is not - it is a prior-year verification reject).
  - Re-trying with slightly different values to "see what works." Each retry that lands on a wrong value is logged; stop guessing and pull the transcript.

If, after pulling the 2023 Return Transcript, the AGI on file at the IRS differs from what you have any record of having filed, that points to either identity-related activity on your account or an amendment you did not authorize. At that point, before resubmitting, contact the IRS (or your tax preparer / CPA) - it is a separate issue from a simple typo, and the fix is not to guess which figure is correct.

If you want, tell me which sub-field your software flagged (AGI vs. IPPIN) and whether your 2023 return was amended, and I can narrow this to the specific retrieval step.

Quick read on the rate: 18 psi lost in ~20 hours is a definite leak, not normal permeation (butyl tubes drift ~1-3 psi per day; latex faster but not this fast) and not just temperature. A small thorn, wire, valve leak, or porous tube all match this rate. Front being fine localizes it to the rear wheel.

Important caveat up front: an outside visual check does not rule out a thorn or wire embedded in the tread from the inside, a casing bruise on the tire's inner surface, a torn rim strip, or a spoke nipple poking through. Plan to inspect the tire's interior before any patch or swap.

Non-destructive leak-check sequence
Do these in order. Stop as soon as you localize the leak.

Phase 1 — wheel still on the bike, inflated
1. Re-inflate to ~60 psi and note the time. Mark the stem position with a piece of tape so you can return the wheel to the same orientation.
2. Valve core check (Schrader): with the cap off, listen at the open valve and brush soapy water on the valve tip and the threaded core. Bubbles or hiss at the core = loose or dirty core; tighten 1/8 turn with a valve tool or a small wrench on the knurled nut, then re-test. For Presta: open the locknut and re-seat the core, then test.
3. Valve-stem base: brush soapy water around the stem where it exits the rim. Bubbles here = the valve isn't sealing against the rim, which usually means rim tape is shifted, torn, or missing over the spoke hole, or the locknut is loose.
4. Tire beads: brush soapy water along both bead lines on both sides of the wheel (where the tire's edge meets the rim). Rotate the wheel slowly. Bubbles at the bead = the tire isn't seated evenly, the rim has a burr, or the rim strip has slipped; usually curable without a new tube.
5. Tread and sidewalls: slosh soapy water across the entire outside tread and both sidewalls, including the inboard sidewall. Bubbles pinpoint an outside puncture. Listen for a faint hiss in a quiet room by holding the inflated wheel near your ear and rotating slowly.

Phase 2 — wheel off the bike
6. Spin the bare wheel in the air near your ear; small leaks sometimes audibly hiss where soapy water won't stay in place (e.g., on a knobby).
7. Submerge test: with the tube inflated inside the tire (still on the rim is fine), dunk the wheel section-by-section in a basin of water — valve area first, then arc the wheel through the water. A steady stream of bubbles marks the leak. Mark with chalk.

Phase 3 — tire off the rim
8. Push one bead off the rim. Before touching anything, run a rag-wrapped finger (or a gloved finger) all the way around the inside of the tire, pressing lightly. You'll feel a thorn, wire, or glass shard that wasn't visible from outside. Pull it out — leaving it in will re-puncture a fresh tube immediately.
9. Inspect the rim strip: look for tears, displacement over a spoke hole, or a missing section. Inspect the rim well for sharp edges, exposed spoke nipples, or debris.
10. Inflate the bare tube (just the tube, valve open) and either submerge it or soap it. This catches pinholes, porous seams, or valve-stem/tube interface leaks.

Decision criteria

Patch the tube if all of these are true:
- Single puncture smaller than ~3 mm.
- Puncture is in the tube's central tread area, not within ~2 cm of the valve stem.
- Tube is otherwise supple (no cracks when flexed, no thin spots, not visibly aged).
- You're using a vulcanizing patch with fresh cement, not a glueless patch as a permanent fix.
- You found and removed the cause on the tire's inside.

Replace the tube if any of these are true:
- Puncture is near the valve stem (patching here is unreliable under pressure).
- More than one puncture found.
- The hole is a slice or tear longer than ~5 mm — patches won't hold.
- The tube is old, stiff, or shows craze cracks when flexed.
- You can't find a leak on the tube itself but the wheel still goes flat — the tube may be porous at the seams or the valve-stem interface; replacement is faster and more certain than chasing it.

Take it to a bicycle shop if:
- The leak persists with a confirmed-new tube and confirmed-clean tire interior — points to rim strip, rim well, spoke nipple, or a tire casing issue you don't want to chase.
- The tire shows a bulge, persistent deformation, or visible casing threads when reinflated — the tire itself is failing and replacement decisions (matching size, folding vs. wire bead, tubeless-ready compat) are worth a pro opinion.
- The bead won't seat or blows off when you reinflate.
- The wheel is out of true enough that you can't confidently remount and re-seat.
- You've done the sequence and still can't localize — a shop will submerge the whole wheel and read the bubble in under a minute.

Two operational notes
- When you reinstall, inflate to half pressure, spin and check the tire tracks centered on the rim, then top up. This catches a poorly seated bead before it ruptures a tube at full pressure.
- If the cause was debris, the new tube's first ride deserves a 24-hour pressure check before you trust it for commuting.

Holding the bike until you've run phases 1-3 is the right call. Start at phase 1 — most slow leaks of this rate are either at the valve or a single small puncture on the tread, and you'll usually know within ten minutes whether you're looking at a 5-minute patch or a tube swap.

Center of the pressure-test: without a pre-adoption rate, the four signals describe the platform's operating state but cannot support any causality claim about effect. Leadership's "six-week measurement approach instead of retroactive causality claim" steer is the right shape — the draft risk is letting a trend line imply one.

Per-signal:

  Adoption across three teams. Denominator, not numerator. Adoption % alone says nothing about quality or effect; it earns its keep as the denominator for the other three (catch rate per adoption, exceptions per adopter, corrections per unit of output). Without binding to output volume or work mix, two teams at 80% adoption can sit in totally different operating regimes.

  Drift-check failures caught before ship. Most useful as a *trend within* the six weeks, not an absolute. Direction tells you the safety net is firing more or less; it does not tell you why. "More caught" cuts three ways: more issues generated, better detection, or the check retuned during the window. Need a category breakdown so the headline count decomposes.

  Exceptions requested vs. accepted. Friction signal. Increasing accepted exceptions could mean defaults misaligned, users learning override levers, or scope creep on what's routed through. Keep request volume and accept rate separate — request = user behavior, accept = platform policy. Selection bias: people who know they can override differ from those who don't.

  Handoff corrections after generation. Slipperiest of the four. Decreasing corrections could be (a) drift-check catching more upstream, (b) platform producing cleaner output, or (c) reviewers fatigued / trusting the platform. Without an independent signal on reviewer behavior, you can't pick. This is the metric most likely to be misread.

Cross-signal — the drift-vs-handoff pairing is the most informative thing in the window. Both up = platform generating more, only partially caught upstream. Caught up + corrections down = upstream catching working. Both down = system genuinely calmer or reviewers fatigued — ambiguous. Lead with this pairing, not the four counts separately.

Within-window confounds to disclose in the writeup: team rotation, task-mix shifts, platform changes during the window, reviewer practice evolving. Anything the platform's own logs emit (drift-check counts, exception events) sits in vendor scope and needs independent verification, not vendor sign-off.

What the six weeks can honestly deliver: operational characterization (where the safety nets fire, what gets overridden, what slips), direction-of-change (not magnitude), cross-team comparison, category-level trends on drift and exceptions.

What it cannot, even with clean data: any "the platform reduced X by Y%" claim, causality, attribution, effect size, or counterfactual.

Reframe for Anya: present it as a *characterization window*, not an *evaluation window*. Describes the system; doesn't judge whether the platform works. Removes the causality trap and gives leadership operational data they can act on without overclaiming.

Ranging over a Go `map[int][]Route` and feeding entries to a hasher in encountered order is non-deterministic — Go's runtime intentionally randomizes map iteration order per `range` to discourage order-dependent code. The fix is to sort by key (and within each key, by route identity) before hashing, so the digest is a pure function of the parsed route set rather than the runtime's iteration order.   - Check him over — ticks often come in groups, especially ears, neck, armpits, between toes, groin.

Here's a safe sequence for Kibo. This assumes an awake, calm cat; if Kibo is painful, fractious, or has many ticks, skip to "vet first."

PREP
  - Fine-tipped tweezers (or a purpose-made tick hook like a Tick Twister)
  - Latex/nitrile gloves
  - Isopropyl alcohol in a small jar with a tight lid (to kill and preserve the tick)
  - Mild antiseptic or chlorhexidine wash, cotton balls
  - Treats and a towel for burrito-wrap restraint if needed
  - A helper, ideally

RESTRAIN
  - Have a second person gently hold Kibo: one hand scruffing/under chest, other steadying hindquarters
  - Speak softly; a towel wrap around the shoulders/front legs keeps claws in
  - Never restrain so hard Kibo struggles — that risks breaking the tick

REMOVE (the critical step)
  - Part the fur so the tick's mouthparts are visible at skin level
  - Grasp the tick with tweezers as close to the skin as possible — at the head/mouthparts, NOT the engorged body
  - Pull straight up with steady, even pressure. Do not jerk, twist, squeeze, crush, or burn
  - Squeezing the body can inject pathogens; twisting can leave mouthparts in the skin
  - If mouthparts break off in the skin: don't dig — clean the area and monitor; call the vet only if it becomes red, swollen, or draining

PRESERVE
  - Drop the intact tick into the alcohol jar; label with the date and where on Kibo it was attached
  - Keep it for 2–4 weeks in case symptoms develop — the vet can ID the species (which informs disease risk: deer ticks carry more, lone star and American dog ticks vary)
  - Note the date, location on body, and how long it was likely attached

AFTERCARE
  - Clean the bite site with antiseptic; don't use hydrogen peroxide on cats (irritating)
  - Wash your hands and the tweezers
  - A small red bump or scab for a few days is normal

MONITOR FOR 2–4 WEEKS
  Daily check for:
    - Lethargy or hiding more than usual
    - Refusing food or water
    - Fever (warm ears, lethargy — no rectal thermometer without training)
    - Lameness, stiff or painful joints
    - Swollen lymph nodes (under jaw, behind knees)
    - Unusual bleeding, pale gums, or yellowing of gums/eyes
    - Wobbliness or weakness in the hind legs (tick paralysis is rare but an emergency)
    - Vomiting or labored breathing
  Check the bite site weekly for an expanding red ring or increasing swelling/drainage.

CONTACT THE VET (same day) IF
  - You couldn't fully remove the tick and the site looks inflamed
  - The bite site is expanding red, draining, or very painful
  - Kibo is lethargic, off food, feverish, or limping within 2–4 weeks
  - You see any of: pale/yellow gums, wobbliness, breathing trouble, bleeding
  - Kibo was exposed to a tick-control product not explicitly labeled safe for cats (many dog products are toxic)

CONTACT THE VET (routine, within a day or two) IF
  - You're unsure how long the tick was attached
  - Kibo has had multiple ticks
  - You want the tick species-identified and a risk assessment

A note on prevention (separate from removal): only use tick products labeled for cats — permethrin and many "spot-ons" sold for dogs are toxic to cats. If you want a preventive, ask the clinic which option fits Kibo's weight and health history.

   - New evidence of pests — droppings, frass, insects — attracted to the area.
   - Adjacent rooms (kitchen floor near sink, wall behind cabinet) developing musty odor, warm spots, or discoloration.

Possible causes to evaluate in order of likelihood: residual odor in panel from prior unknown wetting event, micro-leak history not currently active, external moisture wicking from behind panel. Request: open back panel or use borescope to inspect cavity, inspect wall behind for prior leak evidence, verify all supply/drain seals."
