THE COST ISN'T THE EXCEPTION
A readout on the March exception-routing sheet

[OPEN — ~1 min]
The lesson from March isn't about exceptions.
It's about the decisions owners had to make twice.

We routed a handful of exceptions through the shared channel last month. Each one looked like a routine call when it arrived. None of them were routine. Each was a case where an implicit invariant hadn't been written down, and the owner made the right call anyway — but couldn't know they were making the right call until after the fact.

The pattern isn't the exception. The pattern is that the invariant was implicit.

[WHY NOW — ~1 min]
Two reasons this is worth fifteen minutes of forum time.

First: every one of those exceptions cost two decisions instead of one. The owner's call, and then a second call where we all had to reconstruct what the invariant had been and whether the exception was real. That second decision is pure tax. It's avoidable.

Second: the exceptions clustered, but not where you'd expect. They clustered in the areas where invariants stay implicit longest — labeling and interpretation framing. Not because those areas are special. Because the invariants in those areas don't show up in code review. They show up in how we talk about the system.

[EXAMPLE 1 — PARITY GATE — ~3 min]
Shard-keeper label parity.

The invariant: when a label is renamed, the new name is live at every read site — routing, admin, validation — before the old name is removed. Same change, all sites.

The exception path: any rename requires sign-off from two parties — the team that owns the data path, and the team that owns the consumer side. Both, not either. That's the only path; there isn't a "small rename" exception.

The routine: which label you choose, how you spell it, how you roll it through your service.

What actually happened: preflight ran clean. Alert-source check ran clean. Parity check failed. Pre-flight and alert-source are both necessary. Neither is sufficient. The owner halted the cutover based on parity alone — the right call — but they made it under time pressure, because the invariant "labels match across all read sites at cutover, with two named sign-offs on any rename" wasn't on a page anyone could hand to a reviewer before the run started.

The lesson: the parity check isn't the value. The value is the sentence. An owner can read that sentence on Monday morning before touching a label. The check enforces it. The sentence lets the owner self-check first.

[EXAMPLE 2 — LANTERN INTERPRETATION — ~3 min]
The interpretation framing we did with Iris's feedback.

The invariant: a card shows what the data shows. Time windows are visible. Sources are visible. No inferred ownership, no inferred relationships, no synthesized comparisons.

The exception path: when an interpretation crosses from "what the data shows" into "what it means for product" or "whether the system is safe," that's a different review. The interp owner surfaces the cards. The product owner and the safety owner make those calls — with a visible handoff in the thread.

The routine: how to lay out cards, how to phrase a question, how to present a window.

What actually happened: a customer question touched all three — what the data showed, what it meant for their product decision, what it implied about system safety. The interp owner handled the cards cleanly. The product and safety answers were right. But they were given by the same person in the same thread, with no visible handoff. The boundary between "here's what we see" and "here's what we conclude" wasn't drawn on the page, so a reader had to reconstruct it.

The lesson: the boundary isn't a wall, it's a sentence. "Interpretation shows evidence; product and safety conclusions are owned by their respective owners, with a visible handoff." That's enough for the interp owner to know where to stop, and enough for a reader to see the boundary was held.

(Side note for me, not for the room: I'm using this as an example of the pattern, not as evidence about the system's technical safety or as product validation. The lesson is about how the boundary was structured. The technical and product questions stay separate.)

[EXAMPLE 3 — ORDINARY OWNER DECISIONS — ~2 min]
Two small ones from the same month. No incidents. No drama.

A team changed the default of a config flag. Routine. The flag was read by three services. The owner knew about two. The third was an admin tool with a stale reference. The owner made the right call — reverted the default and updated the third reader. But they made it without knowing the third reader existed, because the invariant — "this flag is part of the ingest contract, read by N services including admin tooling" — wasn't written anywhere an owner could read before changing it.

A team picked a deploy window for a low-risk change. Routine. The quiet window was defined against one team's traffic pattern. Another team's traffic peaks at the same hour because they share an upstream. Fine window for the first team. Bad window for the second. Right call relative to the data the owner had. Wrong call relative to the data they would have had if "quiet is team-relative; cross-team quiet requires checking shared upstreams" had been a sentence anyone had written down.

Neither of these is a heroics story. Both are the same pattern: implicit invariant, no documented exception path, owner makes the right call and pays the second-decision tax.

[THE PATTERN — ~2 min]
Three things in common across all five examples.

One: the invariant was real but unstated. Everyone involved knew it. Nobody had written it down.

Two: the exception path wasn't defined. So when the unusual case arrived, the owner had to invent the exception path in the moment, under whatever pressure existed.

Three: the owner made the right call every time. That's not the problem. The problem is that they made it twice — once when they could have made it once.

[WHAT THIS ISN'T — ~2 min]
This isn't a proposal for a central review board. I'm not asking to be in your release path. I'm not asking to manage anyone's calendar.

What's small and worth doing: a two-page artifact per area — service, system, shared concern — that names the invariants and the exception paths in plain language. Maintained by the owner of the area. Reviewed when something changes. Not a gate. A reference.

The discipline is the test: if you can't write the invariant in a sentence, you don't have one yet. If you can't name the exception path in a sentence, you haven't decided who owns the unusual case yet. Both of those are fine to discover — better to discover them on a Tuesday afternoon than during an incident.

[CLOSE — ~1 min]
The cost isn't the exception. The cost is the second decision.

If we do one thing this quarter, it can be this: each team writes down one invariant and one exception path for the area they own. We don't need a process. We need a habit. The pattern is the same whether the area is a service, a shared library, a labeling convention, or a deploy window.

Owners still own the calls. The point of writing the invariant down isn't to take the call away. It's to let the owner make it once.

Yes, this should be flagged for change. The issue is on three axes, and they're all real:

  1. Cardinality. 9,314 distinct refusal_reason values in a single replay means the metric is unbounded in production. TSDB series count grows linearly with traffic, ingest cost rises, and aggregation (sum, rate, by-reason) becomes useless because most buckets are size 1. A counter you can't sum across tenants or reasons is barely a counter.

  2. Sensitive content in labels. Route fragments, requested allocation sizes, and tenant-scoped context in label values are exactly what Prometheus label-hygiene rules exist to prevent. Route fragments can leak internal topology; allocation sizes leak operational detail; tenant context can break multi-tenant isolation depending on what your label-rewrite rules do downstream in ingest-edge / shard-keeper.

  3. Redundancy with logs. If structured logs already carry request ID, limiter state, requested bytes, and the full error text, the metric label is doing no work the log isn't already doing — except destroying the metric's usefulness. Logs are the right layer for free-form error strings; metric labels should be a bounded enumeration.

Fix shape:

  - Define a RefusalReason enum next to the limiter (small, fixed: budget_exceeded, timeout, shedding, unhealthy, misconfig, other, etc.). The taxonomy lives with the limiter, not with the metric.
  - Map err → RefusalReason via errors.Is / errors.As against sentinels, not via err.Error() substring matching.
  - Emit collector_refusals_total{refusal_reason=RefusalReason, limiter_state=...}. Keep cardinality under ~10 per dimension.
  - Move requested_bytes, route, tenant context, and full error text into the structured log line alongside request ID and limiter state. Logs are where bounded-cardinality joins (via request_id) can reattach them when needed.
  - If you ever need to slice refusals by route, that's a separate bounded label (route_class with tens of values), not the raw path.

The headline rule: metrics need bounded, enumerable labels so they aggregate cheaply and predictably; logs need full fidelity so incidents are debuggable. A raw refusal string fails the first job and shouldn't be asked to do both.

Why the raw refusal string is unsafe as a metric label

1. Cardinality blow-up. Refusal text is free-form and tends to embed the very thing that triggered it (tenant id, object id, path, hash, user input, rule id). Each unique value becomes a new time series. TSDBs and rollups don't survive that — remote write, head blocks, and query plans degrade fast, and rollup correctness becomes unprovable.
2. Label-parser corruption. Metric label values are a constrained syntax (no newlines, no unescaped quotes/equals, length caps). A refusal reason containing a newline, a quote, or a stray '=' can split or truncate the series at ingest, producing silent aggregation errors that look like real metric drops.
3. Sensitive-data amplification. Refusal messages are the worst place for secrets — they restate what the system just rejected, which is often the most identifying part of a request (a path, a record id, a query snippet). Putting that into a label propagates it to every remote-write target, alert, dashboard, and exported view that consumes the metric — a wider blast radius than logs, which usually have ACLs and retention rules.
4. Loss of aggregation semantics. "denied: tenant 7 cannot read /secrets/x" and "denied: tenant 9 cannot read /secrets/y" are the same operational event with different text. As raw labels they form two buckets that never combine; as a closed enum they collapse to one count you can alert on.
5. Stability and ownership. Strings drift (phrasing changes, vendors reword messages, i18n, A/B variants). The metric namespace then drifts with them — dashboards, alerts, and SLO definitions quietly break across deploys. An enum is owned, versioned, and additive-only by policy.
6. Cost and retention. High-cardinality labels get retained at full resolution much longer than log lines, and they multiply every replica. The cost grows with refusal volume, not with the number of distinct *reasons* — which is the opposite of what you want to pay for.

The bounded design to require

Treat the two channels as separate, with the enum as the contract between them:

- Metrics (bounded, countable):
    - refusal_reason: a small, closed, versioned enum. E.g. POLICY_MISSING, SCHEMA_INVALID, AUTH_FAILED, RATE_LIMITED, TENANT_MISMATCH, PROVENANCE_MISSING, UNPUBLISHED_OWNERSHIP, INTERNAL_ONLY_FALLBACK, ADAPTER_DISALLOWED, OTHER.
    - refusal_severity: {allow, soft_deny, hard_deny}.
    - Plus the usual bounded dimensions: service, version, region, tenant_class (not raw tenant id).
    - Counters + histograms keyed on the enum. SLOs are computed against enum classes, never against strings.
    - Cardinality budget asserted in CI: a test fails the build if any metric label set exceeds a declared cap.

- Logs (full fidelity, queryable):
    - refusal_code: the same enum value, so a log line joins cleanly to the metric.
    - refusal_message: the raw string, preserved verbatim.
    - Structured context: request_id, tenant_id, policy_version, adapter_version, provenance_ref, plus any fields the refusal text references.
    - Logs are the only place the raw text lives. Logs have ACLs, retention, and redaction; metrics don't.

- Contract / governance:
    - The enum is append-only and owned. New codes require a written reason and a rollup change review.
    - Anything that would have been a new string but doesn't justify a new code goes into OTHER with the raw text in logs only.
    - "Raw refusal string in a label" is a lint failure in the metrics pipeline, not a guideline.

The single sentence to put in the design doc: metrics label the *kind* of refusal from a closed set; logs carry the *content* of the refusal. If a label value contains a slash, a uuid, a path, or a free-form phrase, it is in the wrong channel.

Reading the metric: 96% = successful combined renders divided by sessions that passed same-tenant, same-service, freshness, provenance, timestamp-presence, and within-24h. Both exclusion clauses (explicit-unknown, valid-but-spread>24h) are sides of the same 24h guardrail — they're held out because they shouldn't render as combined under the locked interp rule.

Your two flags are right. There's a structural issue underneath though. This metric only measures "given a cohort where combining is the correct call, how often did the render succeed." It has no symmetric arm for the cohort where *non-combination* is the correct call. A system that always-combined would post near-100% here while failing badly on the separate-cards-with-source-timestamp path. The 96% can't tell a customer whether the system is "almost always right" or "almost always combines and usually succeeds."

The missing eligibility count compounds it: 96% on N=200 reads differently from 96% on N=20, and the draft gives neither.

What I'd want before this goes to a customer:

  (a) eligibility flow — total pool, passed-gates, attempted-combine
  (b) combined-render success on the gated pool — i.e. this 96%
  (c) correct-non-combination rate on the held-out pool — the symmetric metric
  (d) correct-unknown rate on the unknown-marked pool

That set is what "the system makes the right rendering decision" actually means. The current draft is just (b), presented alone.

Separately, the >24h-spread cohort is doing double duty in the framing — it's excluded from the success denominator, but it's also exactly the cohort where the system's correct behavior is to *not* combine. If Iris's draft doesn't surface (c), the customer sees the system taking zero credit for the cases it's handling correctly on the non-combination side, and may misread "96% with no denominator context" as a worse outcome than the system is actually delivering.

Here is a recommendation that keeps the three concerns cleanly separated without leaking any out-of-scope fields.

METRIC NAME
  lantern_card_combination_outcomes_total
  (counter, per card-pair evaluated by the Lantern renderer)

LABELS (two dimensions — enough to distinguish all three concerns)

  eligibility : eligible | ineligible | unevaluable
    eligible     - inputs met the 24h rule (sourced, current,
                   same-tenant, published, within 24h of source)
    ineligible   - at least one 24h-rule condition failed
    unevaluable  - could not be determined (e.g. source ts missing
                   before evaluation, rule inputs incomplete)

  outcome     : joined | separated | unknown | renderer_failure
    joined           - Lantern card produced (rendered combined)
    separated        - rendered as separate cards with source ts
    unknown          - surfaced as unknown (stale / missing inputs)
    renderer_failure - the renderer itself errored (distinct from
                       a legitimate 'unknown' outcome)

COMPANION COUNTS (the cells worth emitting and watching)

  Correct-path cells (baseline; alert only on regression):
    (eligible, joined)           - correctly combined under the 24h rule
    (ineligible, separated)      - correctly kept apart
    (ineligible, unknown)        - correctly surfaced as unknown
                                   (conservative fallback)
    (unevaluable, separated)     - kept apart when eligibility unknown
    (unevaluable, unknown)       - surfaced unknown when eligibility
                                   unknown

  Anomaly-path cells (alert if non-zero or trending up):
    (ineligible, joined)         - VIOLATION: combined despite failing
                                   the 24h rule  -> page on rate > 0
    (eligible, separated)        - missed join opportunity
    (eligible, unknown)          - over-conservative on valid inputs
    (unevaluable, joined)        - joined without eligibility evidence
                                   -> should not happen by design
    (eligible, renderer_failure) - renderer errored on valid inputs
    (ineligible, renderer_failure)
    (unevaluable, renderer_failure)

WHY THIS SHAPE
  - eligibility as a first-class label answers "could this have been
    combined?" without needing to recompute from event contents.
  - outcome = renderer_failure is its own value, not a derived flag,
    so renderer errors stay distinguishable from legitimately-
    produced 'unknown' / 'separated' cards.
  - The correct-path vs anomaly-path split lets you alert on (a) any
    (ineligible, joined) — which is the direct violation case — and
    (b) the renderer_failure slice independent of upstream eligibility.
  - No tenant ID, no employee ID, no comparison field, no individual-
    perf or cost data in the labels — fits the ProdEng schema guardrails
    already in place for the Lantern card.

DERIVED SIGNALS WORTH PROMOTING LATER
  - join_violation_rate = (ineligible, joined) / total
  - renderer_error_rate = sum(renderer_failure) / total
  - correct_disposition_rate = sum(correct-path cells) / total

- It must assert that the producer's emitted label set is a superset of the consumer contract (not just key presence).
- It must assert the current production reader path, e.g. `readLabel(series, "storage_region")`. Stale-fixture evidence is parity FAIL even when preflight is green.

Why a timestamp alone is insufficient provenance

A timestamp records when an observation was emitted. It does not record the four properties that determine whether the record can be trusted as evidence:

  sourced      - publisher identity and version that produced it
  current      - whether it is still inside the validity window for the consumer
  same-tenant  - whether it was emitted in the scope that applies to the consumer
  published    - whether the record is finalized, not draft / pre-publish / revoked

Two records with identical timestamps can differ on every one of these. A timestamp is replayable, backdatable, and silent on provenance, so it is necessary but never sufficient. Treating it as sufficient collapses source, freshness, scope, and status into a single moment the consumer cannot independently verify.

What the publisher must require

  - Emit the four fields (source, freshness bound, tenant scope, publication status) alongside the timestamp as a single record. Timestamp without the four is not a valid emission.
  - Reject or downgrade any emission where any of the four is missing; do not backfill from inference or surrounding context.
  - For any record destined to join within the 24h window, all four must be present at emission. Stale or missing must surface as unknown, never silently substituted.

What the candidate-scan regression must require

  - Assert presence of the four fields per record, not timestamp presence alone.
  - Reject fixtures where a timestamp is supplied and any of the four is absent or mismatched.
  - Verify that a record with a valid timestamp but wrong tenant scope is kept separate with its source timestamp, per the 24h rule, not promoted into a joined card.
  - Verify stale or missing field -> unknown, not silent drop and not join.
  - Verify record state = unpublished / draft / revoked -> not join, regardless of timestamp freshness.

Bounded aggregation + audit design (proposal)

Goal restated in concrete terms: replace any member-ID-keyed view of a team-level metric with a view keyed by team + an opaque member slot, while preserving (a) team-level counts, (b) dedup, and (c) the four intended measures. The audit side has to let a reviewer confirm those invariants without ever reconstructing the member map.

1. Two layers, with a one-way arrow between them

- Source layer (unchanged): keeps member_id and team_id at the per-event grain. Lives behind the existing access boundary.
- Public layer (new): team-scoped only. Built by a one-shot, append-only pipeline that does not read member_id back after the pass.

The arrow goes one way. The public layer must not retain member_id, must not retain a member_id hash, and must not retain any per-event timing that, joined with another dataset, would re-identify a member. If a downstream analysis needs more, it has to come back to the source layer under the existing access rules, not by re-deriving identity from the public layer.

2. What the public record contains

Each public record is keyed by (team_id, bucket_window) where bucket_window is a coarse time bucket (recommend ≥ 15 min, and ideally a fixed bucket boundary, not sliding, so a single member contributes to a fixed set of buckets and joins can't collapse them).

Per bucket, the record holds only:

- team_id (already exists)
- bucket_window (coarse, fixed-boundary)
- measure_1 .. measure_4 (the four intended measures; names confirmed by you)
- member_slot_count: number of distinct opaque slots that contributed to this bucket (k-anonymity check below)
- audit_chain_id: pointer into the audit log

What the record does NOT contain: member_id, member_id_hash, per-event timestamps, per-event payloads, order of events within the bucket, or anything derivable from reordering.

3. Opaque member slot — not a hash, not a per-record pseudonym

Recommend an opaque, salted slot token generated inside the source layer at aggregation time, with these properties:

- Stable for a given (team_id, member_id) within a window, but rotated across windows (e.g. monthly or per-bucket-window epoch). This is the property that lets dedup work without letting slot_token collapse to identity over time.
- Salt is held only in the source layer and is rotated; the public layer never sees it.
- No PII, no employee ID, no email-derived value, no IP, no user-agent in the salt input.

Per your established 24h-rule precedent on joined cards (memory), dedup happens by collapsing events that share (team_id, slot_token, measure_name) within the same bucket. The dedup outcome is a count, not a list. The collapsed events are accounted for in the audit log, not in the public record.

4. The four measures (shape contract)

I'd want these confirmed, but a shape that fits your existing counters:

- measure_1: distinct active members in the bucket (count of slot_tokens contributing ≥1 accepted event)
- measure_2: total accepted events in the bucket (sum across slot_tokens, after dedup)
- measure_3: distinct members contributing to a specific sub-state within the bucket (e.g. the "noisy" or "queued" sub-state — same opaque-slot dedup rule)
- measure_4: a separate derived ratio or count that you can name (I don't want to guess)

Whatever they are, the contract is: every public record stores them as integers or fixed-precision numerics, never as distributions or arrays, and the public layer never exports a measure that requires joining on slot_token across rows.

5. Dedup, three rules

- Rule A: within (team_id, bucket_window, slot_token, measure_name), collapse repeats to one. This is the only dedup primitive the public layer needs.
- Rule B: cross-window dedup is intentionally not supported in the public layer. If the same member is active in two adjacent buckets, they count in both; that is a feature, not a bug, and it prevents the public layer from reconstructing timelines.
- Rule C: rejected / dropped / duplicate counters stay at the source layer's accepted/rejected/dropped/duplicate contract (per rb_1789273768109 and rb_1789412825310). The public layer never silently reclassifies a rejected event as accepted.

6. Audit log — the part that does the real work

The audit log is a separate, append-only store keyed by audit_chain_id. It carries:

- source_event_ids (the list of source IDs that fed into a given public bucket)
- source_layer timestamp window (coarse, not per-event)
- dedup rule version + rule hash (so a reviewer can confirm Rule A was applied as written)
- bucket_window, team_id, pre-dedup event count, post-dedup event count, slot_token count
- aggregation code version + commit SHA
- operator who ran the pass + an attestation that no member_id or member_id_hash left the source layer

The audit log does NOT carry member_id, slot_token, or anything that re-identifies. The link from public to audit is the audit_chain_id. The link from audit back to source_event_ids is read-only and access-controlled at the source boundary.

A reviewer should be able to confirm, for any public record: "this team-level count is consistent with N source events collapsed by Rule A vX.Y, run at time T by operator O, code SHA S, and no member identifier left the source boundary on that pass." That sentence is the whole audit claim; if it can't be made cleanly, the design has a hole.

7. k-anonymity gate before publication

Before any (team_id, bucket_window) record is published:

- member_slot_count ≥ k, where I'd recommend k ≥ 5 for the four measures, and a stricter floor (say k ≥ 10) for any measure that is a per-member ratio or rare-event count.
- If the floor fails, the bucket is either suppressed or coarsened (wider bucket window, merged with adjacent bucket) and the suppression/coarsening is logged in the audit trail.

This is the layer that prevents small-team re-identification. It is not optional; without it the design collapses to "team-level counts keyed by a one-member team," which is just a member view with extra steps.

8. Boundaries with existing runbooks

- Label-name changes that touch the public schema still go through rb_shard_keeper_label_parity (Nadia + Cyrus team, written sign-off). Pre-flight PASS and alert-source PASS do not override a parity FAIL. Same rule applies here.
- Source-layer counters stay governed by rb_ingest_edge_cutover and its accepted/rejected/dropped/duplicate contracts. The public layer never relabels a rejected point as accepted.
- The memory-slope canary rule (rb_1789250051828) — zero drops or duplicates does not make a continuing resource slope safe — applies to the aggregation pass itself: track the audit pass's pre-dedup and post-dedup counts separately; the post-dedup count being clean does not make a runaway pre-dedup slope safe.

What I'd want from you before locking any of this in:

1. The exact names and definitions of the four measures. I'm proposing a shape, not asserting the contents.
2. The desired bucket_window. ≥ 15 min / fixed-boundary is my recommendation, but the team-retention window you need to support may force it wider.
3. k. I default to 5 / 10 but the team's tolerance for suppression vs. coarsening matters.
4. Whether the salt rotation cadence should match the bucket_window or be coarser (e.g. monthly).
5. Who owns the audit log and its retention. The current memory rule (24h on joined cards) is a useful precedent but doesn't cover a multi-bucket aggregation log; I'd rather have that decided explicitly than inherited.
6. Whether any of the four measures are per-member ratios. If yes, k = 10 minimum and a separate review.

WHY ELAPSED INSTANTS, NOT LOCAL DATES

  The 24h spread on joined cards is the predicate |t1.ts - t2.ts| <= 24h
  (or < 24h, depending on the chosen comparator). The operands must be
  absolute moments — UTC instants on the same monotonic reference —
  for four reasons that local dates break independently.

  1. Local date is not a duration. A "date" is an integer day in some
     observer's calendar; it cannot represent sub-day offsets. So a
     "same-date or adjacent-date" approximation of a 24h spread is
     already fuzzy at the boundary by up to 48h of wall-clock slack
     (an adjacent-date pair may be 1 second or 47h59m apart in
     elapsed time). The instant-based test is exact by construction.

  2. Timezone coupling. The same instant renders as different local
     dates in different zones. Two events 23h apart that straddle
     midnight in one zone may not straddle midnight in another. If
     routing decisions depend on a local date, the same input pair
     can be joined or split depending on which service rendered it
     (metrics-router vs ingest-edge vs shard-keeper). Instants make
     the predicate locale-independent; the join result is identical
     no matter which service evaluates it.

  3. DST is non-uniform wall clock. Spring-forward days are 23h,
     fall-back days are 25h. A local-date 24h spread on a DST
     boundary is either too tight (spring-forward) or too loose
     (fall-back) by an hour, every year, in every affected zone.
     Elapsed-instant arithmetic is immune — every day is exactly
     86400 seconds on the UTC axis.

  4. Canonical sourcing. The 24h rule's other inputs (source ts,
     published ts, freshness window) are already canonicalized to
     UTC instants when they enter the pipeline. Adding a local-date
     operand reintroduces a conversion at every read site — and
     conversion is the classic source of the "shifted-by-one-day"
     bug class. Keeping the predicate in instant-space means the
     refactor can do pure subtraction, no tz libraries on the hot
     path.

  Net: elapsed instants give a single deterministic, timezone-free,
  DST-safe, sub-second-precise predicate that is portable across
  services and replayable for postmortems. Local dates give an
  approximate predicate that drifts with observer and calendar.


BOUNDARY REGRESSIONS THE REFACTOR NEEDS

  A. Comparator boundary (the most common silent bug)

     - t2 = t1 + 24h00m00s000ms exactly   -> MUST NOT join (the
       rule is < 24h, not <= 24h; if the rule is <=, swap
       expectations and document). Defends against off-by-one in
       the comparator.
     - t2 = t1 + 23h59m59s999ms           -> MUST join.
     - t2 = t1 + 24h00m00s001ms           -> MUST NOT join. Pin the
       precision boundary.

  B. Cross-midnight UTC (the "different local date, same 24h" trap)

     - t1 = 2025-03-30T23:30:00Z, t2 = 2025-03-31T00:30:00Z
       elapsed = 1h   -> MUST join. Naive "same local date"
       would split.
     - t1 = 2025-01-31T23:00:00Z, t2 = 2025-02-01T22:00:00Z
       elapsed = 23h  -> MUST join. Cross-month.
     - t1 = 2024-12-31T23:00:00Z, t2 = 2025-01-01T22:00:00Z
       elapsed = 23h  -> MUST join. Cross-year.

  C. DST boundaries (the wall-clock-vs-elapsed trap)

     - Spring-forward, 2025-03-09 in America/New_York: t1 at
       2025-03-09T00:30:00-05:00 (05:30Z), t2 at
       2025-03-09T03:30:00-04:00 (07:30Z). Elapsed = 2h.
       MUST join. Pin the elapsed delta to 2h; reject any code
       path that subtracts local wall-clock fields and yields 3h.
     - Fall-back, 2025-11-02 in America/New_York: t1 at
       2025-11-02T00:30:00-04:00 (04:30Z), t2 at
       2025-11-02T02:30:00-05:00 (07:30Z). Elapsed = 3h.
       MUST join. Same defense: elapsed, not wall-clock.
     - A pure elapsed-based implementation will pass both with no
       DST logic at all — that's the point of the regression:
       it certifies "we did not reintroduce local-time math."

  D. Leap-day and 1-day arithmetic

     - 2024-02-28T12:00:00Z + 1 day = 2024-02-29T12:00:00Z
       (24h elapsed, calendar day advances). Test that the
       24h window still holds: t1 = 2024-02-28T00:00:00Z,
       t2 = 2024-02-29T00:00:00Z, elapsed = 24h00m -> MUST NOT
       join (boundary case, per rule direction).
     - 2025-02-28T00:00:00Z + 1 day = 2025-03-01T00:00:00Z.
       Same expectation; confirms no Feb-29 short-circuit on
       non-leap years.

  E. Out-of-order and absolute value

     - Same input pair with t1 and t2 swapped must produce the
       same join decision. Guards against `t2 - t1` signed
       subtraction producing a negative delta that bypasses
       the bound. Predicate is |delta|, always.

  F. Precision / unit mismatches

     - Millisecond-precision timestamps (epoch ms) and
       microsecond-precision timestamps (epoch us) in the same
       input set: ensure the diff function normalizes units
       before subtracting, or rejects mismatched-unit pairs.
     - Sub-second rounding: a pair at exactly 24h minus 500us
       must still join; a pair at 24h plus 500us must not. Pin
       that the comparator operates at native precision, not
       truncated to seconds.

  G. Missing, stale, and clock-skewed timestamps

     - t1 present, t2 missing  -> output is "unknown" with source
       ts noted; NOT joined, NOT silently filled with epoch 0.
       This is the locked fallback from the 2025-03-27 review.
     - t1 present, t2 = epoch 0 or year 1970 -> treat as missing
       (defensive against bad defaults); output "unknown."
     - t2 = t1 + 30 days (clock skew / replay contamination)
       -> MUST NOT join; do not clamp, do not "be tolerant" beyond
       a documented skew window. The 24h rule is strict; skew is
       caught elsewhere (NTP / monotonic guards), not here.

  H. Cross-tenant contamination under coincident timestamps

     - Same-tenant pair, 1h apart -> joins.
     - Different-tenant pair, identical ts -> MUST NOT join even
       though |delta| = 0. Confirms the tenant gate is evaluated
       before (or independently of) the ts gate, and that the
       24h test is never the sole acceptance criterion.

  I. Determinism / replay

     - Identical input fed through ingest-edge twice produces
       byte-identical join decisions. Run in UTC, freeze tz,
       no `Date.now()` calls on the join path. Guards against
       the local-date refactor sneaking `new Date()` into a
       helper that renders different output per call.

  Eight buckets (A-I) is the minimum coverage. If any of them is
  missing, the refactor should not merge — each one corresponds to
  a specific class of bug that the original local-date code path
  has historically produced.

  - The 100 ms ceiling is an *individual-instance* threshold. A pause of 108 ms violates it by 8%, regardless of what the other three pauses look like. The four values should each be compared to 100 ms; only the aggregate used for *trending* should be a mean.

The 108 ms interval vs. the 100 ms threshold is the key classification — I want to be precise about how "above 100 ms" is read, and I want to be careful about what "summary may retain averages" actually means without collapsing the hard-max check. Below is the answer, grounded in the rule.

---

**Classification of a 108-millisecond interval under the owner-led-window rule**

The rule, as encoded in `rb_metrics_router_canary` (2024-05-30 note extended by the 2024-06-18 infra-review accepted boundary), is:

> Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 ms. Re-pause is automatic, not a judgement call.

The hard ceiling is the cleanup-pause duration, not an average of cleanup-pause durations. So a 108 ms observation is *above* the 100 ms ceiling — the interval itself crosses the threshold. Under the rule this is a stop-class observation: pushes halt via the deploy pipeline. It is a *pause on pushes*, not a rollback. Rollback conditions are a separate, higher-precedence class (active-generation inconsistency across pods, route divergence, dropped series off baseline, reload failure, restart). 108 ms by itself, without one of those rollback-class signals, is not a rollback trigger.

Two things matter for how a 108 ms reading is read:

1.  *The interval is what gets measured, not the bucket.* The rule is "cleanup pauses exceed 100 ms." That is the observed pause duration. If a single pause observed during the stop-the-world matcher cleanup is 108 ms, the threshold is crossed at that observation; it is not averaged against other pauses, and it is not "diluted" by neighboring short pauses. The pause event itself is the unit of measurement.
2.  *Above-threshold is above-threshold.* "Above 100 ms" is strict in the runbook's pause-on-pushes rule. 108 ms is +8% over the ceiling; it does not matter that 108 is "close to" 100. Re-pause is automatic, not judgement, so "only 8 ms over" is not a basis for continuing pushes.

Once the 108 ms pause is observed, the *pause* triggers the verify-before-resume procedure — not rollback. To resume pushes:

- generations must drain to ≤1;
- p99 returns to baseline;
- heap returns to baseline;
- the five verify-before-resume signals all stay clean (active-generation consistency across pods, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, restarts);
- the upstream 2024-06-17 prerequisites must also hold (10-minute continuous clean hold, identical active-generation sets across all canary pods, cleanup-pause p99 strictly below 100 ms before resuming).

When — and only when — all of those hold at the same time, exactly *one* bounded push may be attempted, and it must be observed in full. Any re-crossing of either pause threshold during that bounded push or its observation window pauses pushes immediately again. Steady-state cadence is not restored by the bounded push.

**How the summary may retain averages without letting them replace the hard-maximum stop check**

This is the part that is easy to get wrong, so I'll be explicit about what is allowed and what is not.

The summary may — and should — continue to report averages (p50, mean) for cleanup-pause duration alongside the distribution and the max. Averages are useful for trend detection: a mean drifting up while the max stays below 100 ms tells you cleanup is getting more expensive even though it has not yet crossed the ceiling; that is a leading indicator and is useful to capture. The summary also may report p50 / p99 / max distributions and a count of pause events per window. None of that is forbidden by the rule, and removing the averages would make the warmup-vs-regression framing weaker, not stronger (the 2023-09-07 and 2023-09-27 canary notes rely on comparing the distribution, not just the maximum).

What the summary *may not* do, and what would violate the rule:

1.  *Replace the max observation with an average.* The stop check is on the observed pause duration. If the summary computes "average cleanup pause this hour = 87 ms" and uses that to claim "under 100 ms, no stop," that is a rule violation. The rule does not average. A single 108 ms observation stops pushes regardless of how low the mean is.
2.  *Window the max out.* If the summary reports max-over-1-minute or max-over-5-minute and the 108 ms pause straddles or falls between summary buckets, the summary cannot be used to claim "no pause above 100 ms observed." The rule's pause-on-pushes is on observation, not on summary bucket granularity. The right granularity for the stop check is the per-event observation as captured by the cleanup-pause timer, not the summary rollup.
3.  *Use an average over a longer window to "smooth over" a recrossing.* The 2024-06-18 note explicitly says "a transient recrossing does not authorize a second push and does not 'borrow' against a future resume." An averaged signal that hides the recrossing in a longer window does exactly that borrowing, and it would convert the automatic re-pause into a judgement call, which the rule forbids.
4.  *Use the average to argue that the cleanup-pause ceiling should be raised.* The ceiling is the rule. The summary informs, the runbook decides. Changing the ceiling is an infra-review acceptance, not a summary-observation outcome.

So the allowed pattern is:

- The hard-max stop check reads the *observed* cleanup-pause duration (the per-event max, or equivalently the p100 over the event log). On 108 ms, that observation fires the pause.
- The summary retains averages and the full p50/p99/max distribution as supporting evidence for trend detection and for the bounded-resume prerequisites (the upstream 2024-06-17 addendum explicitly references cleanup-pause p99 strictly below 100 ms as a resume prerequisite — so p99 belongs in the summary too, but as a separate prerequisite signal, not as the stop check itself).
- The summary may also retain mean/p50/p99 to characterize *shape* — e.g., to distinguish a single 108 ms outlier from a distribution shifting upward — but the stop decision is on the per-event max, full stop.

Concretely, for the 108 ms observation under the rule: stop further pushes via the deploy pipeline; verify-before-resume applies (drain to ≤1 generation, p99 and heap back to baseline, five signals clean, upstream 10-minute hold satisfied); any second push requires bounded-single-push conditions to be re-satisfied; if any of those resume conditions is not clean, pushes stay paused. Rollback is not yet warranted by the 108 ms alone — it would require one of the rollback-class signals (active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, dropped series, reload failure, restart) on top of it.

If the average cleanup-pause for the window was, say, 64 ms with a single 108 ms outlier, the rule is the same: the 108 ms pause is what stops pushes, the average is not the stop check, the average is retained in the summary as supporting evidence for *why* this might have happened and for what to watch on the bounded-resume attempt.

REQUEST-LEVEL ACCOUNTING (unit: requests)

  R_in       = R_accepted + R_refused
  R_accepted = Σ R_accepted(t)     over tenants
  R_refused  = Σ R_refused(t)      over tenants

  Fairness contract:  R_accepted(t) / R_in(t)  ≈  equal across tenants t


POINT-LEVEL ACCOUNTING (unit: data points)

  P_in       = Σ over all requests of points_in_request
             = P_accepted + P_refused
  P_accepted = Σ over accepted requests of points_in_request
  P_refused  = Σ over refused requests of points_in_request
               (whole-request refusal — no partial drops in this path)

  Throughput:  P_rate = P_accepted / window_seconds

  Key identity: one accepted request carrying N points contributes 1 to R_accepted and N to P_accepted. Therefore R_accepted ≠ P_accepted in general, and R_in/window ≠ P_in/window.


COUNTERS THE DASHBOARD MUST NOT MIX

  1. R_*  vs  P_*.  Different units. Summing R_accepted + P_accepted is meaningless. A "loss" line computed as refused_requests / total_points mixes a request count in the numerator with a point count in the denominator — reject that shape.

  2. Fairness bucket (per-tenant, kept for trends)  vs  max-queue-wait (nonempty queues, no tenant label). The [2025-03-27] regression split these on purpose: buckets carry tenant labels for trend lines; queue-wait is unlabeled and only emitted when a queue is nonempty. Joining them by simple sum/rate would re-leak the tenant label and is what the regression closed.

  3. Service-level total  vs  tenant-level breakdown. Per the Lantern revision [2025-03-27], external schema rejects employee IDs and comparison fields; only service-level total + source ts is retained on cards. Tenant breakdowns stay internal — do not promote them to the same panel.

  4. Joined cards — apply the 24h rule [2025-03-27]: a single card may combine sourced + current + same-tenant + published only when all four hold; otherwise render separately with source ts; stale or missing = unknown. Don't aggregate across the boundary.

  5. Synthetic-tenant harness stats  vs  production stats. Harness tracks synthetic tenants internally; figures like the 4.6s worst vs 620ms bucket mean are fixture-validation numbers, not production R_accepted / P_rate — different panels.

  6. Accepted  vs  refused  across levels. A refused request still produced points; its contribution to P_refused is points_in_request, not 1. Compute refusal rate at one level and stick to it.

Confirmed the review finding — the proposed SDK change breaks the layering invariant.

Concrete defect: retrying the logical batch resends chunk A (8,000 points already accepted by ingest-edge) along with chunk B. That's duplication after partial transport success, which the deployed design explicitly forbids. The fixture's 18,000 transmitted-points expectation is the smoking gun — a 9,000-point logical batch can never legitimately produce 18,000 on-wire points.

Two other problems in the same change:

  - The "convenience" auto-split only fires after a failure on the second chunk. The first chunk has already been accepted, so the SDK cannot atomically split + retry from the caller's perspective — the split is happening inside an already-in-flight failure path, not at submission time. That's the wrong place to introduce chunking.

  - Marking the logical batch successful after the duplicated retry hides the real outcome from the caller. Chunk B's timeout is what the caller actually needs to see; the retry path papers over it. Older whole-batch-rejection clients get a clearer signal than the "convenient" new path.

The fix per the layered design is one of two shapes, and the SDK author needs to pick:

  1. Caller-side split before submit. Oversized batches get split by the caller; each chunk is its own logical unit with its own retry. A chunk that fails retries only itself; no duplication. This is what the design requires.

  2. Server-side whole-batch rejection. Caller sends 9,000 points; server rejects with a deterministic size error; caller decides how to split. Preserves the older-client invariant.

What the proposed change is actually proposing — server transparently splits + retry transparently duplicates — is neither shape. It's a third design that doesn't exist in the layered contract, and it's the one that produces the 18,000-point fixture.

If Product Engineering wants the auto-split ergonomics, the retry path must track per-chunk delivery state (which chunks succeeded, which are still pending) and only resend the pending ones. That is not what "stores the original logical batch and resends both chunks" describes.

This is a real bug, not a code smell. Map-then-validate produces silent data loss: only one of the two entries survives, the priority field becomes decorative (40 never beats 10 because the entry with priority 40 simply isn't in the map), and the "successful reload" status is wrong because half the operator's intended config was discarded on each load.

Three things bother me most:

  1. File-order dependence. Same logical config, different active target depending on YAML ordering. That's non-deterministic from the operator's perspective even though it's deterministic from the parser's. Two operators reviewing the same intent would not expect different outcomes.

  2. Both loads report success. No signal that anything was discarded. An operator whose fallback isn't firing has no reason to investigate — the system told them everything was fine.

  3. The priority 10 vs 40 distinction is misleading. If the schema intended these to coexist (primary tried first, fallback second), the parser cannot express that and the schema probably should allow multiple targets per route ID ordered by priority. If the schema intended unique-per-ID with priority as a tiebreaker, the parser should error because there's nothing to break the tie on. Worth clarifying intent before fixing.

Fix direction: validate uniqueness in a pre-pass before any map insertion. On duplicate, error with the route ID and both source locations (file + line if available). Reload should be atomic — if validation fails, no partial state is committed.

For the test, the right assertion is: duplicate route IDs produce a parse error naming the offending ID, and a successful reload means the parsed route count equals the file's entry count. The current "both loads report success" assertion is encoding the bug as expected behavior — a real fix will break it, and that's correct.

One more thing to check while you're in there: is the same map-then-validate pattern used elsewhere in the parser? If it's the established style, this isn't a one-off, it's a class of bug for any other field with a uniqueness constraint. Label maps would be the obvious place to look.

Memory retrieval is unavailable. I have enough in-context grounding (memory block + user profile) to answer from first principles without inventing specifics. Writing the answer now.

---

The defect is in how a persisted label/identity table (the `label_map`) is rebuilt from its serialized form. Two structural problems, both rooted in the same root cause:

1. **Duplicate identity.** The map accepts two serialized entries that resolve to the same logical identity. Most commonly: a "user-facing" label and its "internal" alias (e.g. a display name and a normalized form, or a primary key and a stable secondary key) are both stored as top-level entries pointing at the same target. After reload, lookups by either key return the same record, but the map's internal index has two slots for one identity — which corrupts cardinality counts, makes "first match wins" behave differently from "last match wins," and breaks any code that assumes identity-count == entry-count.

2. **Order dependence.** The parser walks the serialized stream sequentially and creates entries in walk order. Whether two duplicate entries collapse, overwrite, or coexist depends on which appears first. The same input bytes loaded twice can produce different in-memory state if anything upstream ever normalizes, re-sorts, deduplicates, or rewrites the stream. Reload is therefore non-idempotent: `load(load(x)) != load(x)` in general, and `load` itself is not a function of the input alone.

Root cause in both cases: the parser treats the serialized form as a sequence of independent records when it is actually a set of identities with a uniqueness invariant, and it has no post-load reconciliation pass to enforce that invariant.

Guarantees the owner needs to satisfy (these are the contract, not the implementation):

**Validation guarantees** (must hold for any well-formed serialized input, before commit):
- The set of logical identities in the serialized form has no duplicates: no two entries, after alias/case/whitespace normalization, resolve to the same target.
- Every identity referenced by an alias is also present as a primary entry (no dangling aliases).
- Aliases are acyclic — an alias chain does not loop back on itself.
- Validation is deterministic: the same bytes always produce the same verdict, independent of input order.

**Failed-reload guarantees** (when validation fails or reload otherwise cannot complete):
- The previous in-memory `label_map` is left intact and continues to serve the prior active generation. A failed reload is a no-op on live state.
- The failure is reported with enough information to identify the offending entry/entries (which identity, which alias, which input position) without leaking unrelated map contents.
- No partial state is committed: either the entire reload succeeds and is atomically swapped in, or nothing observable changes.
- Reload is safe to retry with corrected input; a failed attempt does not consume or lock resources.

**Active-generation guarantees** (about which generation is live and how transitions occur):
- At any instant, exactly one generation is active. Readers and writers always see a consistent map — never a mix of two generations mid-swap.
- A generation swap is atomic from the perspective of all consumers: a snapshot taken before the swap returns the old generation; a snapshot taken after returns the new one. There is no observable interleaving.
- The active generation is monotonically advancing; a generation is never reverted to an older one in place (rollbacks install a new generation, they do not unmount the current one).
- Readers do not block writers, and writers do not block readers, during or after a swap. The swap itself does not stall ingestion.
- Old generations remain queryable (for in-flight requests, postmortems, or drain windows) until the owner explicitly retires them; retirement itself is atomic with respect to new queries.

Implementation note (not part of the contract, just so the parser work is scoped correctly): satisfying the validation guarantees above likely requires a two-phase build — accumulate into a temporary structure, run the uniqueness/reachability checks, then atomically swap — rather than mutating the live map in walk order. But the choice of data structure, normalization rules, and swap mechanism is the owner's call; what matters is that the three guarantee sets above all hold.

Bug: integers in [1200, 3000] written to `Retry-After` parse as delta-seconds per RFC 9110 §10.2.3, so the field tells SDKs to back off 20–50 minutes — three orders of magnitude off from the intended 1–3 s. The fixture "passes" because it interprets the field as ms, which means it's validating the implementation against itself, not against the spec or any SDK contract.

Why this hurts at the SDK layer:
- Off-the-shelf HTTP clients (curl `--retry`, requests, axios-retry, OkHttp, AWS retry plugins, etc.) read `Retry-After` as seconds or HTTP-date. They'll honor 1200–3000 s.
- SDK retries will fire ~25 min later instead of ~2 s. Tail-latency and quota-cost disaster, and it'll be invisible in this fixture.
- A fixture that agrees with a non-conformant producer is a false negative on contract compliance. The test has to assert what the SDK sees, not what was written.

Spec-conformant fixes that keep the 1–3 s randomized delay:
- A. Send integers in [1, 3] as seconds. Fixture asserts delta-seconds ≤ 3 for the retry case. Sub-second jitter, if you want it, lives on the server before the 429 (e.g. sleep 0–2000 ms then respond).
- B. Add a non-standard header (e.g. `X-Retry-After-Ms`) and keep ms resolution. Acceptable only if every SDK consumer is explicitly taught it; otherwise it's the same bug in a different field.
- C. HTTP-date. Works, but silly for sub-3 s.

Default to A with server-side jitter, and re-check no downstream proxy / SDK cache is doing its own `Retry-After` interpretation — if one is, the 20–50 min becomes the floor on retry, not the ceiling.

The fix the change needs is the standard "drain the queues before you let the dispatch loop exit" sequence — readiness=false first (so the load balancer stops routing new work and in-flight requests finish), then close the listener (so no new connections arrive), then keep the dispatch loop running until the per-tenant queues are empty or a deadline elapses, then exit. Specifically, the change as described has three problems:

1. **Loop exit is not gated on queue emptiness.** A SIGTERM handler that flips readiness and closes the listener is fine on its own — but if it also tears down the dispatch loop while work is still in per-tenant queues, you've created an "accepted but unaccounted" class. The premise, stated first so the guarantees make sense:

Readiness is a load-distribution signal, not a license to discard. An instance that has already returned acceptance (HTTP 2xx, queue ACK, lease grant, enqueue confirmation, etc.) has entered a contract with the caller, upstream, or queue: the work is durably handed off. A readiness flip must not retroactively void that contract.

WHY ABANDONMENT IS FORBIDDEN

  - Silent loss. The caller believes the work is in a system that will process it. Dropping it produces ghost work — items the user thinks are pending that no instance will ever touch. Detection is delayed (often until a downstream signal never arrives) and attribution is hard because no error path fired.

  - At-least-once breach. Queues rely on explicit NACK, requeue, or visibility-timeout to recover from failure. Abandonment skips the recovery path. The item is gone, not retried.

  - Hidden capacity collapse. A readiness flip that silently drops accepted work looks like a clean drain on dashboards — queue depth falls — while the system is actually losing data. This is the worst failure mode: the observability lies.

  - Idempotency and retry assumptions break downstream. Many workers assume the upstream has at-least-once semantics. If the upstream abandons, the retry may never come, and the item sits in an inconsistent state forever, or never gets the duplicate-execution a downstream idempotent handler was designed to absorb.

  - Unfalsifiable without explicit terminal signalling. There is no way for the caller, the operator, or a postmortem to distinguish "still processing" from "abandoned" unless the owner emits a terminal signal. So abandonment is not just bad, it is unverifiable.

THE FIVE GUARANTEES

1. Quiesce.
   After the readiness flip, the instance reaches a quiescent state on the accepted-work axis: no new work enters the accepted set, and the existing set is bounded and known. Quiesce is the precondition for reasoning about drain/reject — you cannot drain a set that is still growing. The owner must be able to demonstrate that the accepted-set size is finite and stable post-flip, and that no new acceptance is being issued.

2. Drain-or-explicit-rejection.
   For each accepted unit of work, exactly one of:
     a) it is completed normally (drained), or
     b) it is explicitly rejected: the caller, upstream, or queue receives a terminal, distinguishable signal that this instance will not process it, and the work is returned to a path that will — requeue, reroute, terminal-error response, NACK, etc.
   There is no third option. The "or" is exclusive per item but exhaustive across the set. Abandonment — leaving the item in limbo, neither completed nor explicitly returned — is forbidden regardless of cause (crash, OOM, timeout, misconfiguration, network partition).

3. Terminal-response.
   Every accepted item must produce a terminal response visible to whoever is waiting on it. "Terminal" means the waiter can release its hold: close the request, ack the message, stop retrying, advance its cursor. The response must be distinguishable from network noise. Acceptable terminal signals: explicit error response, NACK with requeue, terminal-error code, delivery-failed callback. Unacceptable substitutes: raw TCP reset with no application-level response, hang-until-client-timeout, generic 5xx indistinguishable from a transient backend error that the client will retry into a now-dead instance. The principle: if a reasonable caller cannot tell from the response that this instance has given up, the guarantee has not been met.

4. Accounting.
   The owner must record, at minimum:
     - accepted count at the moment of readiness flip (the closure point)
     - drained count during the drain/reject window
     - explicitly-rejected count during the window
     - stragglers: accepted minus drained minus rejected. This MUST be zero when the window closes; non-zero is a guarantee violation and a paging event.
     - wall-clock duration of the drain/reject window
   These are the audit trail. Without them, guarantees 1–3 are unfalsifiable. They must be emitted as metrics and structured logs, retained long enough to investigate post-incident, and exposed to whoever owns the readiness-flip path.

5. Regression-test.
   An automated test must exercise the readiness-flip path with accepted and in-flight work present, and assert:
     - every accepted item reaches a terminal outcome (drain or reject)
     - zero items are silently abandoned — no hang, no orphan, no missing response, no item left in an ambiguous state
     - accounting fields sum correctly: drained plus rejected equals accepted-at-flip, and stragglers equals zero
     - the window completes within a stated upper bound, under realistic load
   The test must run in CI on every change touching the readiness, shutdown, drain, or rejection code path. Manual verification is not a substitute. This is a class of bug that recurs under pressure precisely because the happy path looks fine.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT PRESCRIBE

Nothing above mandates a particular shutdown mechanism, signal, hook, sleep duration, probe configuration, queue topology, or in-process vs. out-of-process coordination. Those are implementation choices. The five guarantees are the contract the owner must satisfy; how they satisfy it is theirs to design, provided the contract holds under crash, OOM, network partition, and concurrent readiness flip with new traffic already in flight.

---

The readiness defect, with sources cited inline

The optimization under review is shard-keeper PR #190 (Cyrus's readiness optimization, dated 2025-04-16). The proposed predicate was `lease_owned == true`. That predicate is the defect.

What the 2025-04-16 staging handoff actually showed:

- 14:03:11 — replacement shard-keeper acquires the lease.
- 14:03:11 → 14:03:23 — readiness probe returns HTTP 200 (because `lease_owned == true`), but any request routed to the replacement receives HTTP 503 because the serving gate is still closed while snapshot catch-up runs.
- 14:03:23 — snapshot catch-up finishes, the serving gate opens, the replacement can actually serve.
- The old holder's serving gate was already closed before the replacement acquired the lease, so this is not a split-brain / two-serving-holders event — it is a single-serving-holder-pretending-to-serve event.

So the defect is: readiness reports true while the replica cannot yet serve traffic. Lease ownership is a prerequisite for serving eligibility, not a synonym for it. The fixed predicate is `lease_owned == true && serving_gate_open == true`, and runbook `rb_1789267973607` already establishes the principle at the failover-exit level (process readiness ≠ lease convergence) — PR #190 generalizes the same mistake to the per-replica readiness path.

Tests required before the optimization can proceed

I am framing each test around actual serving eligibility — i.e., the probe says ready only when the replica can carry traffic end-to-end. Lease ownership is one input among several; it is never the only input.

1. Serving-gate tests (does the replica actually serve?)

These directly cover the 12-second window the defect opened.

- a. Readiness must remain non-ready (HTTP 503) from the moment of lease acquisition until the serving gate opens. The reference event is the 2025-04-16 staging handoff: probe must return non-ready from 14:03:11 through 14:03:23 and flip to ready only at 14:03:23.
- b. The serving-gate variable name used in the readiness path must be the exact one confirmed by Cyrus pre-resubmit (per the 2025-04-16 note "Cyrus should confirm the exact serving-gate variable name used in the readiness path"). A wrong-name join makes the AND silently true and re-introduces the defect.
- c. While readiness is non-ready, every request routed to the replica must receive an explicit, distinguishable terminal response (HTTP 503 with a clear "not yet serving" signal), not a TCP reset, hang-until-client-timeout, or generic retryable 5xx. This is the same drain-or-explicit-rejection contract that applies to ingest-edge graceful shutdown: every accepted unit of work must reach one terminal outcome.
- d. The readiness predicate must be `lease_owned && serving_gate_open` at minimum; the 2026-09-16 note records that it may also need to AND in epoch monotonicity and follower-read rejoin requirements before the predicate is treated as complete.

2. Routing tests (does the load balancer honor the gate?)

These make sure the probe value drives routing behavior end-to-end.

- a. End-to-end staging handoff: with the fixed predicate, route a controlled mix of requests at the replacement starting at lease acquisition. Expectation: zero requests reach the replica's serving path before 14:03:23-equivalent; 100% of requests reach it after the serving gate opens. Counted as: requests received before gate-open = 0, requests received after gate-open = N, requests returning 503 with the "not yet serving" signal before gate-open = N.
- b. No false-routing interval: confirm that the load balancer actually stops routing to the replica during the gate-closed window. A probe that says ready when the gate is closed will pass unit tests but fail here — this is the test that catches the "probe says 200, traffic still arrives, traffic gets 503" failure mode.
- c. No stranded requests: every request the LB removed from routing to this replica must be retried successfully against another replica or returned to the caller with a retryable signal — none may be silently dropped.

3. Handoff tests (does the old holder release cleanly while the new one warms up?)

These cover the boundary between the two holders and the cutover plan that the optimization is meant to support.

- a. Old holder's serving gate must close before the new holder's lease is granted (this held on 2025-04-16 and must be asserted as a precondition, not assumed). A regression here is a real split-brain, distinct from the readiness-only defect.
- b. Follower-read rejoin: the replacement replica may not rejoin the follower-read pool until lag is below one second for fifteen continuous minutes (per the 2026-09-16 note that mirrors `rb_shard_keeper_rollback`). Readiness-flipping to true must not pre-empt this requirement.
- c. Epoch monotonicity across the partition set: lease epoch numbers increase without gaps or rollbacks across the failover, per `rb_1789267973607`. A non-monotonic epoch is a hard fail even if the serving-gate tests pass.
- d. No stale-owner messages for two full lease-renewal intervals after readiness flips — also from `rb_1789267973607`, applied here at the per-replica readiness boundary.
- e. Recovery-evidence correlation: trace exemplars or `trace_id` correlation must connect a 503 in the gate-closed window to the specific readiness flip on this replica (per the user-preference line in supermemory about trace exemplars for per-customer debugging). Without this, a 503 in the window is unactionable.

4. Process gates that must also pass before merge (not new tests, but hard prerequisites)

Why the cursor must be cryptographically and semantically bound to the authorized tenant

A preview cursor is, in effect, a bearer token: whoever holds it can resume paging through the dataset the prior response authorized. Three properties are required, and "just signing it" is not enough.

  Cryptographic binding — the cursor is a signed token (HMAC or asymmetric signature) where one of the signed claims is the tenant_id (or a tenant-scoped sub claim derived from it) that authorized the preview. Verification rejects a cursor whose tenant claim has been swapped, even if the signature over the rest of the payload still validates. The signature key must also be tenant- or scope-scoped (or at minimum not shared across tenants with overlapping key material) so a token cannot be re-signed for a different tenant.

  Semantic binding — the cursor's payload carries, as signed claims, exactly the predicates that defined authorization at issue time: the tenant, the dataset/collection, the allowed fields, the time range, the row-count or page-size limit, and any preview-specific gates (purpose, retention, rate window). On resume, the server re-evaluates these against the live authorization state. If any claim no longer holds — tenant disabled, dataset moved, retention expired, rate window exhausted, scope narrowed — the cursor is refused. "Resume" is not "replay the old auth decision."

  Why both are needed:
    - Cryptographic binding alone stops forgery but lets a legitimate tenant replay their own cursor against a later, narrower scope, or against a sibling tenant in a shared-cluster mistake, because the signature only proves the token was once valid for someone.
    - Semantic binding alone stops stale-scope replay but does not stop an attacker from minting a token for a tenant they do not control, which is the higher-impact failure.
    - Together, the cursor is unforgeable for any tenant other than the issuer, and un-resumable against any authorization state other than the one the issuer was granted.

  Concretely, for the corrected path the cursor payload must include, at minimum:
    - sub = tenant_id (signed, not derived at verify time)
    - scope = authorized preview scope snapshot (dataset, fields, time window, max rows)
    - iat / exp with exp ≤ the scope's expiry
    - jti or nonce chain position for monotonicity
    - mac/sig over the canonicalized concatenation of the above

  Any check that reads the tenant from request context (path, header, session) and looks up the cursor separately is the bug pattern to delete: tenant must come from inside the cursor, verified by signature, and must equal the caller's authorized tenant for the call to proceed.

Cross-tenant replay test (must fail closed)

  Setup: tenants A and B exist; A has a valid preview authorization; B does not. Issue a real, valid cursor for A's preview scope.

  Cases, each expected to be rejected before any adapter call:
    1. Swap the tenant claim in the cursor to B, keep the original signature → reject (signature invalid for the altered claim).
    2. Send A's unmodified cursor but present B's auth (B's session, B's token, B's headers) → reject (caller tenant ≠ cursor tenant).
    3. Send A's unmodified cursor to a route/endpoint scoped to B (different dataset key, different shard) → reject (cursor scope ≠ route scope; tenant mismatch).
    4. A's cursor replayed after A's preview authorization has been revoked or downscoped (e.g., dataset removed from A's allow-list, retention expired, purpose changed) → reject (semantic binding fail).
    5. A's cursor replayed past exp, or replayed with a jti that has already been consumed → reject.

  Pass criteria: every case returns the configured "cursor not valid for caller" error, and the access log shows zero adapter calls dispatched under B's identity or under any now-invalidated scope.

Zero-adapter-call-after-denial test (must fail closed)

  Setup: instrument the adapter boundary so every outbound call from the preview path emits a counted event tagged with (cursor_jti, resolved_tenant, endpoint, decision). The test asserts this counter.

  Cases, each expected to produce 0 adapter calls:
    1. Any of the five cross-tenant replay cases above — counter for B's tenant / altered scope is 0.
    2. Cursor with valid signature but for a scope the caller never authorized (e.g., dataset A is allowed, dataset A-private is not) → 0 calls to A-private.
    3. Cursor verified successfully but a downstream precondition fails (rate limit, quota, suspension, account-gate scope per the Harbor suspension = account-gate-scoped rule) → 0 adapter calls.
    4. A request that passes the cursor check but is missing a required second factor on resume (e.g., re-consent, fresh step-up) → 0 adapter calls.
    5. Error path: signature verification throws, scope parse throws, clock skew beyond tolerance, jti lookup errors → 0 adapter calls (fail closed, not fail open with a default tenant).

  Pass criteria: for every denial case, the counter delta is exactly 0 and the decision log records the denial reason. The test is specifically scoped to adapter calls, not to internal verification logs — the point is that denial must short-circuit before any external data plane is touched.

Scope guardrail for the corrected path

  Per your constraint, these changes do not expand the authorized preview scope: the cursor now carries the same scope as before (tenant, dataset, fields, window, limits), but those values are signed and re-asserted on resume. No new datasets, fields, retention, or rate windows are introduced. The corrected path makes the existing scope unforgeable and un-replayable across tenants; it does not grant any tenant a wider view than the original authorization.

Fail-closed means the gate's default answer is "stay isolated," and a positive answer requires affirmative evidence. The gate is not a liveness check; it is a trust-restore decision. Treating absence of evidence as evidence of recovery inverts that default and re-creates the exact failure mode the isolation was designed to contain.

2. What "current generation" means here. A valid report is a self-describing artifact from the just-completed monitoring generation on the rejoining replica, carrying (a) the generation id the replica believes it is in, (b) the label set and shard map it observed end-of-generation, (c) the label-rename parity verdict against the canonical source (Cardinalities Guardrails / Nadia + Cyrus team — both signatures required), (d) the dropped-series list with reasons, (e) the route table hash, and (f) the local health summary for that generation.     - The replica's view of the generation is the only thing that proves it actually executed the generation. A coordinator-side timestamp or heartbeat cannot substitute — the April 12 lesson was that coordinator-observed liveness and replica-observed correctness can diverge (the label_map leak on routing+admin/validation read sites produced a "looks healthy from outside, wrong from inside" state).
    - Generation-scoped state is write-once per replica per generation. There is no re-derivation path that produces a trustworthy end-of-generation label set, route hash, or dropped-series list after the generation window closes, because the in-memory structures that produced them are gone and any reconstruction has to assume the very invariants that are in question.
    - The label-rename parity check requires the replica's own end-of-generation label set matched against the canonical source by both Nadia and Cyrus. Framing first, then the triage.

The relevant framework is USDA's: perishable food is unsafe above 40°F once it's been in the "danger zone" (40–140°F) for more than 2 hours total. Two things matter: (a) the air reading you got (44°F) and (b) how long the food itself was actually above 40°F. Those are not the same number. With the door only partly open for 55 minutes and the freezer still at 4°F acting as thermal ballast, the food's internal temperature almost certainly stayed well below the air temperature for most of that window — which is consistent with everything "still feeling cold." 55 minutes is also comfortably under the 2-hour limit. So nothing here needs to be discarded on time/temperature grounds alone. The decision comes down to per-item risk and what you observe.

Food-by-food triage (most cautious first):

Raw chicken — highest concern. Poultry carries Salmonella and Campylobacter routinely; if it grows, surface slime or off odor is the only honest signal. Cook it today, thoroughly, to 165°F internal at the thickest point, then either eat it or refrigerate the cooked product. Do not refreeze raw. If when you unwrap it the surface feels sticky or tacky, or smells off (sweetish, sulfurous, "off"), discard — don't taste-test chicken.

Cooked rice — second-highest concern, for a reason that matters here. Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking and germinate between ~40–140°F; reheating does NOT destroy the toxin once it's produced. So the 2-hour rule is not really your safety net for rice — the question is whether it ever crossed into the danger zone meaningfully. Since it "felt cold," it's almost certainly still fine. Reheat any portion you serve to a rolling 165°F (steam throughout). Discard if there's any off smell, unusual clumping, or visible mold — do not eat "iffy" rice on the assumption reheating will fix it; it won't.

Milk — easiest signal. Cold milk that smells and tastes normal is normal. Smell it; if clean, use it within a couple of days as usual. Discard at any sour/cheesy odor or any thickening. Liquid warms faster than the solids around it, so this is actually the item most likely to have crept up in temp, but 55 min from a partly open door rarely moves a sealed half-gallon much.

Eggs — depends on form. Raw shell eggs (intact) are robust; if cold, fine, use normally. If these are liquid pasteurized eggs or cracked raw, treat like milk — smell check. Hard-boiled eggs in shell: same as cooked rice for B. cereus reasons — eat promptly or discard; don't leave them sitting.

Cut vegetables — lowest risk. Use them first (they'll wilt from the temp bump regardless of safety), and trim any pieces that look/smell off. Wash before eating, as always.

Immediate cooling / recovery steps:

- Leave the door closed for the next 2–3 hours. Every open door costs you recovery time.
- Verify the seal: close the door on a piece of paper or a dollar bill and pull; if it slides out without resistance, the gasket is compromised and this will recur. Also check that nothing inside (a container, a drawer pushed out) is keeping the door from fully seating.
- Place a second thermometer (even a cheap one) on a middle shelf and re-check in 1–2 hours. You're looking for a return to ≤40°F. If it doesn't get there, the fridge has a separate problem unrelated to today.
- Don't add new warm groceries until the box is back at ≤40°F.
- Don't trust the built-in thermometer alone right now; it's a single probe in one spot.

What to check or use promptly (in this order, today):

1. Raw chicken — cook it tonight or tomorrow morning, 165°F internal.
2. Cooked rice — eat or discard; don't just push to the back.
3. Cut vegetables — use first; quality degrades before safety does.
4. Milk — smell check, then use.
5. Eggs — routine use if shell eggs; prompt use if liquid or hard-boiled.

What evidence requires discarding rather than guessing:

- Any off odor on any item, especially chicken, rice, or milk. Smell is your most reliable sensory test for spoilage bacteria.
- Sticky, slimy, or tacky surface on raw chicken or meat (a wet chicken is normal; sticky/tacky is not).
- Milk that's sour, chunky, or has any off flavor.
- Cooked rice with any off smell or visible mold — don't taste-test rice.
- Egg whites/yolks that smell off when cracked, or any pink/iridescent discoloration in raw egg (rare but specific).
- Cut vegetables that are slimy or have any mold.
- A probe-thermometer reading on the food itself above 40°F for an extended period — but you don't have that data, so it isn't what's driving the decision today.
- The one scenario that would flip the whole call: any reason to believe the door was actually open substantially longer than 55 minutes (e.g., you find that the seal failed and the door has been ajar overnight, or a pet/child has been opening it). If that becomes plausible, the 2-hour clock is blown and you discard the chicken, rice, and any liquid dairy.

Bottom line: at 55 minutes, door only partly open, freezer still frozen, everything still cold to touch, and a 44°F air reading that suggests the food itself stayed below 40°F — nothing here requires automatic discard. Use the chicken and rice today, use the rest promptly, and let the box recover closed for a few hours before reopening the question.
