This is a real metric-design problem, not just an edge case. Let me lay out what the numbers mean and what to push the PR author on.

  caller total latency:        9.2s
  caller deadline (5s total):  breached at 12:00:05, by 4.2s
  handler metric reports:      4.4s (queue delay excluded)
  queue wait:                  4.8s   ← larger than the processing time itself

Two specific failure modes the metric creates:

  1. SLO/alert gap. Anything keyed on this metric — p95, burn-rate alerts, error budgets — will not see this incident. The metric says 4.4s, comfortably under 5s. The caller timed out. Under any load that produces non-trivial queue wait, dashboards built on this metric will systematically look healthier than caller experience.

  2. Queue wait is the dominant term in your example, not the exception. 4.8s wait vs 4.4s processing means the metric is reporting a minority share of total request time. If that's the regime this PR is meant to operate in, the metric is structurally unfit for caller-facing SLOs.

The "new five-second processing context at dispatch" framing is the deeper concern. Two distinct deadlines are being conflated:

  - caller's 5s, from acceptance (already breached at 12:00:05)
  - handler's 5s, from dispatch (met, 4.4s ≤ 5s)

The handler is internally correct against its own deadline and externally violating the caller's. A single "handler duration" metric measuring the internal one is going to be misused as a proxy for the external one unless the gap is filled elsewhere.

What I'd block on, or at minimum require explicit answers to before merge:

  a. Confirm there's a separate acceptance→completion latency metric, and confirm the SLO alerting keys off that one, not this. If yes, the PR description must call out that this metric is not caller-facing and name the metric that is.

  b. The max-queue-wait gauge already exists in ingest-edge (we've touched this area before — no tenant label, synthetic-tenant harness). Make sure it's surfaced alongside this metric on the same dashboard, and that queue-wait alerting exists independently of handler duration. Right now, with the metric scoped the way it is, queue wait is the only thing that would catch this incident.

  c. Decide whether the handler should propagate the original deadline rather than starting a fresh one at dispatch. If dispatch happens after deadline expiry, processing-time is the wrong thing to measure — the request is already a timeout from the caller's perspective. At minimum, the metric should distinguish "processing time on a still-valid request" from "processing time on an already-expired request," or the second case should be excluded / labeled.

  d. If the scope is intentional, name it so. handler_processing_duration_seconds_excluding_queue_wait is ugly but unambiguous. As written, anyone wiring this into a caller-SLO dashboard will silently miss deadline breaches.

Concrete questions for the author:

  - Exact metric name, where in the code path it's emitted, and what scope (handler, dispatch, request) it measures.
  - Which metric do the existing 5s SLO and alert rules use?
  - Where is acceptance-to-completion latency reported today, if anywhere?
  - Is the dispatch-time deadline reset documented, and is there a reason it isn't a continuation of the caller's deadline?

If (a) and (d) are addressed and queue-wait alerting is confirmed live, this is a doc-and-rename follow-up, not a blocker. If the answer to (a) is "no separate metric, this is the only one," it's a blocker — merge as-is and someone will build a caller-SLO dashboard on a metric that excludes the dominant source of latency.

Fuzzing on nylon webbing isn't purely cosmetic — broken outer fibers are how the material starts degrading before any cut or stitch failure shows. Because the patch sits at a load-bearing transition (near the D-ring stitching), my read is: treat as retire-worthy unless you can confirm it's isolated surface scuff from a specific rub point (crate edge, car seatbelt hardware, etc.).

WEBBING & LOAD-BEARING STITCHING — SAFETY INSPECTION CHECKLIST
Method: light hand tension (10–15% stretch, just enough to flatten the weave)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SETUP
- Flat, well-lit surface; clean background so frays/dust show.
- Webbing should be dry — wet hides texture defects.
- Run fingers along the full length first, NO tension, to feel for hard spots, thin spots, raised areas, or stiffness.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
WEBBING UNDER TENSION
Pull each section taut and look along both faces, then backlit if possible.

SUPERFICIAL FUZZING — cosmetic, NOT a replacement trigger
- Raised surface fibers from normal abrasion (pilling like a sweater).
- Fibers still lay flat under thumb pressure; no exposed base weave.
- Webbing width unchanged; uniform across surface, not concentrated at stress points.
- Color slightly dulled but otherwise intact.

COMPROMISED WEBBING — replace now
- Visible thinning: width tapers at any point, or weave looks see-through when backlit.
- Cuts, nicks, or snags — even short ones that break the surface.
- Melted, glazed, or charred spots (heat/friction damage).
- Abrasion exposing inner core fibers (lighter threads visible through the sheath).
- Stiff, waxy, or brittle sections (UV or chemical degradation) — webbing should flex like new.
- Any section that stays narrower under tension than the rest.
- Discoloration concentrated along an edge (often the first sign of breakdown).

QUICK SIDE-LOAD TEST at any suspect spot
- Pinch both sides of the webbing and pull sideways — if it stretches unevenly or you see daylight through the weave, it is compromised.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
LOAD-BEARING STITCHING
Critical zones: buckle attachments, D-ring/anchor loops, handle-to-strap joins, every bartack and X-box.

Hold each stitched junction under light tension and look straight along the stitch line. Count stitches; note gaps.

HEALTHY
- All stitches intact, thread flat against webbing, color uniform, no fraying.

REPLACE IF YOU SEE
- 2 or more adjacent broken, missing, or pulled-through stitches.
- Loose thread loops hanging from the line (stitch has lost tension).
- Thread abrasion, fraying, or discoloration along the stitch line.
- Needle holes elongating under tension (stitches no longer holding the webbing).
- Any bartack or X-box with a visible gap, separation, or lifted thread.
- Hardware-to-webbing junction that shifts, twists, or slides under tension.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
HARDWARE (covered while you're there)
- Plastic buckles: no cracks, all teeth intact, latch returns positively.
- Metal D-rings / O-rings: no gap when closed, no bend, no deep scratches across the load axis, no corrosion pitting.
- Trigger snaps: spring action positive; no drift open under a light shake.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
REPLACEMENT THRESHOLDS — SUMMARY
Replace immediately if ANY one of the following is true:
 1. Cut, melt, char, or abrasion exposing inner fibers.
 2. Visible width reduction or uneven stretch at any point.
 3. 2+ broken or missing stitches at any load-bearing seam.
 4. Any elongated needle hole or pulled-through stitch under tension.
 5. Stiff / brittle / waxy webbing section.
 6. Cracked buckle, bent D-ring, or trigger snap that drifts open.
 7. Hardware-to-webbing junction that shifts under tension.

Cosmetic only — keep using, recheck monthly:
- Uniform surface fuzzing.
- Minor surface scuffs that do not break the weave.
- Light dirt that washes out.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
RE-INSPECTION CADENCE
- Every 1–3 months depending on use intensity.
- Immediately after any pull-event, snag, chew incident, or known chemical/UV exposure.
- Log date and any borderline findings with location on the gear.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

I cannot pull the diff or commit list, so the review below is built entirely from the failure-mode description you sent. If the PR is filed under a different key, send me the actual pr_id and I will re-pull.

Failure-mode classification
- Stale-response fencing defect, not split brain. Your trace description is conclusive: at no point are two serving gates accepting requests concurrently, so the holder-side fence (lease epoch + serving gate) is doing its job. The defect is that the client-side response fence does not exist — responses don't carry the serving epoch, and the client applies them in arrival order, which is the wrong ordering rule.
- Concretely: holder A (epoch 811) accepts a read, then loses the lease and closes the serving gate. Holder B (epoch 812) takes over and serves the retry. A's late response arrives after B's and overwrites B's newer routing value in the client cache. The cache is now wrong (points at A, which has no lease), and any follow-on read from this client will be routed to a holder that won't serve it.

Cross-service impact (metrics-router, ingest-edge — both in your metrics pipeline)
- metrics-router: if any consumer caches shard-keeper holder routing values from read responses, it is exposed to the same stale-wins pattern. During a failover window, stale-wins means reads keep getting routed at A even though A's serving gate is closed. Symptoms are read timeouts / errors until the client's TTL drains or until A finishes draining its in-flight backlog. If A's serving-gate close doesn't actually stop A from emitting responses (slow write-ack path, follower commit log, etc.), the TTL is the only thing protecting the client — and TTL is the wrong fence here.
- ingest-edge: same exposure if it caches holder addresses. The pattern is identical.
- Reference point: shard-keeper runbook rb_1789267973607 ("verify lease convergence after failover") lays out the server-side exit checks for a failover (single owner per partition, monotonic lease epochs, no stale-owner messages for two renewal intervals). That runbook is about the holder layer. Your PR is the missing client-side piece — fencing on responses, not just on requests.
- Net recommendation: audit both consumers' read paths to shard-keeper. For each, confirm the caching key includes serving epoch and the apply rule is monotonic (drop on response.epoch < cached.epoch). Add a per-consumer regression fixture that drives a delayed response after a failover.

Fix recommendations (for the PR)
1. Carry serving epoch on every shard-keeper response — header or body field, your call. Treat it as a fencing token on responses, parallel to the lease epoch on the holder.
2. Client-side apply rule: accept iff response.epoch >= cached.epoch. Drop on response.epoch < cached.epoch (no overwrite). If response.epoch > cached.epoch + N for some small N, drop and log — a leap that large is almost always a stale read of cached state elsewhere, not a real advance.
3. Metric: shard_keeper_stale_response_dropped_total. Cardinality: bound the label space — bucket (response.epoch - cached.epoch) into {1, 2-5, 6+}; do not pass raw epoch values through as label keys (this is the same shape as the Cardinality Guardrails work, and the guardrails will reject unbounded label values pre-flight).
4. Trace: every read response carries the epoch it was served under as a span attribute. This is what makes your staging fixture reproducible end-to-end.
5. Holder-side confirmation: verify A cannot emit a response after the lease is lost. The serving-gate close should be sufficient as described, but check for any async path that can serialize a response after gate close — write-ack fanout, follower commit-log replay, slow-path commit. If any of those exist, that's a separate holder-side fence fix that has to land alongside.

Test coverage to add to the PR
- Fixture A (yours): in-flight read at epoch 811, A loses lease mid-read, B serves retry at 812, A's response arrives delayed. Assert: client rejects A's response, cached epoch stays at 812, metric increments, trace carries both epochs.
- Fixture B: late-arrival is from B at 812, with A at 811 already lost. Tests ordering under non-monotonic cache writes from the other side.
- Fixture C: two consecutive failovers (811 → 812 → 813); A's late 811 arrives after B's 813. Assert drop, cached stays at 813.
- Cross-service fixture: same failover pattern driven from a metrics-router consumer; assert the consumer's routing cache is monotonic on serving epoch.

Frame held to the standing 1:1 decision (12 Sept, with Hema): scope is replay-validation fixture cleanup only — no relabel, cutover thread stays closed absent new evidence. Within that scope the PR is required to demonstrate four things before it can land:

1. Response identity sufficient to reject a prior-epoch result across handoff. Per-holder identity (epoch / term / lease generation — whatever word this service already uses) on the wire, end-to-end, compared at the receiver against current known state. A below-current identity is rejected, not applied. The mechanism should be the existing one — no new protocol introduced here.

2. Four regression fixtures, each asserting the outcome, not just "no crash":
   - Handoff — clean handover; new holder accepts, old holder (now stale) is rejected by identity.
   - Retry — in-flight retry after handoff reaches the new holder and is accepted under the new identity.
   - Delayed old-holder response — old holder's response lands after the new holder is serving; rejected with no state mutation, no cache write, no log line that could be misread as a successful apply.
   - Client-cache ordering — newer cached entry exists, older response arrives later; cache must not move backward. Asymmetric with retry: the new identity is already in cache; the fixture proves a late stale write cannot downgrade it.

3. Explicitly out of scope for this PR: new identity protocols / fence tokens / transport changes; new metrics, dashboards, or alerts; anything that reopens the cutover thread.

The point of the four-fixture set is that "delayed old-holder" and "client-cache ordering" are the two cases where arrival order can quietly move cached routing state backward — they're the actual regression risk, and a request_changes review is the right shape for them to land in fixtures rather than getting papered over with a fix. Good baseline: no load, no damage signs, lights elsewhere live = the fault is likely either at the GFCI itself or downstream of it, and the branch breaker probably never tripped (GFCIs trip themselves; the breaker only trips on overcurrent/short). Here's the non-destructive sequence.

1. Confirm nothing is plugged into the tripped GFCI. Also unplug anything on any other outlet that's on the same kitchen counter circuit (the load side of the GFCI can feed additional outlets, often the other half of the counter, sometimes a dining nook or pantry). If a downstream device is leaking even a little current to ground, the GFCI will refuse to reset.

2. Check for an upstream GFCI on the same circuit. Yes, do this. In older South Slope wiring it's common for a bathroom GFCI, a powder-room GFCI, or even a garage/laundry GFCI to be wired ahead of a kitchen one, either intentionally or as a renovation artifact. Walk the apartment and press TEST then RESET on every GFCI you can find (kitchens, baths, behind the fridge or washing machine if applicable, exterior). If you find one that's tripped, reset it first, then return to the kitchen GFCI. Symptom of this case: the kitchen GFCI's reset button feels normal, clicks, but the outlet stays dead — that's the upstream-trip signature.

3. Try one reset on the kitchen GFCI with all load-side outlets empty. Press TEST firmly (it should click and the outlet should go dead), then press RESET firmly and hold 1–2 seconds. A GFCI that won't latch on an empty circuit has either failed internally or is seeing a real ground fault on its load conductors.

4. Verify whether power is actually reaching the GFCI. Plug in a simple lamp or use a non-contact voltage tester on the hot side of the receptacle (the smaller slot). If there's no voltage at all, the GFCI itself is fine and the problem is upstream. If there is voltage but it won't reset, the GFCI mechanism has failed.

5. Breaker: yes, one reset is reasonable, and only after steps 1–4. At the panel, identify the kitchen small-appliance circuit (often labeled "Kitchen," "Counter," or two 20A breakers for kitchen per code). Fully flip it OFF (firm click past the midpoint), then fully ON. Do not "just push it back" — soft-tripped breakers can look on but aren't actually closed. One attempt only. If it immediately trips again, or if it was already in the fully-on position and the GFCI still won't reset, the breaker is not your problem; leave it alone.

6. Leave the breaker off and stop troubleshooting if any of the following apply:
   - The breaker trips again immediately or within seconds of being reset.
   - The GFCI resets once but trips again the moment any small load is plugged in, or trips on its own within a day or two.
   - You find any of: warm faceplate, discoloration around the receptacle, a buzzing or crackling sound, any burning smell now or later, scorch marks on the plug or cord, or moisture in the box (kitchens back-splash splash zone).
   - The GFCI will not reset with the load side fully cleared and the line side confirmed hot — that points to a failed GFCI or a wiring fault (reversed line/load, a shared neutral issue, a nicked conductor in the wall) that you cannot diagnose without opening the box.
   - You reset it more than twice in a short period, or it has tripped repeatedly in recent weeks — that's a pattern, not a one-off, and the underlying cause needs a licensed electrician.
   - You're not certain which outlets are on the GFCI's load side, or the wiring in the box doesn't match what you'd expect (back-stabbed connections, aluminum conductors, double-tapped terminals).

7. Who to contact. You're renting the South Slope unit with Devika, so the right first call is your management company / landlord, not a private electrician — they own the electrical system and are responsible for GFCI replacement and any branch-circuit fault, and the lease puts repair obligations on them. Ask for a licensed electrician dispatch, specify that a GFCI receptacle will not reset after a blender trip with no load present, and that the breaker has been verified. If they delay or push you to "just keep resetting it," the response deadline in your lease and the NYC tenant repair-rights process apply; do not continue to use a GFCI that has tripped and won't reset cleanly, and do not run an extension cord from another circuit to feed the kitchen counter.

Until it's fixed: don't use that receptacle or anything downstream of it, don't swap in a regular (non-GFCI) outlet as a workaround, and don't keep pressing RESET repeatedly hoping it will take — each failed reset attempt on a real ground fault is just confirming the fault is still there.

Right — those are two different operational states, and Iris's copy collapses them in a way that lets HH/MC infer broader access than Lantern actually has.

Unavailable: the dedup tuple is incomplete (typically source_event_id missing from the upstream), so Lantern can't determine whether the movement is new or a duplicate. It's not "stale data" — it's missing identity for the movement. Lantern doesn't see a value to be stale about.

Explicit Unknown: a permitted source is recognized, but its current value is stale or missing. Lantern only knows the source exists; it isn't seeing more than it should.

Neither state changes the authorized scope. "Unavailable means Lantern has stale data" wrongly suggests Lantern has the value and it's just old, which is the exact thing we don't want HH/MC to conclude.

Suggested revision for Iris to send to HH/MC:

"Lantern reports a deploy as 'Unavailable' when it cannot determine whether the movement is new or a duplicate — typically because the source-event ID is missing from the upstream source. Lantern still only sees what it's permitted to see; 'Unavailable' does not mean the data exists but is old.

A separate state, 'Explicit Unknown,' appears when a permitted source is recognized but its current value is stale or missing."

Plain text below, no headers/asterisks:

1. Safe vs. unsafe normalization steps

Safe (presentation-level only, schema-neutral):

  Parsing the artifacts into a structured form (e.g., a token tree keyed by the schema's declared fields, or the parser's natural keys for an artifact whose schema is implied by the document format). This addresses only byte-vs-tree differences, not token value differences.

  Canonicalizing byte representations that a parser would already collapse: CRLF → LF, NUL-strip, BOM handling at the document boundary, surrogate-pair normalization to a single encoding, trailing newline at EOF. These are not part of any token's value; they are transport artifacts.

  Sorting token keys before comparison. The drift signal that matters is "does the value at this key differ?" — key order is presentation. (Caveat: if the schema's own grouping or the team's review convention is order-sensitive, surface ordering as a separate, named check rather than collapsing it silently.)

  Re-encoding to a single canonical encoding (e.g., UTF-8) for comparison. The bytes that encode a value are not the value.

Not safe unless the schema declares it insignificant:

  Trimming leading/trailing whitespace from a string value. This is a value-level edit, not a presentation-level edit. `"12 px"` and `" 12 px"` are distinct values; the leading space is part of the value. The fixture Anya wrote is exactly the regression case that catches this — it must remain a failing case for any helper that trims.

  Collapsing internal whitespace (e.g., `"12  px"` → `"12 px"`), zero-padding normalization, case folding, unit normalization (`"12px"` vs `"12 px"`), thousands-separator removal, decimal-comma vs decimal-point, locale-driven digit grouping. Each of these is a value-level semantic claim that belongs in the schema, not in a generic normalizer.

  Ignoring or substituting explicit unknowns. If the source marks a value as unspecified, not visible, redacted, or absent, that distinction is part of the contract and must survive comparison.

  Trailing-comma / single-quote / quoted-string tolerance that the parser would normally reject. If a parse is "successful" only because the normalizer silently repaired something the parser would have flagged, you have hidden a real difference.

2. Why token-value whitespace must not be silently normalized unless the schema defines it as insignificant

Three independent reasons that all have to hold:

  Semantic: in design tokens, a leading or trailing space is almost always meaningful. Spacing primitives (`"12 px"`, `" 12 px"`, `"12 px "`) are typically resolved in a specific layout context where the spaces are part of the resolved output. Two tokens that differ only in whitespace will render differently downstream, which is exactly the kind of change a drift checker is supposed to surface. The fixture is doing the checker's job — any helper that makes it pass has weakened the check, not improved it.

  Epistemic: the checker's contract is to surface differences between two artifacts for human review. A silent whitespace normalization turns a question ("is this value different?") into an assumption ("this kind of difference is unimportant"). Once the normalizer makes that assumption, the team can no longer audit whether the assumption was right for the tokens they actually ship. The fixture is the way to keep that assumption from being made implicitly.

  Boundary: the schema is the only place with the authority to declare a class of difference insignificant. If the spec for this artifact type says spacing around numeric primitives is insignificant in this field, then trimming is legitimate — but it must be documented as a schema rule, applied only to fields covered by that rule, and tested with both passing and failing fixtures that pin the boundary. If the schema does not say so, trimming is a unilateral semantic choice made by the normalizer, which is the same shape of problem as a normalizer silently lowercasing email addresses or rounding numbers.

  Practical consequence: trimming does not just fail the one fixture. It changes the failure profile of every fixture and every future artifact comparison in a way that is invisible at the call site. The narrow correct fix is to keep the three presentation-level normalizations Anya already approved (parse to tree, canonicalize line endings, sort keys) and drop the value trim.

3. Original artifacts to retain as evidence

For this kind of review, the originals matter because the whole point of a drift checker is to be re-runnable and to be auditable after the fact. Recommend Anya retain:

  Both input artifacts, byte-for-byte, in their original form (whatever encoding and line endings they were produced with). Store with content-addressed identifiers (e.g., sha256) so the comparison can be re-run deterministically against exactly what was reviewed. Do not store only the parsed/normalized forms.

  The parsed intermediate representation produced by each normalization step, in order, with the diff after each step. This is what makes "which step turned this from a real difference into a silent agreement" answerable later. It also makes it possible to add or remove a normalization step and re-evaluate the same input set without re-collecting the artifacts.

  The normalization rule set as a versioned artifact in its own right: which steps were applied, in what order, with what parameters, and the schema excerpt that authorizes each step. Steps that are presentation-level cite "format spec" or "parser behavior"; steps that are value-level cite the schema clause that declares the value class insignificant. No step without a citation.

  Fixtures, both passing and failing, with the expected verdict for each (which side, what diff). The `"12 px"` vs `" 12 px"` fixture is a failing fixture by design and must stay failing; any future normalizer that makes it pass should cause the test suite to fail loudly and name the offending step.

  The reviewer-visible summary: which artifacts were compared, the rule set version, the overall verdict, the per-key diffs, and who reviewed it. This is the audit trail the team will need if a downstream consumer reports a difference the checker said was not present.

  The original review thread or PR comment that scoped the change, so the rule set's evolution is traceable to a human decision and not just to whoever edited the normalizer last.

The clean separation to keep on the engineering boundary: Anya owns the rule set and the implementation; the role here is to flag that value-level whitespace normalization is a semantic claim the schema must authorize, that the three presentation-level steps she already has are sufficient for the drift signal she described, and that the originals and the per-step intermediates need to be retained so the team can re-litigate any of those decisions later. No rewrites of her code, no opinion on her test framework beyond "keep the failing fixture failing."

Practical comparison — walking vs. wheelchair assistance at LGA

Walking the terminal end-to-end after landing typically means 15–25 minutes on your feet: corridor to the people mover, queue for the people mover (standing), ride, then walk to baggage claim, stand at the carousel, then walk/stand at the curb for pickup. Gates at LGA are long; depending on where you lands, the gate-to-baggage distance is roughly half a mile to three-quarters, and most of it is hard floor with no seats along the way.

Wheelchair assistance works like this: an agent meets her at the gate seat (she waits there, usually 5–15 min for the chair to arrive), then pushes her through the corridors — typically cutting past the people-mover line and any standing stretches — and drops her either at the baggage carousel or directly at the curb. Bags travel separately and meet her at the carousel; she doesn't carry them. Standing drops to near-zero. Total time on the ground is usually similar or a bit shorter, but the time is seated instead of standing.

The "is it excessive" question has a simple practical answer: it's one of the most commonly used services at LGA — agents handle dozens per flight, no one registers it as unusual, and she's in and out faster with less fatigue. She can also use it selectively (gate to carousel, then walk the short curb stretch) if she wants a middle ground. Using it on the arrival flight doesn't commit her to anything for the return; she can decide flight-by-flight.

The framing that fits best: this is energy budgeting for the visit, not a medical accommodation. The walking happens whether or not she does it; the question is whether she wants to spend that energy in the terminal or save it for Nov 12 and the days around it.

The candidate expression is a regression: it substitutes a multiplicative estimator (`count × mean`) for an additive truth the collector already emits. Replay A's match is a mean-reversion coincidence, not a property of the estimator.

Three concrete problems with shipping it as the published metric:

1. The estimator replaces an emitted exact counter with an approximation. The collector publishes refused points directly; PR 309 throws that away and re-derives a number from `attempted - received - k·avg`. Even when the approximation lands, it's a worse source of truth than the one being replaced.

2. Replay A passes by construction, not by validation. The four refused batches (2k + 8k + 11k + 19k = 40k) average to exactly the global mean (10k), so `k·avg` equals the sum. Any other distribution of refused-batch sizes with the same sum — say 1k / 5k / 15k / 19k — would still match. The fixture doesn't exercise the estimator at all; it just confirms `mean(rejected) == mean(all)` happened to hold. Replay B breaks that property by shrinking the refused batches, so `4·10,000` overshoots the actual refused sum and the estimator diverges from the collector's emitted counter.

3. `attempted - received` isn't a closed system. In Replay A the gap `1,000,000 - 920,000 - 40,000 = 40,000` is non-zero, which means there's at least one more bucket (in-flight / pending / lost) beyond received and refused. The estimator masks that bucket only because `k·avg` happens to equal the actual refused, not the residual. The instant a second source of drift enters (queue depth, time-window misalignment), the estimator will silently attribute it to refused points.

The right shape for "separate request accounting from point accounting":

- Keep the emitted exact refused-point counter as the published source of truth for point totals.

A few things to pin down with Wes before this becomes a spec — these are the load-bearing pieces:

  1. Counter updates need to be atomic, not check-then-increment. `tenant_pending < 64` and `global_pending < 2,048` as plain reads are TOCTOU races — two concurrent reservers can each see 63 / 2,047 and both pass. Use CAS, hold the counters under a lock, or atomic add with rollback if a post-check fails.

  2. "Release each held reservation exactly once" only holds if cancel and enqueue-failure paths share a single source of truth for what's currently held. Two reasonable shapes:
       a. Each request carries small state (tenant_held, global_held as bools); release paths toggle those flags, actual decrement runs once per flag.
       b. Reservations live in a defer-style cleanup block keyed off a single `released` flag, cleanup idempotent.
     Either way, explicitly sketch the three failure modes: cancel arriving mid-reservation (between tenant and global); enqueue succeeding but "mark accepted" failing (item in-queue, counters still held); retry of the release path itself.

  3. Cancel-arrives-mid-reservation isn't covered by the current wording. The sequence says "release tenant if global fails," but a concurrent cancel can land after tenant is held and during the global attempt — that should also release tenant.

  4. The enqueue-vs-acceptance gap. If enqueue returns success but "mark accepted" doesn't (crash, dropped response, timeout-then-retry), the batch is in-queue with dangling counters. Two options:
       a. Sweep "enqueued but not accepted" after a TTL and release their reservations.
       b. Fold acceptance into enqueue completion: enqueue success = accepted, decrement on enqueue, no separate mark.
     The sketch's ordering suggests (b) is the intent — make it explicit.

  5. Reservation order has a fairness consequence worth stating as intent: tenant-first throttles one noisy tenant at 64 before it can pressure the global pool. Global-first would let a single tenant burn global down to 2,048 alone. Current order is correct for fairness — flag it so Wes knows it's deliberate, not accidental.

  6. Binding constraint. 2,048 / 64 = 32. With >=32 active tenants, global is the tighter cap; below that, per-tenant binds first. Worth knowing where each cap is expected to bite at typical load.

2) Cancellation regression (caller cancellation inside the bounded response)

  - The bounded response uses the existing retryable backpressure path. 3) Slot-release regression (releasing queue slots on terminal outcomes)

  - The 2,048 global and 64 per-tenant ceilings are capacity budgets. A batch that terminates (accepted, refused, or cancelled) must release its slot deterministically and promptly; otherwise the ceilings behave as effective caps that shrink under load and turn the stop conditions into false positives.
  - Required artifact: a fixture where tenants push the global cap to 2,048, then a burst of terminal outcomes occurs (acceptance, refusal via the retryable path, and caller cancellation) within a small window. the "replay p99=780 ms" Cyrus saw at 16M points/min —

indicating a production condition, which is exactly why
§1's traffic_class filter is mandatory.

sustained form is also required, because the symptom is
what users feel and a 30-second refusal burst followed by
recovery is not a page-worthy event at this stage.

Both clauses use the same sustained-window semantics. No
mixed semantics inside one alert.

------------------------------------------------------------
3. CAUSE-VERSUS-SYMPTOM WORDING
------------------------------------------------------------

The current draft names queue_wait_p99_ms and
retryable_queue_full_ratio as if they were independent
conditions. They are not. The right structure is one
cause rule and one symptom rule, with the symptom rule
explicitly downstream of the cause rule.

Recommended split:

  Alert A — CAUSE (early-warning, queue saturation):
    name:      "metrics-router queue saturation — cause"
    condition: traffic_class="live"
               AND source_class="ingest-edge"
               AND environment="production"
               AND queue_wait_p99_ms > 400
               sustained for 5m
    severity:  warning
    routing:   Nadia-owned dashboard + #infra
               (no paging; investigation channel)
    rationale: queue saturation is the upstream condition.
               It does not by itself mean users are
               impacted; it precedes refusal.

  Alert B — SYMPTOM (user-impact, refusal rate):
    name:      "metrics-router queue refusals — symptom"
    condition: traffic_class="live"
               AND source_class="ingest-edge"
               AND environment="production"
               AND retryable_queue_full_ratio > 0.005
               sustained for 5m
    severity:  page (the user-impact signal)
    routing:   Nadia-owned on-call rotation
    rationale: retryable refusals are the user-facing
               symptom — the API is returning 429-equivalent
               responses. This is what warrants a page.

  Escalation ladder:
    - Cause fires alone (5m sustained q-p99 > 400, refusal
      ratio below threshold): investigate, do not page.
      This is the early warning.
    - Symptom fires alone (refusal ratio > 0.005 sustained,
      p99 not yet above 400): page. This is a real user
      impact condition; investigate cause in parallel.
    - Both fire: page and treat as a queue-control failure
      until proven otherwise.

  - "queue saturation (cause)"
  - "queue refusal rate (symptom)"

hide the relationship. The labels must make the cause-
symptom relationship visible in the alert text itself, so
the on-call reader does not have to reconstruct it.

   PRODUCTION
------------------------------------------------------------

This proposal does not change the rollout boundary. The
queue control mechanism itself remains not live in
production. The alert evaluates real customer traffic on
the live path (OTel/Prometheus), but it does not assume
that any queue-side throttle, shed, or backpressure
control is currently acting on that traffic.

  - The fact that the symptom alert pages on refusal rate

    response, not a control loop.
  - If queue control is later promoted to live in
    production (separate decision, separate rollout), the
    alerts will need to be re-evaluated. Until then, the
    boundary holds and the alert text should say so. Add

If $120 for the super feels off for your building's norms (some buildings quietly suggest amounts on the form itself — worth glancing at), a close alternative is $110 / $70 / $60, which lifts the maintenance share because of the in-unit visits but keeps the super clearly ahead.

Marriage on December 31 = married all year (federal rule)

Because you and Devika were married on December 31, 2025, the IRS treats you as married for the entire 2025 tax year. That means your federal choices are limited to two:

  - Married Filing Jointly (MFJ) - one return, both signatures
  - Married Filing Separately (MFS) - two returns, each spouse files their own

Single and Head of Household are not available to you. New York follows your federal filing status for the state return, with the same two options.

If you choose MFJ, both spouses are jointly and severally liable for the full tax on the joint return - meaning each of you is responsible for the whole amount, including anything attributable to the other spouse's income. That's the one big practical difference from filing as two single people.

Plain-language comparison of MFJ vs MFS for your situation

The dimensions that actually move the needle for a two-W-2 couple like yours, in roughly the order I'd look at them:

  1. Standard deduction. 2025 federal standard deduction is $30,000 for MFJ vs $15,000 each for MFS. If you don't itemize, MFJ almost always wins on this line alone.

  2. Tax brackets. MFJ brackets are wider than the single brackets that MFS uses. Two earners with similar incomes typically pay noticeably less combined under MFJ.

  3. Credits and phase-outs. Under MFS, several things are reduced, eliminated, or have worse phase-outs: the EITC (zeroed out), student loan interest deduction (zeroed out), education credits, Roth IRA contribution limit (drops to a much lower number when MFS), and many other AGI-based thresholds.

  4. Capital losses. MFS cuts the net capital loss you can deduct against ordinary income in half ($1,500 vs $3,000). Probably not relevant to you this year, but worth noting.

  5. HSA contributions. If either or both of you contributed to an HSA in 2025 (very likely given Sphere's HDHP), MFJ lets you share the family contribution limit however you agree. MFS requires a more formal allocation between the two returns. This is paperwork, not a reason to choose one over the other.

  6. Itemized deductions. Some itemized deductions (medical in particular, which has a 7.5% of AGI floor) can sometimes favor MFS when one spouse has large medical expenses and the other has none - because MFS lets each spouse's medical expenses clear the floor against that spouse's lower AGI. Unlikely to matter for you unless one of you had an unusual medical year.

  7. State tax. New York's MFJ benefit is smaller than the federal benefit, but MFJ is still usually better for NY as well. NY's MFS is rarely a win.

The short version: for a two-W-2 professional household with no name change, no exotic deductions, and no specific reason to keep liabilities separate, MFJ is the standard answer and almost always produces the lowest combined tax. MFS is normally only reconsidered when there's a specific trigger (large one-spouse medical expenses, income-driven student loan repayment where joint AGI hurts, or a desire to keep one spouse's tax liability isolated from the other).

One New York / NYC note

You live in Brooklyn (South Slope), which means you're a NYC resident. In addition to the federal 1040 and the NY IT-201, you'll likely need to file an NYC IT-201 or have NYC tax computed inside the state return. Tax software handles all three; just make sure both NY state and NYC boxes are checked when you start. NYC has its own school tax credit and NYC-specific adjustments.

Household document checklist

Before you open the software, gather these for both of you:

  - W-2 from Sphere (Alex)
  - W-2 from the hospital (Devika)
  - Form 1095-C or 1095-B from each employer - shows the months each of you had employer health coverage, needed for the shared responsibility provision and any HSA-related questions
  - 2025 HSA contribution totals - check W-2 Box 12 code W (employer + employee combined for the year) and Form 5498-SA from your HSA custodian (total contributions including any you made directly). If you're both on a family HDHP, decide how to allocate the family limit between your two MFJ lines
  - All 1099s - 1099-INT (bank interest), 1099-DIV (brokerage dividends), 1099-B (any sales), 1099-R (retirement distributions if any). Pull these from each bank/brokerage portal; they don't always come by mail
  - 1098 - mortgage interest statement, if you have one (you rent, so probably N/A, but include if either of you owns property)
  - 1098-E - student loan interest, if applicable
  - Charitable contributions - any written acknowledgments for $250+ donations, plus a total of smaller ones
  - Medical expenses - receipts for anything you might itemize (only worth it if total exceeds the 7.5% of AGI floor, so usually only relevant if there was an unusual year)
  - Daycare / dependent-care receipts - only if you have a qualifying dependent; probably N/A for 2025
  - Estimated tax payments - federal and NY, if either of you paid any during 2025
  - Last year's returns - 2024 returns for both of you, in case any carryover items need to flow forward (capital loss carryovers, charitable carryovers, etc.)
  - Bank account and routing numbers for direct deposit of the refund (or for paying any balance due)
  - Marriage certificate - you have it per the City Clerk. Software won't ask for it, but keep it handy if anything is questioned
  - Social Security numbers - for both of you, plus any dependent you're claiming

A couple of practical sequencing notes

  - Decide on filing status together before either of you starts a return. Once you pick MFJ, both W-2s go on one return; if you accidentally start two MFS returns in the software, you have to start over.
  - If you do choose MFJ, decide who appears as the primary taxpayer on the return - usually the one with the larger income, but it's cosmetic. The software usually defaults to this.
  - Both signatures on a paper return, or both e-file authorizations if you e-file. One spouse can't sign for the other without a power of attorney.

Two things drive most of the gap between a joint and a separate-filer projection for a married couple: the tax brackets, and the long list of deductions and credits that change with status.

1. Brackets and rates. Married Filing Jointly uses wider income brackets than two Married Filing Separately returns — at the same total household income, the marginal rate under MFS kicks in sooner. That alone can move a projection by hundreds to thousands of dollars depending on the income level. Long-term capital gains and qualified dividends are also tiered by income, and the 0% / 15% / 20% thresholds are roughly half as wide under MFS, so a chunk of LTCG that would be tax-free jointly can become taxable separately.

2. Deductions and credits that disappear or shrink under MFS. The list is long and many of these are easy for a projection tool to under-weight:

  - Standard deduction is half per MFS return vs. the full joint amount ($15,000 each vs. $30,000 for 2025).
  - If one spouse itemizes, the other must itemize too — you can't mix standard with itemized.
  - IRA deduction and Roth IRA contribution phase-outs are tighter under MFS, and if spouses lived together all year the Roth contribution phase-out is effectively $0.
  - Student loan interest deduction is not allowed at all under MFS.
  - American Opportunity and Lifetime Learning credits are not allowed under MFS.
  - Child and Dependent Care Credit, Saver's Credit, Adoption Credit, and the Coverdell ESA contribution are not allowed under MFS.
  - Social Security benefits are computed under a separate worksheet that often taxes more of the benefit under MFS.
  - Capital loss limit drops from $3,000 to $1,500.
  - The $25,000 rental real estate passive-loss allowance is generally not available unless spouses lived apart the whole year.
  - Premium Tax Credit for ACA Marketplace coverage is generally not available under MFS unless a narrow exception (e.g., domestic abuse, spouse lived apart) applies.
  - SALT cap: $10,000 combined under MFJ; each MFS spouse effectively has $5,000.

So a projection where joint and separate "look close" is often close because these lost credits and tighter phase-outs are at least partially baked in. If the projection tool isn't fully modeling all of them, the apparent gap can understate the true cost of MFS.

How meaningful the comparison is while the 1098 is missing

Form 1098 reports mortgage interest (and any mortgage insurance premiums) you paid in 2025. If it's not in the input yet, the projection is working from an incomplete itemized-deduction picture. Whether that matters depends on whether you'd itemize at all.

  - If your itemized total without mortgage interest already exceeds the standard deduction by a comfortable margin — state and local income tax capped at $10,000, charitable, medical above 7.5% of AGI, plus other itemized items — then the missing 1098 is a small refinement, not a swing factor. The joint vs. separate comparison is reasonably meaningful.

  - If mortgage interest is the line that pushes you from standard to itemized, the projection is unreliable until the 1098 is in. A couple needs more than $30,000 of itemized deductions for MFJ to benefit; under MFS each spouse needs more than $15,000 individually. The 1098 number can flip which side of that line you land on, and the answer changes from there.

There's also a small subtlety: under MFS, each spouse can claim only the mortgage interest they actually paid (or were allocated under your state's property rules). The 1098 itself won't tell you who paid what — that comes from your own records.

Entries to verify before picking a status or filing

For the itemized side:
  - 1098 mortgage interest for 2025, plus any 1098 from a second property or HELOC (HELOC interest deductibility has its own rules the 1098 doesn't spell out)
  - PMI / MIP amounts if applicable — also on the 1098
  - Property taxes actually paid in 2025 (cash basis — billed-but-not-paid doesn't count)
  - State and local income tax (or sales tax if you elect) paid in 2025, with the $10,000 SALT cap in mind
  - Charitable contributions, with written acknowledgment for any single gift of $250 or more
  - Medical and dental expenses paid (not reimbursed), only the portion above 7.5% of AGI

For the income side:
  - All W-2s for both of you
  - 1099s: NEC, MISC, INT, DIV, B, R, SSA-1099 if any
  - Cost basis for any sales — 1099-B defaults are usually right but sometimes disagree with your records
  - HSA contributions (payroll + direct), and confirmation of the annual limit you each qualified for
  - 401(k) and IRA contributions for 2025
  - Estimated tax payments (federal and state) made during the year

For status-specific items a projection may under-model:
  - If either of you has student loans, an income-driven repayment plan is calculated on the joint-return AGI for most plans regardless of who is the borrower — so an apparent tax savings from MFS doesn't automatically flow through to a lower loan payment. Worth checking before deciding on MFS for that reason.
  - If either of you had Marketplace coverage (Form 1095-A), confirm whether an MFS exception to the Premium Tax Credit lockout applies.
  - Confirm the projection is using live 2025 IRA deduction / Roth phase-outs against your actual MAGI, not stale defaults.

For a sanity check:
  - Your 2024 federal and state returns (AGI, dependents, status, total tax) — useful for anchoring the 2025 numbers and for e-file identity verification.

In short: the joint-vs-separate gap is usually meaningful, but it leans heavily on which credits and phase-outs the projection actually models, and the missing 1098 makes the itemized side provisional. Until the items above are confirmed, treat the numbers as a working draft rather than a basis for filing — and you can decide on the status once they're in.

============================================================
HOW TO ENTER THE ITEM ONCE IN THE JOINT DRAFT
============================================================

Pick exactly one home. The standard home for an item that's a single economic event (one account balance, one transaction, one policy) is the column or schedule where the underlying asset or event lives — not where its tax effect first shows up.

For a typical item that lives on a form/schedule, the rule of thumb:
  - If the item produces a number reported on Form 1040 itself (wages on line 1a, interest on line 2b, dividends on line 3a/3b, capital gains on line 7), it lives on the joint Form 1040 column.
  - If the item produces a number reported on a schedule first (Schedule B interest, Schedule D capital gains, Schedule 1 above-the-line, Schedule A itemized deductions, Schedule B/D/NR etc.), it lives on that schedule's joint column. The joint Form 1040 then pulls the rolled-up total.
  - If the item is itself a schedule or statement (like a crypto transaction-by-transaction worksheet, a rental P&L, or a stock-sale statement), the worksheet/statement is shared — only one copy exists and both spouses' names appear on it. It feeds a single joint schedule.

Don't add a "spouse A" / "spouse B" sub-column. Joint = one economic unit. The only split that ever appears inside a joint return is the rare community-property allocation on Schedule B/D for specific income items, and only if you actually live in a community-property state.

============================================================
HOW TO HANDLE IT ACROSS SEPARATE DRAFTS WITHOUT DOUBLE COUNTING
============================================================

The mechanics depend on whose name owns the item:

1. Owned by one spouse only (account titled in that spouse's name, no joint account designation):
   - In the owner's MFS draft: enter the full amount on the relevant schedule/line.
   - In the non-owner's MFS draft: enter zero / leave blank. Do not enter half. MFS is not joint — each spouse reports only their own items.
   - In the joint draft: enter the full amount once, in the joint column/schedule.

2. Jointly owned account (both names on the account):
   - In each MFS draft: each spouse reports their share according to how the account is actually held. For most states that's 50/50 by default unless you have a written agreement stating otherwise; community-property states have specific allocation rules for certain income.
   - In the joint draft: enter the full amount once.

3. Item that produces a deduction/credit rather than income (e.g., HSA contribution, IRA deduction, charitable contribution from a joint account):
   - Joint draft: enter once on the joint schedule; allocation happens by the form's own rules (e.g., HSA contribution limit on joint is the family limit, not 2x single).
   - Each MFS draft: the item belongs to the spouse who has the legal obligation / whose name is on the account that paid it, or 50/50 if paid from a truly joint account.

The anti-double-counting rule in one line: an item goes where the underlying asset or payment lives, fully, once per return — and never in two different returns when comparing MFJ vs MFS.

============================================================
ACCOUNT-OWNERSHIP / NOMINEE DETAILS TO VERIFY BEFORE TRUSTING THE COMPARISON
============================================================

Before the comparison numbers mean anything, confirm these on every account and item that appears in either draft:

a. Account ownership & titling right now — names on the account, joint vs sole designation, TOD/POD beneficiary designations, and the exact legal registration (individual, joint tenants with right of survivorship, tenants in common, community property, trust, custodial UTMA/UGMA, IRA beneficiary, etc.). Pull a current statement or broker confirmation; don't rely on memory of how it was opened.

b. For jointly held accounts — written agreements if any state that splits ownership other than 50/50, and the residency state at the time the income accrued (community-property states only: AZ, CA, LA, NM, TX, WA, plus WI for specific items; marital property election in some).

c. Nominee / 1099-B/DIV/INT reporting — confirm whether the payor is reporting the income under one spouse's TIN or both, and whether a Form 1099 came in the name of a nominee, custodian, or trust rather than the beneficial owner. The beneficial owner — not the nominee — is who reports it. If a 1099 is in one spouse's name but the account is really jointly held, you adjust the reporting to the joint return; if MFS, you allocate correctly to the beneficial owner.

d. Cost basis & holding period for any sale — confirm basis method (FIFO default vs specified), wash sale tracking, and that both spouses' portions of a joint-account sale use the same basis records.

e. Items that straddle ownership — HSA through Devika's payroll vs Alex's, retirement contributions, charitable contributions paid from a joint checking, medical expenses paid from an HSA, dependent-care FSA. Confirm who funded it and whose limit it counts against.

f. Items with explicit per-spouse limits — IRA deduction limits, Roth IRA contribution limits, earned-income-required items, education credits, savers credit. These do NOT double on joint; they DO allocate or split under MFS by IRS rules.

g. State of residence on Dec 31 and any change during the year — affects MFS allocation rules and state-level comparison.

============================================================
NO-DOUBLE-COUNTING CHECKLIST (SHORT)
============================================================

- [ ] Each income item: identified one owner-or-joint designation; entered once in joint; entered only on owner's MFS (or split per the account's actual ownership in each MFS).
- [ ] Each deduction/credit item: entered once in joint on the joint schedule; entered only on the MFS of the spouse with the legal payment obligation or 50/50 from a true joint account.

- [ ] Per-spouse limit items (IRA, Roth, education, savers) allocated by IRS rules, not duplicated.

What the bank's refusal actually means

The Form 1099-INT reporting is just information — it tells the IRS who got a form, not who actually owns the income. The bank confirmed it won't make that call and won't fix the form. So the allocation is now unambiguously between you two. For spouses, that's a normal state of affairs, not an unusual one.

Two paths, very different outcomes

1. Married Filing Jointly
The cleanest path on this specific question. The joint return covers both of you, so the $364.27 just lands once on Schedule B (which it wouldn't trigger anyway — Schedule B is required only above $1,500 of taxable interest). On a joint return, the two of you can split the interest however you both consent to — 50/50, all to you, anything — and the IRS doesn't second-guess it because both taxpayers signed. No nominee Form 1099-MISC flow is triggered at all, since both parties are on the same return.

2. Married Filing Separately
This is where the nominee issue lives but it's tractable. Per Pub 550, a TIN-recipient whose 1099-INT includes amounts belonging to another person is a "nominee recipient." Formally the nominee issues Form 1099-MISC (Box 3, "Other income") to the actual owner if the amount is $600 or more — yours is $364.27, so no 1099-MISC is required to be issued. The substantive rule still applies though: each MFS return must report the portion the filer actually owns. If you and Devika agree the underlying account is jointly yours, then on MFS returns you'd report your share and she'd report hers (Schedule B not triggered for either at $182 each or for you at $364 either way).

  MFS, all to you:        $2,164 federal refund + $369 NY refund
  MFS, 50/50:             $2,162 federal refund + $369 NY refund

That gap is the standard-deduction doubling ($30,000 MFJ vs $15,000 single) plus wider MFJ brackets, and it's a real swing.

When MFS would still make sense

Absent one of these, MFJ is the obvious move:

  - Income-driven student loan repayment (AGI-driven monthly payment)
  - A means-tested benefit or credit tied to MAGI/AGI thresholds that
    flips adversely when combined
  - Separate-liability protection you actually need for one spouse's
    tax exposure
  - A specific planning reason your preparer has already identified

If none of those apply, the $1,125 swing is what the decision comes down to, and it points to MFJ.

Worth doing now regardless of how you file

  1. That the two sides of the comparison are the things you actually care about (it can pass against the wrong inputs and still be vacuously true).
  2. That the enumeration of "expected generated outputs" is complete — drift compares what was supplied; it does not enumerate what should have been supplied.
  3. That the release candidate is bound to a specific canonical-package version — drift checks bytes, not semantic identity or provenance.
  4. That a missing expected artifact is a hard failure — most drift checks are no-op on absence rather than rejecting.
  5. That the handoff is implementation-ready — implementation-ready is a separate gate (completeness, provenance, contract coverage), not a property drift can certify.

Two routes, complementary demands

  V5 compression: sustained body tension + heel-hook control = whole-body isometric endurance with hip and ankle engagement. Failure mode is forearms blowing out before the heel-hook transition if grip outpaces tension. Forearm cost is HIGH because you rarely get to relax the grip.

  V6 vertical/small edges: balance + grip economy + foot precision = a quieter route in absolute terms but technically punishing. Failure mode is feet slip -> overgrip -> pop. Forearm cost is LOWER per move but spikes on errors.

Why they pair well: V5 teaches you to climb on tension (less grip); V6 teaches you to climb on feet (less grip). Working both retires the "hold tighter" default. The V5 heel-hook transition is the harder motor pattern to acquire; the V6 foot sequence is the easier one to acquire but at a higher grade. Expect V5 to be the longer project; expect V6 to be more sendable in 4 sessions IF footwork clicks.

Rehab framework (still in effect per Ren): longer warmup than feels necessary, gradual load, stop if forearm pain >2/10, symptoms >=30 min, or any next-day symptoms. No active restriction right now, so the plan leans forward — but the stop rules are not optional.


Four-session structure
(built for 2x/week. If you're running 4x/week, drop attempt counts by ~30% and keep total time at or below the cap.)

SESSION 1 — Recon + movement vocabulary (60 min cap)
  Warmup (25-30 min): easy traverse, wrist/finger/shoulder mobility, 2 V0-V1 full-body climbs, 1 V2-V3 at fluid limit, then 2 priming climbs — one compression-feel problem and one footwork-feel slab.
  Drills (15 min):
    - Heel-hook-toe-hook transitions on a juggy V1-V2 (5 reps each side, focus on hip rotation under load)
    - Silent-feet vertical climbing on V0-V1 (no readjustments, no scraping)
  Attempts (10-15 min): 1-2 easy burns on each route, just the opening 3-4 moves. Stop after you have a beta sketch, not after you're pumped.
  Stop when: 60 min elapsed, OR first clear forearm "thickness" or pump signal, OR movement starts looking rushed.

SESSION 2 — V5 focus, V6 footwork primer (75 min cap)
  Warmup (25-30 min, same shape as S1 plus a compression-feel primer).
  V5 work (30 min): 3-5 attempts with the heel-hook transition as the explicit goal each burn. Between burns: heel-hook mechanics drill on easier terrain (3-5 reps), then 7-10 min rest before the next burn.
  V6 preview (10 min): 1-2 attempts, opening moves only. End on the route while forearms are still quiet.
  Stop when: 4 V5 attempts OR 75 min OR the heel-hook starts slipping due to fatigue (not skill).

SESSION 3 — V6 focus, V5 polish (75 min cap)
  Warmup (25-30 min, with footwork-feel primer).
  V6 work (30 min): 3-5 attempts focused on getting through the small-edge crux with feet-first movement. Between burns: silent-feet drill on moderate terrain, then 7-10 min rest.
  V5 polish (10 min): 1 burn on V5, only the heel-hook transition. End with that move feeling repeatable.
  Stop when: 4 V6 attempts OR 75 min OR foot placement starts requiring readjustment.

SESSION 4 — Send push + consolidation (90 min cap)
  Warmup (30 min, full, with both compression-feel and footwork-feel primers).
  Order matters: start on the route with fresher forearms. If V5 is closer to sending, lead with V5; if V6 is closer, lead with V6. 3-4 quality burns on the lead route, 7-10 min between. If the lead route sends, switch to the other for 1-2 burns; if not, switch to movement drills on the weak link (heel-hook for V5, silent-feet for V6) and finish with one final attempt.
  Stop when: send on one OR clear fatigue signal on the lead route OR 90 min.


Spacing rules across all sessions
  Hard burns: 7-10 min passive rest, shake out fully
  Movement drills between burns: keep the system warm without taxing forearms
  Hydration and a small snack between sessions if back-to-back days


Stopping signal hierarchy
(use the first one that fires — don't negotiate with yourself past it)
  1. Forearm pain >2/10 or symptoms >=30 min -> stop, contact Ren
  2. Movement quality degrades (form breaks before strength fails) -> stop, you've learned the day's lesson
  3. Three consecutive "worse than the last" burns -> stop, motor learning is saturated
  4. Time cap reached -> stop


If next-morning forearm symptoms appear, drop the next session to drills-only on easier terrain or rest entirely. The 4-session arc is a suggestion; the rehab signals are not. Sending one of the two — or neither, with both movement patterns noticeably cleaner — both count as a successful project.

Two separate decisions, two different lock-up behaviors.

1) MEDICAL PLAN (HDHP vs PPO) — locks at the deadline

   - You elect one plan during OE. After 10/23 17:00 ET the election is generally fixed for the full plan year; mid-year switches require a qualifying life event (marriage, new dependent, loss of other coverage, etc.), not a routine change of mind.
   - This single choice sets: biweekly premium deduction, deductible, coinsurance rate, out-of-pocket max, network/access rules, and — importantly — whether you are HSA-eligible at all. A standard PPO does not open HSA eligibility; only HDHP does.
   - Because you have to project the whole year in one shot, this decision is about expected utilization and risk tolerance, not a per-paycheck tuning knob.

2) HSA PAYROLL CONTRIBUTION — prospectively adjustable

   - The per-paycheck employee HSA contribution (separate from the $900 employer contribution paid as $225 × 4 quarterly) is a number you enter on the OE form, but you can raise or lower it mid-plan-year through HR/payroll without a qualifying event, as long as you stay under the IRS annual ceiling.
   - The OE entry is just a starting point. You can submit $0/period and increase later, or set a high number and dial it back. Mid-year adjustments are normal and expected, not exceptions.
   - The $900 employer contribution is automatic once you elect HDHP and open the HSA; it does not depend on what you elect for your own per-paycheck amount.

What still has to be decided before 10/23 17:00 ET:

   (a) HDHP or PPO. This is the only decision that cannot be revisited casually after the lock.

   (b) An initial HSA per-paycheck employee contribution if you go HDHP. This number is a placeholder and can be changed prospectively during the plan year — including up to the IRS annual cap — without waiting for the next OE. If you go PPO, this row is N/A (no HSA account to contribute to).

What does NOT have to be decided by 10/23:

   - The final HSA annual total. The only ceiling is the IRS annual limit, and you can approach it incrementally across 26 paychecks.

So the practical distinction is: the medical-plan choice is a one-shot annual commitment with utilization uncertainty, while the HSA contribution is a per-paycheck dial you can turn in either direction all year. Only (a) is truly deadline-sensitive; (b) only needs a defensible starting number.

SESSIONS 3 & 4 — REVISED ARC
You have two sessions left. Banked: sessions 1 (Oct 10) and 2 (Oct 21, tonight). Below: cadence, per-line attempt caps, drills, rest spacing, and observable stopping points. Different bottlenecks, different structures — that's the whole point.

CADENCE
~7 days between sessions (target Oct 28 and Nov 4). V5 compression load and V6 skin wear both want ≥5 days to clear. A week between sessions preserves quality on both lines at once; anything tighter risks compounding one without recovering the other. If a session slips a few days, take the slip rather than compress.

WARMUP (both sessions)
Ren's longer warmup — 25-30 min total: easy traverse (10 min), wrist/shoulder mobility (5 min), progressive moves ramping to project grade (10-15 min). No project attempts until the warmup is fully complete. This is non-negotiable per the rehab protocol.

V5 COMPRESSION LINE — quality is the bottleneck
The new hip position is the breakthrough. The job is to bank the pattern under fatigue-light conditions before fatigue overwrites it.

Drills (BEFORE counting hard attempts):
  - 8-10 min on an easier V3-V4 compression problem rehearsing the hip shift + heel-hook sequence. Goal: lock the motor pattern at low load.
  - 2-3 "rehearsal runs" on the project — link only the setup into the heel-hook transition, then lower off. These are skill reps, not attempts.
  - Drills do NOT count against the hard attempt cap.

Attempt caps:
  - Session 3: 3 quality attempts
  - Session 4: 4 quality attempts (pattern is grooved; this is the send push)

Rest spacing:
  - 4-5 min between hard attempts. Compression drains the forearms faster than vertical — these rests run long for a reason.
  - Stand up, shake out, do 2-3 easy moves between sets.

Stopping points (any one triggers stop on this line):
  - Hip drifts out of position on a 2nd consecutive attempt
  - Heel-hook placement requires a re-adjustment (should land clean on first try)
  - Forearm pump arrives before the transition
  - Pain >2/10 — Ren protocol, contact Ren

Drills (BEFORE counting hard attempts):
  - 10 min on vertical terrain at sub-project grade doing silent-feet drills — place foot, no scraping, no readjustment

  - 2-3 "opening sequence from hang" reps on the project — climb only the linked sequence you already have, starting from a hang at the first hold. Banks precision reps without spending skin on the upper (unfinished) holds.

Rest spacing:
  - 3 min between attempts

Stopping points (any one triggers stop on this line):
  - Visible hot-spot, flapper forming, or any skin tearing
  - Two attempts in a row fail at the same precision crux (diminishing returns — the pattern needs a reset, not more reps)

ATTRIBUTION PROBLEM

The 64-pending-batch cap is a pre-acceptance backpressure control. It refuses new batches before Mosaic accepts the work, returns a retryable response, and never starts processing. By construction:

  - no compute is consumed
  - no result is produced
  - no accepted-work record exists
  - no cost is incurred
  - no accepted-work SLA is touched

The current wording frames the refusal as tenant misuse, excess cost, or an accepted-work failure. Each claim is wrong on the mechanism:

  1. Misuse — the tenant did nothing wrong. They hit a capacity signal that exists to protect Mosaic (the 2,048 global / 64 per-tenant cap was deployed precisely so this event isn't a tenant-quality event). Refusal is the system's normal response, not a tenant defect.
  2. Excess cost — there is nothing to attribute because nothing was accepted. Tagging cost on a refused request invents spend that didn't happen and creates billing / trust disputes when tenants see charges for work Mosaic didn't run.
  3. Accepted-work failure — the work was not accepted. There is no failure to assign. The control fires at the door, not after entry.

Consequences of misattribution: it pollutes the tenant's record with a fault flag tied to a system-side capacity event; it conflates a capacity-protection signal with a tenant-quality signal (different control planes, should not share a label); and it leaks the 64 cap and cost framing into customer-facing surfaces, exposing internal capacity tuning that the customer has no need to see.

  "Retryable pre-acceptance refusal: per-tenant pending-batch cap (64) reached.

  - Names the control (pre-acceptance refusal) so it reads as capacity, not fault.
  - Names the cap (64) for operator triage — that's the number ops needs to act on.
  - States the outcome (no work accepted) so downstream systems do not infer an accepted-work failure or attribute cost.

- Two-person handoff at the door: one of you stays in Kibo's room, the other answers. If both of you need to be at the door, gate the hallway AND shut the room door so he can't stage in the hall.

LEASH / GATE
- Use a closed door as the primary barrier. A baby gate in the hallway is a useful second layer, not a substitute.
- Skip the harness/leash unless Kibo is already harness-trained for sustained wear. For 3 hours of intermittent openings, a closed door is more reliable and less stressful.
- If he cries at the door: ignore for short bursts, rotate in for comfort, do not open the front door while he's loose in the hall.

CANDY & WRAPPER STORAGE
- Have ONE sealed plastic bin or large ziplock at the door for incoming candy. No open bowls.
- After each group, sort immediately:
  - Chocolate → sealed bin, then move the bin into a closed cabinet or high shelf out of sight. Baking chocolate and dark chocolate are the most concerning.
  - Sugar-free candy (anything with xylitol / "sugar alcohol" on the label) → same sealed bin, same closed storage. Even small amounts can drop blood sugar in cats, and many also cause GI upset.
  - Wrappers → straight into a small trash bag, tied off, into a closed trash can. Foil and plastic wrappers cause linear-obstruction risk if chewed.
- Empty the candy bin into the cabinet at the end of the night — do not leave a bag of "leftovers to sort tomorrow" by the door.
- Drop the trash down the chute / take it out before bed.

DOOR PROTOCOL
- Door opens → one person physically blocks the gap with their body, other hands candy out. No open-door conversations in the hallway.
- Costume bags, glow sticks, props, and any tote with handles go straight into the sealed bin or a high hook — not on the floor or a low chair.

FOOD
- 2.25 cups total for the day, same as a normal day. Split on your usual schedule. Confined cats sometimes eat out of boredom; if he finishes early, do not refill — use the puzzle feeder with a portion of his ration instead.

IF YOU SUSPECT AN INGESTION
1. Move Kibo away from the source. Secure any remaining candy and wrappers so you can account for what's missing.
2. Note: what (chocolate, gum, sugar-free candy, wrapper, raisin, macadamia, etc.), approximate amount, time window, and his current behavior. Keep the wrapper/packaging.
3. Call your vet's emergency line (have the number saved in your phone tonight). If you can't reach them, the ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center is 24/7 at 888-426-4435 (a consultation fee may apply; they will tell you whether an ER visit is needed).
4. Do NOT induce vomiting unless a vet specifically tells you to. Cats aspirate easily and some substances cause more damage coming back up.
5. Watch for the next 24–48 hours: vomiting, diarrhea, drooling, lethargy, restlessness, tremors, stumbling, increased thirst/urination, pale gums, or seizures. Any of these → ER immediately.
6. If he loses consciousness, seizes, or collapses: go straight to the nearest emergency vet; do not wait for a callback.

QUICK TONIGHT PREP
- Pick the room and put his bed / litter / water in place now so it's not a scramble at 5 PM.
- Charge phones, locate the sealed bin, and put your vet's emergency number + ASPCA APCC in both your phones.
- Decide who's on Kibo duty and rotate so neither of you is stuck for the full 3 hours.

Kibo-walk-friendly soba bowls. Walk at 6:30, you eat ~7:15, Devika reheats at home ~8:00.

The trick to no-gummy leftovers: cold-rinse the noodles, dress at the plate, never ahead of time. Sauce stays separate.

QUANTITIES (2 generous portions):
- 8 oz dry soba (one standard pack)
- 1 block firm tofu (~14 oz), pressed 10 min
- 1 medium head broccoli (~4 cups florets)
- 3 scallions, whites and greens split
- 3 garlic cloves
- Sauce: 3 tbsp soy + 1 tbsp rice vinegar + 1 tsp sesame oil + 1 heaping tsp chili crisp, to taste
- Neutral oil for the pan

SEQUENCE

  5:30  Press tofu between paper towels, weighted.
  5:40  Sauce in a jar, shake to combine. Slice scallions, mince garlic,
        cut broccoli. Pot of water on to boil.
  6:00  Boil soba 4 min. Drain, RINSE COLD until cool, shake, toss with
        1 tsp sesame oil. Set aside in a container. Do NOT add sauce.
  6:05  Same pan, oil, fry tofu cubes (1/2 in) undisturbed ~3-4 min per
        side until golden. Remove.
  6:15  Same pan: garlic + scallion whites 30 sec, add broccoli + 2 tbsp
        water, cover 2 min until crisp-tender. Combine with tofu.
  6:20  Split noodles and tofu-broccoli between two containers. Sauce
        jar in the fridge.
  6:30  Walk Kibo.
  7:15  Your bowl: splash 1 tbsp water on noodles, microwave 60 sec OR
        hot-pan toss 1 min. Add half the sauce, scallion greens. Eat.
  8:00  Devika's bowl: same reheat, rest of sauce, scallion greens.
        2 min, she can do it herself when she walks in.

WHY IT WORKS
- Cold rinse strips surface starch so noodles don't clump.
- Sesame-oil coat keeps them from sticking together in the fridge.
- Sauce held separately means noodles don't soak and swell.
- Reheat with a splash of water brings back the fresh-cooked bounce.

Quick answer, since you're on the clock (oven by 2:15):

PRIMARY FIX — ADD 1/2 CUP MORE BREADCRUMBS

  Your ratio is dry-light for that volume of wet ingredients. Two eggs and 1 cup
  of crumbs is roughly enough binder for ~2.5 cups of dense material; you've got
  closer to 3.5-4 cups once the mushrooms and lentils are factored in, plus
  cremini weep moisture during baking which is what will slump the loaf in the
  oven even if it seems okay raw. Bumping crumbs to 1.5 cups total absorbs that
  without changing flavor.

  Alternatives if you've run out of breadcrumbs:
    - 1/4 cup all-purpose or oat flour (works, slightly denser crumb)
    - 1 extra beaten egg (only if you want the loaf richer; egg alone won't
      fix the moisture-weep issue)

  Don't reach for flour + egg together — that's over-binding and the loaf goes
  dense and gummy.

TEXTURE TEST BEFORE SHAPING

  Scoop a heaping tablespoon of mixture into your palm. Press into a patty about
  2 inches across. Hold your hand flat for 10 seconds, then tilt it 45 degrees.

    - Holds shape, no slump, no crack = ready to shape and bake.
    - Slumps at the edges = add another 1/4 cup breadcrumbs, retest.
    - Cracks dry on the sides = over-corrected; fold in 1 tablespoon milk or
      water and retest.

  Aim for slightly firmer-than-borderline raw. The loaf firms up only modestly
  in the oven; if it's marginal in your hand, it will slump at the 35-40 min
  mark.

BAKING TIME — NO MEANINGFUL CHANGE

  350°F for 45-55 minutes in a parchment-lined loaf pan, until an instant-read
  thermometer in the center reads 160°F+ and the top springs back when pressed.
  Tent loosely with foil at the 30-minute mark if the top is browning faster
  than the center is setting. Rest 10 minutes in the pan before unmolding and
  slicing — that's when the loaf finally locks up.

SEQUENCE FOR THE NEXT 2 HOURS

  12:10  add the 1/2 cup crumbs, mix, run the patty test, adjust
  12:20  shape into pan, settle on counter for 5 min (push out air pockets)
  12:25  into 350°F oven
  ~1:10  check internal temp, tent if needed
  ~1:20  pull at 160°F+, rest 10 min
  ~1:35  unmold onto rack; cover loosely
  by 2:15  done and held; re-warm at 325°F for 8-10 min right before plating at 5

  That buffer also absorbs any Kibo-outing disruption without touching the
  rest of the menu.
