Given Thursday was dinner (Nov 26), today is Friday Nov 27, and you want to eat through Sunday Nov 29, here is what to do.

FREEZE NOW
- Apple pie, all 3 slices. Wrap each slice in plastic wrap, then foil or a freezer bag. Pie is one of the best freezer candidates and is noticeably better eaten from frozen than from day 3-4 in the fridge. Keeps 2-3 months.
- Half the mushroom-lentil loaf, unless you are sure you will eat every slice by Sunday. Lentil loaf freezes well. Slice it now, slide parchment or wax paper between slices, wrap the stack tightly in plastic then foil, freeze. Press plastic wrap directly onto the cut face of whatever you leave in the fridge so it does not dry out.

REFRIGERATE, EAT BY SUNDAY EVE (Monday at the very latest)
- 2 cups mashed potatoes. Do not freeze them. Dairy-heavy mash turns watery and grainy on thaw and never quite recovers. Keep in a sealed container, finish by Sunday.
- 1 cup roasted green beans. Do not freeze them. They go limp and soggy on thaw. Keep in a sealed container, finish by Sunday. One cup is small, easy to clear.
- The refrigerated half of the loaf (if you did not freeze it all).

Anything still in the fridge Tuesday morning should be tossed. Three to four days is the safe window for cooked leftovers, so you are right at the edge by Sunday night.

REHEATING

Mushroom-lentil loaf - oven is the only method that holds up
- 325 F oven. Slice about 1/2 inch thick, lay in a small baking dish.
- Spoon a little vegetable broth or water over each slice and add a small pat of butter on top.
- Cover tightly with foil.
- Heat 15-20 minutes until warmed through (165 F if you check).
- From frozen, same setup, foil-covered, 35-45 minutes. Thaw overnight in the fridge first if you can - better result.

Mashed potatoes - low and gentle, never high direct heat
- Best: stovetop. Put them in a saucepan with a small splash of milk and a knob of butter, low heat, stir gently until warmed through, about 5-7 minutes. High heat scorches the dairy and makes them gluey.
- Oven: 350 F, spread in a baking dish, drizzle 2-3 tablespoons of milk or cream across the top, cover with foil, 20-25 minutes, stir once halfway.
- Microwave only if you must: 50 percent power, covered, stir every minute, 3-5 minutes. Splash of milk before you start.

Roasted green beans - just warm, do not cook further
- Skillet: a little olive oil, medium heat, 2-3 minutes, toss. Best texture by far.
- Oven: 375 F, 5-7 minutes on a sheet pan.
- Microwave: covered, 60-90 seconds.

Apple pie from frozen - do not thaw first or the bottom gets soggy
- Place slices on a baking sheet (catches drips), 350 F oven, 25-35 minutes from frozen until heated through and the crust has re-crisped.
- For one slice fast: 350 F toaster oven, 8-12 minutes from frozen.

Two small things that pay off: press plastic wrap directly onto the cut face of anything you are storing, and let the loaf and potatoes come out of the fridge 15-20 minutes before reheating so they heat evenly instead of staying cold in the middle.

In the meantime, the safe-in-the-meantime part I can answer generically — the same trick works on almost any zippered compartment:

Short-term securing (no zipper damage)
1. Stop forcing it. If the slider is off the track, forcing it usually shaves more teeth off the coil and turns a $5 slider fix into a full zip replacement.
2. Keep it closed with a small removable cable tie, twist tie, or a binder clip through the two pull holes. These grip the *pull*, not the teeth, so they don't deform the coil. Anything softer than the teeth (rubber band, thin paracord) works too — loop through the pulls and snug it.
3. For jackets / soft bags only: a small safety pin through the tape just below the bottom stop keeps the slider from wandering off. Don't pin through the teeth or through the coil itself.
4. For luggage / hard items: skip the pin and stick with the cable tie or twist tie through the pulls.

Don't use until it's properly fixed:
- Pushing the slider back on by hand with force (no pliers, no bending) — that's fine and actually the standard field fix. Pliers or bending the slider is what causes real damage.
- Superglue, tape across the teeth, or staples. They buy a day and cost you the rest of the zip.
- Forcing the bag shut with a luggage strap and ignoring the broken zip — it flexes the bad spot every time you move it.

Reply with what the item and failure are and I'll give you a real repair-vs-replace verdict (most common case: if the slider is intact and only a few teeth are missing near the bottom, repair is clearly cheaper; if the coil has split along the body of the zip or the slider is chewed up, replacement wins).

Failure mode 2 — source_timestamp = clock.Now() on every export.

  - Even when pending_batches is absent, the emit carries the current export time, not a snapshot-relative time.
  - Downstream freshness / staleness checks on metrics-router treat the record as freshly observed. The panel's "last seen" age gets reset by exports that carry no observation.
  - Cross-system impact: staleness alarms wired off source_timestamp will not fire on a stuck or partitioned producer. Combined with failure mode 1, you get the worst pairing — telemetry is genuinely missing AND the panel reports it as fresh-and-zero. That is the exact pattern that survives a SLO breach on a Friday night because every dashboard is green.

Why the fixture is part of the bug, not evidence against it.

  - The fixture omits pending_batches and expects below_limit + current time. That bakes failure modes 1 and 2 into the contract.
  - "Production is unchanged" is true in the sense that no existing path regresses — but this PR is establishing the shape of the export that metrics-router will start consuming. The fixture is the spec.

  1. Three-state limit_state: below_limit, at_limit, absent (or unknown). absent is the only correct answer when pending_batches is omitted. Decoder must not coerce missing → 0; return a sentinel or a pointer.
  2. source_timestamp must come from the snapshot (snapshot.observed_at or equivalent), not clock.Now(). When the snapshot has no observation, do not emit a record at all, or emit one with a sentinel timestamp and a separate has_observation=false flag the panel can key off.

The fixture isn't showing a clean dedup hit — it's showing a bug. After normalization, "Batch-A" and "batch-a" collide on the same row, the lookup returns request 1's terminal result with no payload comparison, and P2 is silently shadowed. Worse than a drop: the caller of P2 acts on a response that was computed from P1's payload, which can mask client bugs or enable key-reuse footguns.

Recommendation: don't approve as-is.

What the change should do:
- Keep the key normalization (ToLower + TrimSpace) — that's fine and helpful.
- On lookup, compare payload hash against the stored hash for that (tenant_id, normalized_key) row.
- Mismatch → reject with a 409 / "idempotency-key-reuse with different payload" (Stripe-style). Do not return the cached terminal result.
- Add a fixture case asserting rejection on same-key-different-payload, not silent return.

Two side notes while the author is in there:
- ToLower + TrimSpace doesn't normalize Unicode whitespace (e.g. U+3000). If you want true normalization, use NFKC + trim, or document the gap.
- State in the API contract that key normalization is server-side. Clients shouldn't rely on it as a safety property.

The "tenancy scopes this so it's safe" pushback won't hold: tenant scoping prevents cross-tenant collision, not same-tenant reuse of a key with a different payload. Those are orthogonal failure modes.

Four things, four roles:

  Preventive visit
    The wellness exam itself. Under ACA-compliant plans (your Sphere
    HDHP included), preventive services coded correctly are covered at
    100% — no deductible, no coinsurance. Billed with a preventive E/M
    code (99381-99397 or G0438/G0439) and a Z00.xx ICD-10. Anything the
    doctor addresses beyond prevention (new complaint, condition
    management) can be billed separately as a problem-focused visit
    (99213/99214) and then hits your $2,300 deductible and 10%
    coinsurance.

  Separately processed lab work
    A different claim, often from a different provider (Quest,
    LabCorp, hospital lab). Labs ordered at a preventive visit are
    not automatically preventive. Z-coded screening labs (USPSTF-
    recommended) stay 100%. Symptom- or condition-coded labs are
    diagnostic and apply to deductible + coinsurance. The lab sends
    its own EOB and its own bill, independent of the doctor's.

  EOB (Explanation of Benefits)
    Comes from your insurer. Not a bill. For each claim it shows:
    provider, date of service, billed amount, plan/network discount,
    amount applied to deductible, plan paid, and patient
    responsibility. You receive one even when you owe $0.

  Provider bill
    Comes from the doctor or lab. The amount they're asking you to
    pay. Should equal the EOB's "patient responsibility" line.

Verification sequence before paying anything:

  1. Wait for both the EOB (insurer) and the bill (provider) for every
     claim tied to the visit — the visit claim plus any lab claims.
     Don't pay the provider bill before the EOB arrives.

  2. Match by patient name, date of service, provider/facility,
     billed amount, and CPT/ICD codes. Stop on any mismatch.

  3. Confirm preventive coding on the visit:
       - CPT is a preventive E/M (9938x/9939x, G0438/G0439), not
         99213/99214
       - ICD-10 starts with Z00 (encounter for examination)
     If a problem-focused code appears, ask whether that component
     was necessary and whether it can be re-coded.

  4. Confirm lab coding:
       - Z-codes -> 100% preventive
       - symptom/condition codes -> deductible + coinsurance
     Call the lab's billing line if the diagnosis isn't obvious on
     the EOB.

  5. Check the EOB math:
       billed
       - plan/network discount
       - amount applied to deductible ($2,300 on your HDHP)
       - coinsurance (10% after ded)
       = patient responsibility
     The provider bill must equal that final number, nothing more.

  6. Confirm in-network status for every claim — rendering physician,
     lab, any facility fee. Out-of-network changes the allowed
     amount and your cost share.

  7. If it still doesn't reconcile, call provider billing first
     about coding; then the insurer about plan rules, applied
     amounts, and network status.

Ask about coding or a mismatch when:

  - Scheduled preventive visit but EOB shows 99213/99214
    (problem-focused) instead of a preventive E/M code.
  - Labs ordered at a preventive visit came back with a diagnostic
    code instead of a Z-code.
  - EOB shows patient responsibility on a service you expected to
    be preventive.
  - Provider bill differs from the EOB "patient responsibility"
    line (higher or lower).
  - Provider on the EOB isn't who you actually saw (covering
    physician, different NPI, different facility).
  - Same service appears twice (visit + same-day add-on that should
    have rolled in).
  - Date of service, billed amount, or CPT/ICD on the bill doesn't
    match what you received.
  - Claim processed as out-of-network when you booked in-network.

HDHP nuance worth keeping in mind: preventive stays 100% before the
deductible by ACA rule, so a clean preventive visit plus clean
preventive labs should produce $0 patient responsibility across both
EOBs. Anything that flips to diagnostic reverts to the $2,300
deductible, then 10% coinsurance.

PRACTICAL NYE FIREWORKS PLAN FOR KIBO
(preventive, non-medication; current status sounds stable)

LONG WALK — TIMING
  Take it now or finish by ~5:30 PM at the latest. Residential fireworks in South Slope typically ramp after dinner; a 45–60 minute sniff-walk that ends 60–90 minutes before the first expected bangs lowers his baseline arousal better than anything you'll do indoors tonight.
  - Front-clip harness + 4–6 ft standard leash. Skip retractable — they fail at distance and at sudden noises.
  - Quiet blocks only. Skip the park entrance and wide intersections. ID tags on, microchip visible.
  - Skip dog parks and busy stoops today.
  - He doesn't need to "work it off" — the goal is mild fatigue and familiar scent exposure, not exhaustion.

FOOD
  Feed dinner earlier and slightly smaller than usual, by ~5:30 PM. A full stomach right before a stress event raises vomiting risk. No new foods, no table scraps. Water available, don't force intake.

BRIEF LATER BATHROOM TRIPS (after dark)
  Plan for one short outing between 6:30 and 7:00 PM if he has normal evening needs, while it's still the early part of the window.
  - Y-harness + short leash, treats in your pocket, business only, straight back inside.
  - If he freezes, trembles hard, or pulls toward home at a distant pop, follow him in — don't drag. Use the leash and your voice to guide; carry only if you can do it safely without being bitten.
  - After ~8:00 PM, skip outdoor trips unless he absolutely insists. He can hold it; outside is the highest bolt-risk window.
  - Set up a pee pad on the floor of the safe area as insurance, so you don't have to leash up mid-event for a sudden need.
  - If he potties inside from stress, no correction. Clean silently and move on.

SECURE QUIET AREA + NOISE MASKING
  Pick one interior room with the least exterior wall exposure — bathroom, interior bedroom, or central hallway.
  - Move his bed, water bowl, a worn t-shirt of yours or Devika's, and a long-lasting chew (stuffed Kong, lick mat with peanut butter, snuffle mat) into that room now.
  - White noise: fan + air purifier, or low-volume TV/radio at a steady tone. Steady mid-frequency masking beats silence — silence makes individual pops louder by contrast.
  - Close and latch every window before dusk. Draw curtains fully on street-facing rooms; even sheers let flashes through. Move any window-perch beds down to floor level.
  - Close interior doors so he can't bolt across the apartment at a loud pop. Move breakables and sharp-edged items off the floor wherever he's pacing.
  - If he already gravitates to a den-like spot (closet, under a desk), let him have it — work with his choice, don't move him.
  - Do NOT introduce a Thundershirt or compression wrap cold tonight. Only use one if you've already fit-trained him on it.
  - Do NOT use essential oil diffusers in the safe room — concentrated oils irritate canine airways.

APARTMENT DOOR
  Building entry door: it stays locked; nothing for you to do.
  Apartment door: deadbolt it if you have one. If he tends to door-watch or scratch at the door during bangs, put a baby gate or a chair across the inside of the apartment door to block his view of the hallway — corridors echo.
  Don't open the apartment door for anyone you don't know tonight.
  If he bolts to the apartment door at a bang, don't grab him. Use your body and a treat tossed a few feet behind him (away from the door) to redirect.

COMFORT MEASURES
  Be boring. Sit in the safe area, read, scroll. No "it's okay baby," no sustained eye contact when he's stressed. Brief calm touch is fine; sustained petting can rev some dogs up. Forced reassurance reinforces worry.
  Mental work beats idle pacing: stuffed Kong (freeze it earlier today), lick mat with peanut butter, snuffle mat. Licking and chewing are physiologically settling.
  A worn t-shirt or small unwashed blanket of yours or Devika's in the safe spot — familiar scent calms more than a clean bed.
  If he's already crate-trained and crate-comfortable, the crate with a blanket draped over three sides works. If he isn't crate-trained, skip the crate — a mid-panic crate causes injury.
  Don't restrain, hug, or physically "ground" him. For noise-phobic dogs, restraint escalates panic.
  Don't shout, scold, or correct. He isn't being disobedient.
  Don't run the vacuum, blender, dishwasher, or anything loud that competes with your masking setup.
  Stay with him. Both of you being present in the safe area matters more than any specific behavior.

SIGNS — EMERGENCY VET (call or go now, do not continue comforting at home)
  Any one of these is enough:
  - Collapse, fainting, or sudden inability to stand
  - Gums pale, white, blue/gray, or bright brick red. Lift his lip now while he's calm and memorize his baseline color so you can compare later.
  - Difficulty breathing: very rapid, very labored, or persistent open-mouth panting that won't slow even in the quiet safe room
  - Seizure (paddling, loss of consciousness, uncontrolled tremors, loss of bladder/bowel)
  - Non-productive retching or dry heaving (deep-chested dog = bloat/GDV risk), repeated vomiting, or any blood in vomit or stool
  - Bloated, hard, or visibly distended abdomen
  - Bleeding from anywhere
  - Body hot to the touch combined with hard panting that won't slow
  - Unresponsive to you or to his name when normally responsive
  - Self-injury: broken nail, cut, jammed tooth, scraped pads from panic
  - Suspected ingestion of anything (dropped food, trash, foreign object)

SIGNS — CALL REGULAR VET TOMORROW (continue comforting tonight)
  - Won't eat or drink for 12+ hours after the noise ends
  - Hides and won't come out for 4+ hours after the last bang
  - Persistent shaking that doesn't resolve within an hour of quiet
  - Indoor accidents continuing into the daytime
  - Limping, lethargy, or appetite loss tomorrow
  - Any new behavioral change that persists into tomorrow

VET LOGISTICS — DO THIS BEFORE 6 PM
  I don't have a stored emergency vet number for you (your contacts list came back empty), so before the noise ramps: program the nearest 24-hour ER into your phone now. Realistic options in / near South Slope are Veterinary Emergency Group (VEG) Brooklyn on Atlantic Ave, BluePearl Brooklyn on Atlantic Ave, and Animal Medical Center on the Upper East Side — pull the current number yourself rather than trusting one from memory. Your regular South Slope vet's after-hours line is the other fallback. Save the address too, in case you need to go.
  If you do need to go: carrier or seat-belt harness for transport. Don't walk him out at peak noise; if you don't have a car staged, use a rideshare.

THROUGH YOUR 6:00–10:00 PM WINDOW
  6:00 PM: home, dinner for you, his earlier dinner already done. Move into the safe area.
  6:30–7:00 PM: short potty outing if needed, then back inside.
  7:00–10:00 PM: movie in the safe area, fan + low-volume audio masking, both of you present, low-key.
  10:00 PM onward: NYE residential noise in Brooklyn often peaks closer to midnight and can run later than July 4. Plan to stay with him past 10 if he hasn't settled — stress response can outlive the last pop by 30–90 minutes, so don't read a quiet stretch as "done."

Quantities (3 adults, generous portions)

- Frittata: 8 of the 10 eggs, 4 oz spinach (wilted), 6 oz mushrooms (sautéed), 1/3 cup grated cheese (optional, but helps bind), 2 tbsp olive oil, salt, pepper. Save 2 eggs for another use.
- Roasted potatoes: all 1.5 lbs, cubed 3/4", tossed with 2.5 tbsp olive oil, salt, pepper, optional garlic or rosemary.
- Salad: 5–6 oz greens; vinaigrette in a jar — 3 tbsp olive oil, 1 tbsp lemon juice (or vinegar), 1 tsp dijon, salt, pepper.
- Toast: 4–6 thick slices sourdough, butter softened.
- Fruit: wash, slice, plate; a squeeze of citrus keeps it bright.

Prep timeline (working back from 1:00 PM)

11:30  BOTH — mise en place.
        Cube potatoes; cold-water parboil 5 min, drain, toss with oil/salt/pepper.
        Slice mushrooms; sauté in a dry pan until they release water, then add oil and brown ~6 min. Wilt spinach in same pan; squeeze very dry and chop.
        Whisk 8 eggs with salt, pepper, cheese; fold in veg.
        Wash and spin greens; shake up vinaigrette in a jar.
        Wash and chop fruit onto a platter; slice sourdough.
        Wipe counters now, not later.

11:50  Potatoes spread on sheet pan, room temp.
12:00  Potatoes into 425°F oven. Set 20-min timer.
12:15  Pour frittata mix into a buttered 10" cast iron (or any oven-safe skillet).
12:20  Potatoes out, onto a covered tray to hold heat. Oven to 375°F. Frittata in. Set 22-min timer.
12:25  One of you starts Kibo's 25-min walk (back ~12:50).
12:47  Frittata out; rest on the stovetop 5 min (it continues to set).
12:50  Plate-up sprint (~10 min):
          - Potatoes to serving dish (covered keeps them hot).
          - Dress and toss salad at the table or in a bowl.
          - Toast under the broiler 60–90 sec (or toaster).
          - Slice and plate frittata.
          - Load dishwasher, soak skillets, wipe counters, take trash/recycling out.

 1:00  Anya arrives. Eat ~1:05.

Cleanup-play checklist (do before Anya walks in)
  - Counters wiped
  - Cutting boards, knives, prep bowls in dishwasher or soaking
  - Spent towels in the laundry
  - Stovetop and oven knob area wiped
  - Trash and recycling out
  - Kitchen towel replaced with a fresh one

Why this works
  - Parboiling the potatoes gets you crispy outside / fluffy inside in 20 min at 425°F instead of 35–40.
  - Cooking mushrooms DRY first keeps the frittata from going watery; squeezing the spinach is non-negotiable for the same reason.
  - Everything that diries the kitchen (sauté pans, cutting boards, sheet pan) is either loaded into the dishwasher or soaking by 12:55, so the visit starts with a clean kitchen.

Buffer tip
  The frittata mix can be made at 11:30, poured into the skillet, covered, and refrigerated; bake it at 12:20 as above. That gives you slack if Kibo's walk runs long.

For a paw that's just pink with a couple of licks and otherwise looks and acts normal, the goal tonight is to get the salt off, get the paw dry, and watch. Here is the non-medication plan.

Immediate cleaning and drying (no products):

1. Lukewarm water rinse of the affected paw. A shallow bowl or a low faucet works; let it soak 30–60 seconds and swish gently so water reaches between the toes. Plain water is enough; soap is not needed.
2. Use a soft, damp cloth to wipe gently between the toes if you see any crusted or gritty residue.
3. Pat dry thoroughly with a clean towel. The webbing between the toes is the part that needs the most attention — trapped moisture is what lets irritation worsen.
4. Distract him for a few minutes while the paw finishes drying so the licking cycle breaks.
5. Check the other three paws the same way; salt typically affects more than one.

Do not put anything on the paw tonight — no ointment, balm, spray, or medicated wipe. If this is contact irritation from salt, the rinse and dry is what helps. If something else is going on, a clean, uncoated paw is what you want a vet to see.

Limiting salt contact on later walks:

- Wipe or rinse all four paws at the door before he comes fully inside. A damp washcloth or a paw-rinse cup at the entry is the single biggest habit change. Doing it every walk matters more than how fancy the setup is.
- Dog boots are a physical barrier, not a medication, and they are the most reliable option if you walk regularly on treated sidewalks. Fit matters; a short indoor acclimation period helps.
- Choose routes that avoid heavily treated pavement when you can (untreated side streets, parks, snow-covered grass).
- Keep walks shorter on heavy-salt days.
- Wipe paws again before he lies down or sleeps after a walk.

Signs that mean call your South Slope vet (same-day, not an emergency):

- Pinkness still there or worse after 24 hours
- It spreads to other toes or other paws
- Licking becomes more frequent or more intense
- New redness, swelling, or warmth
- A sore, scab, or raw spot appears
- Foul smell from the paw

Signs that mean go straight to urgent or ER evaluation:

- Bleeding from the paw that does not stop with a few minutes of gentle pressure
- Swelling that is visibly and quickly getting worse
- Any cut, torn nail, or puncture you didn't see before
- Discharge — pus, blood-tinged fluid, anything wet and new
- Lameness, reluctance to put the paw down, or whimpering when the paw is touched
- Red streaks running up the leg
- Lethargy, hiding, food refusal, or a behavior change that lasts more than a few hours
- Any vomiting or general illness alongside the paw issue

If tonight stays where it is — mild pink, a few licks, normal walking, eating, behaving — this can be watched at home and rechecked in the morning. If anything on either list above shows up, that's the threshold to act. Your South Slope vet is the right first contact for the non-urgent list; the urgent list points at an ER hospital.

Recommendation: Option A (reusable, size 3), with one caveat.

Why A over B:
- Hook-and-loop straps materially help retention. If a boot is on the snug side, a strap that closes above the paw is the difference between "still on at the end of the block" and "lost two blocks ago." That matters more than paw-width tolerance here.
- Textured flexible sole gives real traction on the slushy/salted surface the barrier exists for. Option B's no-sole build is mostly a grip risk on slick pavement.
- Reusable beats 12 disposables once Kibo is past the initial fit trial. A disposable pack makes sense if you expect to size-adjust or rotate through wear; you don't.
- Four boots = one full set for a four-paw dog, which is the correct unit of purchase for this use case.

Caveat / what to do:
- Try one boot on a back paw before committing to the full set. At 2.2" against a 2.25" minimum, the back fit is the variable that determines whether this works. If the back paw is clearly compressed or the boot won't slide on without effort, neither option is the right boot and you want a sub-2.25" size before Kibo walks salted sidewalks in something too tight.
- If A fits the back paw, the front paw is comfortably mid-range and you're done.

Net: A is the right call given stated constraints; the back-paw fit is the one thing to physically verify before treating the purchase as final.

Kibo boot sizing comparison

Option A — reusable fabric boot, size 3
- Spec range: 2.25–2.50 in paw width
- Front paws (2.4 in): fit cleanly within range
- Back paws (2.2 in): 0.05 in below the stated minimum
- Tradeoff: structured, reusable, more secure — but compresses if back paws are forced in

Option B — disposable natural-rubber boot, size medium
- Spec range: 2.25–2.75 in paw width
- Front paws (2.4 in): fit cleanly within range
- Back paws (2.2 in): same 0.05 in gap below minimum
- Tradeoff: stretchier rubber + no rigid sole/strap — accommodates shape better but disposable and less secure on a sidewalk

More plausible size: Option B medium, narrowly. The disposable rubber's stretch gives the most forgiveness for the under-spec back paws, and the lower price per unit makes trial-and-error cheaper. Option A size 3 was previously your preferred baseline, but it compresses back paws that fall under its minimum — the prior note explicitly said to drop a size below 2.25 in if it won't slide on, which makes Option A the riskier pick.

Safe indoor fit check (before any outdoor use)
- Acclimate indoors only for the first several sessions — paws on the carpet, treat-based, short intervals.
- Slide each boot on with two fingers; it should go on without forcing. If you have to tug or the fabric bunches, that boot is wrong.
- Walk Kibo across the room on a non-slip surface. Confirm: (a) he moves naturally and does not flick the boot off, (b) the gait looks even across all four legs, (c) no material pinches at the dewclaw or between toes.
- Check the cuff seal — you should be able to fit one fingertip between cuff and leg, no more.
- Time the session; first attempts should be 2–5 minutes, then extend.

Signs to remove the boots immediately
- Limping, head-bobbing, or a shorter stride on any leg
- Stopping, sitting, or trying to bite at a boot
- Boot slipping, twisting, or coming off mid-walk
- Skin visible at the cuff edge, fur pressed flat, or any blanching around the top of the paw
- Whimpering, excessive panting unrelated to temperature, or refusal to move

Standing paw rule (already in your memory): swelling, discharge, odor, bleeding, or limping → stop the walk and inspect.

One operational note for back paws specifically: because both options spec a 2.25 in floor and Kibo's back paws measure 2.2 in, the fit test on the back paws is the deciding data point. If Option B medium back paws still gap or slip, the prior guidance applies — drop a size below the stated minimum rather than sizing up.

Based on the indoor test, here's my read on the fit and what I'd recommend:

Fit assessment

Front paws (~2.4"): good. The 2.4" paw sits comfortably in the middle of the listed 2.25-2.50" range, and the boots stayed oriented through ten minutes of walking.

Rear paws (~2.2"): fails. The 0.05" below the lower size bound isn't the only problem, it's also the *type* of problem. A woven fabric boot doesn't compress like natural rubber; strap snugness can close the circumference, but it can't narrow the internal footprint. The rotation you saw on one rear boot is the warning that this set will rotate on outdoor terrain where the substrate is uneven, wet, or icy. A rotated boot = water/snow/debris ingress, abrasion, or a lost boot. Ten minutes on a flat floor under controlled conditions isn't supposed to produce rotation; that's the boot telling you it doesn't fit.

Recommendation

Avoid the four-boot set for outdoor use. Don't go mixed-sizing on this brand either — your data point is the rear fit, and a half-size down would drop you below the listed range on the front paws too. You end up trading one problem for another.

Switch the rear paws to the medium disposable natural-rubber barriers. Stretch accommodates the undersized rear paw better than woven fabric, and disposables are cheaper than a vet visit from a torn-off-rotated-boot injury. Keep the front pair of the reusable set (front paws genuinely fit), or use four disposables if you'd rather have one rule for all four paws outdoors.

Signs a boot must come off immediately

- Boot has rotated, slipped off, or is hanging by a strap
- Any limping, head-down posture, or repeated lifting of the paw
- Redness, moisture, or compressed fur visible at the cuff
- Chewing or licking at the boot
- Strap that has loosened (recheck the two-finger rule)
- Wet sock liner or boot interior (wet fabric against skin macerates fast)

If any of these appear, stop the walk, remove the affected boot, and check the paw before continuing. For the rear paws, the rotation you already saw indoors means the medium disposables are the safer outdoor choice — don't retest this fabric pair outside.

5. Walk + sit + lie-down cycle, ~10 steps each. Watch the gait: a slight high-step for the first few steps is normal; a persistent skip or toe-drag is not.
6. Check the gait on a turn — this is where 2/17's rotation showed up. If the boot spins on a hard turn indoors, it will spin outdoors too.

  - Boot has rotated or slipped off the paw shape (not just shifted slightly on the cuff).
  - Kibo is favoring the paw, skipping, or doing a sustained high-step beyond the first few strides.
  - Chewing or biting at a specific boot (not casual licking).

  - Any bleeding, blister, or raw spot — even tiny.

Assessment, metrics-router staging, gen 744 / 2,184 routes, raw-hash mismatch on the canary-isolated instance

What it is: serialization artifact. The hash input is JSON emitted directly from a Go map, and Go map iteration order is non-deterministic across processes. Two semantically identical snapshots therefore hash to different values even when route-table content matches. Sorted-by-route-key shows identical (key, target) pairs across A and B, and both report the same generation and route count, so the route-table content is identical.

Why this does not warrant firing the canary or treating the hash as a consistency gate in its current form:

  - 2024-08-07 rollback triggers (active-generation inconsistency across pods, route divergence from the previous-generation table, dropped series off baseline, reload failure, or restart): none engaged.
  - 2025-02-17 staging comparison: identical replay input, only the snapshot-serialization toggle changed — same shape of mismatch, not treated as a consistency failure.
  - 2023-11-21 canary: a validation-only signal was treated as validation-only rather than as a rollback or canary-failure trigger. This is structurally the same kind of signal.

Production is unchanged, no route change, no dropped write, no downstream parity movement — consistent with no real inconsistency.

Recommendation:

  - Do not widen the alert to fire on raw-hash mismatch in this form. Doing so creates false canary isolation on serialization noise with no underlying content drift, and erodes trust in the canary signal over time.
  - If you want the snapshot hash to actually gate, the executable change is canonicalize-then-hash: sort keys before emitting JSON, or switch the encoder to a canonical form, then hash. That makes the hash reflect (key, target) identity and gives the gate a real meaning. Owner-runnable; no cross-service surface change.
  - The current A/B state is consistent. The canary isolation is the bug, not a symptom.

If Wes wants, the staging validation change framing from 2025-06-10 fits the same shape — staging-only, validation-only, no production impact, owner-run executable to make the signal meaningful.

WHY THIS IS OBSERVABILITY/SERIALIZATION, NOT SEMANTIC ROUTE-CONSISTENCY

  A semantic route-consistency failure means the routes themselves diverge: a route added or dropped, a predicate changed, a destination remapped, an identity duplicated. The detector would fire on two route tables whose set of identities or whose per-identity fields actually differ.

  What we have is the opposite shape. The reproducer is identical replay input — same generation, same route table source — yielding different bytes. Nothing in the semantic content moved. The label_map is treated (and documented) as a set of identities with a uniqueness invariant, not as a sequential record, so insertion order carries no meaning. Length-delimited provenance-digest encoding already prevents concatenation ambiguities. The only thing left to leak is byte-order from a Go map that hasn't been canonicalized before serialization.

  That places the defect in the serialization/observability layer: the generator emits semantically equal content, the parser/detector compares raw bytes, and the comparison misclassifies equality as inequality. It is not a route-consistency failure because no guardrail trip on real divergence has occurred. It is also not a generation defect because the inputs to generation are equal.

  The framing matters because the remediations are disjoint:
    - If this is misframed as semantic route-consistency, the next move is to harden the generator and re-audit the guardrail — which does not touch the actual bug.

  1. Canonical or semantic hashing for snapshot identity
     - The snapshot/provenance identity must be derived from a canonical or semantic form, not from raw emitted bytes.
     - Acceptable: a canonical serializer that sorts/orders map keys deterministically and applies length-delimited framing before hashing.
     - Preferred: a semantic hash over the normalized identity set (route keys, predicates, destinations) so that any byte-equivalent encoding of the same route table collides to the same digest.
     - The PR must show, for at least one round-trip, that two serializations of the same route table (different key orders, different label_map layouts) produce the same snapshot identifier.
     - The provenance-digest encoding (already length-delimited) must continue to round-trip; do not regress it to a concatenation form.

  2. Continued fail-closed behavior on real content differences
     - The canonicalization must be lossless with respect to the route-table identity set. Two route tables that differ in any field that carries semantic meaning (route added, route removed, predicate changed, destination changed, label_map identity set changed) must produce different snapshot identifiers.
     - Specifically: collapsing the label_map to a set must still distinguish {a,b} from {a,b,c} and from {a,c}, and must still distinguish a label_map whose per-identity fields differ even when the identity keys are equal.
     - No "best-effort" matching. If the consumer cannot decide equality losslessly, the system must fail-closed, not pass.
     - The guardrail and the snapshot-identity check must continue to trip on every reproducer the current detector trips on, plus any reproducer it currently misses due to byte-order leakage (a missed trip is itself a defect to file, not to fix silently).

  3. Regression coverage
     - Insertion-order permutations:
         * Same route table built with N different insertion orders (route addition order, label_map identity insertion order, nested-map key order) must produce byte-identical canonical output and identical snapshot identifiers.
         * At minimum: a fixture with ≥3 routes and ≥3 label identities, permuted across at least 6 orderings, all colliding.
         * Coverage must include the empty case, single-element case, and a case where one label identity's field-set ordering is varied independently of its siblings.
     - Genuine route mutations:
         * Each of the following must produce a different snapshot identifier from the baseline:
             - one route added;
             - one route removed;
             - one route's predicate changed (single field);
             - one route's destination changed;
             - one label_map identity added;
             - one label_map identity removed;
             - one label_map identity's value field changed (with the identity key held constant — this is the load-bearing case for "set with per-identity fields").
         * Each mutation case must be paired with an identical-content control to confirm the detector is responding to the mutation, not to incidental ordering noise.
     - Cross-run determinism:
         * The same fixture replayed under the toggle-on and toggle-off paths (the PR's serialization optimization) must produce the same snapshot identifier on the toggle-on path across ≥10 invocations, and must produce the same snapshot identifier as the toggle-off path on identical input.
     - Crash-window coverage (#2094 specific):

  - Should not move the canonicalization into the generator. The generator's job is to emit the route table faithfully; canonicalization belongs at the snapshot-identity boundary so it covers every producer, present and future.
  - Should not require production traffic to validate. Identical replay-input methodology is sufficient and is the standing rule.

SUNDAY BRUNCH — Spinach-mushroom strata for 3 + yogurt & fruit
- 8 eggs
- 2 cups milk
- 10–12 oz bread (roughly one loaf), cubed
- 8 oz mushrooms, sautéed (the other half of the bag)
- Remaining ~6 oz frozen spinach, thawed and squeezed
- 1 small onion, Dijon mustard, salt, pepper; cheese if you have it (pantry)
- Side: 1.5 cups yogurt + washed/portioned fruit
- Coffee (on hand)

FRIDAY-EVENING PREP (~30–40 min, mostly hands-off)
1. Move frozen spinach to the fridge to thaw (or quick-thaw in a colander under cold water).
2. Cube bread for the strata; spread on a sheet pan and leave out overnight, or dry 8–10 min at 300°F.
3. Sauté 8 oz mushrooms with a pinch of salt; cool.
4. Squeeze both portions of spinach dry.
5. Grease a 9x13 dish. Layer bread, mushrooms, spinach. Whisk 8 eggs + 2 cups milk + a spoonful of Dijon + salt + pepper; pour over. Press bread down so it soaks, cover, refrigerate.
6. Wipe and portion fruit into a bowl for Sunday.
7. Set aside: Saturday's canned tomatoes, onion, garlic, and 4 bread slices on the counter so nothing needs deciding tomorrow.

What you've already flagged is right. Both problems are real, and they're worse together than apart.

Unbounded-cardinality, concretely:

- `service_pair` — bounded by the service catalog. Fine.
- `owner_email` — bounded by owner roster. Fine in principle, see below for the PII angle.
- `pull_request` (raw repo + PR number) — unbounded. PR numbers accumulate forever, every merged/closed exception PR becomes a permanent label value the TSDB must index. Time-series with high-cardinality labels don't drop cleanly without losing history, so this grows monotonically until it hurts query latency and storage.
- `exception_reason` — unbounded, and worse than unbounded: free text. "Missing idempotency key", "idempotency key missing", and "no id key" become three buckets. Reviewer phrasings diverge even when the underlying failure mode is identical, so the metric will systematically over-count distinct reasons and under-count recurrences of the same one.

Unnecessary employee-identifier surface:

- `owner_email` as a label value lands PII into every dashboard, alert query, exported CSV, screenshot, and shared link downstream. Owner identity is needed for joining to ownership data, but that's what an opaque stable `owner_id` is for. Email is also less stable than people think — aliases change, contractors rotate, contractors offboard — and you'll lose join continuity precisely when you most want it.
- If reviewers ever include external contractors or vendors on a cross-service exception, you've now also exported their contact info into the metrics surface.

Failure modes this metric would introduce if shipped as-proposed:

- TSDB index growth driven by `pull_request` and `exception_reason`. Bounded only by exception-review volume × human phrasing variation.
- Same-bucket fragmentation: identical failure modes reported under N different reason strings, defeating the "group by reason" use case the dashboard wants.
- Owner-rotation blind spots: dashboard groups by email; an alias change silently splits one person's history into two rows.
- Misleading throughput signal: a count-per-owner-per-pair grouping rewards volume, not boundary quality. 50 routine exception sign-offs and 2 critical invariant violations look identical on a totals view. If the intent is governance signal, totals is the wrong primitive.

Fix the record, then a narrow metric on top is fine.

PART 1 — CARDINALITY AND IDENTIFIER RISKS

Cardinality is the count of distinct time series a metric produces under its label set. Each unique label combination is one series. Series count drives TSDB index size, ingestion bandwidth, remote-write cost, query latency, and per-scrape alert evaluation cost.

Risks from using raw identifiers as metric labels:

  - Unbounded growth. tenant_id, proposal_id, owner_id, request_id, trace_id, raw route paths, raw error messages are effectively unbounded in production. Prometheus-style TSDBs retain a series in the head block until the staleness window expires, so a burst of new IDs can permanently bloat the index and push out legitimate series.

  - Tenant / PII leakage. A tenant_id label on a shared or cross-team dashboard silently becomes a per-tenant view. Even internally it breaks the "aggregate operational visibility" goal because every aggregation is implicitly per-tenant.

  - Pager correctness. Alerts that filter on unbounded labels are either non-selective (page on every value) or rely on regex / negative-match that breaks when a new value appears. Cardinality Guardrails treats this as "bounded label shape is necessary but not sufficient" — paging needs bounded selectors.

  - Cost and quota blowup. A single misconfigured label multiplies ingest cost by orders of magnitude in a day. Series budget per metric is finite and shared.

  - Aggregation collision. Sum / rate across labels still works, but per-series averages and percentiles become one-observation-per-series and lose cohort meaning.

  - Audit / ownership ambiguity. Raw identifiers leak the underlying entity (owner, proposal, customer) into the metric stream, which makes access control, retention, and redaction harder than if those entities lived in audit records with explicit policy.

PART 2 — DESIGN PRINCIPLES

  1. Labels are bounded classifications, never raw identifiers. Every label value set must be closed (enum) or have a documented cardinality ceiling. Open value sets belong in logs.

  2. Raw identifiers live in logs and audit records, not metrics. tenant_id, proposal_id, owner_id, request_id, raw_route, raw_error_message stay as log fields. Metrics and logs correlate via time window and bounded labels; high-cardinality drilldown happens in the log layer.

  3. Aggregate operational visibility is preserved by bucketing — tenant_tier, source_class, region, status_class, error_class, deploy_epoch, route_class. The bucket boundaries are the unit of visibility; they are owned and versioned.

  4. Owner, cardinality ceiling, and re-cut trigger are required audit metadata per label. They are not stored as labels.

PART 3 — BOUNDED LABEL SCHEMA (example)

  source_class    : enum over the service inventory. Ceiling <= 1.5x current service count. Owner: platform-svc. Re-cut when a new service class appears.

  tenant_tier     : enum — {free, pro, enterprise, internal}. Ceiling <= 6. Owner: billing. Re-cut requires pricing-model migration plan.

  region          : enum over deployment topology. Ceiling <= 12. Owner: sre. New region needs on-call rotation and runbook before label is added.

  status_class    : enum — {success, client_error_4xx, auth_error_4xx, rate_limited_4xx, server_error_5xx, timeout, circuit_open, dependency_error}. Ceiling <= 12. Owner: per-service.

  error_class     : canonical error taxonomy, one value per dependency or failure mode. Ceiling <= 30. Owner: per-service with platform-svc review on additions.

  deploy_epoch    : enum — {current, previous}. Ceiling 2. Owner: release-eng. Re-cut is automatic per deploy; previous ages out.

  route_class     : bounded route buckets — {public_read, authed_read, write, admin, internal_health}. Ceiling <= 20. Owner: per-service. Raw path lives in logs.

  is_canary       : bool. Ceiling 2.

Cardinality budget per metric is explicit. Example:

  ingest_edge_requests_total ceiling
    = source_class(<=10) * tenant_tier(<=4) * region(<=6)
    * status_class(<=8) * deploy_epoch(2) * route_class(<=10)
    * is_canary(2)
    = 76,800 series

Observed should stay <= 50% of ceiling. Trigger re-cut when observed exceeds 70%, or when a new value class appears that does not fit the existing taxonomy.

PART 4 — LOGS AND AUDIT (high-cardinality fields, NOT labels)

  - tenant_id, customer_id, account_id
  - proposal_id, owner_id, author_id
  - request_id, trace_id, span_id
  - raw_route_path
  - raw_error_message, stack frames
  - source_event_id, provenance_source, published_service_id  (dup-deploy dedup key)
  - deploy_id, git_sha, build_id

Drilldown pattern: dashboard / alert fires on bounded metric aggregate, jump to logs filtered by source_class + deploy_epoch + time window, then filter by high-cardinality field (e.g., tenant_id) inside the log query. Owner and runbook mapping live as a doc, not as a label.

PART 5 — ALERT AND DASHBOARD PATTERN

  Alert selector (bounded):
    ALERT IngestEdgeServerErrorBudget
      IF
        sum by (source_class, region, deploy_epoch) (
          rate(requests_total{source_class="ingest_edge", status_class="server_error_5xx"}[5m])
        )
        /
        sum by (source_class, region, deploy_epoch) (
          rate(requests_total{source_class="ingest_edge"}[5m])
        )
        > 0.01
      FOR 10m
      LABELS {owner="ingest-edge-oncall", runbook="ingest-edge/5xx-budget"}

  Dashboard grouping: by source_class, tenant_tier, region, status_class, error_class. Group-by tenant_id is forbidden on shared dashboards; tenant drilldown is a log filter.

  Alert preflight: verify the selector is bounded (no regex over an open set, no negative match on unbounded values). A bounded label shape is necessary but not sufficient for paging.

PART 6 — AUDIT RECORD PER LABEL (runbook or doc)

  label
  value_set             (versioned list)
  cardinality_ceiling   (integer)
  observed_cardinality_max (last 30d)
  re_cut_trigger        (condition, e.g. observed > 70% of ceiling, or new class appears)
  owner                 (team + on-call rotation)
  review_cadence        (quarterly or on change)
  last_reviewed         (date)
  migration_plan_ref    (doc id, if a re-cut is in progress)

PART 7 — PREFLIGHT FOR ANY NEW LABEL PROPOSAL

  1. Is this a raw identifier? If yes — refuse as a label, route to logs.
  2. Is the value set closed or bounded? If no — refuse, or escalate as "expected high-cardinality" with explicit owner and series budget (rare; requires platform-svc signoff).
  3. Is the label namespaced to the stream that owns it (e.g., source_class owned by platform-svc, not each service)? If no — fix ownership first.
  4. Are owner, ceiling, and re-cut trigger recorded in an audit entry before merge?
  5. Does any paging rule depend on this label? If yes — verify the selector is bounded.
  6. Are raw proposal and owner details preserved in logs / audit records, not in metric labels?

I have the prior context now. The three options that were on the table for the 2027-03-27 work-room chair problem, and the status of the warranty cylinder.

## The three options compared

1. **Manufacturer warranty claim — free replacement cylinder, 7–10 day delivery, user-installs.**
   Cost: $0. Time: 7–10 days. Effort: moderate (swap the cylinder yourself; warranty cylinders are user-installable in most office-chair designs, but if you've never done it the job is finicky — the seat has to come off, the existing cylinder hammered or pressed out, and the new one seated cleanly).

2. **Local repair service — $85, next-business-day, on-site.**
   Cost: $85. Time: next business day. Effort: none for you. This is what was recommended on 3/27.

3. **Buy a new chair — ~$430.**
   Cost: ~$430. Time: same-day if a retailer has stock, otherwise days. Effort: assembly, and disposal of the old chair. Throws away a chair that is otherwise fine — only the cylinder failed.

## Recommendation

**Pay the $85 and book the local service.** It's the cheapest practical path, gets you off the dining chair fastest, and doesn't waste a working chair. The warranty cylinder is still worth filing for (see below), but it shouldn't be the thing you're waiting on.

## Is the warranty cylinder reasonable?

Yes — file the claim regardless. A gas cylinder is a wear item in the chair's bill of materials, so a free replacement under warranty is unusually generous and not worth leaving on the table. Three reasons it still makes sense even though you're paying for the local repair:

- You get a free spare. Cylinders fail repeatedly over a chair's life; having a known-good spare turns the next failure into a 10-minute swap instead of a service call.
- Seven to ten days lines up with how long office-chair cylinders are expected to last once one has already failed — you're not losing much by letting the local fix buy you the working chair now and the warranty cylinder showing up as a backup.
- Cost is zero and the only risk is a short return-window if you decline the spare.

Don't expect the warranty cylinder to be your primary fix — treat it as the spare.

## Using the chairs safely while you wait

- **Work room:** use the dining chair only for short, seated-at-height tasks (laptop, reading, eating). Don't raise it to standing-desk height — dining chairs aren't stable on a footing built for a chair with a 5-star base and casters, and the seat height is wrong for monitor ergonomics anyway.
- **Work chair post-repair:** once the local service swaps the cylinder, do a sit-test before you trust it — sit, bounce gently, raise and lower three or four times, then load it with your normal working weight for a few minutes. New cylinders can fail within the first day if the seal wasn't seated.
- **Monitor height:** with the dining chair at the desk, the top of the screen is almost certainly below eye level. Stack something solid under the monitor (a closed book, a box) for the day or two until the work chair is back — neck strain from a low monitor for a week is the real ergonomic risk here, not the chair itself.
- **Old cylinder:** keep it after the swap. If the warranty cylinder arrives and the local-installed one ever sticks, you can compare them and you'll have a fallback.
- **Spare (warranty) cylinder when it arrives:** store it horizontally in a dry spot, not under load, and label it with the chair model and the date. Gas cylinders lose pressure slowly over years sitting unused; a spare from a known batch is more trustworthy than one bought fresh in three years when the next one fails.

Scope: candidate "precompile all route matchers before opening readiness" at the 40,000-route staging fixture.

Failure
  At 40,000 routes, cold startup is 42s. The deploy readiness gate is 30s. Observed in staging: three replacement instances were terminated before readiness and restarted without joining service. Production is unchanged, so this is still a pre-merge window.

Why
  The precompile step sits on the readiness-critical path. Wall-clock cost (42s) exceeds the gate (30s), so the deploy pipeline never sees a ready signal and kills the instance.

Production failure modes if this ships
  1. Deploy / redeploy — every metrics-router rollout fails; new version never reaches healthy.
  2. Autoscaling — new instances during traffic spikes are killed before serving; capacity cannot grow.
  3. Crash recovery / restart — restarted instances are killed before readiness; recovery stalls.
  4. Any process restart (kernel upgrade, config-reload restart, OOM kill).
  Blast radius: metrics-router cannot roll, cannot scale, cannot recover. That is not a price worth a 7% steady-state match speedup.

Headroom is also bad
  Linear extrapolation: 30s / 42s × 40,000 ≈ 28,500 routes already trips the gate. This fixture is roughly 30% inside the timeout. Any route-table growth without retuning either the gate or the compile path makes this strictly worse — even before considering growth in matcher cost.

Mitigation options (informational, not approval)
  - Compile per-shard or parallel across cores so wall-clock fits inside the gate.
  - Mark ready with empty or partial matcher cache; finish compilation in the background; route cache-hit traffic to compiled matchers, fall back to the slow path on miss.
  - Lazy compilation: compile on first match of each route; evict on table reload.
  - Raise the readiness gate (operational change, masks the regression rather than fixing it).
  Each of these preserves the steady-state win without putting it on the readiness-critical path.

Recommendation
  Do not merge the candidate as designed. It will fail every production rollout at the current gate. Move precompile off the readiness-critical path, or do not precompile. The 7% steady-state gain does not offset the deploy / scale / recovery blast radius.

Ownership note
  Implementation, release, and rollback for metrics-router remain with Wes. This is a failure-mode review only — no release-gate authority is asserted here.

Fifteen-minute pre-ride, in order. Plain text below — I'll keep it tight.

TIRES (3 min)
- Inflate to the sidewall-rated psi; cold reference ~55-60 if you're in that band.
- Squeeze both tires for feel, then visual scan sidewalls and tread for cuts, bulges, embedded debris.
- Spin each wheel; watch for true run and sidewall wobble.

Stop & service if: sidewall bulge or cut, casing visible through a tread cut, wire/glass still embedded, tire won't hold air, lateral wobble >~2 mm or hop you can feel.

BRAKES (2 min)
- Squeeze each lever: firm bite, no sponginess, reserve travel left.
- Walk the bike and pull each brake — wheel should lock (or skid on a wet day).
- Check pad thickness and that the rotor/rim contact is centered.

Stop & service if: lever bottoms out or feels soft (hydraulic), pads <1.5 mm rim or <0.5 mm disc, rotor rub that doesn't quiet with caliper re-seating, brake fails to grip.

DRIVETRAIN (3 min)
- Run the chain through all gears by hand or on a stand; no stiff links, no rust pitting.
- Eyeball the cassette for bent/missing teeth; check derailleur hanger is straight.
- Shift through the full range both directions; limit screws clean at the ends.

Stop & service if: a stiff link that won't free, bent hanger, audible skip under load, chain drops off the chainring or cassette, cracked cog tooth.

WHEEL RETENTION (2 min)
- Confirm front + rear axle/QR: fully seated in dropouts, lever closes with firm resistance.
- Lift the bike, strike the tire down — wheel shouldn't shift in the frame.
- Disc centered in caliper with light, even pad gap.

Stop & service if: axle won't torque to spec, lever closes with no resistance, wheel moves in the dropouts, rotor drags hard enough to slow you.

LIGHTS (2 min)
- Front: clean lens, charged/battery fresh, mount snug, beam level (not aimed at drivers or straight down).
- Rear: steady + flash both work, mount snug, visible from behind at riding height.

Stop & service if: either light won't turn on, mount slips under handlebar/seatpost shake, beam is dead-aimed.

LOADED TEST (3 min)
- Pack the bag/pannier as you'll actually carry it.
- Walk the bike 20 m first — listen for new creaks, clicks, rubs.
- Ride 3-5 min in a low gear on flat ground; bars tight, headset no knock, rear light still on.

Stop & service if: any new front-end noise, vibration, or wander; a creak that only appears loaded; brake rub returns under load; light fails mid-ride; anything you wouldn't want to discover 10 miles out.

Quick overall rule: if anything in the loaded test feels different from how the bike felt pre-pause — sound, feel, tracking — don't talk yourself out of it. Walk home and book the shop.

INTERIM OBSERVATION — exception vs. ordinary-owner intake (framing only)

Scope note: this distinguishes the structural shape of the two request types as they appear in intake. It does not characterize the current batch, because the current intake records do not surface a labelled set of three bounded exception requests and six ordinary-owner requests; the distinction below applies whenever those shapes appear.

What makes a request a bounded exception
- It asks to operate outside an existing rule, fence, or stated stop condition for a named, time-boxed reason.
- It carries an explicit envelope: which rule is being relaxed, for how long, what evidence will be produced, and what reverts the relaxation.
- It does not request a permanent change to the rule itself; ownership of the rule stays where it was.
- The asker is not the rule owner; the request is addressed to whoever owns the boundary.

What makes a request an ordinary owner request
- It is in-scope for the asker's own service or boundary: they are the owner of the code path, runbook, metric, or doc it touches.
- No existing rule has to be bent to honor it; the answer can be "yes / no / later" within the asker's own remit.
- It moves work forward rather than carving out an exception, even when the work is non-trivial.

Failure mode: the `cancelled_total` increment is unconditional (runs before the CAS), while the `success_total` increment is conditional (runs only if the CAS wins). That asymmetry is the bug.

Failure modes in the described interleaving (cancel loses the CAS, completion wins):

1. Phantom cancellation accounting. The caller receives one success result, yet `cancelled_total` is already +1. The counter no longer tracks the terminal actually delivered.

2. Reconciliation breaks. `success_total + cancelled_total != accepted_total` (and worse if error is also a terminal). Any dashboard or alert that sums terminals drifts from request volume.

3. Multiplicative over-count under racing. The cancel path increments before every CAS attempt. If a single request can be raced multiple times in the terminal window (deadline expiry + client disconnect + explicit cancel clustered near each other), each attempt adds to `cancelled_total` even though only one ever actually contended the terminal CAS.

4. Alerting / SLA pollution. Anything keyed on the `cancelled_total` rate — SLA panels, churn analysis, fairness dashboards — picks up phantom cancellations on every completion-via-race request.

5. Diagnostic ambiguity. From the counters alone, "cancel lost, request completed normally" and "cancel lost, request errored later" both produce a +1 on `cancelled_total` with no terminal actually delivered there. You can't reconstruct what happened.

Symmetric fix — move the increment inside the CAS-winning branch on both sides:

    cancellation: CAS to cancelled -> on win, increment cancelled_total
    completion:   CAS to success   -> on win, increment success_total

That restores one-to-one correspondence between per-terminal counters and delivered terminals, makes the sum reconcile, and removes the asymmetry. Loser-side paths become no-ops on the counters.

The queue-occupancy and processing-duration measurements being separate is fine and unaffected; the bug is isolated to the terminal-result counters.

Not in scope for me to call the design approved or to characterize implementation progress — flagging the failure mode only.

The terminal-result improvement correctly emits one terminal result per request. It does not, on its own, deliver exactly-once accounting. The remaining race:

  - Completion commits terminal-state selection, then applies accounting contributions (outbox write, in-flight decrement, terminal metric, source_event_id mark).
  - Cancellation observes terminal-state as not-yet-durable (or durable without an accounting snapshot), terminates the request, and skips accounting.
  - Restart cannot tell from durable state whether a terminal result had its accounting committed, so it either re-finalizes (double-applies) or discards (drops accounting).

Completion and cancellation therefore select terminal state and apply different accounting sets. Exactly-once requires that, for any request reaching a terminal state, the same terminal-state selection and the same accounting contribution commit atomically — regardless of whether the request completed or was cancelled.

Required to unblock:

  1. Terminal-state selection is committed atomically with its accounting contribution set: accounting applies iff and only iff the surviving terminal selection commits.
  2. Cancellation is not a path that elides accounting entries that completion would have applied; it selects the same terminal-state-derived accounting set and commits it through the same idempotent channel.
  3. Terminal-state selection is the single source of truth across restart, so recovery cannot both re-finalize a terminal result and apply a fresh accounting contribution.

Without these, "one terminal result" and "exactly-once accounting" remain different properties; the improvement is structural, not a fix for this fence.

Note: this comment identifies a structural property of the terminal-result improvement; it does not assert specific line-level findings in this revision.

Beacon (Dutchess County, NY) round-trip distance from a Brooklyn pickup: ~120 miles one-way → ~240 miles round trip. Even with some local driving around Beacon plus the return, total is ~260 miles. A typical rental-car fuel tank holds 12–14 gallons; a compact/sedan on the highway at 32–35 mpg uses about 7.5–8 gallons for 260 miles.

At current NY metro gas ~$3.50/gal, that's ~$26–30 of fuel to refill. So:

- Prepaid-fuel option: $64, locked in. Saves zero if I'd return with the tank roughly where I got it; loses ~$34–38 if I return nearly full. Refund-true-equal point is when my actual refill cost lands at $64, which would require burning ~18 gallons — i.e. essentially the whole tank going unused, which won't happen on a Beacon weekend.
- Return-full (status quo): I refill locally before drop-off, ~$26–30, keep the difference vs. the $64 prepaid.

Cost call: **return-full wins by roughly $34–38.** The $286 base reservation is unchanged either way.

Risk call:
- Prepaid: no refueling needed on return, zero risk of a missed-window refueling fee or a misjudged-tank upcharge. Small upside if I returned the car full by accident (irrelevant here).
- Return-full: I have to find a gas station within a sensible distance of the drop-off point on Sunday, in the right window. Mild hassle; risk of being late or paying an inflated airport-style price if I leave it to the last mile. Cheap to mitigate: refill in Beacon or along the Hudson corrider before heading back.

Net: prepaid is convenience-only insurance at a steep markup here, because the trip is short and the math clearly says I'll use far less than a tank.

**Recommendation: stick with return-full.** Keep the $64 credit on the prepaid offer, plan to refill at a Beacon-area station (not the airport/vicinity) before returning, and leave ~10 minutes of slack in the Sunday return leg. No reservation changes, no driver or itinerary changes — just decline the prepaid add-on when they offer it at the counter.

   - Aiming for a non-diarreal, formed sample is fine; even a small amount is usable.
   - Seal the container tightly.

   - Write directly on the container or on tape affixed to it:
     "Kibo [last name] / 4/30/27 / [time collected, e.g. 7:15 AM] / AM walk"

   - Refrigerate (not freeze) in the container, in a sealed plastic bag to contain odor, until you leave.
   - The clinic's 12-hour guideline is designed around refrigeration, so fridge-stored AM sample is fine until you walk out the door.

   - Keep the container cool in transit: sealed plastic bag inside a small cooler pack or insulated lunch bag. Avoid direct ice contact (don't let it sit in meltwater or freeze).
   - Bring it into the clinic at drop-off, not left in a hot car.

6. Hygiene
   - Wear a glove or baggie during collection; wash hands + the scooper thoroughly after.
   - Wipe any surface the sample touched with an enzymatic cleaner or diluted bleach solution.
   - Wash your hands again before food prep.

The slip pattern — foot pops at the moment of hip shift, with grip fine and no fatigue — points to sequencing and foot pressure, not strength. The right foot is going passive as you turn into the next hand move.

Three likely mechanisms (any one can cause it; identify which on the wall):

  1. Pressure not driven. As hips shift, force through the right foot drops below the threshold that keeps rubber engaged on the small edge. Fix: drive force into the wall through the foot for the entire hip turn — don't let it relax until the hand is set.
  2. Foot orientation. The foot was placed for the old body position; as you turn, toe/heel rotates off the optimal edge-engagement angle. Fix: pre-rotate or flag the foot before committing the hip shift.
  3. Timing. The hip shift happens before the hand commits, so the right foot absorbs a lateral/rotational load it isn't braced for. Fix: commit the hand first, then turn — or swap feet before the hand move.

Ren can probably see which of these is happening from the ground in real time, which is faster than solo trial-and-error.

Overall: structurally sound for a narrow "is this RC's canonical_package_version coherent across its artifacts" check. The three failure classes are sequentially gated (presence → metadata → version match), so they're mutually exclusive per output — that's clean. But there are three real gaps worth raising with Anya before this lands.

Concerns, in order of severity:

1. No output/member identifier in the report. You can answer "did this RC pass or fail, and how?" but you cannot answer "which outputs do I need to fix?" For a release-gate fixture, triage requires re-running the predicate and inspecting artifacts directly. This also conflicts with the exception-review intake pattern (owner + class + concrete condition) — class is present, but concrete condition is missing, and ownership is at RC granularity rather than per-output. At minimum the report should carry the manifest output identifier for the failing row; ideally a per-output owner too.

2. `canonical_package_version` field semantics are ambiguous when the failure class is 1 (missing output) or 2 (missing metadata). Is this the expected version from the handoff, the observed version from metadata, or null on the early failure classes? If it's "expected," class 1/2 rows are noise. If it's "observed," class 1 rows are empty. Pick one and say so in the field description — downstream consumers will otherwise parse it inconsistently.

3. No guard for a malformed handoff record. If the handoff's `canonical_package_version` is missing or empty, every artifact fails class 3, which buries the actual root cause (the handoff is bad, not the artifacts). Worth either rejecting the run up front ("no handoff version → fixture not runnable") or adding a fourth failure class: `handoff_version_missing`.

Two smaller observations, take or leave:

4. The predicate is one-directional (manifest → artifacts) and does not flag undeclared artifacts. If North Pier needs to catch surprise outputs, add a fourth class: `undeclared_artifact`.

5. Class 1 (entirely missing output) is qualitatively more severe than class 3 (version drift) — the former means the artifact store is broken or the build is incomplete, the latter means rebuild and re-check. Consider a `severity` field or letting class 1 short-circuit the rest of the run, so a single missing output doesn't get reported alongside dozens of meaningless downstream version comparisons.

Questions worth bringing back to Anya:

  - What's the consumer of this report? If it's a human triaging an RC, the missing output identifier is a blocker. If it's an automated gate that just flips yes/no, the current shape is closer to adequate.
  - Is there a separate fixture for artifact integrity (hashes, build timestamps, upstream refs)? If so, this narrow version-coherence check is fine as-is. If not, the scope may be too thin for a release gate.
  - What's the expected behavior when the handoff record is itself malformed — fail the run, or fail every artifact?

Provenance defect

Two intertwined properties are lost in Cyrus's proposal, and they are not independent:

1. Authoritative transition timestamp. `source_timestamp` is the time the event occurred in the source system. What survives compaction is `observed_at` = compaction time. These are different quantities. Audit queries like "what was the lease state at time X" or "show transitions for tenant Y in [a,b]" are keyed on event time, not on when someone ran a job. Replacing one with the other is not a rename; it changes what the field means.

2. Signed transition evidence. The signed envelope is the producing service's (shard-keeper or ingest-edge) cryptographic attestation over a specific `(source_timestamp, content)` pair. Discarding the envelope and keeping only a compacted row means:
   - no non-repudiation that the producer attested to that specific timestamp,
   - no tamper evidence against post-compaction edits, and
   - no cross-service reconciliation against the producer's signed chain.

The signature is over the timestamp. Lose the timestamp and the surviving signature no longer corresponds to anything it was signing — it attests to compacted content, not to the original event.

Scope check. "Prod+customer paths unchanged" is correct for query and realtime paths. Audit is what compliance review, post-incident analysis, and cross-tenant dispute resolution depend on. Staff-only is not low-stakes; it's the path that gets read after something has already gone wrong.

Evidence-quality gap (what the requirement has to close)

The audit-compaction path Cyrus has proposed deletes signed transition envelopes after 7d and reconstructs history with compaction time as `observed_at`. Two consequences for tenant-scoped evidence:

  1. The original `source_timestamp` is unrecoverable for any envelope older than the retention window.
  2. The signed envelope itself (the proof of authority at a given moment) is gone, but the authority record's identity — the latest-lease-state row's stable ID — is retained.

That means any join that tries to re-establish "what was true for tenant T at time X" by walking signed envelopes will silently degrade once the window passes. The gap is not "we lost data"; the gap is "the join key becomes ambiguous between a deleted proof and a retained identity." A tenant-scoped join that doesn't anchor on the retained identity will start substituting compaction `observed_at` for the original `source_timestamp` and quietly rewrite the authoritative timestamp — which is the exact failure mode the requirement has to prevent.

Bounded requirement — deterministic tenant-scoped join via retained authority record identity

  Scope: read-side join only. No writes, no schema migrations, no retention-window changes. Implementation ownership stays with Product Engineering; the April 1–June 15 evidence cycle stays open and unfrozen (evidence collection continues on its current cadence; this requirement does not pause, redirect, or re-freeze it).

  Functional requirement
    - The tenant-scoped join key is the retained authority record identity (the stable ID of the latest lease-state row for the (tenant_id, authority_scope) pair). It is not derived from a signed transition envelope's hash, not derived from `observed_at`, and not derived from processing or replay time.
    - The join is deterministic: same inputs (tenant_id + authority record ID) yield the same joined row set regardless of when the join runs. Replays against historical inputs must reproduce.

  Invariants (the "must nots" the request calls out explicitly)
    - No substitution of processing time. The join must not use "when this query ran" or "when compaction last ran" as a stand-in for any temporal field on the joined row.
    - No refresh of the authoritative timestamp. The authority record's `source_timestamp` (the original event time on the retained lease-state row, not the compaction `observed_at`) is preserved bit-for-bit through the join. A row whose `source_timestamp` is absent must surface as absent, not be backfilled.
    - No dependency on signed envelopes. The join must not require an envelope that may be outside the 7-day retention window. If the only way to answer is from a possibly-deleted envelope, the join returns "insufficient retained evidence" — it does not synthesize a value.

  Contract for the join
    - Inputs: (tenant_id, authority_record_id).
    - Output: joined tenant-scoped evidence rows tagged with the authority record's original `source_timestamp` (or an explicit "no retained source_timestamp" marker) and the authority record's stable ID.

`last_checked_by` shouldn't be a handoff-check decision input. The decision rests on three artifact-level properties: manifest output presence, artifact metadata, and canonical_package_version match. An actor field isn't a property of the artifact — gating the decision on it makes the check non-deterministic (two identical artifact states produce different outcomes depending on who clicked) and brittle to human availability. A blocked handoff caused by a missing `last_checked_by` would be a tooling artifact, not a real fault, and would mask the actual signal.

For diagnosis we still want the evidence — just not as a gate. Keep `last_checked_by` as audit metadata, and preserve the signals that actually answer "why is this handoff blocked?": per-check timestamps, expected-vs-actual for any mismatch (metadata fields, canonical_package_version), and a reason code on the block. Diagnosis then comes from the artifact data, not from who's on call.

Bounded review — shared ownership boundary

Scope
- Owner: Cyrus (mapped implementation + release owner; Data Platform owner path).
- Exception class: ownership.
- Review scope: shared ownership boundary only. No implementation change recommended, no release approval, no PR or deploy action taken.
- State: staff-only staging lookup. No production or customer-path change has occurred; this is a pre-release condition, not an incident. No rollback, no comms.

At-risk condition (as stated)
- Two signed, published owner-map records exist for the same (tenant, canonical_service).
- Their effective intervals overlap.
- The two records name different owners.
- The candidate query returns whichever record was processed last, rather than resolving by effective-interval semantics.

Finding (boundary-level)
- The shared ownership boundary is the published owner-map lookup contract: given two valid signed records for the same (tenant, canonical_service), the candidate query must return a single, deterministic owner that matches the actual effective-interval semantics, not the mutable order in which records happened to be processed.
- "Whichever was processed last" is a processing-order tie-break. It is non-deterministic from the caller's view (any two replays can flip the answer if the candidate query touches the records in a different order), and it is independent of effective-interval semantics (a record whose effective window has not yet started, or has already closed, can still win if it was processed later).
- Overlapping effective intervals with different owners are exactly the case the lookup contract has to be defined for: a tenant+service has one owner at any moment in time, and the boundary requires the candidate query to honor that. Selecting by processing order breaks the contract at the moment two overlapping records coexist, which is the moment the contract matters most.
- This is a boundary defect even with no production or customer-path impact: the staff-only staging lookup is exercising the same lookup the production path would exercise once records of this shape are published, so the failure mode is latent, not hypothetical.

Required boundary property (the criterion Cyrus's path must satisfy; not an implementation prescription)
- Determinism: for a fixed (tenant, canonical_service) and a fixed query time, the candidate query returns the same owner across replays.
- Effective-interval honesty: the returned owner is the one whose effective interval covers the query time; records whose effective interval does not cover the query time cannot win regardless of processing order.
- Single-writer invariant on the lookup: when two valid records' effective intervals both cover the query time, the boundary requires the system to either (a) resolve to the unique owner for that point in time per the records' own semantics, or (b) fail closed. "Last processed wins" violates (a) and is not an acceptable substitute for (b).
- Auditable ordering: any ordering the candidate query uses must be derived from authoritative, immutable record metadata (e.g., the signed envelope's source_timestamp / sequence, as already established for signed-envelope records in this domain), never from a mutable processing counter or insert/update clock.

Why this stays on Cyrus's path
- How the candidate query orders records, how it sources its tie-break, how it surfaces a fail-closed result, and how it is released are all implementation and release decisions that belong to Cyrus's Data Platform owner path. I am not prescribing any of those.
- The role of this review is to confirm that the shared ownership boundary contract above is the contract the candidate query must meet, and that the at-risk condition as stated fails that contract. That is the entire scope of my sign-off.
